Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Had Allah intended to take a son, He would have chosen from what He creates whatever He wills﴾ [Az-Zumar 39:4]:
* In this noble verse: a demonstration of the perfection of Allah's sovereignty, glorified and exalted, and that if He willed anything, nothing could prevent Him, as His saying shows: ﴿He would have chosen from what He creates whatever He wills﴾. From another aspect, it is a refutation of their assertions or claims that the angels are daughters of Allah, or the Messiah, or 'Uzayr. It says: if Allah had willed to take a son, He would have chosen whatever He wills, without taking what they claimed.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of Allah's will (irada), azza wa jall, based on His saying: ﴿If Allah had desired to take a son﴾. Allah's will regarding His own act is agreed upon; we do not think anyone disputes that Allah wills His own act. But does it extend to the act of the created being or not?

On this there is disagreement between the People of the Sunnah and the People of innovation. Among them are those who said: it extends to the act of the created being, and they went to an extreme in this, saying that the created being has no will at all. This is the view of the Jahmiyya Jabriyya.

Among them are those who said: it extends to the act of the created being, but not in the manner of compulsion (jabr). This is the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah and the Community (Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah). And among them are those who said: it does not extend to the act of the created being, and that the created being is independent in its act, with no will of Allah regarding it. This is the doctrine of the Qadariyya, the Magians of this Ummah. Yes.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of Allah's voluntary acts (al-af'al al-ikhtiyariyya), azza wa jall, based on His saying: ﴿He would have chosen what He wills from what He creates﴾. Allah's voluntary acts are established by both revelation (al-sam') and reason (al-'aql). As for revelation, the acts which Allah attributes to Himself are very numerous. As for reason, the agent who acts by choice is more perfect than one who does not act. The Ash'aris and others among the Mu'attila (those who deny Allah's attributes) went to the view that voluntary acts do not subsist in Allah, azza wa jall, on the argument that a newly occurring act necessitates the occurrence of the agent. There is no doubt that this view is false and entails false consequences, among them that Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, is unable to act, and this is a deficiency in Allah, azza wa jall, and a denial of His many reports which affirm action for Him, too many to be enumerated.

* Among the benefits of this verse: affirmation of Allah's volition (mashi'a), based on His saying: ﴿He would have chosen what He wills from what He creates﴾. Concerning volition we say what we said about will with respect to its scope: it applies to the acts of Allah, and does it apply to the acts of the created being? This is subject to the earlier disagreement which we explained regarding will. But here there is a matter that must be noted: will is divided into two types, legislative will (al-irada al-shar'iyya) and universal/decreed will (al-irada al-kawniyya). As for volition (al-mashi'a), it is one type only. Universal will is synonymous with volition, having the same meaning: if you say, "What Allah wills occurs," it means "What Allah wills occurs."

As for legislative will, it is synonymous with love (al-mahabba), meaning it relates to what Allah, azza wa jall, loves. So you say: Allah wills from us that we thank Him. This will is legislative.

The difference between legislative and universal will is in two respects:

The first respect: universal will encompasses what Allah loves and what He does not love. Universal will: He wills faith, He wills disbelief, He wills obedience, and He wills wickedness by universal will.

As for legislative will, it relates only to what He loves. So you cannot say that Allah wills wickedness, meaning loves it; this is impossible.

Second, the second difference: universal will necessarily entails the occurrence of what is willed; that is, if He wills something by universal will, it must occur. Legislative will may occur or may not occur: He, subhanahu wa ta'ala, wills from us faith and obedience, and they may exist or may not exist. This is the difference between them.

With this, the objections which the Qadariyya raised against the People of the Sunnah are resolved. They said to them: If you affirm that Allah's will relates to everything, even sins, it follows that Allah wills evil, and so Allah would be evil according to their statement. We ask Allah for well-being. What do we say? We say: As for legislative will, Allah can never will evil at all. As for universal will, He wills what He wishes, but His universal will concerning evil has profound and numerous wisdoms that are well known.

He says: * Among the benefits of this noble verse: the declaration of Allah's transcendence, subhanahu wa ta'ala, above everything the disbelievers and deniers attribute to Him, based on His saying: ﴿Glory be to Him﴾.

* Among its benefits: affirmation of Allah's names: Allah, the One (al-Wahid), and the Subduer (al-Qahhar), three names. Every name Allah affirms for Himself includes the attribute from which it is derived. So "Allah" is derived from divinity (al-uluhiyya), so it includes the affirmation of divinity as one of His attributes. "The One" (al-Wahid): oneness (al-wahdaniyya), so it includes the affirmation of oneness for Allah, azza wa jall. "The Subduer" (al-Qahhar): subjugation (al-qahr), so it includes the affirmation of subjugation for Allah, azza wa jall, and that He is the Subduer, the Overpowering, who prevails over everything.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you⁠﴾ [Az-Zumar 2]. When He stated that the revelation of the Book is from Allah, He specified to whom it was sent down, saying: (﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you⁠﴾ O Muhammad). The word ﴿We have sent down⁠﴾ is a plural pronoun, but when it refers to Allah it is definitely not plural; rather it is for majesty. The Christian has been confused by this kind of plural and has said that God is the third of three, because Allah the Exalted refers to Himself with a plural form, and the least plural is three. Our reply to him is that this is from the deviation of the Christians: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate⁠﴾ [As-Saff 5], and they followed the ambiguous (mutashabih) verses of the Qur'an. Had they referred this ambiguous matter back to the clear (muhkam) verses, they would have known that they were in extreme error. That is because Allah has stated clearly in many verses that He is one God, saying: ﴿And your God is one God; there is no deity except Him, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful⁠﴾ [Al-Baqarah 163]. This is a clear, definitive (muhkam) text. As for "nā" (we), which is the plural pronoun, in the Arabic language in which the Qur'an was revealed it is suitable both for plurality and for one who refers to himself in majesty. Therefore it is from the ambiguous, because when a word admits two meanings it is called ambiguous (mutashabih), and the ambiguous must be referred back to the clear (muhkam).

He said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book⁠﴾. ﴿To you⁠﴾ here is the goal (endpoint), and the address is to the Messenger ﷺ. ﴿The Book⁠﴾ means the written thing, which is the Qur'an, and the reason it is called a book has already been mentioned.

(﴿with truth⁠﴾ is connected to "sent down"). ﴿With truth⁠﴾: the letter "bāʼ" here indicates association (mulābasah) and transitivity (taʻdiyah); that is, the Book itself was sent down as truth from Allah, not from anyone else. ﴿We have sent down⁠﴾ with truth, meaning with certainty: that We sent it down to you from Us. We have also said it is for transitivity, meaning that the Book was sent down with truth; that is, whatever the Qur'an contains is true.

So according to the first view, the meaning of "truth" is the affirmation that it was sent down from Allah, and according to the second view, the meaning is that everything the Qur'an contains, of reports, commands, prohibitions and other things, is true.

So ﴿with truth⁠﴾ has two meanings:
The first meaning: that the Qur'an was sent down from Allah as truth, not falsehood.
The second: that whatever the Qur'an contains is true: commands, prohibitions, reports, stories, all of them are true.

He said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book with truth⁠﴾. He said "(connected to 'sent down')" and did not say "connected to ﴿We have sent down⁠﴾", because what is connected is connected to the verb, whereas "nā" (we) is a pronoun separate from the verb.

He said: ﴿So worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion⁠﴾. The "fāʼ" here is the fāʼ of consequence (tafrīʻ), and the sign of the fāʼ of consequence is that what follows it is arranged upon what precedes it. The meaning is: because of Our sending down the Book to you, worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion. ("Worship⁠" is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ), and his saying ﴿sincere⁠﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "worship". Sincerity (ikhlāṣ) in a thing is purifying it of impurities and removing what mixes with it. So when one is sincere to Him in religion, the meaning is that you purify your religion of every shirk. Hence the author said: (﴿sincere to Him in religion⁠﴾ from shirk), that is, monotheistic toward Him, that is, toward Allah.

As for his saying ﴿to Him the religion⁠﴾: "religion" (dīn) means action, and what is meant here is the specific action, which is worship, due to His saying ﴿So worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion⁠﴾. He did not say "sincere to Him in worship", because "dīn" is the action for which the doer seeks recompense; hence the saying: "as you do, so you will be repaid."

Know that "dīn" is applied to an action for which recompense is sought, and it is also applied to the recompense itself, which is the reward for the action. The first usage is like this verse ﴿sincere to Him in religion⁠﴾, and like His saying: ﴿For you is your religion, and for me is my religion⁠﴾ [Al-Kafirun 6], and like His saying: ﴿And I have approved for you Islam as religion⁠﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 3]; that is, an action by which you worship.
An example of the second is His saying: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment⁠﴾ [Al-Fatihah 4], meaning the Day of recompense for deeds, and His saying: ﴿And what can make you know what the Day of Recompense is? Then what can make you know what the Day of Recompense is?⁠﴾ [Al-Infitar 17-18], that is, the Day of recompense for deeds.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs the pure religion⁠﴾ [Az-Zumar 3]. ﴿Unquestionably⁠﴾ is a particle of opening, a letter used to draw attention. What did we say?
* Student: ﴿Unquestionably⁠﴾ is a particle of alerting.
* Shaykh: A particle of alerting, yes.
* Student: ﴿Unquestionably⁠﴾ is a particle of opening.
* Shaykh: ﴿Unquestionably⁠﴾ is a particle of opening, and it is a letter used to draw attention. ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs the pure religion⁠﴾: this is a particle of opening, a letter used to draw attention, because when the speaker says "unquestionably", the listener pays attention. His saying ﴿to Allah belongs the pure religion⁠﴾: the prepositional phrase is the predicate placed first, and ﴿the religion⁠﴾ is the postponed subject. Placing the predicate first conveys restriction (ḥaṣr), that is: to Allah alone.

His saying ﴿the religion⁠﴾ means the action for which reward is sought, and His saying ﴿the pure⁠﴾ means free from impurities and shirk. That is, a rational person must make the pure religion belong to Allah alone; for how is it fitting for a rational person to worship Allah in truth for the sake of seeking nearness to another? This goes against reason. If a person stands to pray so that people may see him, he is foolish in his mind and astray in his religion. How can you make the pure truth belong to people? Action that is for people belongs to people, but action that is for Allah must be for Allah. Hence He said: ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah⁠﴾ alone ﴿the pure religion⁠﴾, so it is not permissible to make it for anyone else.

Hence He said: ﴿And those who take besides Him protectors⁠﴾, saying: ﴿We do not worship them⁠﴾ and so on to the end. The "wāw" here is for resumption, "those who" is the subject, "took" is the relative clause, and the predicate of the subject is omitted, its estimated form being: they say, "We do not worship them", or: they said, "We do not worship them".

His saying ﴿And those who take besides Him protectors⁠﴾: ﴿took⁠﴾ here means "made", as in His saying: ﴿And Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend⁠﴾ [An-Nisa 125], meaning He made him. And His saying: ﴿Have you seen one who takes his desire as his god?⁠﴾ [Al-Jathiyah 23], that is, made his desire his god. When "took" means "made", it requires two objects: the one made and the one it is made into.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (the idols are ﴿protectors⁠﴾). Accordingly, the first object is omitted and the second is ﴿protectors⁠﴾, and omitting an object when there is evidence for it is permissible. Ibn Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said in the chapter on the subject and predicate:

"And omitting what is known is permissible, as you say 'Zayd' after 'who is with you two'."

("Omitting what is known is permissible"): the reality is that this line is in the chapter on the subject and predicate, but is it general? Yes, it is general: omitting what is known is permissible. It may even be eloquence and rhetoric to omit it. The principle is that what is known may be omitted, while what is not known may not be omitted, because speech must clarify the speaker's intent, and this cannot happen if what is not known is omitted.

So the first object is omitted, with the estimate: the idols; the second is present, which is His saying ﴿protectors⁠﴾. ("Protectors") is the plural of "walī", meaning they take them as protectors in worship: they humble themselves before them, prostrate to them, make vows to them, give charity for them. But they do not believe that these idols benefit or harm them by themselves, nor that they create or provide sustenance; rather they claim that they have taken them as a means.

Hence he says: (﴿And those who take besides Him protectors⁠﴾ are the disbelievers of Mecca). Restricting this verse to the disbelievers of Mecca is deficient, and we should not explain the general by something more specific except as an example. As for specifying the meaning so that a word in the Qur'an is general and then we explain it by a more specific sense, this is in reality deficiency, is it not? But if the person intends this explanation as an example, that is, like the disbelievers of Mecca, there is no harm. However, a reader of such a statement by the author does not doubt that the author intended this restriction, and this is clearly problematic. The obligation is to keep the general indication of the verses, and likewise the hadiths, as they are, until a rational proof or a verbal indicator shows that the intended meaning is specific.

He says: (the disbelievers of Mecca said: ﴿We do not worship them⁠﴾). The word "said" is omitted here because it is known from the context, and it is valid to estimate "they say: ﴿We do not worship them⁠﴾". Perhaps this is more suitable than the author's "said", as a narration of the state they were in. In any case, the omitted sentence is the predicate of the subject, namely ﴿And those who took⁠﴾, and it is not permissible to make ﴿We do not worship them⁠﴾ the predicate, because the meaning would be corrupted.

He said: ﴿We do not worship them except that they bring us near to Allah in nearness⁠﴾. This is a restriction of their purpose in worshipping these idols: that is, we do not worship them except for this purpose, ﴿that they bring us near to Allah in nearness⁠﴾. This is an admission and acknowledgment from them that they worship the idols, as shown by their saying "we do not worship them", and that this worship is a means to a nobler end, which is nearness to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This is from their ignorance, because if they worship them, they have made them the goal; the aim is to reach Allah, and reaching Allah is only through worshipping Him. So by worshipping them, they have made them the goal. Hence, God willing, we will show that this is from their foolishness.

﴿That they bring us near to Allah in nearness⁠﴾: "nearness" (qurbā) is a verbal noun meaning "bringing near" (taqrīban). The author says it is a verbal noun, but a moral (maʻnawī) verbal noun, because it agrees with its governing verb in meaning but not in wording. A verbal noun may be verbal (lafẓī) or moral (maʻnawī): if it matches its verb in wording it is verbal, like "I stood a standing (qiyāman)"; if it differs in wording but not in meaning, it is moral, like "I stood standing (wuqūfan)".

"I sat a sitting (quʻūdan)"?
* Student: Verbal.
* Shaykh: Verbal. "I sat a sitting (julūsan)"?
* Student: Moral.
* Shaykh: Moral, good.

He says: "Draw near to Allah in nearness (zulfā)"; he says it means nearness (qurbā), and qurbā also means bringing near. The author only said it means bringing near so that it corresponds to the verb: the verb (qarraba) has the present tense yuqarribu, and the corresponding verbal noun is taqrīban, not qurbā.

But it is known that a verbal noun may agree with its governing verb in wording without matching it in letters, and this is called in their terminology a "noun of verbal noun" (ism maṣdar), as in His saying: ﴿And Allah has made you grow from the earth as a growth⁠﴾ [Nuh 17]. Had it been a verbal noun it would have said "ināb̲atan"; since it said "nabātan" with fewer letters than its verb, it is called a noun of verbal noun. The point is that they say: "We do not worship these idols except so that they bring us near to Allah in nearness."

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them concerning that in which they differ⁠﴾. ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them⁠﴾: this sentence is resumptive, explaining the end of those who took the idols as protectors; that is, what will their final state be? Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them concerning that in which they differ⁠﴾. Now, ﴿between them⁠﴾: the author said "and between the Muslims", indicating that the other party of the distinction (or of being between, according to the more correct view) is omitted, namely "and between the Muslims". This estimate is not indicated by the context: had he said "between you", it would have been correct that the meaning is between you and them. But he said ﴿between them⁠﴾, that is, between these disbelievers. It seems the author, may Allah have mercy on him, thought there is no disagreement among the disbelievers, but this is not so; rather disagreement among them exists in this world and the Hereafter. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He will say, "Enter among nations that have passed on before you of jinn and mankind into the Fire." Every time a nation enters, it will curse its sister, until, when they have overtaken one another therein, the last of them will say of the first⁠﴾ [Al-A'raf 38], and so on through the verses: exchange, dispute, enmity. Allah judges between them, and He has mentioned this in several verses. So the correct view is that the pronoun in ﴿between them⁠﴾ refers to the disbelievers, and that disagreement exists among them themselves.

The Jews and Christians have disagreement between them: ﴿And the Jews say, "The Christians are not on anything," and the Christians say, "The Jews are not on anything"⁠﴾ [Al-Baqarah 113]. This is an established disagreement among the disbelieving nations. Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning what they differ about in matters of religion, admitting the believers to Paradise and the disbelievers to the Fire. This is according to what the author held.

But according to the view that is the apparent meaning of the noble verse, ﴿Allah will judge between them concerning that in which they differ⁠﴾, each person is placed in his rank, as Allah the Mighty and Majestic explained in His saying: ﴿And We will put shackles around the necks of those who disbelieved. Will they be recompensed except for what they used to do?⁠﴾ [Saba 33], when He mentioned the dialogue between the oppressed and the arrogant.

In these two verses there are benefits:
* First: the virtue of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the loftiness of his rank, through the sending down of the Book of Allah to him, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you⁠﴾.
Here we ask: is the sending down of the Qur'an to the Messenger a sending down to us? Yes, it is sent down to us, because he is our Messenger, and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O mankind, there has come to you a proof from your Lord, and We have sent down to you a clear light⁠﴾ [An-Nisa 174]. So what is sent down to the Messenger of Allah is sent down to us, but he is the one directly receiving this sending down and conveying it to us.
* From the benefits of the verse: what was mentioned before, that the Qur'an is sent down from Allah, so it is His speech.
* And among them: the exaltation of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, because descent can only be from above (...).
This is indicated by the Book, the Sunnah, reason and natural disposition: five kinds of evidence, all establishing Allah's exaltation above His creation. Two groups have opposed this:
The first group: the Hulūliyyah, who say that Allah in His essence is in every place. They say: Allah Himself, may He be glorified, is in every place: in the mosque, in the market, in the house, on the roof, in the room, in the most vile place, and we seek refuge in Allah. I say that these are disbelievers; but whoever is mistaken must be informed and the truth explained to him, and if he persists, he is a disbeliever.
The second opposing group: the Mu'attilah, who deny, saying that Allah the Exalted is neither above nor below, neither right nor left, neither connected nor separated. These describe Allah as nonexistent, as Mahmud ibn Subuktakin, may Allah have mercy on him, said to Ibn Furak when he said that Allah is neither existent nor nonexistent... to the end. Mahmud ibn Subuktakin said to him: you have described Allah the Exalted as nonexistent. He was right: if we wanted to describe a nonexistent thing, we would find no description more encompassing of the nonexistent than this.

Now, Allah guided those who believed to the truth about what they differed in, by His permission, and they said that Allah the Exalted Himself is above everything, as this Book, the Sunnah, the consensus, reason and natural disposition indicate.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the Book is truth from Allah, which the Prophet ﷺ did not fabricate against his Lord; rather it is from Allah. For His saying: ﴿We have sent down to you the Book with truth⁠﴾ means it is truth from Allah the Mighty and Majestic. Allah the Glorified and Exalted said: ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have severed from him the aorta⁠﴾ [Al-Haqqah 44-46].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verse 2–4 (part 2 of 4):

There is no harm in discussing this verse. He says: ﴿And if he had invented against Us some sayings﴾, after He had said: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble Messenger. And it is not the word of a poet; little do you believe. Nor is it the word of a soothsayer; little do you remember. [It is] a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Haqqah 40–43]. This is lest someone imagine that, because He said ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble Messenger﴾, the Qur'an came from the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and that he was the one who said it. So He said: ﴿And if he had invented against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have cut from him the aorta. And none of you could have prevented Us from him﴾ [al-Haqqah 44–47].

* Among the benefits of this verse: that everything in the Qur'an is true, in the second sense: its reports, its stories, its commands and its prohibitions. So its reports contain no falsehood in any way. Its stories are not meant to pass the time or waste time; rather they are beneficial narratives. The rest will come, God willing (...).

* * *

* The student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿Surely, to Allah belongs the sincere faith. And those who take protectors besides Him say, "We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to Allah in position." Indeed, Allah will judge between them concerning that over which they differ. Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a liar and ungrateful. Had Allah intended to take a son, He would have chosen from what He creates whatever He wills. Exalted is He! He is Allah, the One, the Subjugator. He created the heavens and the earth in truth. He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night, and He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term. Unquestionably, He is the Exalted in Might, the Oft-Forgiving﴾ [az-Zumar 3–5].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Surely, to Allah belongs the sincere faith﴾. What is the meaning of this phrase of the verse?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That is not it.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The meaning of the verse; we do not want detail.
* The student: A reminder that the religion of Allah, blessed and exalted, is a pure religion.
* The Shaykh: Pure from shirk, and that any religion in which shirk has entered, Allah does not accept it. Good, yes.

His saying: ﴿And those who took protectors besides Him﴾. How do we parse this clause?
* Student: The waw is a conjunctive particle for resumption, and ﴿those﴾ is a subject (mubtada').
* The Shaykh: Yes. Where is its predicate?
* The student: Its predicate is the object of the saying, ﴿We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to Allah﴾; the estimated reading is: they say (...).
* The Shaykh: You say: the predicate is the object of the saying, and you say: there is an omitted element whose estimate is "they say." What (...)?
* The student: ﴿We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to Allah﴾ is the object of the saying.
* The Shaykh: Where is the predicate of (those)?
* The student: Omitted.
* The Shaykh: What is the estimate?
* The student: They say.
* The Shaykh: They say. Yes, good. If they were saying: ﴿We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to Allah﴾, then here they made the means into an end?
* The student: It is the worship of idols; they made the means...
* The Shaykh: Yes, but here they made the means an end.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: (...) They say: we do not make it (...) rather we make it a means.
* The Shaykh: My brother, they said: ﴿We only worship them﴾, so they worshipped them so that this would be a means to bring them near to Allah. Thus they made the means into an end, because the purpose of drawing near to Allah is to worship Him. Here they reversed the reality and made the means an end.
Now, is the condition of some people at graves like the condition of these? Yes, there are people who circumambulate graves, make vows to them, prostrate to them, and say: these are saints who bring us near to Allah, just like these. And do these grave-worshippers exist?
* Student: Now, yes.
* The Shaykh: Now they exist.
* The student: Those who worship (...).
* The Shaykh: I described to you the condition of those who circumambulate graves and worship them, and I said: do they resemble the condition of the polytheists? You said to me: yes. So I now say to you: do such people exist now in the Islamic world or not?
* The student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: They exist.

Now the author said: (﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them﴾, and between the Muslims). So what is the extent of the correctness of this interpretation?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them﴾. The author says: (and between the Muslims). So what is the extent of the correctness of this interpretation?
* The student: It is not correct.
* The Shaykh: It is not correct. What is the correct one?
* The student: The correct one is that (...).
* The Shaykh: Well done, meaning between the disbelievers themselves.

Now, can you show me an example of the disbelievers' disagreement?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, a verse that testifies that there will be disagreement among them.
* The student: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not differ except after knowledge had come to them﴾ [Al 'Imran 19].
* The Shaykh: No, that is on the Day of Resurrection; their disagreement is on the Day of Resurrection, because Allah judges between them on the Day of Resurrection.
* The student: Like His saying, exalted is He (...): ﴿Their latter will say to their former, "Our Lord, these are the ones who misled us"﴾ [al-A'raf 38].
* The Shaykh: Well done. Just as He said: ﴿Those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant, "Were it not for you, we would have been believers"﴾ [Saba' 31], and the verses on this are numerous.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾.
* Among the benefits of this verse: that the sending down of the Qur'an is a proof upon people that obligates them to worship Allah; this is from His saying: ﴿So worship﴾, and this fa' is for consequence; i.e., because the Book was sent down to you, worship Allah.
* And among its benefits: that whoever has not received the Book is not obligated to worship, and other verses support this, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We would not punish until We send a messenger﴾ [al-Isra' 15], and His saying: ﴿Messengers as bearers of good tidings and warners, so that mankind will have no argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ [an-Nisa' 165], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the cities until He sends into their mother [city] a messenger reciting to them Our verses. And We would not destroy the cities unless their people were wrongdoers﴾ [al-Qasas 59].
And like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "By the One in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, no one from this nation hears of me, Jew or Christian, and then does not believe in what I have been sent with, except that he will be among the companions of the Fire"[[Reported by Muslim (153 / 240) from Abu Hurayrah.]]. He said: "hears of me." The texts on this meaning are many: that whoever has not been reached by the call of the messengers is not obligated to worship.

The applied evidence for this issue consists of several examples. Among them: the hadith of 'Ammar ibn Yasir, may Allah be pleased with him, that "the Prophet ﷺ sent him on an expedition, and he became junub and did not find water, so he rolled himself in the dust as a beast rolls, thinking that this was what was required of him, and prayed. He informed the Prophet ﷺ of this, and the Prophet ﷺ explained to him that it would suffice him in place of washing that he strike the earth with his hands, then wipe his face and palms, and he did not order him to repeat the prayer"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (338), and Muslim (368 / 112) from 'Ammar.]].

Likewise the man who came and prayed without being calm in his prayer, and the Prophet ﷺ said to him: "You have not prayed," and he said: "By the One who sent you with the truth, I cannot do better than this"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (757), and Muslim (397 / 45) from Abu Hurayrah.]]. The Prophet ﷺ taught him and did not order him to repeat what had passed of his prayer, even though he had not been praying a prayer that would suffice him.

Likewise the woman who suffered istihadah and thought it was menstruation, so she did not pray, and the Prophet ﷺ did not order her to repeat [prayers]¹. [[Reported by Ahmad (27631) from Fatimah bint Abi Hubaysh.]] Similar examples are many.

Accordingly, if a man embraced Islam in a land of disbelief or in a remote land not reached by the rulings of the Shariah, and he left the prayer for a period, then afterward learned of the obligation of prayer, we do not order him to repeat what he left, but only to pray the prayers whose time has come.

Likewise, if a woman in a remote place reached puberty by menstruation while still young, and did not fast Ramadan, but she is in a place with no scholars around her to ask, and ignorance has overcome her, like the desert dweller for example, then we do not order her to make up the fasts she left, because of her ignorance. This is what befits the Islamic Shariah, which is built on ease and facility, and on the fact that Allah, exalted is He, does not burden a soul beyond its capacity, and does not burden a soul except with what He has given it. And the verse before us may contain an allusion to what was mentioned: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you﴾, ﴿so worship﴾: after the sending down, he was commanded to worship.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the obligation of sincerity to Allah in worship, from His saying: ﴿sincere to Him in religion﴾. Sincerity is the purification of a thing from what mixes with it. This is why the authentic hadith states that Allah said: "I am the most self-sufficient of partners in regard to association. Whoever does an action in which he associates others with Me, I abandon him and his association"[[Reported by Muslim (2985 / 46) from Abu Hurayrah.]]. So if a person gives charity with wealth but does so ostentatiously in order to be praised, he has not worshipped Allah; he is sinful and not rewarded. And if he prays in order to be praised, he has not worshipped Allah; he is sinful and not rewarded, because Allah commanded a specific worship, which is sincerity: ﴿sincere to Him in religion﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that worship is a religion (dīn) that a person adheres to, and the meaning of its being a religion is that he acts in order to be rewarded.

* It follows from this benefit that a person should, during worship, be mindful of this meaning, namely that he acts in order to be rewarded; for when he feels this, he will perfect the work, since reason guides a person to know that reward is in proportion to the deed: if you do the deed well, the reward is good, and if you fall short, the reward decreases. I believe that this matter, I mean the awareness that a person works for reward, escapes many people who do not pay attention to it.

* Among its benefits also: an indication of the intention of the one for whom the act is done: when you act, you intend to draw near to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by complying with His command. For example, when you want to perform wudu', you intend that you are performing wudu' in compliance with the command of Allah when He said: ﴿O you who have believed, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾ [al-Ma'idah 6]; so that you feel the worship and the pleasure of worship, not merely to free your duty by doing what is obligatory upon you of purification for prayer. There is no doubt that this is a good intention, but better than it is that you sense that you are complying with the command of Allah, so that you feel the pleasure of worship and that you are truly a servant of your Lord, the Mighty and Majestic. These are matters a person should attend to in his worship, and this is why He said: ﴿sincere to Him in religion﴾.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Surely, to Allah belongs the sincere faith﴾.

* Among the benefits of this phrase: that Allah does not accept except a sincere religion: ﴿Surely, to Allah belongs the sincere faith﴾. As for what is other than that, it does not belong to Allah, even if you associate it with Allah — pay attention, O brothers — because what is "the religion belongs to Allah"? It is the sincere one, pure from the impurities of shirk.

If someone says: if an action is sincere at its beginning but associated with shirk at its end, does the whole action become void, or only the part containing shirk, or what?

We say: there is detail in this. If the worship in which shirk occurred in its course is such that its parts depend upon one another, then it becomes void, like the prayer: a man began prayer sincerely for Allah, and during it he heard someone near him and showed off in his prayer during the act of worship. What do we say? We say: the prayer becomes void, all of it, because its beginning and its end are built upon one another.

But if its parts do not depend upon one another, then what was sincere is valid and what was mixed is not valid. For example, a man who was giving charity had a thousand riyals; whenever a poor person came, he gave him some of it. He spent five hundred riyals sincerely for Allah, and during the spending some people appeared and he showed off to them. Does the first charity, which was sincere, become void? No. Why? Because some of it does not depend on the rest; each dirham or each riyal is separate from what precedes it. This is an important matter.

The second matter: sometimes showing off attacks the heart and a person resists it. Does this affect his sincerity?

The answer: it does not affect it as long as he resists it and turns away from it, because he is now in struggle against his enemy, and Satan always comes to a person from every direction. Allah the Exalted said of him in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾ [al-A'raf 16]; meaning: in every place. He comes to a person to deter him from worship, deters him from seeking knowledge, deters him from maintaining kinship ties and from kindness to parents, and similar things that Allah has obligated upon you. When he sees that you are determined to perform worship, he comes from another direction, which is exaggeration in worship, adding to it, extremism and over-strictness. If he is unable to do that, he comes from the direction of intention, saying that you are showing off. But a person must resist Satan to the extent he can, seeking help from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* From the benefits of the noble verse in His saying: ﴿Surely, to Allah belongs the sincere faith﴾: the self-sufficiency of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, complete self-sufficiency.

The reasoning for this: if Allah does not accept except what is sincere, this indicates His independence from the deeds of the servants; for, and far is He from that, if He were poor and needing it, He would be satisfied with what came to Him from them even as a partnership. Just as a needy person accepts from you what is exclusively his and what is shared. Since Allah accepts only what is sincere, it is known from this that He is independent of the servants. To this points His saying, exalted is He, in the sacred hadith: "I am the most self-sufficient of partners in regard to association."[[Reported by Muslim (2985 / 46) from Abu Hurayrah.]]

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those who took protectors besides Him, [saying], "We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to Allah in position"﴾, and so on to the end.

* Among the benefits of this verse: that idol-worshippers have taken the idols as allies and made them protectors.

* And among its benefits: that they — i.e., the idol-worshippers — deceive people, saying: we only worship them for a purpose, namely that they bring us near to Allah in position.

* And among its benefits: that this ruling can be extended to all people of falsehood, who claim that they do good while they are liars.

Let us give an example of this with the people of ta'til (denial of divine attributes). The people of ta'til claim that by their denial they are exalting Allah, and that their aim is to glorify Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, above deficiency and resemblance to creation. They are lying in this, because when they strip Him of the perfection of His attributes, that is the opposite of tanzih (glorification). These people say: we only worship them that they may bring us nearer to Allah in position; but the reality is that this worship distances them from Allah by many distances.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the acknowledgment by the polytheists that they worship their idols, ﴿We only worship them﴾; they openly state that they worship them, but they do not say: we worship them so that we may draw near to them, rather: so that they may bring us near.

* And among its benefits: that the polytheists in the time of the Messenger ﷺ acknowledged the existence of Allah, and that He is greater than every great one; this is from their saying: ﴿that they may bring us nearer to Allah﴾. So they acknowledged Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that He is greater than their idols; for this reason they made them a means to Him or a means of drawing near to Him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verses 2–4 (part 3 of 4):

* Among its benefits: there will be a dispute and contention between these polytheists and those they took as allies on the Day of Resurrection. This is shown by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them concerning that in which they differ﴾ [Az-Zumar 39:3].
* Among its benefits: judgment belongs to Allah alone, Mighty and Majestic, on that day, meaning the Day of Resurrection, and the return is to Him.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a liar and ungrateful﴾ [Az-Zumar 39:3]. This sentence is emphasized, as you can see, by ﴿Indeed (inna)﴾. His saying ﴿does not guide﴾ refers to guidance of tawfiq (divine enabling and granting of success), whereas guidance of dalala (guidance by showing the way) is the proof of Allah against His creation, which must reach everyone, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And as for Thamud, We showed them guidance, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat 41:17]. Did We show them guidance (hidaya)?

* Student: Dalala.
* Shaykh: Dalala. So ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide﴾ means tawfiq, not dalala. Rather, the guidance of dalala is established for everyone. ﴿Does not guide one who is a liar and ungrateful﴾. ﴿One who is﴾ means: the one who is a liar.

The author said: (concerning the attribution of a son to Him). Those who attributed a son to Him were the Jews, the Christians, and the polytheists, three groups. The Jews said: "'Uzayr is the son of Allah." The Christians said: "The Messiah is the son of Allah." The polytheists said: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." The verse, as you see, ﴿one who is a liar﴾ is general, but it seems the author restricted it to the attribution of a son to Allah, based on His later saying: ﴿Had Allah intended to take a son, He would have chosen from what He creates whatever He wills﴾ [Az-Zumar 39:4].

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It seems the author restricted it to attributing a son to Him, based on the saying of Allah: ﴿Had Allah intended to take a son﴾. Otherwise, if we look at the verse ﴿a liar﴾, it would be unrestricted, not limited to attributing a son to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. But the author restricted it on the basis of context or an indicator from the context.

﴿Ungrateful (kaffar)﴾: this may be an intensive form (sigha mubalagha, a form expressing emphasis or repetition), and it may be a form of attribution (nisba). If it is attribution, it becomes a permanent description, as we say: carpenter, blacksmith, woodworker, builder, and the like. If it is an intensive form, it is not a permanent description but indicates abundance. In any case, whether for emphasis or attribution, it means one who disbelieves in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

The author said: (by worshipping other than Allah). There is no doubt that this is disbelief: worshipping other than Allah. Restricting disbelief here to worshipping other than Allah is supported by the context, namely His earlier saying: ﴿And those who take protectors besides Him, [saying]: "We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to Allah"﴾ [Az-Zumar 39:3].

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Had Allah intended to take a son﴾, as they said: "The Most Merciful has taken a son," ﴿He would have chosen from what He creates whatever He wills﴾). ﴿Had﴾ (law) here is conditional. Its condition is ﴿intended﴾ and its response is ﴿He would have chosen from what He creates whatever He wills﴾. Know that when the response of a conditional "law" is affirmative, it most often is joined with the particle lam (la): "Had Allah intended, He would have chosen." It may come without lam, as in His saying: ﴿Had We willed, We would have made it salty﴾ [Al-Waqi'a 56:70]. When the response is negated, it is not joined with lam. Yes, this is the case in most examples, but it may be joined with lam, as in the poet's saying:

"Had we been given the choice, we would not have parted, / but there is no choice with the nights."

﴿Had Allah intended to take a son﴾: "intended" here is a universal will (irada kawniyya), so it means will in the sense of desire (mashi'a). That is: if Allah had willed to take a son, meaning to make a son for Himself, as they said: "The Most Merciful has taken a son." ﴿He would have chosen (la-stafa)﴾: "istafa" comes from safwa, the best of a thing, so "istafa" means to choose. ﴿He would have chosen from what He creates﴾, meaning from among what He creates, ﴿whatever He wills﴾. Here "ma" is the object of "istafa," meaning: He would have chosen whatever He wills from what He creates. The saying ﴿from what He creates﴾ is a relative construction with "ma," and the returning pronoun is:

* Student: Omitted.
* Shaykh: Omitted. The estimate is: "from what He creates." He expressed it with "ma" rather than "man," although they said: "The angels are the daughters of Allah," "'Uzayr is the son of Allah," and "the Messiah is the son of Allah." He used "ma" because it is more general than "man." This is one aspect. Another aspect: when the attribute is intended to be considered, one uses "ma" for "man." Here the attribute is intended to be considered, which is worship. Look at an example that clarifies what we said. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [An-Nisa' 4:3], and did not say "man." This is because the intended meaning is not the specific woman but the attribute, so He used "ma" for "man."

﴿He would have chosen from what He creates﴾, meaning from His creatures that have will and consciousness, such as 'Uzayr, the Messiah, the angels, and others, and also inanimate things such as carved idols and the like. (﴿whatever He wills﴾ and taken it as a son).
The saying ﴿from what He creates whatever He wills﴾: we say about ﴿whatever He wills﴾ what we said about ﴿from what He creates﴾.
(And taken it as a son, other than those who were said to be the angels, daughters of Allah). ("Inna" or "min"? "Other than those who said"?) Do all of you have "inna"?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (Other than those among the angels whom they said were daughters of Allah, and 'Uzayr, son of Allah, and the Messiah, son of Allah.) Yes. The meaning is: if Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, had willed to take a son, no one could have prevented Him. He would have chosen from what He creates whatever He wills, from what they said or from something else. He, the Mighty and Majestic, has perfect dominion, but He does not take a son, as He said: ﴿It is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son﴾ [Maryam 19:92], meaning it is utterly impossible for Him to take a son. For this reason He said here: (﴿Glory be to Him﴾, exalting Him above taking a son. ﴿He is Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ over His creation).

﴿Glory be to Him﴾ means: exalted above it. "Subhan" is a verbal noun (ism masdar) from "sabbaha," whose verbal noun is "tasbih." Know that "subhan" is always joined with an annexed noun (idafa), though it may occasionally come without it, rarely or irregularly. It may be joined with "al," as in "dhas-subhan." But the rule is that it is always annexed, and it is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), and its governing verb is always omitted. The meaning is: exaltation of Him.

The author's saying (concerning taking a son) specified taking a son because the context concerns that. Otherwise He is exalted above taking a son and above every defect and deficiency.

If someone asks: is there a defect in taking a son?
The answer: yes, there is a defect, because it indicates that the father needs the son. This is why you find that when a person does not have a son, he sees himself as lacking, and wishes above all that a son would come to help him with life's affairs and keep his memory alive after his death. So taking a son is a deficiency, and for this reason Allah exalted Himself above it.

Second: a son comes for the sake of preserving the species from which he is born, and Allah, Glorified and Exalted, has no need of that, for He is the One, the Everlasting, the Mighty and Majestic.

Third: a son is similar to his father, and we do not hear, nor have we heard, that a human was given a he-goat. Is that not so?
Rather, a person is given a son like himself. So if it were assumed that Allah had taken a son, the son would be like Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and Allah, the Exalted, is exalted above having anyone similar to Him.

So from these three aspects it becomes clear that a son is impossible for Allah in the utmost degree of impossibility. Then Allah also mentioned a fourth obstacle, which is that He has no wife. He said, the Exalted: ﴿And He did not have a companion, and He created all things, and He is Knowing of all things﴾ [Al-An'am 6:101]. So He made clear that He has no wife, and how then would a son come? A son came from Adam, for example, as a miraculous sign.

Then ﴿He is Allah, the One﴾: He is Allah. If He had a son, that son would share in divinity, but divinity belongs to Him alone. ﴿The One﴾: if He had a son, there would be two, because a son must be similar to his father, while Allah is One with no second, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿The Subduer (al-Qahhar)﴾ is an intensive form and an attributive form, meaning He possesses constant, repeated subjugation. How many people and nations of tyranny has Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, subdued!

* Among the benefits of this verse: whoever is a liar and ungrateful, Allah does not grant him success, as He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a liar and ungrateful﴾ [Az-Zumar 39:3].
* Among its benefits: a warning against lying and the traits of disbelief, and that lying is a cause of being denied guidance. This is because when a ruling is linked to a description, it is found when that description is present and absent when it is absent. This is the rule from which this benefit can be applied. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Beware of lying, for lying leads to immorality, and immorality leads to the Fire." [Agreed upon by al-Bukhari (6094) and Muslim (2607/105), from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud.]
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: truthfulness is a cause of guidance. Its reasoning: if lying is a cause of error, then its opposite is a cause of the opposite, so truthfulness becomes a cause of guidance.
From this benefit follows encouragement to truthfulness. But truthfulness with whom? Truthfulness with Allah, with His Messenger, and with the servants of Allah. Truthfulness with Allah is through sincerity to Him; with the Messenger, through following him; with the servants of Allah, through good dealing. So hold fast to truthfulness, "for truthfulness leads to righteousness, and righteousness leads to Paradise. A man continues to speak the truth and seeks to be truthful until he is recorded with Allah as a truthful one." [Agreed upon by al-Bukhari (6094) and Muslim (2607/103), from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud.] May Allah make us and you among them.
Some foolish people say: "Lying is a means of salvation." Some merchants say: "Lying is the nails of goods." Is this correct? What do we say? We say: lying is destruction, and truthfulness is salvation. As for the merchants who buy and sell and say: "Lie so that goods are sold, like nails for doors," what do we say to him? We say: rather, be truthful, for truthfulness is the real nail, the one that establishes blessing. Lying may move goods, but it erases gain.

* Also among the benefits of this verse: disbelief is a cause of error, as He said: ﴿one who is a liar and ungrateful﴾ [Az-Zumar 39:3]. This is supported by His saying: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [As-Saff 61:5].
* Among its benefits: a warning against the traits of disbelief. This is because when a ruling is linked to a description, it is established when the description is present and removed when it is absent. The traits of disbelief that do not lead to absolute disbelief may, Allah forbid, be a cause of error, such as slandering lineage, wailing over the dead, and killing a protected Muslim. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Cursing a Muslim is wickedness, and fighting him is disbelief." [Agreed upon by al-Bukhari (48) and Muslim (64/116), from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud.]

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Had Allah intended to take a son, He would have chosen from what He creates whatever He wills﴾ [Az-Zumar 39:4]:
* In this noble verse: a demonstration of the perfection of Allah's sovereignty, glorified and exalted, and that if He willed anything, nothing could prevent Him, as His saying shows: ﴿He would have chosen from what He creates whatever He wills﴾. From another aspect, it is a refutation of their assertions or claims that the angels are daughters of Allah, or the Messiah, or 'Uzayr. It says: if Allah had willed to take a son, He would have chosen whatever He wills, without taking what they claimed.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of Allah's will (irada), azza wa jall, based on His saying: ﴿If Allah had desired to take a son﴾. Allah's will regarding His own act is agreed upon; we do not think anyone disputes that Allah wills His own act. But does it extend to the act of the created being or not?

On this there is disagreement between the People of the Sunnah and the People of innovation. Among them are those who said: it extends to the act of the created being, and they went to an extreme in this, saying that the created being has no will at all. This is the view of the Jahmiyya Jabriyya.

Among them are those who said: it extends to the act of the created being, but not in the manner of compulsion (jabr). This is the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah and the Community (Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah). And among them are those who said: it does not extend to the act of the created being, and that the created being is independent in its act, with no will of Allah regarding it. This is the doctrine of the Qadariyya, the Magians of this Ummah. Yes.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of Allah's voluntary acts (al-af'al al-ikhtiyariyya), azza wa jall, based on His saying: ﴿He would have chosen what He wills from what He creates﴾. Allah's voluntary acts are established by both revelation (al-sam') and reason (al-'aql). As for revelation, the acts which Allah attributes to Himself are very numerous. As for reason, the agent who acts by choice is more perfect than one who does not act. The Ash'aris and others among the Mu'attila (those who deny Allah's attributes) went to the view that voluntary acts do not subsist in Allah, azza wa jall, on the argument that a newly occurring act necessitates the occurrence of the agent. There is no doubt that this view is false and entails false consequences, among them that Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, is unable to act, and this is a deficiency in Allah, azza wa jall, and a denial of His many reports which affirm action for Him, too many to be enumerated.

* Among the benefits of this verse: affirmation of Allah's volition (mashi'a), based on His saying: ﴿He would have chosen what He wills from what He creates﴾. Concerning volition we say what we said about will with respect to its scope: it applies to the acts of Allah, and does it apply to the acts of the created being? This is subject to the earlier disagreement which we explained regarding will. But here there is a matter that must be noted: will is divided into two types, legislative will (al-irada al-shar'iyya) and universal/decreed will (al-irada al-kawniyya). As for volition (al-mashi'a), it is one type only. Universal will is synonymous with volition, having the same meaning: if you say, "What Allah wills occurs," it means "What Allah wills occurs."

As for legislative will, it is synonymous with love (al-mahabba), meaning it relates to what Allah, azza wa jall, loves. So you say: Allah wills from us that we thank Him. This will is legislative.

The difference between legislative and universal will is in two respects:

The first respect: universal will encompasses what Allah loves and what He does not love. Universal will: He wills faith, He wills disbelief, He wills obedience, and He wills wickedness by universal will.

As for legislative will, it relates only to what He loves. So you cannot say that Allah wills wickedness, meaning loves it; this is impossible.

Second, the second difference: universal will necessarily entails the occurrence of what is willed; that is, if He wills something by universal will, it must occur. Legislative will may occur or may not occur: He, subhanahu wa ta'ala, wills from us faith and obedience, and they may exist or may not exist. This is the difference between them.

With this, the objections which the Qadariyya raised against the People of the Sunnah are resolved. They said to them: If you affirm that Allah's will relates to everything, even sins, it follows that Allah wills evil, and so Allah would be evil according to their statement. We ask Allah for well-being. What do we say? We say: As for legislative will, Allah can never will evil at all. As for universal will, He wills what He wishes, but His universal will concerning evil has profound and numerous wisdoms that are well known.

He says: * Among the benefits of this noble verse: the declaration of Allah's transcendence, subhanahu wa ta'ala, above everything the disbelievers and deniers attribute to Him, based on His saying: ﴿Glory be to Him﴾.

* Among its benefits: affirmation of Allah's names: Allah, the One (al-Wahid), and the Subduer (al-Qahhar), three names. Every name Allah affirms for Himself includes the attribute from which it is derived. So "Allah" is derived from divinity (al-uluhiyya), so it includes the affirmation of divinity as one of His attributes. "The One" (al-Wahid): oneness (al-wahdaniyya), so it includes the affirmation of oneness for Allah, azza wa jall. "The Subduer" (al-Qahhar): subjugation (al-qahr), so it includes the affirmation of subjugation for Allah, azza wa jall, and that He is the Subduer, the Overpowering, who prevails over everything.

Then He, exalted is He, said: (He created the heavens and the earth in truth) [Zumar 5]. The phrase [بِالْحَقِّ] (in truth) is related to [خَلَقَ] (created).

This verse came after the refutation of those who claim that God has a son, to show that the Creator of the heavens and the earth is free of need for a son and has no need of one, because everything belongs to Him. Only one who does not fully possess dominion needs a child.

As for His saying [خَلَقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ] (He created the heavens): [السَّمَاوَاتِ] is the plural of [سَمَاءٌ] (sky/heaven), and the word [سَمَاءٌ] is used with two meanings:

The first meaning: height, even if it is below the heavens.

The second meaning: the well-known heavens, the canopy that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, constructed.

From the first meaning is His saying: ﴿He sends down water from the sky﴾ [Zumar 21]. [مِنَ السَّمَاءِ] here means from the clouds. The sky is not attached to the ceiling of the heavens, but is in the height. From the same usage is His saying: ﴿Let him stretch a rope to the sky﴾ [Hajj 15], meaning up to the height. As for the second meaning, which is the construction, it is frequent. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Then He turned to the sky while it was smoke, and said to it and to the earth: "Come willingly or unwillingly." They said: "We come willingly." (11) So He completed them as seven heavens in two days﴾ [Fussilat 11-12].

From the same usage is this verse, [خَلَقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ]. It is plural because it is the plural of "seven heavens," as stated in the Qur'an and in the Prophetic Sunnah.

[وَالْأَرْضَ] refers to the earth that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, laid out for creation, on which they live, as He said: ﴿And the earth He laid out for the creatures﴾ [Rahman 10]. The Qur'an does not explicitly mention the number of the earths. That is, the Qur'an does not state explicitly that the earths are seven, but their number has been indicated not by explicit statement, such as His saying: ﴿Allah is He who created seven heavens and of the earth the like thereof﴾ [Talaq 12]. "The like thereof" is alike in number but not alike in attributes, because of the difference between the heavens and the earth in their characteristics. As for the Sunnah, it is explicit that the earths are seven. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever usurps a span of land unjustly, it will be hung around his neck from the seven earths on the Day of Resurrection."[[Recorded by Muslim (1610/137) from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd.]]

The apparent meaning of the texts is that these earths are layered, meaning some are beneath others, like the heavens, because His saying, peace and blessings be upon him, "it will be hung around his neck from the seven earths," would not make sense unless they were layered, so that one would be punished with what is beneath the uppermost earth. So they are layered. But the scholars who discuss the creation of the earths have asked: are these earths separate from one another, or are they one mass? Our answer to this question is: Allah knows best; we do not know. However, we must believe that there are seven earths, as the texts state.

As for His saying [بِالْحَقِّ] (in truth), which is related to [خَلَقَ] (created): this means that His creating them was in truth, that is, He created them truly, with no creator of them besides Him. This is one meaning. The second meaning of [بِالْحَقِّ] is for the sake of truth, not in vain, as He said: ﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve﴾ [Sad 27]. Is it [السَّمَوَاتِ] or [السَّمَاءَ]? ﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve﴾.

He, the Exalted, also said: ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play (38). We did not create them except in truth﴾ [Dukhan 38-39].

And Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has spoken truly, for in the creation of the heavens and the earth there is evident truth. Through them Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is known, and His signs in the cosmos and His legislative signs are manifest. Through them creatures live. In this session we cannot encompass all the truth in the creation of the heavens and the earth: ﴿He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night﴾ [Zumar 5].

The author said: [يُكَوِّرُ] means "causes to enter" [يدخل].

There is no doubt that Allah causes the night to enter into the day and the day to enter into the night, as in other verses. But does the meaning of [التَّكْوِيرُ] (wrapping) here mean [الإيلاج] (causing to enter), namely that the day enters upon the night so that it lengthens, and the day enters upon the night so that it lengthens?

The apparent wording rejects this, because Allah said [يُكَوِّرُ], and [التَّكْوِيرُ] means [التَّدْوِيرُ] (rotating, making round). It is the rotating. From it comes [كَوَّرَ الْعِمَامَةَ] (he wound the turban), meaning he wrapped it around. The turban's layers are called [أَكْوَارًا]. So [يُكَوِّرُ] means He rotates the night over the day, and this resembles His saying: ﴿He covers the night over the day, pursuing it swiftly﴾ [A'raf 54]. When this is the apparent meaning of the wording, it is obligatory to keep the wording on its apparent meaning, because the apparent meaning is what comes to the mind of the hearer.

If someone says: why do you not take the matter as the author said, so as to interpret the Qur'an by the Qur'an, and make [يُكَوِّرُ] mean [يُولِجُ] (causes to enter)?

We say: this is not correct, for two reasons.

The first reason: it contradicts the apparent wording. And what is the apparent wording of [يُكَوِّرُ]? It means to rotate and to fold up.

Second: it loses the meaning derived from the word [يُكَوِّرُ]. As for the meaning derived from causing to enter, this is known from other verses, so we gain a new benefit distinct from the benefit of entering.

As for His, the Exalted, causing the night to enter the day and the day to enter the night, this is well known and indicated by other verses: [وَيُكَوِّرُ النَّهَارَ عَلَى اللَّيْلِ] (and He wraps the day over the night).

He said: (and He subjected the sun and the moon) [meaning] made them subservient. [التَّسْخِيرُ] (subjugation), may Allah have mercy on you, means [التَّذْلِيلُ] (making subservient). That is, He made them subservient. For what purpose? For the benefit of the servants, as shown by His saying: ﴿And He subjected for you the night and the day, the sun and the moon﴾ [Nahl 12].

So the subjugation here is for the benefit of the servants. The sun and the moon are well known and need no definition. If we wanted to define them by what astronomers know, we would only add obscurity. If we said: "The sun is a burning, flaming mass of fire," and so on, people would wander around asking: "Where is it? What is it? A mass?"

The moon is likewise a rocky, solid, cold, dark mass, and so on, which also leads the mind in every direction. But if we say: the sun is what we see, the sign of the day, and the moon is the sign of the night, everyone knows them more clearly than anything else. [سَخَّرَ] made them subservient in their movement and in the variation of this movement. That they revolve around the earth and differ in length and shortness is without doubt for the benefit of the servants: ﴿each runs for a specified term﴾ [Zumar 5].

[كُلٌّ] (each) of what? Of the sun and the moon. [يَجْرِي] means it moves in its orbit. [الْفَلَكُ] (orbit) is the round thing, and they revolve in a clear circular path, though this differs with the alternation of night and day.

His saying [لِأَجَلٍ] means "up to a term," that is, an end, [لِأَجَلٍ] meaning for a goal, a specified term determined by whom? By Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is the specified term. The author said: (the Day of Resurrection).

The proof of this is His saying: ﴿When the sun is wrapped up (1), when the stars fall (2), when the mountains are set in motion﴾ [Takwir 1-3], until He said: ﴿Then a soul will know what it has presented﴾ [Takwir 14]. When will this happen? On the Day of Resurrection, as He said: ﴿On the Day every soul will find what it has done of good present﴾ [Al 'Imran 30]. These two run until the Day of Resurrection. When the Day of Resurrection comes, people's need for them ends, and [...].

﴿Unquestionably He is the Mighty, the Forgiving﴾ [Zumar 5]. [أَلَا] is an introductory particle used to draw attention. [هُوَ] refers to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. [الْعَزِيزُ] (the Mighty): the author said: "the one overpowering in His command, who takes vengeance on His enemies." This is one of the meanings of might which He affirmed for Himself. It was previously stated that it has a second and third meaning: might of rank, and might of inaccessibility, in addition to might of dominance.

Allah, glorified and exalted, is perfectly characterized by might: ﴿To Allah belongs all might﴾ [Fatir 10], ﴿Indeed, all might belongs to Allah﴾ [Yunus 65]. So all types of might are established for Allah, glorified and exalted.

His saying [الْغَفَّارُ] (the Forgiving) is an intensive form derived from [الْغَفْرُ], or a relational form. [الْغَفْرُ] or [الْغُفْرَانُ] means covering a sin and overlooking it. It is not sufficient to say that forgiveness is merely overlooking a sin, because the derived meaning rejects this. Forgiveness [الْمَغْفِرَةُ] is derived from [الْمِغْفَرُ] (helmet), and the helmet is an item placed on the head to protect it from the arrows of enemies. So in this helmet there is covering and protection. For this reason we say about the meaning of [الْغَفَّارُ]: He is the one who forgives sins, that is, the one who covers the sin and overlooks it.

* In this noble verse: affirmation of the creation of the heavens and the earth. From this benefit follows a refutation of the naturalists and philosophers who claim the world is eternal, that it has no beginning, and that these heavens have always existed. This verse refutes them, because it says: ﴿He created the heavens﴾, meaning He brought them into existence after non-existence.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the heavens are a number, indicated by the plural form, because the plural points to a number, and other texts have clarified that they are seven.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the creation of the heavens and the earth is in truth, and its opposite is falsehood, so they were not created in vain [...] or in play.

* Among its benefits also: the Creator of the heavens and the earth is Allah, from His saying [بِالْحَقِّ] according to one of the two meanings we indicated.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: affirmation of the spherical shape of the earth, from His saying: ﴿He wraps the night over the day﴾. It is known that night and day alternate over the earth, so if their movement is a wrapping, this shows that the earth is spherical.

* Among its benefits: affirmation of Allah's power by wrapping the night and the day. Allah pointed to this in His saying: ﴿Say: "Have you considered, if Allah made the night perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what god other than Allah could bring you light? Will you not then hear?" (71) Say: "Have you considered, if Allah made the day perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what god other than Allah could bring you a night in which you may rest? Will you not then see?"﴾ [Qasas 71-72].

Even if all creation gathered to bring the night in place of the day, or the day in place of the night, they could not do it. In this is a demonstration of the perfection of Allah's power, as He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: demonstration of Allah's blessing upon us by subjecting the sun and the moon, from His saying: ﴿And He subjected the sun and the moon﴾.

* Among its benefits: the sun and the moon run in their orbits. This is a refutation of those who claim that the alternation of night and day occurs by the rotation of the earth. The verse is explicit that the sun runs and the moon runs. At least we say that it is apparent in this. When we have an apparent meaning from the Book and the Sunnah, it is not permissible for us to depart from this apparent meaning except by a clear proof that justifies opposing it, because Allah addressed us with His speech in the Arabic tongue. It is therefore obligatory for us to follow what the Arabic language requires, unless there is evidence to the contrary. They now say that the sun and the moon do not run, that the moon revolves around the sun, that the earth also revolves around the sun, and that the alternation of night and day occurs by the earth's rotation. All of this contradicts the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, so it carries no weight, unless we know something by which we can counter Allah's speech by taking it out of its apparent meaning. Otherwise, it is obligatory to keep it on its apparent meaning.

Even if we were to accept that the earth rotates, it does not follow that the sun does not revolve around it, because some people say: if you acknowledge that the earth rotates, then it follows that the difference between night and day is caused by the earth's rotation.

We say: it does not follow, because when the earth's rotation differs from the sun's rotation, the alternation of night and day occurs, and there is no obstacle.

In any case, the important point is that we must follow the apparent meaning of Allah's speech, because Allah is the Creator, His report is true, and He addressed us with what we understand in our language, the language of the Arabs. It is not permissible for us to deviate from the apparent meaning except by sensory evidence, which we present to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, on the Day of Resurrection. If He asks us: why did you believe that the earth is what rotates and that night and day occur by its rotation?

That would be our argument. We would say: because we perceived this. Now, if it is supposed, though it seems distant, that it were proven that night and day occur by the rotation of the earth and not by the rotation of the sun, how would we answer the apparent wording?

We say: [the sun] runs according to human perception, because when a thing is stationary while another thing rotates, the one above it, which is still, is thought to be the one that moves and rotates. If this is established, we say: they run according to human observation, even though they are stationary and the earth is what rotates. Yes.

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: No, in general, the apparent meaning is general, because when Allah legislates something, He cannot legislate something He dislikes.

* Student: It may be beloved to another, a benefit for another.

* Shaykh: Like what?

* Student: I do not recall.

* Shaykh: What (...) legislative matters are connected to what He loves.

* Student: Like jihad, which involves killing, but there is a benefit in it.

* Shaykh: Yes, it is disliked by us: ﴿Fighting has been enjoined upon you while it is hateful to you﴾ [Baqarah 216]. But for Allah it is not hateful, because Allah loves that His servant fight in His cause and be killed.

* Student: (...) the language of the Arabs (...) likewise for emphasis (...).

* Shaykh: No. [كُلٌّ] is the subject (mubtada').

* Student: [كُلٌّ] is the subject (...) for emphasis.

* Shaykh: That is, for emphasis in meaning.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: The sentence here is for generality. As for [كُلٌّ يَجْرِي], it is a resumptive clause (isti'nafiyyah). I do not think it is in the accusative position; it is a resumptive clause. Yes.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿He created you from a single soul, then made from it its mate, and He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock. He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation, in three darknesses. That is Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs dominion. There is no god but Him, so how are you turned away? (6) If you disbelieve, indeed Allah is free of need of you, yet He does not approve disbelief for His servants. And if you are grateful, He approves it for you. No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you of what you used to do. Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ [Zumar 6-7].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾ [Zumar 5]. What is the meaning of His saying [بِالْحَقِّ]?

* Student: (...) He created them in truth.

* Shaykh: That is one. The second meaning: He created them in truth, meaning no one else created them.

* Student: That is, for the sake of truth.

* Shaykh: For the sake of truth. Good, what is the evidence for the second meaning?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, the evidence for the second meaning is that Allah created them for the truth?

* Student: ﴿We did not create the sky and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾.

* Shaykh: ﴿The sky and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ is another verse: ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play (38). We did not create them except in truth﴾ [Dukhan 38-39]. Yes. Is there anything in the Qur'an that indicates the number of the earths?

* Student: Yes, in the Qur'an His saying: ﴿and of the earth the like thereof﴾.

* Shaykh: ﴿Allah is He who created seven heavens and of the earth the like thereof﴾ [Talaq 12]. Yes. If someone said: "the like thereof" in attributes?

* Student: Does this mean it is a question?

* Shaykh: Yes.

* Student: We say: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, did not specify them (...) by number (...).

* Shaykh: He did not say that. He did not say: alike in number.

* Student: Because it came in a hadith.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verse 5 (part 2 of 2):

* The Shaykh: No, we want it from the verse itself.
* A student: Because Allah said about the heavens the number: seven heavens. So the likeness in the earth is in number.
* The Shaykh: (...) If someone said: "Similar to them in attribute," because when you say "So-and-so is like So-and-so," you mean in attribute.
* The student: Because Allah mentioned ﴿He created seven heavens﴾, so it will be (...).
* Another student: (...) originally (...) in number and manner, but there is no likeness between the earth and the heavens in terms of attribute; it is entirely different from them.
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, likeness in attribute is impossible. The heavens are great, lofty, and encompass the earth, and the earth cannot be like them in attribute. Therefore it is established that it is like them in number, because He said: ﴿seven heavens and of the earth, the like thereof﴾, meaning in number, not in attribute. Alright, did you not attend? Alright, ﴿He wraps the night over the day﴾, what did the author say about ﴿yukawwiru﴾?
* Student: (...) it revolves.
* The Shaykh: No, the author's words.
* The student: The author's words (...).
* The Shaykh: No.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: He said: its meaning is "yadkhul" (enters). "He wraps the night over the day," i.e., the night enters into the day, so the night increases; and "wraps the day over the night," so the day increases. Alright, what is the apparent meaning?
* The student: That it turns (yudir).
* The Shaykh: That it turns. What is the evidence that this is the apparent meaning?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The meaning of al-takwir (wrapping) and al-idara (turning around). And from it?
* The student: "Kawwara al-'amama" (he wrapped the turban).
* The Shaykh: "Kawwara al-'amama" (he wrapped the turban).

The Almighty's saying: ﴿He has subjected the sun and the moon﴾. What is the meaning of ﴿sakhkhara﴾?
* Student: It means "dhallala" (made subservient).
* The Shaykh: Made subservient. For what?
* Student: For the servants.
* The Shaykh: For the servants. What is the evidence that the intended meaning is making them subservient to the servants?
* The student: The Most High's saying in another verse: ﴿He has subjected to you the night and the day, and the sun and the moon﴾ [al-Nahl 12].
* The Shaykh: Well done. ﴿Has subjected to you﴾. Yes. His saying: ﴿each runs for a specified term﴾, ﴿each runs﴾. What is meant by ﴿each﴾?
* Student: The sun and the moon.
* The Shaykh: ﴿Each﴾ refers to the sun and the moon. And the meaning of ﴿yajri﴾?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It revolves, or it proceeds, it moves. Alright, His saying: ﴿for a specified term﴾, what is meant by the term here?
* Student: (...).
