* A student: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord? Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know? Only the people of understanding remember. Say: O My servants who believe, fear your Lord. For those who do good in this world there is good, and Allah's earth is spacious. Only the patient will be given their reward without measure﴾ [az-Zumar 9-10].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance﴾ [az-Zumar 8]. Who is meant by "man" here?
* A student: The disbeliever.
* The Shaykh: The disbeliever. Why do we not take it in its general sense, as we took His saying ﴿and man was created weak﴾ [an-Nisa 28] in its general sense?
* A student: (...) by the indication of the context.
* The Shaykh: What is the context?
* The student: The indication of context regarding the disbeliever: ﴿and sets up rivals to Allah﴾ [az-Zumar 8].
* The Shaykh: ﴿and sets up rivals to Allah﴾. Well done.
Is it permissible in Arabic for a general term to be used to mean a specific one?
* A student: Yes, much.
* The Shaykh: Much. Is there anything from beyond this verse?
* A student: His saying: ﴿Those to whom people said, "Indeed the people have gathered against you, so fear them"﴾ [Al 'Imran 173].
* The Shaykh: His saying ﴿those to whom people said, "Indeed the people have gathered against you"﴾: the first "people" is one man, and the second is a group of people, not all people.
His saying: ﴿Then when He bestows upon him a favor from Himself﴾ [az-Zumar 8]: what is the meaning of (khawwalahu)?
* A student: He gave him.
* The Shaykh: He gave him. And from it His saying: ﴿and you have left what We bestowed upon you﴾ [al-An'am 94]. A favor?
* A student: The author explained it as "bestowal," and this is wrong, because bestowal is an act of Allah, the Exalted.
* The Shaykh: The correct view is better than your saying "this is wrong." The correct view is that the meaning is "He gave him a favor," because He bestowed upon him the thing bestowed, not the bestowal; the bestowal is an act of Allah.
His saying: ﴿and sets up rivals to Allah so that he may lead astray﴾ [az-Zumar 8]: are there two readings?
* A student: With fatḥa on the yā', and with ḍamma on the yā', with ḍamma and fatḥa.
* The Shaykh: Recite them.
* The student: ﴿li-yuḍilla﴾ and ﴿li-yaḍilla﴾.
* The Shaykh: Yes, well done.
What is the meaning of the lām on both readings?
* The student: With fatḥa on the yā' it is for consequence; with ḍamma on the yā' it is...
* The Shaykh: For causation.
Our brother has explained that the lām entering the imperfect is for consequence and for causation, as in this verse. Does it have a third meaning? Come on, brother, we think you are a grammarian.
* A student: Extra.
* The Shaykh: Extra; like what?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, the one that enters the imperfect is not the lām that enters the noun.
* A student: The imperfect?
* The Shaykh: Yes, it comes extra, but we want the example now.
* The student: It comes meaning "al".
* The Shaykh: There is no power nor strength except with Allah!
* A student: Like ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ [an-Nisa 26].
* The Shaykh: ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾: the lām here?
* The student: Extra.
* The Shaykh: Extra. Why? Because desire indicates its own meaning; if Allah the Mighty and Majestic said "Allah desires that He make clear to you," it would be correct.
* A student: Correct.
* The Shaykh: Correct, the sentence stands.
Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Say: Enjoy your disbelief for a little﴾ [az-Zumar 8]. We stopped at (yuḍilla)?
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿so that he may lead astray from His way﴾ or ﴿so that he may go astray from His way﴾ [az-Zumar 8]. ﴿His way﴾ means His religion, i.e., His path that leads to Him; the path of Allah that leads to Him: this is the way of Allah.
The "way" is attributed to Allah at times, as in this verse and many others, and attributed to a created being, as in His saying: ﴿Say: This is my way; I call to Allah﴾ [Yusuf 108]. So what is the reconciliation between them?
The reconciliation is that it is attributed to Allah in that He is the one who established it and it leads to Him; and it is attributed to other than Allah, to the created being, in that he is the one who walks it.
So "the way of Allah" means He is the one who legislated this way and set it for the servants, and it leads to Allah. The way of the Messenger, ﴿This is my way; I call to Allah﴾ [Yusuf 108], means my path that I walk. The same is said of the path: ﴿the path of Allah﴾ [ash-Shura 53] and ﴿the path of those You have blessed﴾ [al-Fatihah 7]. The path of Allah is so called because He is the one who established it and it leads to Him, and ﴿the path of those You have blessed﴾ is so called because they are the ones who walk it.
As for His saying ﴿so that he may lead astray from His way﴾, the author said: (the religion of Islam). This is an explanation of the word according to its intended meaning, because the explanation of the Qur'an is sometimes a verbal explanation and sometimes a explanation of meaning.
Verbal explanation: explaining the word by its literal equivalent. Explanation of meaning: explaining the word by what is intended by it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verse 8–9 (part 2 of 5):

For example: the religion of Islam does not correspond to the literal meaning of "sabil" (path), because "sabil" linguistically means "road." If someone were asked to explain "sabil," you would say: it means "tariq" (road).

But the "sabil" intended here is the religion of Islam, because the religion of Islam, which is the laws of Islam, leads to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the One who established it is Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

So, does the author explain "sabil" here by its literal meaning or by its intended meaning? That is, that what is meant by it is such and such.

As for his saying "the religion of Islam," it is clear that it is the path of Allah, because Allah is the One who legislated it, glorified and exalted be He; and because whoever follows it is led to Allah.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: "Enjoy your disbelief for a little while (the remainder of your term); indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire."﴾ [Az-Zumar 8] I seek refuge in Allah.

"Say" is addressed to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and it may also be addressed to everyone who can be addressed; that is: say, O human, to this disbeliever or to this person described with these attributes: ﴿Enjoy your disbelief for a little while.﴾

﴿Enjoy your disbelief for a little while⦆ is an imperative, but it is not on its apparent meaning; rather the imperative here is intended as a threat, like His saying: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [Al-Kahf 29]. It is known that a person does not have the choice between faith and disbelief, but this is by way of threat.

So here, ﴿Enjoy your disbelief for a little while﴾ does not mean that We permit him to enjoy disbelief, or command him to enjoy his disbelief; rather We threaten him, so the imperative here is for threat.

If someone asks: what removed it from its original meaning?

The answer: what removed it from its original meaning is the context: ﴿Say: Enjoy your disbelief﴾, meaning: disbelieve and enjoy disbelief, because the disbeliever enjoys his disbelief like cattle enjoy themselves, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those who disbelieve enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat, and the Fire is their residence﴾ [Muhammad 12]. The disbeliever, may Allah protect us, does not bind himself to any act of worship: not prayer, nor zakat, nor fasting, nor Hajj, nor any other acts of worship. Rather he follows his desire and enjoys himself as a donkey enjoys itself. In the end He said: ﴿Indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire﴾, like His saying: ﴿they enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat, and the Fire is their residence﴾ [Muhammad 12]. How quickly he arrives at the Fire! For the worldly life is little, that is, a short time. However long your life is, when your appointed term comes, it will be as though you had not remained except an hour of a day. If you want to verify this, consider what has passed of your life against what remains. Consider what has passed. Now, each of us differs from the other in age, but each of us is as though born this very hour; that is, all that has passed is as though it had never been. Likewise the remainder of life, however long a person's life may be, when his term comes it is as though it had not been. For this reason He said: ﴿Enjoy your disbelief for a little while⦆, even if your life is long; he says: (the remainder of your term).

﴿Indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire﴾ [Az-Zumar 8]: this sentence is emphasized with "inna," meaning: however much you enjoy yourself, your end is the Fire: ﴿indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire﴾. And "companions of the Fire" is used only of those who will abide in it forever. The sinful believer, although he deserves punishment in the Fire, is not called one of the companions of the Fire, because the basic meaning of companionship is long continuous association. This is the basic principle of companionship, long continuous association, except in one matter. What is it?

* Students: The Companions (al-Sahaba).

* The Shaykh: Who? The Companions, the Companions of the Messenger ﷺ. If someone met the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while believing in him, even for a moment, he became one of his companions.

He says: ﴿Indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire﴾. The Fire is the abode that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, prepared for the disbelievers. Allah has explained in the Book, and His Messenger ﷺ has explained in the Sunnah, the kinds of punishment in it: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Our signs, We will surely drive them into a Fire. Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins that they may taste the punishment. Indeed, Allah is ever Exalted in Might and Wise﴾ [An-Nisa 56]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqum, the food of the sinful, like murky oil, boils in the bellies like the boiling of scalding water. Seize him and drag him into the midst of the Blazing Fire. Then pour over his head the torment of scalding water. Taste! Indeed, you were the mighty, the honorable﴾ [Ad-Dukhan 43–49]. I seek refuge in Allah. "Pour over his head the torment of scalding water": the water that is extremely hot. "Taste! Indeed, you were the mighty, the honorable" is said in mockery of him: where is your might, and where is your honor? In the worldly life he saw himself as a noble lord, but in the Hereafter he is humiliated with this humiliation.

The point is: the kinds of punishment in the Fire, may Allah protect us, if a person imagines them, becomes clear to him how severe is what these people encounter of severe punishment. We seek refuge in Allah from the Fire, we seek refuge in Allah from the Fire, we seek refuge in Allah from the Fire.

He, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during periods of the night, prostrating and standing...﴾ to the end [Az-Zumar 9].

﴿Amman huwa﴾: he said: (﴿Amman﴾ with the mim lightened). So the word is composed of the interrogative hamza and "man," the interrogative "man." He says: rather, "man" is the relative pronoun: the hamza of interrogation and the relative "man," meaning: is the one who is devoutly obedient, to the end.

(﴿huwa qanit﴾: standing in the performance of acts of obedience.) Qunut is used with several meanings:

Among them: humility, as in His saying: ﴿And stand before Allah in devout obedience﴾ [Al-Baqarah 238].

Among them: supplication in the witr or in obligatory prayers during calamities.

Among them: constancy in obedience, as in His saying: ﴿And she believed in the words of her Lord and His scriptures, and she was among the devoutly obedient﴾ [At-Tahrim 12].

An example of the first: ﴿Guard the prayers and the middle prayer, and stand before Allah in devout obedience﴾ [Al-Baqarah 238], meaning: humbly submissive. For this reason, when this verse was revealed, the Companions were commanded to be silent and forbidden to speak.

So here, ﴿qanit﴾ is in which of the three meanings?

* A student: Constancy in obedience.

* The Shaykh: Constancy in obedience. ﴿Amman huwa qanit﴾ [Az-Zumar 9]. The author said: (standing in the performance of acts of obedience), meaning persisting in them.

(﴿Aana' al-layl﴾: its hours. ﴿Sajidan wa qa'iman﴾: in prayer.)

﴿Sajidan wa qa'iman﴾: the text specifies prostration and standing, but not bowing or sitting, because prostration is noble in its posture and standing is noble in its remembrance. How?

Prostration is noble in its posture: the best posture of the one praying is to be prostrating; for this reason the servant is closest to his Lord when he is prostrating.

Standing is noble in its remembrance: what is its remembrance? The Qur'an, which is the speech of Allah, and the speech of Allah the Exalted is the noblest speech. Therefore He specified these two matters, or these two pillars of the pillars of prayer: standing and prostration. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, when he prostrated, there was a sound from his chest like the boiling of a cauldron (Abu Dawud? — recorded in al-Musnad (16312) and al-Nasa'i in al-Mujtaba (1214) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn al-Shikhkhir). And the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, when he stood, did not pass a verse of mercy without asking, nor a verse of punishment without seeking refuge, nor a verse of glorification without glorifying (recorded by Abu Dawud (873), al-Nasa'i in al-Mujtaba (1132), and Ahmad in al-Musnad (23980) from the hadith of Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i). This indicates that one who stands in prayer at night should observe this: observe the intensity of humility in prostration and weeping, and also observe presence of heart during recitation, so that when he passes a verse of mercy he asks, a verse of punishment he seeks refuge, a verse of glorification he glorifies, standing, sitting, prostrating and standing.

(﴿Yahdharu al-akhirah﴾: he fears its punishment. ﴿Wa yarju rahmata rabbihi﴾: Paradise, ﴿his Lord﴾.)

Here his saying: ﴿yahdharu al-akhirah⦆ is a circumstantial clause, the state of his fearing the Hereafter, in conjunction with ﴿sajidan wa qa'iman﴾, meaning: while he is in his prostration and standing, he fears the Hereafter; that is, he fears it, not fears its occurrence, since its occurrence is certain, but fears its punishment, fears that he will be punished.

﴿Wa yarju rahmata rabbihi⦆: the author says: His Paradise. There is no doubt that mercy here is intended as Paradise, as Allah said to Paradise: "You are My mercy; I show mercy through you to whom I will" (Bukhari (4850), Muslim (2846/36) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah).

But mercy may also be understood in another sense, namely Allah's act toward the servant, that is, His mercy to the servant. Which of these is preferable in this verse?

* A student: Mercy in the sense of Paradise: ﴿yahdharu al-akhirah⦆, that is, he fears the punishment of the Hereafter, and hopes for Allah's mercy, meaning he fears the Fire and hopes for Paradise.

* The Shaykh: Yes, this is what the author adopted. But why do we not say: he hopes that Allah will show mercy to him, and the mercy meant here is Allah's mercy which is His act; that is, he hopes that Allah will show mercy to him in both respects, by salvation from the Fire and by entry into Paradise. This meaning is better, because what generally comes to mind from the word mercy is that it is Allah's act; that is, that Allah shows mercy to you.

Also, if we say "Allah's mercy," he hopes to be saved from the Fire, or from the punishment of the Hereafter, and to succeed in Paradise.

﴿Wa yarju rahmata rabbihi⦆: he said: (like one who is disobedient through disbelief or otherwise).

Through this estimation, may Allah have mercy on him, the author has informed us that in this verse Allah makes clear that this and that are not equal. Are those who are devoutly obedient during the night, prostrating and standing, equal to those who are disobedient through disbelief and otherwise?

The answer: No. And this is from the eloquence of the Qur'an: the Qur'an contains many things that are omitted, since the mentioned indicates the omitted, and this is from eloquence. How is it eloquence? Because when something is omitted, the addressee gains two benefits:

The first benefit: brevity of speech.

The second benefit: intensified attention, because when a verse contains something omitted, the mind looks forward to that omitted thing, so you find the person pausing, thinking, reflecting: what was omitted, and what is its estimate? But if the speech came without it, this pause and reflection would not occur. Now, if you recited the noble verse: ﴿Amman huwa qanit aana' al-layli sajidan wa qa'iman yahdharu al-akhirah wa yarju rahmata rabbihi. Qul hal yastawi alladhina﴾ [Az-Zumar 9], you would find yourself looking forward to what? To something else; the speech is not complete, there must be something else. Then your attention intensifies and your reflection on the meaning increases. So what is the aspect of eloquence?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: That is, brevity. And the second?

* The student: Focus.

* The Shaykh: What is focus?

* A student: Intensity of attention.

* The Shaykh: Yes, intensity of attention. How? The first, brevity, we understood clearly: removing something from speech requires less speech and briefer speech. But the second?

* The student: Because if the expression is short, it is easier for the addressee and more intense...

* The Shaykh: No.

* A student: That when something is omitted (...), whereas if the speech were complete (...) it would pass over him without full attention.

* The Shaykh: Because this omitted element is necessary, so the person looks forward: what is this omitted thing? The speech now is incomplete; that is, the speech needs something, so the person looks forward to knowing this thing, and then his contemplation increases. This is from the eloquence of the Qur'an. I mean that it is sometimes omitted: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, omits things the addressee needs, for this benefit, indeed for these two benefits.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (And in a reading: ﴿Am man﴾). What does this reading add to the first? (Am).

The author's saying "in a reading" (fi qira'ah) is part of the author's terminology: when he says "in a reading," or says "with fathah of such and such and dammah of such and such," or says "with ta' and ya'," the reading is canonical (sab'i). But when he says "wa qri'a" (it was recited), sometimes he expresses it as "wa qri'a," and the reading is shadh (irregular), not canonical. Take note of this terminology: when he mentions two equivalent readings, such as saying "in a reading," or with dammah and fathah, or with ya' and ta', and similar expressions, the reading is canonical; but when he says "wa qri'a" in the passive form, the reading is irregular.

Based on this rule, is the reading ﴿Am man﴾?

* Students: Canonical.

* The Shaykh: Canonical, because he said: (And in a reading ﴿Am man﴾, so "am" has the meaning of "bal" (rather) and the hamza). That is: rather, is it he who... rather, is it he who is devoutly obedient during the night. So it is for transition (idrab). And is this idrab here cancelling (ibtali) or transitional (intiqali)?

* A student: Transitional.

* The Shaykh: Transitional. Is it certain, everyone? It is certain that it is a transitional idrab. The difference between transitional and cancelling idrab is that in cancelling idrab the first is void and the reliance is on the second, whereas in transitional idrab the first remains as it is, and the second is a new statement with no connection to the first.

﴿Qul hal yastawi alladhina ya'lamuna wa alladhina la ya'lamun﴾ [Az-Zumar 9]: (Say) to whom? O Muhammad, or say, O whoever can be addressed.

﴿Hal yastawi alladhina ya'lamuna wa alladhina la ya'lamun﴾: an interrogative with the meaning of negation. ﴿Are those who know equal to those who do not know?⦆

The answer: No, those who know and those who do not know are not equal. This is general in every knowledge, so the knowledgeable and the ignorant are not equal, even in the knowledge of carpentry, blacksmithing, chemistry and others, the one who knows and the one who does not know are not equal. But this does not imply that the knower is praiseworthy, because among the sciences there are some whose ignorance is better than their knowledge. So if knowledge is blameworthy and we say "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?", then the non-knower is better. And if knowledge is praiseworthy and we say "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?", then the knower is better.

Now, if this word or this sentence comes in the science of the Sharia?

* Students: The knower is better.

* The Shaykh: The knower is better. In the science of grammar?

* Students: The knower is better.

* The Shaykh: Good. In the science of kalam (theology)?

* Students: The ignorant is better.

* The Shaykh: The ignorant is better, yes, as some of the early scholars said: ignorance of kalam is knowledge, because the knowledge of kalam led its people to destructions, to the extent that the great scholars of theirs, at the point of death, wish that they had died upon the religion of old women, and the religion of old women is safer, even if it is ignorance, than a knowledge that leads them, may Allah protect us, to doubt and bewilderment.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verse 8–9 (part 4 of 5):

* Among the benefits of this noble verse is the threat to those disbelievers who set up rivals besides Allah. It is taken from His saying: ﴿Say: "Enjoy your disbelief for a little while; indeed you are among the companions of the Fire."﴾ Allah, glorified and exalted, has explained the nature of this enjoyment when He said: ﴿And those who disbelieve enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat, and the Fire is their residence﴾ [Muhammad 12].
* Among the benefits of this verse: that the worldly life, however long it lasts, is little and cannot be compared to the Hereafter. For this reason Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And the Hereafter is better for you than the first [life]﴾ [al-Duha 4], addressing the Messenger ﷺ, and He says to people in general: ﴿Rather, you prefer the worldly life, while the Hereafter is better and more enduring﴾ [al-A'la 16–17]. The Prophet ﷺ also said: «The place of a whip of one of you in Paradise is better than the world and all that is in it»[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2892) from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi.]]. "The place of a whip": the whip is a short stick. "Better than the world and all that is in it": which world? All of it, from its beginning until the Hour, with its adornments, amusements and finery. For this reason He said: ﴿enjoy a little while﴾. So this enjoyment for the disbeliever, even if he attains his desire, is small in duration, small in quantity, and small in quality.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the disbelievers are constantly bound to the Fire and will not leave it. This is shown by His saying: ﴿companions of the Fire﴾, since the companion (ṣāḥib) is the one who remains constantly with something.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: addressing a person in a manner suited to his condition. This stubborn disbeliever, who has replaced Allah's blessing with disbelief, is addressed with this harsh address: ﴿Enjoy your disbelief for a little while; indeed you are among the companions of the Fire.﴾ Whereas if the matter were one of calling to the faith, we would not respond to him in this way. We do not say to one whom we invite to Islam: "Enjoy your disbelief for a little while; indeed you are among the companions of the Fire." Rather, we say this to one who is obstinate, arrogant, and has replaced Allah's blessing with disbelief.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the Fire, from His saying: ﴿indeed you are among the companions of the Fire﴾.
Regarding the affirmation of the Fire, two things are obligatory for us:
The first: affirming that it now exists and is present. The Prophet ﷺ was shown Paradise and the Fire during the prayer of the eclipse, and he witnessed them and saw those who are being punished in it. He saw in it a woman being punished because of a cat that she had imprisoned until it died, and he saw in it the owner of the hooked staff being punished[[Narrated by Muslim (904/10) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.]]. The owner of the hooked staff is a man who had a mihjan (hooked staff); do you know the mihjan?
* The students: A stick.
* The Shaykh: In our colloquial dialect it is called mihjan. A mihjan is a stick with a bent head. This man would pass by pilgrims and hook their belongings, the pilgrim's goods, with the head of the staff. If the owner of the goods noticed him, he would say: "By God, this is a hooked staff; hold on to it, excuse me," or he may not say it, though some people do say this. If the owner did not notice, he would take it. The Prophet ﷺ saw him being punished in the Fire with his hooked staff while he was performing the prayer of the eclipse. Then the Prophet ﷺ moved back, fearing that the blaze of the Fire might reach him. So his seeing it was a sensory seeing. This is one point.
The second: we must believe that the Fire is everlasting, forever and ever, its people being punished in it and not being brought out of it. It is eternal forever, because Allah, exalted, mentioned its eternity in three places in the Quran. The first place is in Surah al-Nisa, the second is in Surah al-Ahzab, and the third is in Surah al-Jinn. And the brother will show us the first place in Surah al-Ahzab.
* A student: The verse...
* The Shaykh: In Surah al-Nisa, I mean?
* The student: What?
* The Shaykh: That Allah mentioned that the Fire is everlasting.
* The student: I don't know.
* Another student: ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blaze﴾ [al-Ahzab 64].
* The Shaykh: No, in Surah al-Nisa.
* A student: After the verse of tayammum.
* Another student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: The saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits﴾ [al-Nisa 14].
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and do wrong, Allah will never forgive them, nor will He guide them to a path, except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Nisa 168–169].
* The Shaykh: Excellent, correct. This is explicit: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾.
The second place is in Surah al-Ahzab. Who?
* A student: The saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blaze (64), abiding therein forever; they will find no protector or helper﴾ [al-Ahzab 64–65].
* The Shaykh: Yes, ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blaze (64), abiding therein forever; they will find no protector or helper.﴾
The third place is in Surah al-Jinn?
* A student: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, then indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein﴾ [al-Jinn 23].
* The Shaykh: Where is the eternity?
* The student: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger⁠—﴾...
* The Shaykh: ﴿then indeed for him⁠—﴾...
* The student: ﴿then indeed for him is the fire of Hell⁠—﴾...
* The Shaykh: Yes, where is the eternity?
* The student: ﴿abiding therein forever.﴾
* The Shaykh: ﴿abiding therein forever,﴾ correct.
After this, we cannot accept a statement from any scholar who says that the Fire is not everlasting, nor do we set against this clear text any analogies. The saying of Allah, "Indeed My mercy precedes My wrath"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7422) and Muslim (2751/15), and the wording is al-Bukhari's, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]], is a sound, established text and a true report. But a report may be specified, so we say: the people of the Fire are not deserving of mercy, and Allah's punishment of them with eternity is part of the perfection of His justice and wisdom. Just as they spent their lives in disbelief, and spent all of the worldly life in disbelief, so the Hereafter also passes for them in recompense and punishment. This is justice and this is wisdom. Isn't that so?
We say: your entire life in this world passed in disbelief, so your life in the Hereafter passes in recompense and punishment. You will have no life in the Hereafter just as you had no life in this world through obedience to Allah.
Then Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing...﴾ to the end [al-Zumar 9].
* From the benefits of this verse: the noble Quran opens the way for a person to rational inference, meaning that it presents matters in a rational manner, by calling for reflection and understanding.
For example, one who is devoutly obedient and one who is disobedient: when the condition of this one and that one is presented to a rational person, what does he say? He says: they are not equal; the one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night is not like the disobedient one.
This is one of the methods that the student of knowledge should adopt in debate as a means to silence the opponent, because many opponents may not be convinced by textual evidence alone, so we present to them rational evidence, especially in the present time, when many people, if not most of them, have taken the path of Iblis as a way: opposing revelation with what they think is reason, meaning opposing the texts with what they assume to be reason. We know with certainty that there is nothing in the texts that contradicts clear reason at all; rather, there is in the texts what clear reason confirms, and each of them strengthens the other.
Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned in his Nuniyya that we have four evidences, each of which bears witness to the others: they are the Book, the Sunnah, reason, and natural disposition (fitrah). These four evidences cannot contradict or conflict; rather, some of them confirm and witness to others. And Allah knows best.
* A student: Regarding the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Or do you think that most of them hear or reason?﴾ [al-Furqan 44], does it indicate (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, there are among them those who hear and reason. Or does every disbeliever not hear or reason?
* The student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Some people whom Allah has blessed with guidance, when Allah bestows guidance upon them, they leave disbelief.
* The student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, that is, in the future; that is, ﴿they hear or reason﴾ [al-Furqan 44] in the future. It may be that Allah will bestow it upon them, but as long as they are in this state, they do not hear or reason. For this reason He said: ﴿They are only like cattle; rather, they are further astray in way﴾ [al-Furqan 44]. So the verse you mentioned agrees with this verse: the disbeliever has no hearing and no reason.
* A student: Was it not said about Shaykh al-Islam that he held the view that the Fire will perish?
* The Shaykh: That is not correct. And let us suppose that the one who said the Fire will perish, and far be it from him to do so, was Abu Bakr, a thousand times better than Shaykh al-Islam. Would we accept it in the presence of the verses? No, we would not accept it. In reality, when we find a statement that contradicts the Book and the Sunnah from any speaker, our position is to excuse him, not to make his statement a proof against the words of Allah and His Messenger, whoever he may be. Nobody is infallible, no one is protected from error except those whom Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has protected, such as the messengers.
* A student: Could we say that the reading ﴿li-yuḍilla﴾ is more eloquent than the reading ﴿li-yaḍilla﴾?
* The Shaykh: No, but we can say: he went astray, and so he led others astray. For he went astray, and then he led astray, so the combination of the two readings has a benefit that is not achieved by either one alone (...).
* * *
* A student: ﴿Say: O My servants who have believed, fear your Lord. For those who do good in this world there is good, and Allah's earth is spacious. Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account (10). Say: Indeed I have been commanded to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion (11). And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims (12). Say: Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous day (13). Say: It is Allah I worship, being sincere to Him in my religion (14). So worship what you will besides Him. Say: Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss﴾ [al-Zumar 10–15].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan.
Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord...﴾ to the end [al-Zumar 9].
* In this verse there is a clarification of the difference between people in the worship of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that there is no equality between one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, and so on, and one who is disobedient and far from Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
* Among the benefits of the verse: its apparent meaning is the continuity of obedience, "during the hours of the night" in prostration and standing, meaning in prayer. But the Sunnah has clarified this, and that the best of night prayer is to sleep half of the night, pray one third, and sleep one sixth. This is restricting the Quran by the Sunnah.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the virtue of night prayer, from His saying: ﴿during the hours of the night﴾. The Sunnah has also indicated this, as the Prophet ﷺ said: «The best prayer after the obligatory prayer is the night prayer»[[Narrated by Muslim (1163/202) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].
* Among the benefits of this verse: the virtue of standing and prostration among the pillars of prayer. We have explained the reason for this during the commentary: standing is noble because of its mention, and prostration is noble because of its form.
* Among the benefits of the verse: that a person should, in his journey to Allah, combine fear and hope; from His saying: ﴿fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord﴾.
But should these two be equal, or should the side of hope be given precedence, or the side of fear?
On this there are statements from the people of spiritual conduct (arbab al-suluk). Some of them said: a person's hope and fear should be equal, like the two wings of a bird: if one of them tilts, its flight is disturbed. Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: one's fear and hope should be equal; whichever prevails, its counterpart is destroyed, because if the side of fear prevails it leads him to despair and hopelessness, and if the side of hope prevails it leads him to feel secure from Allah's plan.
Some people of spiritual conduct said: the side of hope should be given precedence, based on Allah's saying in the Hadith Qudsi: «I am as My servant thinks of Me; if he thinks well of Me, then it is for him, and if he thinks ill of Me, then it is for him»[[Narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (9076) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, and its origin is in the two Sahihs.]]. Accordingly, the side of hope is given precedence.
Some scholars said: when performing acts of obedience, the side of hope should be given precedence, so when one performs an act of obedience, he should give precedence to the expectation of acceptance over the expectation of rejection. But in committing a sin, it is better to give precedence to the side of fear, so as not to fall into the sin.
Some of them said: in a state of illness, the side of hope is given precedence, and in a state of health, the side of fear is given precedence, because the Prophet ﷺ said: «None of you should die except while thinking well of Allah»[[Narrated by Muslim (2877/81) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.]]. The sick person has the cause of death present in him, which is the illness, so the side of hope is given precedence, so that he dies while thinking well of Allah.
If someone said: this is referred back to the person himself, and a person is the physician of his own soul; if he sees in himself an inclination toward committing sins and prohibited acts, then let him admonish it, indeed let him threaten it with punishment until it refrains, and if he sees in himself strength to obey Allah, persistence in it, and standing in it, then let him give precedence to the side of hope until he thinks well of Allah. This is referred back to the person himself, and at times a person gives precedence to one of these and at other times to the other.
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, that is, if this were said, it would be better.
* From the benefits of the verses: the affirmation of the punishment of the Hereafter, from His saying: ﴿fearing the Hereafter﴾. Something is only feared when its existence is established; what is not established is not feared.
* Among the benefits of the verse: that in matters of recompense and rulings, the aspect of lordship (rububiyyah) is given precedence, from His saying: ﴿and hoping for the mercy of his Lord﴾, because lordship is that by which disposal and authority are exercised.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that those who know and those who do not know are not equal, from His saying: ﴿Say: Are those who know and those who do not know equal?﴾
* Among its benefits: that this negation is an acknowledged matter, since it came in the form of a question. We have mentioned that when a question is intended to negate, it carries the meaning of a challenge.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the virtue of knowledge.

But it must be known that knowledge is honored according to the honor of its subject. On this basis, the best of the sciences is the knowledge of Allah's Names and Attributes, because this is the most noble subject of knowledge. Then comes knowledge of His rulings, "Whomever Allah intends good for, He grants him understanding of the religion" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (71) and Muslim (1037 / 98), from the hadith of Mu'awiyah]. Then the other sciences follow according to their ranks. The most base of the sciences are those that turn people away from the path of Allah and the way of the pious predecessors (al-salaf al-salih), such as the science of philosophy (falsafah), kalam (scholastic theology), and what resembles them. However, if a person learns them in order to refute their adherents with them, then learning them may at that point be obligatory, because whatever an obligation cannot be fulfilled without is itself obligatory. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded Zayd ibn Thabit (may Allah be pleased with him) to learn the language of the Jews [narrated by al-Bukhari (7195) from the hadith of Zayd ibn Thabit], even though learning foreign languages is not in itself praiseworthy nor enjoined. But since it was a means to knowing what writings came from the Jews and to responding to them in their own language, the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered him to learn the language of the Jews. Zayd learned the language of the Jews within sixteen days, because Zayd ibn Thabit (may Allah be pleased with him) was among the intelligent people, so he learned it. Moreover, the Hebrew language is close to the Arabic language, so learning it was easy.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that people of intellect are the ones who take admonition, based on His saying: ﴿Only those of understanding remember﴾.

* And among its benefits: that whoever does not remember is deficient in intellect, because if only people of understanding remember, then whoever does not remember is, without doubt, deficient in intellect, and the deficiency of his intellect is in proportion to his deficiency in remembrance.

The rational basis for this, from a theoretical standpoint, is that a sensible person cannot choose for himself except what brings salvation, and there is no salvation from the punishment of Allah except through remembrance and taking admonition. Therefore, sound intellect necessitates that a person remember and take admonition in order to seek what is most beneficial and advantageous for the soul: ﴿And the Hereafter is better for you than the first [life]﴾ [al-Duha 4].

* And among the benefits of the verse: praise of those endowed with intellect, in that He made them the ones who remember, take admonition, and benefit from what they hear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verse 8–9 (part 1 of 5):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance﴾ [az-Zumar 8].
﴿When it touches﴾ means: when it reaches him.
And as for ﴿man﴾, the author says: the intended meaning is (the disbeliever).
This general term was made specific because of the apparent context of the verse, as will become clear; otherwise the basic principle is that "man" (al-insan) is one of the words of generality. The "al" in it is for the comprehensiveness of the category, and the sign of the "al" that denotes comprehensiveness is that it can be replaced by (kull), i.e., "every person."
But the author, may Allah have mercy on him, made it a general term by which a specific meaning is intended, by the indication of the context, for the context shows that what is meant is the disbeliever, since what the context describes cannot apply to a believer.
﴿When harm touches man﴾: ﴿harm﴾ is an indefinite noun in a conditional context, so it is general; i.e., any harm that may occur, to his body, his family, his wealth, whether great or small, any harm that may occur falls under the phrase ﴿harm﴾.
﴿He calls upon his Lord﴾: note His saying ﴿calls upon his Lord﴾ and not "calls upon Allah." In this state, i.e., at the onset of harm, he recognizes his Lord, and that there is no refuge from it except in Him, so he calls upon his Lord, believing Him to be his Lord who owns whatever He wills and disposes of whatever He wills.
The author said: (tadarra'a, "humbly beseeches"), meaning he explained ﴿calls upon﴾ as meaning (tadarra'a), based on the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾ [al-A'raf 55]. Tadarru' is submission and abasement before Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
(﴿turning﴾ returning ﴿to Him﴾) So when he calls upon his Lord turning to Him, Allah removes his harm, because He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿Is not He who responds to the distressed one when he calls upon Him, and removes evil, and makes you successors on the earth?﴾ [an-Naml 62].
Allah's responding to the distressed one includes both the disbeliever and the Muslim, even the disbeliever whom Allah knows will disbelieve after his distress is lifted: He answers his supplication. ﴿And when they board ships, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion; but when He delivers them to the land, immediately they associate others with Him﴾ [al-'Ankabut 65]. He, Mighty and Majestic, knows that they will associate others with Him after deliverance, yet He answers them, because His mercy precedes His wrath. In a state of necessity the turning of man to his Lord is true, because he knows that none removes harm except Allah. So when he returns to his Lord, glorified and exalted, His mercy precedes His wrath, and He answers him out of mercy toward him.
Here the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Then when He bestows upon him a favor from Himself﴾ to the end [az-Zumar 8].
He said: ﴿Then when He bestows﴾ meaning, as if this, and Allah knows best, is an indication that after he is overwhelmed by blessing and continues in it for a time, he then disbelieves.
And His saying: ﴿when He bestows upon him a favor﴾. He said: (a'taahu, "gave him") is an explanation of ﴿bestows﴾.
(in'aaman, "a bestowal") is an explanation of ﴿a favor﴾.
As for explaining ﴿bestows﴾ as (a'taahu), it is clear; but explaining ﴿a favor﴾ as (in'aam, "bestowal") has no basis, because what is given is not the bestowal but the favor. Accordingly, leaving the verse on its apparent meaning is better than what the author, may Allah have mercy on him, adopted.
If we take it as "a bestowal," the sentence does not stand. Why? Because bestowal is an act of Allah, whereas what is given is the favor, not the act of Allah. So leaving the verse on its apparent meaning is without doubt the one that agrees with reality.
He says: ﴿Then when He bestows upon him a favor from Himself﴾. ﴿From Himself﴾: the (min) here is for origin; i.e., a favor proceeding from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by which it becomes clear that it is pure grace from Allah.
(﴿forgets﴾ abandons ﴿what he used to call upon﴾, supplicate humbly ﴿to Him before﴾, and that is Allah.) Look, my brother: he used to humbly beseech Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that He remove the harm from him; Allah removed the harm from him and gave him a favor beyond the removal of harm. What then is his state?
He said: ﴿forgets what he used to call upon Him for before﴾. Forgetting here means heedlessness, not the forgetfulness of the heart; what is meant is heedlessness that implies abandonment. Among its examples is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So woe to those who pray, who are heedless of their prayer﴾ [al-Ma'un 4-5], i.e., heedless of their prayer.
﴿forgets what he used to call upon Him for before﴾: he says (﴿what he used to call upon﴾ humbly beseech ﴿Him for before﴾).
The pronoun ﴿Him﴾ refers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
And ﴿what﴾ refers to Allah. For this reason the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (fa-"ma" is in the place of "man"). The "ma" in His saying ﴿what he used to call upon﴾ is in the place of "man." The author's intent is that "ma" means "man," i.e., he forgot whom he used to call upon before, meaning whom he used to direct supplication to, or as the author said: (humbly beseeches Him, who is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic), so he became heedless, and "ma" is as if Allah had bestowed upon him the removal of harm and the granting of favor.
﴿He forgets what he used to call upon Him for before, and sets up rivals to Allah﴾ [az-Zumar 8].
The rivals are those he became heedless of, while the One, the Subduer, he became heedless of, may Allah protect us, even though the rivals did not benefit him and he did not humbly beseech them when harm touched him; yet he turns to them and abandons the One who bestowed favor upon him.
﴿and sets up rivals to Allah﴾ (partners).
Andad is the plural of nid, and the nid is the equal who rivals his counterpart, the like of him. So he sets up rivals to Allah in what? In worship: he worships these idols as he worships Allah, vows to them as he vows to Allah, sacrifices to them as he sacrifices to Allah, and so on.
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿so that he may lead astray from His way﴾ (with the yā' vocalized with fatḥa or ḍamma) ﴿from His way﴾ (the religion of Islam).
﴿rivals so that he may lead astray﴾: this lām is either for causation (ta'līl) or for consequence (ʿāqiba). On the reading with fatḥa, ﴿li-yaḍilla﴾, the lām is for consequence, meaning that by setting up rivals to Allah he ends in misguidance. If the yā' is vocalized with ḍamma, ﴿li-yuḍilla﴾, the lām is for causation, meaning that he set up rivals to Allah so that others would follow him and go astray. The verse has two readings: ﴿yaḍilla﴾ and ﴿yuḍilla﴾; ﴿yaḍilla﴾ refers to himself and ﴿yuḍilla﴾ refers to others. Both readings are sound, or both are sound, and each conveys a meaning that completes the other: he goes astray himself and also leads others astray. We said the lām is for consequence; when? On which reading?
* Students: ﴿li-yaḍilla﴾.
* The Shaykh: On the fatḥa reading; meaning that when he takes rivals, his end is misguidance. And for causation, on which of the two readings?
* Students: The ḍamma.
* The Shaykh: On ḍamma; meaning he set up rivals to Allah so that he would be followed and others would go astray.

Does the lām for consequence occur in the Arabic language? Yes, it occurs. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas 8]. Did the family of Pharaoh pick up Moses so that he might become their enemy and grief? Never. They said: ﴿Perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son﴾ [al-Qasas 9], but the outcome was that he became an enemy and a grief.
And the lām may occur as an extra particle (za'ida), as in His saying: ﴿Allah only intends to remove from you the uncleanness﴾ [al-Ahzab 33]: ﴿Allah only intends to remove from you﴾, i.e., to remove. And as in His saying: ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ [an-Nisa 26]: ﴿Allah desires to make clear﴾, i.e., to make clear. They said it is extra because (arada, "desire") takes its object directly, not with the lām, and it cannot be for causation, since causation is already derived from the act of desiring. Accordingly, they parse it as extra. Thus it becomes clear that the lām that enters the imperfect verb may be extra, causative (which is the most common), or consequential.

* The Shaykh: Yes, correct.

* The Shaykh: Well done. He is pleased that the disbeliever should submit, but He did not will that he submit; so here..
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That is it. This is the point: there is no necessary connection, since pleasure may exist without will, will may exist without pleasure, and pleasure and will may both exist.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What does Allah be pleased with from the disbeliever? That he submit. He is not pleased with disbelief; Allah is not pleased with disbelief. He is pleased with gratitude, so He is pleased that this disbeliever be grateful and believe. But did Allah will that he be grateful and believe? If Allah had willed it, it would have happened.
* A student: O Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, O Shaykh, how do we reconcile ﴿and no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾ [az-Zumar 7] with what is reported: "The dead person is punished by the weeping of his family over him"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1290), Muslim (927/19), from Ibn 'Umar.]]?
* The Shaykh: Yes, this is also correct, and it should be raised against the verse. It is established from the Messenger ﷺ that "the dead person is punished by the weeping of his family over him." 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "The intended meaning is the disbeliever."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1288), Muslim (929).]] Without doubt she, may Allah be pleased with her, was a human who errs and is correct, because the disbeliever is punished whether or not his family weep over him. But she wanted to say that the meaning of the hadith is that the disbeliever is punished while his family weep over him; she made this the meaning of the hadith and cited the verse as evidence.
But we say: this interpretation does not stand. Rather the meaning of the verse is that the punishment intended is psychological suffering, not physical suffering. A parallel to this is the Messenger ﷺ's saying: "Travel is a piece of punishment"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1804), Muslim (1927/179), from Abu Hurayrah.]], though the traveler is not physically tormented. He may be among the most pleasant of situations when the land is fertile, the camels good, and the companions friends; what is travel then? Recreation. Yet it is still a piece of punishment of the heart, is it not?
We in the airplane are comfortable, air-conditioned, warm in winter and cool in summer, drinking coffee and juice, eating dates, and whatever we ask for comes; yet the heart is pained, unlike a person settled in his house. So the punishment in the grave is this kind of punishment.
Some scholars said: he is punished with physical punishment, a bodily penalty, but this applies to one who instructed his family to wail over him, though this is not mentioned in the hadith; the hadith is taken to mean what other texts require.
Some of them said: this applies to a man whose family he knows will wail over him and he does not forbid them. The difference between this view and the previous one is clear: the previous one instructed them, while this one did not forbid them; he did not instruct them but knew they would do it and did not forbid them. So these are four views on the hadith, and the soundest is that the intended punishment is psychological punishment, not physical punishment, because of His saying: ﴿and no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾ [az-Zumar 7].

* A student: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord? * The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance﴾ [az-Zumar 8]. Who is meant by "man" here?
* A student: The disbeliever.
* The Shaykh: The disbeliever. Why do we not take it in its general sense, as we took His saying ﴿and man was created weak﴾ [an-Nisa 28] in its general sense?

Is it permissible in Arabic for a general term to be used to mean a specific one?
* A student: Yes, much.
* The Shaykh: Much. Is there anything from beyond this verse?
* A student: His saying: ﴿Those to whom people said, "Indeed the people have gathered against you, so fear them"﴾ [Al 'Imran 173].
* The Shaykh: His saying ﴿those to whom people said, "Indeed the people have gathered against you"﴾: the first "people" is one man, and the second is a group of people, not all people.
His saying: ﴿Then when He bestows upon him a favor from Himself﴾ [az-Zumar 8]: what is the meaning of (khawwalahu)?
* A student: He gave him.
* The Shaykh: He gave him. And from it His saying: ﴿and you have left what We bestowed upon you﴾ [al-An'am 94]. A favor?

* The Shaykh: The correct view is better than your saying "this is wrong." The correct view is that the meaning is "He gave him a favor," because He bestowed upon him the thing bestowed, not the bestowal; the bestowal is an act of Allah.
His saying: ﴿and sets up rivals to Allah so that he may lead astray﴾ [az-Zumar 8]: are there two readings?
* A student: With fatḥa on the yā', and with ḍamma on the yā', with ḍamma and fatḥa.
* The Shaykh: Recite them.
* The student: ﴿li-yuḍilla﴾ and ﴿li-yaḍilla﴾.
* The Shaykh: Yes, well done.
What is the meaning of the lām on both readings?
* The student: With fatḥa on the yā' it is for consequence; with ḍamma on the yā' it is...
* The Shaykh: For causation.
Our brother has explained that the lām entering the imperfect is for consequence and for causation, as in this verse. Does it have a third meaning? Come on, brother, we think you are a grammarian.

* The Shaykh: Extra; like what?

* The Shaykh: No, the one that enters the imperfect is not the lām that enters the noun.

* The Shaykh: Yes, it comes extra, but we want the example now.

* The Shaykh: Extra. Why? Because desire indicates its own meaning; if Allah the Mighty and Majestic said "Allah desires that He make clear to you," it would be correct.

Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Say: Enjoy your disbelief for a little﴾ [az-Zumar 8]. We stopped at (yuḍilla)?
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿so that he may lead astray from His way﴾ or ﴿so that he may go astray from His way﴾ [az-Zumar 8]. ﴿His way﴾ means His religion, i.e., His path that leads to Him; the path of Allah that leads to Him: this is the way of Allah.
The "way" is attributed to Allah at times, as in this verse and many others, and attributed to a created being, as in His saying: ﴿Say: This is my way; I call to Allah﴾ [Yusuf 108]. So what is the reconciliation between them?
The reconciliation is that it is attributed to Allah in that He is the one who established it and it leads to Him; and it is attributed to other than Allah, to the created being, in that he is the one who walks it.
So "the way of Allah" means He is the one who legislated this way and set it for the servants, and it leads to Allah. The way of the Messenger, ﴿This is my way; I call to Allah﴾ [Yusuf 108], means my path that I walk. The same is said of the path: ﴿the path of Allah﴾ [ash-Shura 53] and ﴿the path of those You have blessed﴾ [al-Fatihah 7]. The path of Allah is so called because He is the one who established it and it leads to Him, and ﴿the path of those You have blessed﴾ is so called because they are the ones who walk it.
As for His saying ﴿so that he may lead astray from His way﴾, the author said: (the religion of Islam). This is an explanation of the word according to its intended meaning, because the explanation of the Qur'an is sometimes a verbal explanation and sometimes a explanation of meaning.
Verbal explanation: explaining the word by its literal equivalent. Explanation of meaning: explaining the word by what is intended by it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verse 8–9 (part 2 of 5):

For example: the religion of Islam does not correspond to the literal meaning of "sabil" (path), because "sabil" linguistically means "road." If someone were asked to explain "sabil," you would say: it means "tariq" (road).

But the "sabil" intended here is the religion of Islam, because the religion of Islam, which is the laws of Islam, leads to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the One who established it is Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

So, does the author explain "sabil" here by its literal meaning or by its intended meaning? That is, that what is meant by it is such and such.

As for his saying "the religion of Islam," it is clear that it is the path of Allah, because Allah is the One who legislated it, glorified and exalted be He; and because whoever follows it is led to Allah.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: "Enjoy your disbelief for a little while (the remainder of your term); indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire."﴾ [Az-Zumar 8] I seek refuge in Allah.

"Say" is addressed to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and it may also be addressed to everyone who can be addressed; that is: say, O human, to this disbeliever or to this person described with these attributes: ﴿Enjoy your disbelief for a little while.﴾

﴿Enjoy your disbelief for a little while⦆ is an imperative, but it is not on its apparent meaning; rather the imperative here is intended as a threat, like His saying: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [Al-Kahf 29]. It is known that a person does not have the choice between faith and disbelief, but this is by way of threat.

So here, ﴿Enjoy your disbelief for a little while﴾ does not mean that We permit him to enjoy disbelief, or command him to enjoy his disbelief; rather We threaten him, so the imperative here is for threat.

If someone asks: what removed it from its original meaning?

The answer: what removed it from its original meaning is the context: ﴿Say: Enjoy your disbelief﴾, meaning: disbelieve and enjoy disbelief, because the disbeliever enjoys his disbelief like cattle enjoy themselves, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those who disbelieve enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat, and the Fire is their residence﴾ [Muhammad 12]. The disbeliever, may Allah protect us, does not bind himself to any act of worship: not prayer, nor zakat, nor fasting, nor Hajj, nor any other acts of worship. Rather he follows his desire and enjoys himself as a donkey enjoys itself. In the end He said: ﴿Indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire﴾, like His saying: ﴿they enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat, and the Fire is their residence﴾ [Muhammad 12]. How quickly he arrives at the Fire! For the worldly life is little, that is, a short time. However long your life is, when your appointed term comes, it will be as though you had not remained except an hour of a day. If you want to verify this, consider what has passed of your life against what remains. Consider what has passed. Now, each of us differs from the other in age, but each of us is as though born this very hour; that is, all that has passed is as though it had never been. Likewise the remainder of life, however long a person's life may be, when his term comes it is as though it had not been. For this reason He said: ﴿Enjoy your disbelief for a little while⦆, even if your life is long; he says: (the remainder of your term).

﴿Indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire﴾ [Az-Zumar 8]: this sentence is emphasized with "inna," meaning: however much you enjoy yourself, your end is the Fire: ﴿indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire﴾. And "companions of the Fire" is used only of those who will abide in it forever. The sinful believer, although he deserves punishment in the Fire, is not called one of the companions of the Fire, because the basic meaning of companionship is long continuous association. This is the basic principle of companionship, long continuous association, except in one matter. What is it?

* Students: The Companions (al-Sahaba).

* The Shaykh: Who? The Companions, the Companions of the Messenger ﷺ. If someone met the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while believing in him, even for a moment, he became one of his companions.

He says: ﴿Indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire﴾. The Fire is the abode that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, prepared for the disbelievers. Allah has explained in the Book, and His Messenger ﷺ has explained in the Sunnah, the kinds of punishment in it: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Our signs, We will surely drive them into a Fire. Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins that they may taste the punishment. Indeed, Allah is ever Exalted in Might and Wise﴾ [An-Nisa 56]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqum, the food of the sinful, like murky oil, boils in the bellies like the boiling of scalding water. Seize him and drag him into the midst of the Blazing Fire. Then pour over his head the torment of scalding water. Taste! Indeed, you were the mighty, the honorable﴾ [Ad-Dukhan 43–49]. I seek refuge in Allah. "Pour over his head the torment of scalding water": the water that is extremely hot. "Taste! Indeed, you were the mighty, the honorable" is said in mockery of him: where is your might, and where is your honor? In the worldly life he saw himself as a noble lord, but in the Hereafter he is humiliated with this humiliation.

The point is: the kinds of punishment in the Fire, may Allah protect us, if a person imagines them, becomes clear to him how severe is what these people encounter of severe punishment. We seek refuge in Allah from the Fire, we seek refuge in Allah from the Fire, we seek refuge in Allah from the Fire.

He, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during periods of the night, prostrating and standing...﴾ to the end [Az-Zumar 9].

﴿Amman huwa﴾: he said: (﴿Amman﴾ with the mim lightened). So the word is composed of the interrogative hamza and "man," the interrogative "man." He says: rather, "man" is the relative pronoun: the hamza of interrogation and the relative "man," meaning: is the one who is devoutly obedient, to the end.

(﴿huwa qanit﴾: standing in the performance of acts of obedience.) Qunut is used with several meanings:

Among them: humility, as in His saying: ﴿And stand before Allah in devout obedience﴾ [Al-Baqarah 238].

Among them: supplication in the witr or in obligatory prayers during calamities.

Among them: constancy in obedience, as in His saying: ﴿And she believed in the words of her Lord and His scriptures, and she was among the devoutly obedient﴾ [At-Tahrim 12].

An example of the first: ﴿Guard the prayers and the middle prayer, and stand before Allah in devout obedience﴾ [Al-Baqarah 238], meaning: humbly submissive. For this reason, when this verse was revealed, the Companions were commanded to be silent and forbidden to speak.

So here, ﴿qanit﴾ is in which of the three meanings?

* A student: Constancy in obedience.

* The Shaykh: Constancy in obedience. ﴿Amman huwa qanit﴾ [Az-Zumar 9]. The author said: (standing in the performance of acts of obedience), meaning persisting in them.

(﴿Aana' al-layl﴾: its hours. ﴿Sajidan wa qa'iman﴾: in prayer.)

﴿Sajidan wa qa'iman﴾: the text specifies prostration and standing, but not bowing or sitting, because prostration is noble in its posture and standing is noble in its remembrance. How?

Prostration is noble in its posture: the best posture of the one praying is to be prostrating; for this reason the servant is closest to his Lord when he is prostrating.

Standing is noble in its remembrance: what is its remembrance? The Qur'an, which is the speech of Allah, and the speech of Allah the Exalted is the noblest speech. Therefore He specified these two matters, or these two pillars of the pillars of prayer: standing and prostration. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, when he prostrated, there was a sound from his chest like the boiling of a cauldron (Abu Dawud? — recorded in al-Musnad (16312) and al-Nasa'i in al-Mujtaba (1214) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn al-Shikhkhir). And the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, when he stood, did not pass a verse of mercy without asking, nor a verse of punishment without seeking refuge, nor a verse of glorification without glorifying (recorded by Abu Dawud (873), al-Nasa'i in al-Mujtaba (1132), and Ahmad in al-Musnad (23980) from the hadith of Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i). This indicates that one who stands in prayer at night should observe this: observe the intensity of humility in prostration and weeping, and also observe presence of heart during recitation, so that when he passes a verse of mercy he asks, a verse of punishment he seeks refuge, a verse of glorification he glorifies, standing, sitting, prostrating and standing.

(﴿Yahdharu al-akhirah﴾: he fears its punishment. ﴿Wa yarju rahmata rabbihi﴾: Paradise, ﴿his Lord﴾.)

Here his saying: ﴿yahdharu al-akhirah⦆ is a circumstantial clause, the state of his fearing the Hereafter, in conjunction with ﴿sajidan wa qa'iman﴾, meaning: while he is in his prostration and standing, he fears the Hereafter; that is, he fears it, not fears its occurrence, since its occurrence is certain, but fears its punishment, fears that he will be punished.

﴿Wa yarju rahmata rabbihi⦆: the author says: His Paradise. There is no doubt that mercy here is intended as Paradise, as Allah said to Paradise: "You are My mercy; I show mercy through you to whom I will" (Bukhari (4850), Muslim (2846/36) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah).

But mercy may also be understood in another sense, namely Allah's act toward the servant, that is, His mercy to the servant. Which of these is preferable in this verse?

* A student: Mercy in the sense of Paradise: ﴿yahdharu al-akhirah⦆, that is, he fears the punishment of the Hereafter, and hopes for Allah's mercy, meaning he fears the Fire and hopes for Paradise.

* The Shaykh: Yes, this is what the author adopted. But why do we not say: he hopes that Allah will show mercy to him, and the mercy meant here is Allah's mercy which is His act; that is, he hopes that Allah will show mercy to him in both respects, by salvation from the Fire and by entry into Paradise. This meaning is better, because what generally comes to mind from the word mercy is that it is Allah's act; that is, that Allah shows mercy to you.

Also, if we say "Allah's mercy," he hopes to be saved from the Fire, or from the punishment of the Hereafter, and to succeed in Paradise.

﴿Wa yarju rahmata rabbihi⦆: he said: (like one who is disobedient through disbelief or otherwise).

Through this estimation, may Allah have mercy on him, the author has informed us that in this verse Allah makes clear that this and that are not equal. Are those who are devoutly obedient during the night, prostrating and standing, equal to those who are disobedient through disbelief and otherwise?

The answer: No. And this is from the eloquence of the Qur'an: the Qur'an contains many things that are omitted, since the mentioned indicates the omitted, and this is from eloquence. How is it eloquence? Because when something is omitted, the addressee gains two benefits:

The first benefit: brevity of speech.

The second benefit: intensified attention, because when a verse contains something omitted, the mind looks forward to that omitted thing, so you find the person pausing, thinking, reflecting: what was omitted, and what is its estimate? But if the speech came without it, this pause and reflection would not occur. Now, if you recited the noble verse: ﴿Amman huwa qanit aana' al-layli sajidan wa qa'iman yahdharu al-akhirah wa yarju rahmata rabbihi. Qul hal yastawi alladhina﴾ [Az-Zumar 9], you would find yourself looking forward to what? To something else; the speech is not complete, there must be something else. Then your attention intensifies and your reflection on the meaning increases. So what is the aspect of eloquence?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: That is, brevity. And the second?

* The student: Focus.

* The Shaykh: What is focus?

* A student: Intensity of attention.

* The Shaykh: Yes, intensity of attention. How? The first, brevity, we understood clearly: removing something from speech requires less speech and briefer speech. But the second?

* The student: Because if the expression is short, it is easier for the addressee and more intense...

* The Shaykh: No.

* A student: That when something is omitted (...), whereas if the speech were complete (...) it would pass over him without full attention.

* The Shaykh: Because this omitted element is necessary, so the person looks forward: what is this omitted thing? The speech now is incomplete; that is, the speech needs something, so the person looks forward to knowing this thing, and then his contemplation increases. This is from the eloquence of the Qur'an. I mean that it is sometimes omitted: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, omits things the addressee needs, for this benefit, indeed for these two benefits.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (And in a reading: ﴿Am man﴾). What does this reading add to the first? (Am).

The author's saying "in a reading" (fi qira'ah) is part of the author's terminology: when he says "in a reading," or says "with fathah of such and such and dammah of such and such," or says "with ta' and ya'," the reading is canonical (sab'i). But when he says "wa qri'a" (it was recited), sometimes he expresses it as "wa qri'a," and the reading is shadh (irregular), not canonical. Take note of this terminology: when he mentions two equivalent readings, such as saying "in a reading," or with dammah and fathah, or with ya' and ta', and similar expressions, the reading is canonical; but when he says "wa qri'a" in the passive form, the reading is irregular.

Based on this rule, is the reading ﴿Am man﴾?

* Students: Canonical.

* The Shaykh: Canonical, because he said: (And in a reading ﴿Am man﴾, so "am" has the meaning of "bal" (rather) and the hamza). That is: rather, is it he who... rather, is it he who is devoutly obedient during the night. So it is for transition (idrab). And is this idrab here cancelling (ibtali) or transitional (intiqali)?

* A student: Transitional.

* The Shaykh: Transitional. Is it certain, everyone? It is certain that it is a transitional idrab. The difference between transitional and cancelling idrab is that in cancelling idrab the first is void and the reliance is on the second, whereas in transitional idrab the first remains as it is, and the second is a new statement with no connection to the first.

﴿Qul hal yastawi alladhina ya'lamuna wa alladhina la ya'lamun﴾ [Az-Zumar 9]: (Say) to whom? O Muhammad, or say, O whoever can be addressed.

﴿Hal yastawi alladhina ya'lamuna wa alladhina la ya'lamun﴾: an interrogative with the meaning of negation. ﴿Are those who know equal to those who do not know?⦆

The answer: No, those who know and those who do not know are not equal. This is general in every knowledge, so the knowledgeable and the ignorant are not equal, even in the knowledge of carpentry, blacksmithing, chemistry and others, the one who knows and the one who does not know are not equal. But this does not imply that the knower is praiseworthy, because among the sciences there are some whose ignorance is better than their knowledge. So if knowledge is blameworthy and we say "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?", then the non-knower is better. And if knowledge is praiseworthy and we say "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?", then the knower is better.

Now, if this word or this sentence comes in the science of the Sharia?

* Students: The knower is better.

* The Shaykh: The knower is better. In the science of grammar?

* Students: The knower is better.

* The Shaykh: Good. In the science of kalam (theology)?

* Students: The ignorant is better.

* The Shaykh: The ignorant is better, yes, as some of the early scholars said: ignorance of kalam is knowledge, because the knowledge of kalam led its people to destructions, to the extent that the great scholars of theirs, at the point of death, wish that they had died upon the religion of old women, and the religion of old women is safer, even if it is ignorance, than a knowledge that leads them, may Allah protect us, to doubt and bewilderment.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verse 8–9 (part 4 of 5):

* Among the benefits of this noble verse is the threat to those disbelievers who set up rivals besides Allah. It is taken from His saying: ﴿Say: "Enjoy your disbelief for a little while; indeed you are among the companions of the Fire."﴾ Allah, glorified and exalted, has explained the nature of this enjoyment when He said: ﴿And those who disbelieve enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat, and the Fire is their residence﴾ [Muhammad 12].
* Among the benefits of this verse: that the worldly life, however long it lasts, is little and cannot be compared to the Hereafter. For this reason Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And the Hereafter is better for you than the first [life]﴾ [al-Duha 4], addressing the Messenger ﷺ, and He says to people in general: ﴿Rather, you prefer the worldly life, while the Hereafter is better and more enduring﴾ [al-A'la 16–17]. The Prophet ﷺ also said: «The place of a whip of one of you in Paradise is better than the world and all that is in it»[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2892) from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi.]]. "The place of a whip": the whip is a short stick. "Better than the world and all that is in it": which world? All of it, from its beginning until the Hour, with its adornments, amusements and finery. For this reason He said: ﴿enjoy a little while﴾. So this enjoyment for the disbeliever, even if he attains his desire, is small in duration, small in quantity, and small in quality.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the disbelievers are constantly bound to the Fire and will not leave it. This is shown by His saying: ﴿companions of the Fire﴾, since the companion (ṣāḥib) is the one who remains constantly with something.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: addressing a person in a manner suited to his condition. This stubborn disbeliever, who has replaced Allah's blessing with disbelief, is addressed with this harsh address: ﴿Enjoy your disbelief for a little while; indeed you are among the companions of the Fire.﴾ Whereas if the matter were one of calling to the faith, we would not respond to him in this way. We do not say to one whom we invite to Islam: "Enjoy your disbelief for a little while; indeed you are among the companions of the Fire." Rather, we say this to one who is obstinate, arrogant, and has replaced Allah's blessing with disbelief.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the Fire, from His saying: ﴿indeed you are among the companions of the Fire﴾.
Regarding the affirmation of the Fire, two things are obligatory for us:
The first: affirming that it now exists and is present. The Prophet ﷺ was shown Paradise and the Fire during the prayer of the eclipse, and he witnessed them and saw those who are being punished in it. He saw in it a woman being punished because of a cat that she had imprisoned until it died, and he saw in it the owner of the hooked staff being punished[[Narrated by Muslim (904/10) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.]]. The owner of the hooked staff is a man who had a mihjan (hooked staff); do you know the mihjan?
* The students: A stick.
* The Shaykh: In our colloquial dialect it is called mihjan. A mihjan is a stick with a bent head. This man would pass by pilgrims and hook their belongings, the pilgrim's goods, with the head of the staff. If the owner of the goods noticed him, he would say: "By God, this is a hooked staff; hold on to it, excuse me," or he may not say it, though some people do say this. If the owner did not notice, he would take it. The Prophet ﷺ saw him being punished in the Fire with his hooked staff while he was performing the prayer of the eclipse. Then the Prophet ﷺ moved back, fearing that the blaze of the Fire might reach him. So his seeing it was a sensory seeing. This is one point.
The second: we must believe that the Fire is everlasting, forever and ever, its people being punished in it and not being brought out of it. It is eternal forever, because Allah, exalted, mentioned its eternity in three places in the Quran. The first place is in Surah al-Nisa, the second is in Surah al-Ahzab, and the third is in Surah al-Jinn. And the brother will show us the first place in Surah al-Ahzab.
* A student: The verse...
* The Shaykh: In Surah al-Nisa, I mean?
* The student: What?
* The Shaykh: That Allah mentioned that the Fire is everlasting.
* The student: I don't know.
* Another student: ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blaze﴾ [al-Ahzab 64].
* The Shaykh: No, in Surah al-Nisa.
* A student: After the verse of tayammum.
* Another student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: The saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits﴾ [al-Nisa 14].
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and do wrong, Allah will never forgive them, nor will He guide them to a path, except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Nisa 168–169].
* The Shaykh: Excellent, correct. This is explicit: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾.
The second place is in Surah al-Ahzab. Who?
* A student: The saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blaze (64), abiding therein forever; they will find no protector or helper﴾ [al-Ahzab 64–65].
* The Shaykh: Yes, ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blaze (64), abiding therein forever; they will find no protector or helper.﴾
The third place is in Surah al-Jinn?
* A student: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, then indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein﴾ [al-Jinn 23].
* The Shaykh: Where is the eternity?
* The student: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger⁠—﴾...
* The Shaykh: ﴿then indeed for him⁠—﴾...
