* Student: The sentence: ﴿For them are chambers﴾ [Az-Zumar 20].
* Shaykh: The sentence ﴿For them are chambers﴾: a prepositional phrase serving as a fronted predicate for (ghuraf, chambers).
* We take the benefits. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The promise of Allah; Allah does not fail in (His) promise﴾ [Az-Zumar 20]. ﴿Promise﴾ (wa'd). The author says: (in the accusative by an implied verb). That is: they were promised the promise of Allah. Or, according to another possible opinion, the estimate is: the promise of Allah was fulfilled for them, meaning Allah fulfilled His promise to them. On this view it is in the accusative by a verb supplied from outside its own verb. As for the author's view, it is a verbal noun (masdar) with its governing verb omitted.
He, may Allah have mercy on him, says: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The promise of Allah; Allah does not fail in (His) promise﴾. The commentator said: (His promise). This indicates that the definite article (al) here stands in place of a pronoun, and that al-mi'ad (the promise) means al-wa'd (the promise). His saying: ﴿Allah does not fail in the promise﴾ means that He does not fail in what He promised by anything else, because (akhlafa, to fail/break) indicates the replacement of one thing by another, as Allah said: ﴿And whatever you spend, He will replace it﴾ [Saba' 39]. Unlike (khalafa), which indicates that one thing succeeds another; one says khalafahu, meaning he came after him. Akhlafahu means he made a substitute for him. For this reason the afflicted person says: "O Allah, reward me in my affliction and give me in exchange something better than it," meaning give me a substitute for it.
His saying: ﴿Allah does not fail in the promise﴾ is so because of the perfection of His truthfulness and the perfection of His power, since failing in a promise is either due to the lying of the promiser or due to his inability, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is exalted above both. So He is perfect in truthfulness and perfect in power.
In this verse, ﴿Is then one against whom the word of punishment has been justified﴾, to its end, there is evidence. Among its benefits: whoever has the word of punishment justified against him has no guide. Supporting this is His saying: ﴿Whomever Allah sends astray, there is no guide for him, and He leaves them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [Al-A'raf 186].
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the speech of Allah, for the one who decrees the punishment is Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and no other. So the word of punishment proceeds from Allah, and in this is the affirmation of speech for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The whole Qur'an, every letter of it, affirms the speech of Allah. Why?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No. In every letter of the Qur'an there is an affirmation of the speech of Allah.
* Student: Because it is with words, sound and letters.
* Shaykh: Because it is the speech of Allah, so every letter of it is the speech of Allah, since the speech of Allah consists of letters and sound.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Prophet (ﷺ) cannot save those in the Fire. And if this holds for the Messenger (ﷺ), then it holds for others all the more.
* Among its benefits: whoever has the word of punishment justified against him is in the Fire, because we said that the apparent noun here stands in place of the pronoun, and the estimate is: "Will you save him?"
* Among the benefits of this verse: the eloquence of the Qur'an and the severity of its warnings, for it presents this severe style that cuts through the heart that is alive and aware: ﴿Is then one against whom the word of punishment has been justified, will you save one who is in the Fire?﴾ [Az-Zumar 19]. This is a very severe style, and there is no doubt that a severe style in its proper place counts as eloquence (balaghah), because eloquence is for speech to correspond to what the situation requires, meaning what the situation calls for of gentleness, severity, extension or brevity.
* Among the benefits of this verse: the affirmation of the Fire. The Fire is the second abode in which humans and jinn settle. It is the abode of those who transgress and disbelieve. It exists now, and it will remain forever and ever.
Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿But those who feared their Lord﴾, to its end. In this is a clarification of the high rank of the God-fearing, for the istidrak here is as if it lifts them out of what was mentioned earlier of the severe threat to those against whom the word of punishment has been justified.
* Among its benefits: piety is a cause for entering Paradise, by His saying: ﴿For them are chambers﴾, to its end.
* Among its benefits: their fear of Allah has a prior cause and a subsequent cause. The special lordship in His saying ﴿their Lord﴾ required that they fear Him, and they fear their Lord who will reward them. So piety has a cause, which is Allah's care for them, the Mighty and Majestic; this is the prior cause. And it has a subsequent cause, which is the reward from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that they hope for. All of this is attributed to piety. He is their Lord in that He granted them success in piety, and He is their Lord in that He rewarded them for it.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the dwellings of Paradise are chambers built one above another, by His saying: ﴿For them are chambers, above them are chambers built﴾ [Az-Zumar 20]. Do these chambers differ according to the deeds? The answer is yes. The Messenger (ﷺ) explained that there are two gardens of Paradise made of gold, their vessels and what is in them, and two gardens made of silver, their vessels and what is in them.[Narrated by al-Bukhari (4878) and Muslim (180/296) with their chains from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Two gardens of silver, their vessels and what is in them, and two gardens of gold, their vessels and what is in them..." — the hadith.]
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the perfection of bliss, for these chambers have rivers flowing beneath them, and in them are trees and everything a person could wish for, and even more than that.
* Among the benefits of the verse: this bliss is established by the promise of Allah, by His saying: ﴿The promise of Allah﴾.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation that Allah does not fail in His promise, because of the perfection of His truthfulness and His power. In it is the affirmation of perfect truthfulness and the affirmation of perfect power.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verse 21–22 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Have you not seen﴾ [Az-Zumar 21], meaning: do you not know, ﴿that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾ to the end of the verse. The hamzah here is the interrogative particle. Generally, when the interrogative hamzah (hamzat al-istifham) comes before a negation, it is for confirmation (taqrir). So the meaning of ﴿Have you not seen﴾ is: you have indeed seen. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [Ash-Sharh 1], meaning: We have indeed expanded for you your breast. Thus the interrogation here is for confirmation. As for (lam) (lam, a particle of jussive negation and reversal), it is a particle of jazm (jussive), nafy (negation) and qalb (reversal).

The author's explanation of (tara, "you see") as (ta'lam, "you know") carries the possibility that the seeing here is seeing of knowledge (ru'yat al-'ilm), and it carries the possibility that the seeing is seeing of the eye (ru'yat al-basar). If it is something a person witnesses, being around him, then it is seeing of the eye, followed by seeing of knowledge. If it is something distant that one hears about, then it is seeing of knowledge. The address in His saying ﴿Have you not seen﴾ is either to the Prophet ﷺ, or to everyone who is addressable, i.e., whoever is fit to be addressed.

﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾ [Az-Zumar 21]. ﴿From the sky﴾: from the height. The intended meaning of "sky" is not the preserved ceiling, because it is known that rain falls from the clouds, and Allah has explained in another verse that the clouds are subjugated between the sky and the earth. On this basis, "sky" means height, and His saying ﴿water﴾ is the rain.

﴿Then He makes it flow as springs in the earth﴾ [Az-Zumar 21]. (Salaka) means "made it enter," and from it comes (silk al-kharaz), the string into which beads are inserted until they are strung. His saying ﴿springs﴾ is the plural of (yanbu', spring). The author says: that is, He caused it to enter places of springs; He made it enter the earth as springs, meaning it springs forth whenever a person wills. This is part of the completeness of wisdom and the completeness of mercy, because if this water remained on the surface of the earth it would rot and spoil, and it would spoil other things as well. So it was from the mercy of Allah that He makes it enter the earth to store it, as He said in another verse: ﴿And We sent down from the sky water in measure, then We settled it in the earth﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 18], and ﴿And you are not its guardians﴾ [Al-Hijr 22].

And His saying: ﴿springs in the earth; then He brings out thereby crops of varying colors﴾ [Az-Zumar 21]. ﴿Then﴾ indicates sequence with a delay, because what comes out by the rain does not come out immediately, but gradually, since it is Allah's way, glorified and exalted, that things come about gradually, so that collision does not occur in the universe.

﴿He brings out thereby crops﴾: ﴿thereby﴾ (bihi) the ba' indicates causation, i.e., by means of it. The rain is not what creates this vegetation; rather it is a cause for it.

﴿Crops of varying colors﴾: ﴿varying﴾ is an attribute of (crops). But is it the crops that vary, or their colors?
* Student: No, their colors.
* The Shaykh: ﴿Its colors﴾. So here the attribute has returned to something other than the described noun in meaning. The grammarians call this type of adjective the causal adjective (na't sababi), because its meaning returns to other than the modified noun. It follows the modified noun in i'rab (grammatical case), but its meaning belongs to something else. As when you say: "I saw a generous man whose father is generous." Who is generous?
* Student: His father.
* The Shaykh: The father. And the attribute, in terms of i'rab, applies to whom?
* Student: His father.
* The Shaykh: No, to the man. That is why you say "generous" is an adjective of "man," even though the real description belongs to someone else. This is called a causal adjective. ﴿Varying its colors﴾: how does the variation of these colors work? Is the intended meaning of "colors" the shapes, or the coloring, or both?
* Student: Both.
* The Shaykh: It includes this or that. So "its colors" means its kinds, and it also means color. This crop that comes out of the earth by rain, you see it differing in its colors and differing in its shapes. Go out, if you wish, to the nearest street from here and you will find the amazing variety. Two trees side by side, yet this one's leaves differ from that one's, and its color differs from the other's. You find the flowers on them differ too, and the fruit that comes from them differs, even though the water is one and the earth is one.

He says: (﴿varying its colors. Then it dries up﴾ [Az-Zumar 21], i.e., dries out), so you see it, after greenness, for example, yellowed. This plant that came out, pleasing to the observers, varying in colors, has been struck by wind or intense heat, or with the passage of time, it dries up, meaning it withers. ﴿Then you see it yellow﴾, after it had been green. ﴿Then He makes it debris﴾ [Az-Zumar 21], crushed fragments, because when it dries it breaks, and then it is crushed.

﴿Indeed in that is a reminder﴾ [Az-Zumar 21], a reminder for people of understanding, i.e., those of intellects who are reminded by it, because it indicates the oneness and power of Allah. ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder﴾: ﴿in that﴾ refers to everything mentioned before: the sending down of rain from the sky, its entering into springs in the earth, the bringing forth of crops by it, the crops' return to yellowing and crushing. These are several things that remind a person of the sending down from the sky, its entering the earth, the bringing out of crops by it, and the variation of colors. All of this is a reminder by which people of understanding are reminded of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, of His mercy, and of His wisdom.

﴿Then it dries up, so you see it yellow﴾ [Az-Zumar 21] to the end. People of understanding are reminded by it that everything that becomes complete in this world returns to deficiency. This indicates that this is among the intended meanings, as shown by His saying: ﴿The example of the life of this world is only like water We sent down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingled with it, of which men and livestock eat, until when the earth has taken its adornment and is beautified, and its people think they have power over it, Our command comes to it by night or by day, and We make it a harvest as if it had not flourished yesterday﴾ [Yunus 24].

So the reminder here is not merely a pointing to Allah's oneness and power; rather it is more comprehensive, and among its most important points is the indication that whatever is complete in this world ends in deficiency. Health ends in sickness, life ends in death, and in this manner measure everything in the world by this example.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam, so that he is upon light from his Lord﴾ [Az-Zumar 22] like one whose heart is sealed? The hamzah is the interrogative, and the fa' is conjunctive to something omitted, or to what preceded, according to what we explained yesterday.

﴿Is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam﴾: (sharaha) means "widened," as in our saying: "So-and-so explained (sharaha) the book of so-and-so," i.e., widened it. ﴿Allah expanded his breast for Islam﴾. Is the intended meaning "what is in the breast," or the breast itself opening up?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, it may mean what is in the breast, that Allah widens the heart and makes it open, making it open to Islam so that he is not constricted by it. And it may mean the breast itself, because a person feels that when he is distressed his breast constricts; the breast itself constricts, and when something pleasing comes to him the breast itself expands, even though the origin is the heart. But the place of the heart itself has expansion and constriction. This is observable. Keeping the verse on its apparent sense, that the breast means its reality, is preferable. So the breast expands to Islam and accepts all its laws. If he is commanded to do something, he expands to accept and act on it; if he is forbidden something, he expands to accept and avoid it; if he is informed of something, he expands to accept and affirm it, and so on.

Compare this with a corrupt man: if you command him to pray, you find his breast constricting, and he may say: "I won't pray for you, leave me alone," and the like. Some people, when you command and remind them, rejoice and their breast expands. Allah has described in Surat al-An'am a close and near image of this meaning, when He, glorified and exalted, said in Surat al-An'am: ﴿Whoever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast for Islam, and whoever He wills to leave astray, He makes his breast tight and constricted﴾ [Al-An'am 125], meaning very tight, ﴿as if he were climbing up into the sky﴾ [Al-An'am 125], meaning as if, when Islam is presented to him, he is climbing up into the sky, i.e., he is forcing himself to ascend.

The scholars have differed on the meaning of ﴿climbing up into the sky﴾: is it what is now well known, that a person as he rises in the air experiences increasing pressure, or does it mean climbing a lofty, towering mountain, tiring himself in ascending it?

The earlier exegetes, without doubt, did not know about the matter of pressure; the later ones know it, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, knows both. The verse is suitable for both meanings, because if you imagine a mountain difficult to climb and high (meaning in the sky, meaning lofty), and a person climbs it, does he exert himself or not? He certainly exerts himself, especially if he is weak, he becomes very tired.

If we say that the intended meaning is that a person ascends into the sky beyond the atmosphere, that is also clear. Then He, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam﴾ [Az-Zumar 22].

We said: the sign of an expanded breast is accepting the report, and affirming it; accepting the command and carrying it out; accepting the prohibition and avoiding it. He has no hesitation. There is no doubt that Allah, glorified and exalted, makes him, as He said: ﴿so that he is upon light from his Lord﴾ [Az-Zumar 22]. The author said: (so he was guided). The author has informed us that the verse contains an omission, its estimate being: "so he was guided," and it is supported by ﴿so he is upon light﴾. But in reality there is no need for this estimate: whoever Allah expands his breast for Islam ﴿is upon light from his Lord﴾; merely that Allah expands his breast for Islam means he is upon light, and when Allah expands his breast for Islam he will certainly be guided. Is His saying ﴿upon light from his Lord﴾ sensory light or non-sensory light?
* Student: Non-sensory, Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: Non-sensory. So he is upon light, even if he is in a dark room; he finds himself walking in light. His saying ﴿upon light from his Lord﴾ includes the light of this world and the light of the Hereafter. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿On the Day you see the believing men and believing women, their light running before them and at their right hands﴾ [Al-Hadid 12].

His saying ﴿from his Lord﴾: the lordship here is attributed to the one whom Allah expanded his breast for Islam, and it is a special lordship, since it is attributed to the one whom Allah guided. In the verse there is something omitted indicated by the hamzah, which the exegete, may Allah have mercy on him, estimated by his saying: (like one whose heart is sealed).

Had the author said "like one whose breast is constricted from Islam," that would have been more fitting in the contrast, because the counterpart of a thing should be its opposite, and you should not bring in something else. For example, if Allah the Exalted had said, "Is one whose heart Allah has widened," then the suitable estimate would be as the author said. But for ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has expanded﴾ we say: "like one whose breast Allah has constricted for Islam, so that he is distressed by it?" The answer is no, so the interrogation with the estimate is for negation.

Whoever his breast is not expanded for Islam, is he in darkness? Yes: whoever Allah has not expanded his breast for Islam, his heart is dark, we seek refuge in Allah, having no light, neither the light of knowledge nor the light of faith.

Allah said: ﴿So woe﴾, a word of punishment, ﴿to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾. ﴿So woe to those hardened﴾: (woe) is the subject, ﴿to those hardened﴾ is its predicate, and ﴿against the remembrance of Allah﴾ is attached to (hardened). The author said (woe) is "a word of punishment," and what the author said is more correct than what has been said, that it is a valley in Hell, because a person is told "woe to you for such-and-such" outside of Hell too: ﴿So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they earn﴾ [Al-Baqarah 79]. So it is a word of punishment and threat.

﴿to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾: (hardened) is an active participle, and ﴿their hearts﴾ is its agent. The hard is the opposite of the soft; the soft is the heart of the believer, and the hard is the heart of the disbeliever. His saying ﴿against the remembrance of Allah﴾ means: away from accepting the Qur'an. The exegete, may Allah have mercy on him, indicated that (min) means (an), and that the remembrance of Allah means the Qur'an; that is: woe to those whose hearts harden away from the Qur'an. But it is better to keep the verse on its apparent sense, that His saying ﴿from the remembrance of Allah﴾ means that (min) is causal: their hearts harden because of the remembrance of Allah, and that the remembrance of Allah is broader than the Qur'an. The meaning is that whenever Allah is remembered, their hearts harden, and the reason is that they do not want the remembrance of Allah; when they dislike the remembrance of Allah, the heart hardens as a punishment for them. This is supported by Allah's saying: ﴿And when a surah is sent down, some of them say: "Which of you has had his faith increased by this?" As for those who believe, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice. But as for those in whose hearts is a disease, it adds uncleanness to their uncleanness, and they die while they are disbelievers﴾ [At-Tawbah 124–125].

So you find these people, meaning the believers, the surah increases them in faith, while the others, in whose hearts is disease, it increases them in uncleanness upon their uncleanness.

So we say: "those whose hearts are hardened from the remembrance of Allah," meaning those who, when Allah is remembered, their hearts harden against accepting it, meaning they do not accept it. When they do not accept it, their hearts grow harder from the remembrance of Allah. Allah said: ﴿Those are in manifest error﴾ [Az-Zumar 22]. ﴿Those﴾ refers to whom?
* Student: Those whose hearts are hardened.
* The Shaykh: Those whose hearts are hardened, ﴿in manifest error﴾. The author said: (clear). His saying ﴿in error﴾: ﴿in﴾ indicates enclosure, and how excellent it is in this position, indicating that error has surrounded them on every side, as a room surrounds its occupant. If error has surrounded them on every side, no good is hoped for them, we seek refuge in Allah, because they are in manifest error.

Compare this, ﴿Those are in manifest error﴾, with His saying ﴿so he is upon light from his Lord﴾; it becomes clear to you that the light in the verse is the light of knowledge and the light of faith, and the opposite of knowledge is error.

* We take the benefits. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾ [Az-Zumar 21] to the end. * Among the benefits of this verse: the demonstration of Allah's power in sending down this rain from the sky, since no one can possibly send it down. Allah said: ﴿Indeed, with Allah is the knowledge of the Hour, and He sends down the rain﴾ [Luqman 34].
* And among its benefits: the wisdom and mercy of Allah, in that He made this water descend from the sky. For if it sprang from the earth, the whole earth would not benefit from it in every respect, and it would not reach the mountaintops unless it drowned the people beneath the mountains. So it was part of wisdom that it descends from the sky to cover both the high and the low, and to encompass the whole earth.
* Among the benefits of this verse also: the demonstration of Allah's wisdom regarding the manner of this water's descent. How does it descend? It descends in drops. If it descended in a pour, like the mouths of waterskins pour, it would destroy people and demolish buildings; but by Allah's mercy, it descends in drops.
* Among the benefits of this verse: that "sky" is applied to height, and from this benefit follows that His saying ﴿Are you secure from the One who is in the sky?﴾ [Al-Mulk 16] may be understood to mean the One who is on high.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's power and His mercy toward the servants, in that He made this water flow as springs in the earth, and did not leave it stagnant on its surface, because of the wisdom and mercy in that; it is stored in the earth, and when people want it, they extract it.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the demonstration of Allah's power, in that by this water He brought forth that crop of varying colors.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of causes: ﴿then He brings out thereby﴾, the affirmation of causes.
* Among its benefits: that a cause does not by itself have independent effect upon the caused; this is shown by His saying ﴿then He brings out﴾, where He attributes the bringing out to Allah. This is what the early generations of the Ummah and its imams held: that causes have an effect on their effects, but their effect comes by Allah's action and does not return to them independently.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim, Tafsir of the Noble Qur'an) on surah 39, verses 21–22 (part 2 of 3):**

* Among the benefits of this noble verse is the demonstration of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in that He brings forth this crop of varying colours, although it is nourished by one water and from one soil. This is in His saying: ﴿varying in its colours﴾.
* Among its benefits: the perfection of this world signals its decline, because Allah has struck this as a parable for the worldly life, as in the verse we cited in the tafsir.
* Among the benefits of this verse: those who take heed of the signs of Allah in the cosmos are the people of understanding, whereas whoever does not take heed by them, and says, "This is a nature that interacts and flows along," has no intellect.
* Among the benefits of this verse: a person should employ his intellect in the creatures of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so that he may be reminded by them, either of the benefits of these creatures or of the greatness of the Creator that is in them, because He said: ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder for those of understanding﴾ [Az-Zumar 21].

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord...﴾ [Az-Zumar 22] to the end. In this verse is the negation of equality between the two groups: the one whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam and the one whose breast He has not expanded. This is because the interrogative here carries the meaning of negation.

* Among its benefits: guidance is in the hand of Allah, as in His saying: ﴿Is he whose breast Allah has expanded﴾. And from this benefit it follows that whenever a person knows that guidance is in the hand of Allah, he does not turn, in seeking guidance, except to Allah.

Also, if he knows that guidance is in the hand of Allah, he will not be self-admiring when he is guided, but will say to himself: "Had Allah not guided him, he would have been astray." So he does not say, "I was only given it on account of knowledge I possess," or say, "This is mine," but rather acknowledges the favour of Allah upon him, and that had Allah not guided him, he would not have benefited.

* * *

(...) until the Day of Judgement. We open our summer sessions this year on this day, Saturday, the eighteenth of the month of Muharram in the year one thousand four hundred and thirteen [AH], and we ask Allah, glorified and exalted, to bless our work and our knowledge. Our study is varied: it includes tafsir (exegesis of the Qur'an), hadith, fiqh (jurisprudence), tawhid (monotheism) and usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence), and these are distributed across the days, except for tafsir, hadith and fiqh, for these three are fixed every day.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord? Woe then to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah. Those are in manifest error (22). Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book consistent and repeating; the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver from it; then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah. That is the guidance of Allah; He guides by it whom He wills, and whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide (23). Is one who shields his face with his body from the terrible punishment on the Day of Resurrection [like one who is safe]? And it will be said to the wrongdoers, "Taste what you used to earn" (24). Those before them denied, and the punishment came to them from where they did not perceive (25). So Allah made them taste disgrace in the life of this world, but the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew﴾ [Az-Zumar 22–26].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord﴾. The hamza here is the interrogative particle, and the fa' is a conjunctive particle. The thing conjoined to is what preceded, according to one of the two opinions among the grammarians. It has also been said that the fa' is conjoining to something implied after the hamza, and the implied sense is: "Have you been heedless and so did not perceive this matter? So whoever Allah has expanded his breast to Islam, he is upon a light from his Lord, unlike one who was not so." And we (...).
* Student: ﴿...from before them, so the punishment came to them from where they did not perceive (25). So Allah made them taste disgrace in the life of this world, but the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew﴾ [Az-Zumar 25–26].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord﴾.
* Student: ﴿So Allah made them taste disgrace in the life of this world, but the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew﴾ [Az-Zumar 26].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord﴾ [Az-Zumar 22]. The hamza here is the interrogative, and the fa' is a conjunctive particle, and the thing conjoined to is what preceded, according to one of the two opinions among the grammarians (i'rab scholars).

It has also been said that the fa' is conjoining to something implied after the hamza, and the implied sense is: "Have you been heedless and so did not perceive this matter?"

So whoever Allah has expanded his breast to Islam, he is upon a light from his Lord, unlike one who was not so.

We have a principle: when the grammarians differ on a matter, we follow the easier view, because the matter is one of ijtihad (independent reasoning). If that is so, we hold that the hamza is interrogative, the fa' conjoins to what precedes, and the position of the hamza is after the fa' of conjunction. The implied sense is: fa-aman (so is it the one whom) Allah has expanded his breast to Islam [...].

As for His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Allah has expanded his breast﴾, the word sharaha means widened (wassa'a), and from it comes sharh al-kitab (commentary on a book), because it is widened and spread out.

As for His saying: ﴿Allah has expanded his breast to Islam﴾, the intended "breast" here is the heart, because it is its locus, so it is expressed by it. It may also be said that the intended "breast" is literally the chest, as is evident from the fact that when a person is distressed he finds his chest constricted, as if the millstone were upon him, from the tightness, without realising that this touches his heart. So the expansion here refers to the expansion of the chest itself, and the outcome is one.

As for His saying: ﴿to Islam﴾, it means: for accepting it and committing to it. Islam has two meanings: the first is general, and the second is specific.

The general meaning encompasses everyone who submitted to Allah, the Exalted, by obeying Him (...) while the sharia (revealed law) was in force. It includes everyone who submitted to Allah by obeying Him while the sharia was in force. On this basis, the Jews in the time of Musa were Muslims, and in the time of 'Isa they were disbelievers; the Christians in the time of 'Isa were Muslims, and in the time of Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, they are disbelievers. For this reason we find that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, describes the people of Nuh and those after them as Muslims.

As for the specific meaning of Islam, it is what is specific to the sharia of Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family. So people after the mission of Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, are either Muslims or disbelievers. The Muslims are those who follow the Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, and no one else; this is called specific Islam.

So His saying: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Aal 'Imran 19]: what does it mean? It means the Islam with which Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, was sent. And no one can claim to be a Muslim after the Prophet's mission, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, unless he follows him, because after his mission Islam became specific to those who follow his sharia. So here, ﴿Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam﴾: shall we interpret it by the general meaning or by the specific meaning?

* Students: The specific.
* The Shaykh: If we interpret it by the general meaning, it includes whoever Allah expanded his breast to Islam in the era of the earlier prophets, and whoever Allah expanded his breast to Islam in the era of the Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family. So which do you see?
* Student: The specific.
* Students: The general.
* The Shaykh: The general, because among those who came before, there were those whose breasts Allah expanded to Islam. Musa, peace be upon him, said: ﴿My Lord, expand for me my breast (25), and ease for me my affair﴾ [Ta-Ha 25–26].

However, if the address is directed to the period after the Messenger's mission, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, then it is necessary that the intended meaning be the specific one.

As for His saying: ﴿so he is upon a light from his Lord﴾, the fa' here is conjoining for consequence; meaning: so he, when Allah has expanded his breast, is upon a light from his Lord.

It is an inner light by which a person proceeds upon the sharia of Allah, as if he had a lamp in his hand guiding him to the path, because Allah expanded his breast to Islam, so it does not constrict him.

﴿so he is upon a light from his Lord﴾. There remains the hamza in ﴿Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam﴾, which is interrogative. So where is its counterpart? Its counterpart is what corresponds to it in meaning: that which corresponds in meaning to the expansion of the breast is one whose breast is constricted with Islam. Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam like one whose breast is constricted by it?

The answer: yes or no? That is, is the one whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam equal to the one whose breast is constricted by it? No.

So the counterpart, or the equivalent, if you wish, is omitted, indicated by the context, and the meaning is: "Is he who is in such a state like one who is not in such a state?" The one whom Allah has expanded his breast is not like the one to whom Allah has not expanded his breast. There is no doubt that the difference between them is great, farther than between the heaven and the earth. For the one whom Allah has expanded his breast to Islam, and I ask Allah to make me and you among them, finds himself receptive to the laws of Islam, rejoicing in them. He rejoices when he performs an act of obedience to Allah, and grieves when he commits an act of disobedience to Allah. Those who have reached the utmost in this are distressed by what happens to them of imperfection, even if it was not intentional. That is, if he misses an act of worship, he finds himself in distress and sadness, without being aware of it.

Let me illustrate this with the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. When he ended the prayer after two rak'ahs of the Zuhr prayer, what did he do? He turned from his prayer as if he were distressed. He stood, contrary to his custom, against a wooden post in the qiblah side of the mosque, leaned upon it, and placed his hands like this, as if he were angry. Why? Because his prayer was not complete, so his soul contracted without his being aware of it. But this is due to the perfection of his degree, peace and blessings be upon him, that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, places in a person's soul a contraction, even if he is not aware of it, because he did not complete the worship required of him. He leaned upon it and interlaced his fingers like this, the posture of one who is distressed, until he was reminded [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (482) and Muslim (573/97), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].

So whoever Allah has expanded his breast to Islam finds himself at ease and rejoicing in carrying out the laws of Islam, and conversely, if he neglects any of them or violates one of the prohibitions of Allah.

As for His saying: ﴿so he is upon a light from his Lord; then woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾ [Az-Zumar 22].

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, the commentator (al-Mufassir), said: "(﴿Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam﴾) so he was guided (﴿so he is upon a light from his Lord﴾) like one whose heart is sealed. This is indicated by His saying: (﴿so woe﴾)," and so on to the end.

This is what the author, may Allah have mercy on him, held in his tafsir: that is, he inferred the omitted element from what is mentioned afterward. If we wanted to infer the omitted element from what is mentioned after it, in strict correspondence, we would say: "like one whose heart has hardened," and we would not say "like one whose heart has been sealed," because Allah said: ﴿woe to those hardened﴾. And if you want to deduce the answer from what is mentioned, make it correspond to it, and then we say: "like one who has hardened." However, what we mentioned first is the correct view: that the equivalent is mentioned in contrast to what was stated, so the meaning is: "Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam like one whose breast Allah has constricted from Islam, or like one whose breast Allah has not expanded to Islam?"

﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾. The author said: "﴿So woe﴾." Here, perhaps we will explain or interpret according to what we have, and then return to the author's words, so that our discussion is not cut off.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾. ﴿Woe﴾ is the subject, and ﴿to those hardened﴾ is its predicate: ﴿so woe to those hardened﴾.

And "woe" (al-wayl), according to the preponderant view, is a word of warning (wa'id, threat). It was also said that it is a valley in Hell, but the more correct view is that it is a word of threat. What permitted beginning with it, though it is indefinite (nakirah), is that it is a threat. It may also be said that what permitted beginning with it, though it is indefinite, is that it indicates a severe attribute: meaning, "great woe," or "severe woe," to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah.

As for His saying: ﴿to those whose hearts are hardened﴾, al-qaswah means hardness, to such a degree that when you press something, it does not yield to your pressure, like a stone. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, struck the hardness of the heart with stones, saying: ﴿Then your hearts hardened after that, so they became like stones, or even harder in hardness﴾ [Al-Baqarah 74].

Here the questioner asks: why did He not say "like iron," since iron breaks stones, while stones do not break iron?

The answer to that: we say, iron softens, by what? By heating it in fire. Stones do not soften. Therefore the hardness of hearts was likened to stones.

"Those whose hearts are hardened" means: those that became hard and did not soften to the truth. We ask Allah for well-being.

As for His saying: ﴿against the remembrance of Allah﴾, the "min" (from) has been said to mean "'an" (away from); "hardened from" is like "hardened against". However, the more apparent view is that it retains its own meaning, and that the sense is: their hearts harden from the reminder, instead of what was expected, which is that they should soften. This meaning is supported by His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And when a surah is revealed, some of them say, "Which of you has this increased in faith?" As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice (124). But as for those in whose hearts is disease, it adds defilement to their defilement﴾ [At-Tawbah 124–125]; that is, it increased them in hardness and stiffness.

On this basis we say: "those whose hearts are hardened from the reminder," meaning: whenever Allah is remembered, their hearts harden, contrary to the believer, for whenever Allah is remembered his heart softens. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble before the remembrance of Allah?﴾ [Al-Hadid 16].

﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah; those are in manifest error﴾. ﴿Those﴾ refers to those whose hearts are hardened. He pointed to them with the demonstrative for the distant, to signal their lowliness and the debasement of their rank, because the distant demonstrative sometimes indicates elevation of rank and sometimes indicates debasement of rank.

Thus in His saying: ﴿That is the Book﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2], it indicates elevation of rank, while in His saying here: ﴿those are in manifest error﴾, it indicates debasement of rank.

If someone asks: these meanings differ while the wording is one; what determines which of the two meanings is intended?

We say: the context and the circumstances of the one spoken about determine it, because the context and the indicators each determine what is meant. ﴿Those are in manifest error﴾: ﴿in error﴾ (dalal): the meaning is bewilderment and failure to reach the truth. So these are in error, that is, they are bewildered and have not reached the truth.

And "manifest" (mubin) here may be derived from abana, intransitive, or from abana, transitive. Let us keep together: there are two verbs, bana and abana. Is bana intransitive or transitive?

* Students: Intransitive.
* The Shaykh: Intransitive. You say: "the matter became clear" (bana al-amr), "the morning appeared" (bana al-subh), "the meaning became evident" (bana al-ma'na).

With the hamza, it can be transitive or intransitive, depending on the context. For example, you say: "the dawn became clear" (abana al-fajr), meaning it appeared, that is, it became manifest. And you say: "the man made the truth clear" (abana al-rajul al-haqq), meaning he made it manifest.

So here, ﴿those are in manifest error﴾: is it intransitive or transitive?

* Student: Intransitive.
* The Shaykh: The apparent view is that it is intransitive, that is, in error that is clear and evident.

Let us return to the author's words, may Allah have mercy on him: "(﴿Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam﴾) so he was guided (﴿so he is upon a light from his Lord﴾) like one whose heart is sealed, indicated by (﴿so woe﴾) a word of punishment," and so on to the end.

The author's statement regarding "like one whose heart is sealed" is open to question. If we want to say that the omitted element is indicated by what is mentioned, it must be estimated to correspond to what is mentioned, so we say: "like one whose heart has hardened." That is because the more correct view is what we previously established: that the equivalent is mentioned in meaning as the counterpart of what? Of what is mentioned. So it is said: "whoever Allah has expanded his breast is like one whose breast Allah has not expanded."

Then the author said: (﴿Woe, then, to those whose hearts are hardened﴾ is a word of punishment).

Had he said "a word of warning," it would have been better, because it is a threat. Even in our customary usage today you say "woe to you," meaning you threaten him with this, with whatever you wish.

And His saying: ﴿to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾, i.e., against accepting the Qur'an. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, took the word "dhikr" (remembrance) to mean the Qur'an, and took "min" (مِن, "from") to mean "'an" (عن, "against").

As for "dhikr" meaning the Qur'an, there is no doubt that the Qur'an is a remembrance. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾ [Yasin 69], and He the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and your people﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 44].

However, the better course is to interpret "the remembrance of Allah" here in a more general sense. We say: it certainly refers to the Qur'an, since it is part of the remembrance of Allah, and it also encompasses more than that, such that we say: whenever Allah is mentioned, their hearts harden, whether through the Qur'an or through other than the Qur'an. This is the more correct view.

As for "min" meaning "'an," we have already said that the correct view is that it retains its own meaning.

His saying that "min" replaces "'an" is based on a disputed question between the Kufan and Basran grammarians: when a particle comes in other than its proper place, is it a substitute for a particle that suits the context, or is the verb governing it understood with a meaning that suits the particle? Are you following? Good.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿a spring from which the servants of Allah drink﴾ [Al-Insan 6]. One does not drink *with* a spring; one drinks *from* a spring. Here the grammarians differed: is the "bi" (ب, "with") in the sense of "min" (from), so that one particle stands in for another; or is ﴿yashrabu﴾ (drink) in the sense of "yarwa" (to quench one's thirst), so that the servants of Allah quench their thirst with it, the drinking being implicitly given the meaning of quenching, and quenching includes drinking and something more, it includes drinking and more? On this there is a disagreement between the Kufan and Basran grammarians. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, favours the second view: that the verb is understood with a meaning that suits the particle. Because when we say the verb is understood with another meaning, we gain two benefits: we gain the meaning of what is stated, and the meaning of what is implied. For when you say "yarwa bihā" (they quench their thirst with it), we learn that they drink and also quench their thirst. But if we say "yashrabu bihā" (they drink from it), we gain only one meaning. So implication adds meaning, whereas replacing one particle with another adds no further meaning. Thus the preponderant view in this matter is what Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, held: that the verb is understood with a meaning that suits the particle. ﴿Woe, then, to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾.

The author said: Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Those are in clear error﴾ — "clear" is explanatory). So, is "mubin" (clear) here intransitive or transitive?
* Students: Intransitive.
* The Shaykh: Intransitive.

Then He said: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech, a Book﴾ [Az-Zumar 23]. The benefits, correct?
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: showing that people differ in their acceptance of the truth, and that some accept the truth with open hearts, while others do not.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever Allah has opened his breast to Islam, so that he accepts the truth, is upon a light from Allah.
* Branching from this: an increase in his knowledge, for knowledge is light, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O mankind, there has come to you a proof from your Lord, and We have sent down to you a clear light﴾ [An-Nisa 174].
* Also branching from it, from this same benefit: strength of insight (firasah). Allah the Exalted gives a person insight by which he knows what is in people's hearts from the glances of their faces, and more than that: he infers the unseen from the seen, and Allah gives him conclusions that others do not have. Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned in his book Madarij al-Salikin, in his discussion of insight, remarkable statements of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, concerning his own insight, though he mentioned some things that may not be accepted; but he mentioned much. He supports this with His saying: ﴿so he is upon a light from his Lord﴾.
* This noble verse also indicates that whoever Allah has opened his breast to Islam has a special lordship and special care from Allah. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿from his Lord﴾, for this special lordship is distinct from the general lordship. The lordship of Allah the Exalted over His creation is of two kinds: general and special.
The general is like His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [Al-Fatihah 2].
The special is like the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, about those of understanding who reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾ [Ali 'Imran 191], to the end.
Both kinds are combined in His saying about the magicians of Pharaoh's people: ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun"﴾ [Al-A'raf 121–122]. The first is general, the second is special.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the severe warning for whoever's heart is hardened against the remembrance of Allah, by His saying: ﴿Woe, then, to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾.
* Among its benefits: when you find in your heart a lack of softness toward the remembrance of Allah, then treat your soul, treat it, so that you may be spared this warning. People often complain of this, and we too complain of it. Sometimes the heart hardens and does not soften; it reads the mighty, deterrent verses but is not affected; and sometimes it reads the very same verses and is affected. So if you recognise hardness of heart in yourself, turn to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, ask Him to soften your heart to His remembrance, and prepare yourself for the warning if Allah does not overtake you with His kindness and forgiveness.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: hearts are divided into two kinds: hearts that soften at the remembrance of Allah, and hearts that harden against it.
If someone asks: how can one thing produce two opposite results? Is the question clear? One thing produces two contrary results. We say: this is possible, because the recipient of this thing differs. This is not strange, neither in matters of meaning nor in matters of the senses.
In matters of meaning, as you have seen with the speech of Allah the Mighty and Majestic: just as a person gives a lesson to a group, some of whom devour it, understand it completely, and find it delightful, while others are closed to it and do not understand it; and if one word closes off to them, the whole lesson becomes closed and they are unable to understand. The teacher is one, and the subject is one.
Likewise, we find dates, the well-known date of the palm, eaten by two men: for one it is a sickness, and for the other a nourishment, is that not so? A diabetic who eats dates is harmed by them, while a healthy person is not. We find water flowing over land: one land receives it, drinks it, and grows plants, while another land does not accept it, and the water pours over it without benefit. Likewise, the remembrance of Allah the Mighty and Majestic comes upon a soft heart, and it benefits from it, and upon a hard heart, and it grows harder, and we seek refuge in Allah.
* Among the benefits of this verse: those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah are the opposite of those whose breasts Allah has opened to Islam. Whoever Allah has opened his breast to Islam is upon light, and whoever's heart is hardened against the remembrance of Allah is in clear error.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah have plunged completely into error. From where is this taken?
* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: Because "fi" (في, "in") indicates enclosure, and the container surrounds what is contained. The contained is inside the container. So it is as if these people have been submerged in error, and it has encompassed them as a container encompasses what it holds: ﴿Those are in clear error﴾. We ask Allah for us and for you guidance and light (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verse 21–22 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Have you not seen﴾ [Az-Zumar 21], meaning: do you not know, ﴿that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾ to the end of the verse. The hamzah here is the interrogative particle. Generally, when the interrogative hamzah (hamzat al-istifham) comes before a negation, it is for confirmation (taqrir). So the meaning of ﴿Have you not seen﴾ is: you have indeed seen. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [Ash-Sharh 1], meaning: We have indeed expanded for you your breast. Thus the interrogation here is for confirmation. As for (lam) (lam, a particle of jussive negation and reversal), it is a particle of jazm (jussive), nafy (negation) and qalb (reversal).

The author's explanation of (tara, "you see") as (ta'lam, "you know") carries the possibility that the seeing here is seeing of knowledge (ru'yat al-'ilm), and it carries the possibility that the seeing is seeing of the eye (ru'yat al-basar). If it is something a person witnesses, being around him, then it is seeing of the eye, followed by seeing of knowledge. If it is something distant that one hears about, then it is seeing of knowledge. The address in His saying ﴿Have you not seen﴾ is either to the Prophet ﷺ, or to everyone who is addressable, i.e., whoever is fit to be addressed.

﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾ [Az-Zumar 21]. ﴿From the sky﴾: from the height. The intended meaning of "sky" is not the preserved ceiling, because it is known that rain falls from the clouds, and Allah has explained in another verse that the clouds are subjugated between the sky and the earth. On this basis, "sky" means height, and His saying ﴿water﴾ is the rain.

﴿Then He makes it flow as springs in the earth﴾ [Az-Zumar 21]. (Salaka) means "made it enter," and from it comes (silk al-kharaz), the string into which beads are inserted until they are strung. His saying ﴿springs﴾ is the plural of (yanbu', spring). The author says: that is, He caused it to enter places of springs; He made it enter the earth as springs, meaning it springs forth whenever a person wills. This is part of the completeness of wisdom and the completeness of mercy, because if this water remained on the surface of the earth it would rot and spoil, and it would spoil other things as well. So it was from the mercy of Allah that He makes it enter the earth to store it, as He said in another verse: ﴿And We sent down from the sky water in measure, then We settled it in the earth﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 18], and ﴿And you are not its guardians﴾ [Al-Hijr 22].

And His saying: ﴿springs in the earth; then He brings out thereby crops of varying colors﴾ [Az-Zumar 21]. ﴿Then﴾ indicates sequence with a delay, because what comes out by the rain does not come out immediately, but gradually, since it is Allah's way, glorified and exalted, that things come about gradually, so that collision does not occur in the universe.

﴿He brings out thereby crops﴾: ﴿thereby﴾ (bihi) the ba' indicates causation, i.e., by means of it. The rain is not what creates this vegetation; rather it is a cause for it.

﴿Crops of varying colors﴾: ﴿varying﴾ is an attribute of (crops). But is it the crops that vary, or their colors?
* Student: No, their colors.
* The Shaykh: ﴿Its colors﴾. So here the attribute has returned to something other than the described noun in meaning. The grammarians call this type of adjective the causal adjective (na't sababi), because its meaning returns to other than the modified noun. It follows the modified noun in i'rab (grammatical case), but its meaning belongs to something else. As when you say: "I saw a generous man whose father is generous." Who is generous?
* Student: His father.
* The Shaykh: The father. And the attribute, in terms of i'rab, applies to whom?
* Student: His father.
* The Shaykh: No, to the man. That is why you say "generous" is an adjective of "man," even though the real description belongs to someone else. This is called a causal adjective. ﴿Varying its colors﴾: how does the variation of these colors work? Is the intended meaning of "colors" the shapes, or the coloring, or both?
* Student: Both.
* The Shaykh: It includes this or that. So "its colors" means its kinds, and it also means color. This crop that comes out of the earth by rain, you see it differing in its colors and differing in its shapes. Go out, if you wish, to the nearest street from here and you will find the amazing variety. Two trees side by side, yet this one's leaves differ from that one's, and its color differs from the other's. You find the flowers on them differ too, and the fruit that comes from them differs, even though the water is one and the earth is one.

He says: (﴿varying its colors. Then it dries up﴾ [Az-Zumar 21], i.e., dries out), so you see it, after greenness, for example, yellowed. This plant that came out, pleasing to the observers, varying in colors, has been struck by wind or intense heat, or with the passage of time, it dries up, meaning it withers. ﴿Then you see it yellow﴾, after it had been green. ﴿Then He makes it debris﴾ [Az-Zumar 21], crushed fragments, because when it dries it breaks, and then it is crushed.

﴿Indeed in that is a reminder﴾ [Az-Zumar 21], a reminder for people of understanding, i.e., those of intellects who are reminded by it, because it indicates the oneness and power of Allah. ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder﴾: ﴿in that﴾ refers to everything mentioned before: the sending down of rain from the sky, its entering into springs in the earth, the bringing forth of crops by it, the crops' return to yellowing and crushing. These are several things that remind a person of the sending down from the sky, its entering the earth, the bringing out of crops by it, and the variation of colors. All of this is a reminder by which people of understanding are reminded of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, of His mercy, and of His wisdom.

﴿Then it dries up, so you see it yellow﴾ [Az-Zumar 21] to the end. People of understanding are reminded by it that everything that becomes complete in this world returns to deficiency. This indicates that this is among the intended meanings, as shown by His saying: ﴿The example of the life of this world is only like water We sent down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingled with it, of which men and livestock eat, until when the earth has taken its adornment and is beautified, and its people think they have power over it, Our command comes to it by night or by day, and We make it a harvest as if it had not flourished yesterday﴾ [Yunus 24].

So the reminder here is not merely a pointing to Allah's oneness and power; rather it is more comprehensive, and among its most important points is the indication that whatever is complete in this world ends in deficiency. Health ends in sickness, life ends in death, and in this manner measure everything in the world by this example.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam, so that he is upon light from his Lord﴾ [Az-Zumar 22] like one whose heart is sealed? The hamzah is the interrogative, and the fa' is conjunctive to something omitted, or to what preceded, according to what we explained yesterday.

﴿Is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam﴾: (sharaha) means "widened," as in our saying: "So-and-so explained (sharaha) the book of so-and-so," i.e., widened it. ﴿Allah expanded his breast for Islam﴾. Is the intended meaning "what is in the breast," or the breast itself opening up?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, it may mean what is in the breast, that Allah widens the heart and makes it open, making it open to Islam so that he is not constricted by it. And it may mean the breast itself, because a person feels that when he is distressed his breast constricts; the breast itself constricts, and when something pleasing comes to him the breast itself expands, even though the origin is the heart. But the place of the heart itself has expansion and constriction. This is observable. Keeping the verse on its apparent sense, that the breast means its reality, is preferable. So the breast expands to Islam and accepts all its laws. If he is commanded to do something, he expands to accept and act on it; if he is forbidden something, he expands to accept and avoid it; if he is informed of something, he expands to accept and affirm it, and so on.

Compare this with a corrupt man: if you command him to pray, you find his breast constricting, and he may say: "I won't pray for you, leave me alone," and the like. Some people, when you command and remind them, rejoice and their breast expands. Allah has described in Surat al-An'am a close and near image of this meaning, when He, glorified and exalted, said in Surat al-An'am: ﴿Whoever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast for Islam, and whoever He wills to leave astray, He makes his breast tight and constricted﴾ [Al-An'am 125], meaning very tight, ﴿as if he were climbing up into the sky﴾ [Al-An'am 125], meaning as if, when Islam is presented to him, he is climbing up into the sky, i.e., he is forcing himself to ascend.

The scholars have differed on the meaning of ﴿climbing up into the sky﴾: is it what is now well known, that a person as he rises in the air experiences increasing pressure, or does it mean climbing a lofty, towering mountain, tiring himself in ascending it?

The earlier exegetes, without doubt, did not know about the matter of pressure; the later ones know it, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, knows both. The verse is suitable for both meanings, because if you imagine a mountain difficult to climb and high (meaning in the sky, meaning lofty), and a person climbs it, does he exert himself or not? He certainly exerts himself, especially if he is weak, he becomes very tired.

If we say that the intended meaning is that a person ascends into the sky beyond the atmosphere, that is also clear. Then He, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam﴾ [Az-Zumar 22].

We said: the sign of an expanded breast is accepting the report, and affirming it; accepting the command and carrying it out; accepting the prohibition and avoiding it. He has no hesitation. There is no doubt that Allah, glorified and exalted, makes him, as He said: ﴿so that he is upon light from his Lord﴾ [Az-Zumar 22]. The author said: (so he was guided). The author has informed us that the verse contains an omission, its estimate being: "so he was guided," and it is supported by ﴿so he is upon light﴾. But in reality there is no need for this estimate: whoever Allah expands his breast for Islam ﴿is upon light from his Lord﴾; merely that Allah expands his breast for Islam means he is upon light, and when Allah expands his breast for Islam he will certainly be guided. Is His saying ﴿upon light from his Lord﴾ sensory light or non-sensory light?
* Student: Non-sensory, Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: Non-sensory. So he is upon light, even if he is in a dark room; he finds himself walking in light. His saying ﴿upon light from his Lord﴾ includes the light of this world and the light of the Hereafter. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿On the Day you see the believing men and believing women, their light running before them and at their right hands﴾ [Al-Hadid 12].

His saying ﴿from his Lord﴾: the lordship here is attributed to the one whom Allah expanded his breast for Islam, and it is a special lordship, since it is attributed to the one whom Allah guided. In the verse there is something omitted indicated by the hamzah, which the exegete, may Allah have mercy on him, estimated by his saying: (like one whose heart is sealed).

Had the author said "like one whose breast is constricted from Islam," that would have been more fitting in the contrast, because the counterpart of a thing should be its opposite, and you should not bring in something else. For example, if Allah the Exalted had said, "Is one whose heart Allah has widened," then the suitable estimate would be as the author said. But for ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has expanded﴾ we say: "like one whose breast Allah has constricted for Islam, so that he is distressed by it?" The answer is no, so the interrogation with the estimate is for negation.

Whoever his breast is not expanded for Islam, is he in darkness? Yes: whoever Allah has not expanded his breast for Islam, his heart is dark, we seek refuge in Allah, having no light, neither the light of knowledge nor the light of faith.

Allah said: ﴿So woe﴾, a word of punishment, ﴿to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾. ﴿So woe to those hardened﴾: (woe) is the subject, ﴿to those hardened﴾ is its predicate, and ﴿against the remembrance of Allah﴾ is attached to (hardened). The author said (woe) is "a word of punishment," and what the author said is more correct than what has been said, that it is a valley in Hell, because a person is told "woe to you for such-and-such" outside of Hell too: ﴿So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they earn﴾ [Al-Baqarah 79]. So it is a word of punishment and threat.

﴿to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾: (hardened) is an active participle, and ﴿their hearts﴾ is its agent. The hard is the opposite of the soft; the soft is the heart of the believer, and the hard is the heart of the disbeliever. His saying ﴿against the remembrance of Allah﴾ means: away from accepting the Qur'an. The exegete, may Allah have mercy on him, indicated that (min) means (an), and that the remembrance of Allah means the Qur'an; that is: woe to those whose hearts harden away from the Qur'an. But it is better to keep the verse on its apparent sense, that His saying ﴿from the remembrance of Allah﴾ means that (min) is causal: their hearts harden because of the remembrance of Allah, and that the remembrance of Allah is broader than the Qur'an. The meaning is that whenever Allah is remembered, their hearts harden, and the reason is that they do not want the remembrance of Allah; when they dislike the remembrance of Allah, the heart hardens as a punishment for them. This is supported by Allah's saying: ﴿And when a surah is sent down, some of them say: "Which of you has had his faith increased by this?" As for those who believe, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice. But as for those in whose hearts is a disease, it adds uncleanness to their uncleanness, and they die while they are disbelievers﴾ [At-Tawbah 124–125].

So you find these people, meaning the believers, the surah increases them in faith, while the others, in whose hearts is disease, it increases them in uncleanness upon their uncleanness.

So we say: "those whose hearts are hardened from the remembrance of Allah," meaning those who, when Allah is remembered, their hearts harden against accepting it, meaning they do not accept it. When they do not accept it, their hearts grow harder from the remembrance of Allah. Allah said: ﴿Those are in manifest error﴾ [Az-Zumar 22]. ﴿Those﴾ refers to whom?
* Student: Those whose hearts are hardened.
* The Shaykh: Those whose hearts are hardened, ﴿in manifest error﴾. The author said: (clear). His saying ﴿in error﴾: ﴿in﴾ indicates enclosure, and how excellent it is in this position, indicating that error has surrounded them on every side, as a room surrounds its occupant. If error has surrounded them on every side, no good is hoped for them, we seek refuge in Allah, because they are in manifest error.

Compare this, ﴿Those are in manifest error﴾, with His saying ﴿so he is upon light from his Lord﴾; it becomes clear to you that the light in the verse is the light of knowledge and the light of faith, and the opposite of knowledge is error.

* We take the benefits. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾ [Az-Zumar 21] to the end. * Among the benefits of this verse: the demonstration of Allah's power in sending down this rain from the sky, since no one can possibly send it down. Allah said: ﴿Indeed, with Allah is the knowledge of the Hour, and He sends down the rain﴾ [Luqman 34].
* And among its benefits: the wisdom and mercy of Allah, in that He made this water descend from the sky. For if it sprang from the earth, the whole earth would not benefit from it in every respect, and it would not reach the mountaintops unless it drowned the people beneath the mountains. So it was part of wisdom that it descends from the sky to cover both the high and the low, and to encompass the whole earth.
* Among the benefits of this verse also: the demonstration of Allah's wisdom regarding the manner of this water's descent. How does it descend? It descends in drops. If it descended in a pour, like the mouths of waterskins pour, it would destroy people and demolish buildings; but by Allah's mercy, it descends in drops.
* Among the benefits of this verse: that "sky" is applied to height, and from this benefit follows that His saying ﴿Are you secure from the One who is in the sky?﴾ [Al-Mulk 16] may be understood to mean the One who is on high.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's power and His mercy toward the servants, in that He made this water flow as springs in the earth, and did not leave it stagnant on its surface, because of the wisdom and mercy in that; it is stored in the earth, and when people want it, they extract it.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the demonstration of Allah's power, in that by this water He brought forth that crop of varying colors.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of causes: ﴿then He brings out thereby﴾, the affirmation of causes.
* Among its benefits: that a cause does not by itself have independent effect upon the caused; this is shown by His saying ﴿then He brings out﴾, where He attributes the bringing out to Allah. This is what the early generations of the Ummah and its imams held: that causes have an effect on their effects, but their effect comes by Allah's action and does not return to them independently.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim, Tafsir of the Noble Qur'an) on surah 39, verses 21–22 (part 2 of 3):**

* Among the benefits of this noble verse is the demonstration of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in that He brings forth this crop of varying colours, although it is nourished by one water and from one soil. This is in His saying: ﴿varying in its colours﴾.
* Among its benefits: the perfection of this world signals its decline, because Allah has struck this as a parable for the worldly life, as in the verse we cited in the tafsir.
* Among the benefits of this verse: those who take heed of the signs of Allah in the cosmos are the people of understanding, whereas whoever does not take heed by them, and says, "This is a nature that interacts and flows along," has no intellect.
* Among the benefits of this verse: a person should employ his intellect in the creatures of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so that he may be reminded by them, either of the benefits of these creatures or of the greatness of the Creator that is in them, because He said: ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder for those of understanding﴾ [Az-Zumar 21].

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord...﴾ [Az-Zumar 22] to the end. In this verse is the negation of equality between the two groups: the one whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam and the one whose breast He has not expanded. This is because the interrogative here carries the meaning of negation.

* Among its benefits: guidance is in the hand of Allah, as in His saying: ﴿Is he whose breast Allah has expanded﴾. And from this benefit it follows that whenever a person knows that guidance is in the hand of Allah, he does not turn, in seeking guidance, except to Allah.

Also, if he knows that guidance is in the hand of Allah, he will not be self-admiring when he is guided, but will say to himself: "Had Allah not guided him, he would have been astray." So he does not say, "I was only given it on account of knowledge I possess," or say, "This is mine," but rather acknowledges the favour of Allah upon him, and that had Allah not guided him, he would not have benefited.
