(...) until the Day of Judgement. We open our summer sessions this year on this day, Saturday, the eighteenth of the month of Muharram in the year one thousand four hundred and thirteen [AH], and we ask Allah, glorified and exalted, to bless our work and our knowledge. Our study is varied: it includes tafsir (exegesis of the Qur'an), hadith, fiqh (jurisprudence), tawhid (monotheism) and usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence), and these are distributed across the days, except for tafsir, hadith and fiqh, for these three are fixed every day.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord? Woe then to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah. Those are in manifest error (22). Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book consistent and repeating; the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver from it; then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah. That is the guidance of Allah; He guides by it whom He wills, and whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide (23). Is one who shields his face with his body from the terrible punishment on the Day of Resurrection [like one who is safe]? And it will be said to the wrongdoers, "Taste what you used to earn" (24). Those before them denied, and the punishment came to them from where they did not perceive (25). So Allah made them taste disgrace in the life of this world, but the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew﴾ [Az-Zumar 22–26].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord﴾. The hamza here is the interrogative particle, and the fa' is a conjunctive particle. The thing conjoined to is what preceded, according to one of the two opinions among the grammarians. It has also been said that the fa' is conjoining to something implied after the hamza, and the implied sense is: "Have you been heedless and so did not perceive this matter? So whoever Allah has expanded his breast to Islam, he is upon a light from his Lord, unlike one who was not so." And we (...).
* Student: ﴿...from before them, so the punishment came to them from where they did not perceive (25). So Allah made them taste disgrace in the life of this world, but the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew﴾ [Az-Zumar 25–26].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord﴾.
* Student: ﴿So Allah made them taste disgrace in the life of this world, but the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew﴾ [Az-Zumar 26].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord﴾ [Az-Zumar 22]. The hamza here is the interrogative, and the fa' is a conjunctive particle, and the thing conjoined to is what preceded, according to one of the two opinions among the grammarians (i'rab scholars).

It has also been said that the fa' is conjoining to something implied after the hamza, and the implied sense is: "Have you been heedless and so did not perceive this matter?"

So whoever Allah has expanded his breast to Islam, he is upon a light from his Lord, unlike one who was not so.

We have a principle: when the grammarians differ on a matter, we follow the easier view, because the matter is one of ijtihad (independent reasoning). If that is so, we hold that the hamza is interrogative, the fa' conjoins to what precedes, and the position of the hamza is after the fa' of conjunction. The implied sense is: fa-aman (so is it the one whom) Allah has expanded his breast to Islam [...].

As for His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Allah has expanded his breast﴾, the word sharaha means widened (wassa'a), and from it comes sharh al-kitab (commentary on a book), because it is widened and spread out.

As for His saying: ﴿Allah has expanded his breast to Islam﴾, the intended "breast" here is the heart, because it is its locus, so it is expressed by it. It may also be said that the intended "breast" is literally the chest, as is evident from the fact that when a person is distressed he finds his chest constricted, as if the millstone were upon him, from the tightness, without realising that this touches his heart. So the expansion here refers to the expansion of the chest itself, and the outcome is one.

As for His saying: ﴿to Islam﴾, it means: for accepting it and committing to it. Islam has two meanings: the first is general, and the second is specific.

The general meaning encompasses everyone who submitted to Allah, the Exalted, by obeying Him (...) while the sharia (revealed law) was in force. It includes everyone who submitted to Allah by obeying Him while the sharia was in force. On this basis, the Jews in the time of Musa were Muslims, and in the time of 'Isa they were disbelievers; the Christians in the time of 'Isa were Muslims, and in the time of Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, they are disbelievers. For this reason we find that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, describes the people of Nuh and those after them as Muslims.

As for the specific meaning of Islam, it is what is specific to the sharia of Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family. So people after the mission of Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, are either Muslims or disbelievers. The Muslims are those who follow the Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, and no one else; this is called specific Islam.

So His saying: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Aal 'Imran 19]: what does it mean? It means the Islam with which Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, was sent. And no one can claim to be a Muslim after the Prophet's mission, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, unless he follows him, because after his mission Islam became specific to those who follow his sharia. So here, ﴿Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam﴾: shall we interpret it by the general meaning or by the specific meaning?

* Students: The specific.
* The Shaykh: If we interpret it by the general meaning, it includes whoever Allah expanded his breast to Islam in the era of the earlier prophets, and whoever Allah expanded his breast to Islam in the era of the Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family. So which do you see?
* Student: The specific.
* Students: The general.
* The Shaykh: The general, because among those who came before, there were those whose breasts Allah expanded to Islam. Musa, peace be upon him, said: ﴿My Lord, expand for me my breast (25), and ease for me my affair﴾ [Ta-Ha 25–26].

However, if the address is directed to the period after the Messenger's mission, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, then it is necessary that the intended meaning be the specific one.

As for His saying: ﴿so he is upon a light from his Lord﴾, the fa' here is conjoining for consequence; meaning: so he, when Allah has expanded his breast, is upon a light from his Lord.

It is an inner light by which a person proceeds upon the sharia of Allah, as if he had a lamp in his hand guiding him to the path, because Allah expanded his breast to Islam, so it does not constrict him.

﴿so he is upon a light from his Lord﴾. There remains the hamza in ﴿Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam﴾, which is interrogative. So where is its counterpart? Its counterpart is what corresponds to it in meaning: that which corresponds in meaning to the expansion of the breast is one whose breast is constricted with Islam. Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam like one whose breast is constricted by it?

The answer: yes or no? That is, is the one whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam equal to the one whose breast is constricted by it? No.

So the counterpart, or the equivalent, if you wish, is omitted, indicated by the context, and the meaning is: "Is he who is in such a state like one who is not in such a state?" The one whom Allah has expanded his breast is not like the one to whom Allah has not expanded his breast. There is no doubt that the difference between them is great, farther than between the heaven and the earth. For the one whom Allah has expanded his breast to Islam, and I ask Allah to make me and you among them, finds himself receptive to the laws of Islam, rejoicing in them. He rejoices when he performs an act of obedience to Allah, and grieves when he commits an act of disobedience to Allah. Those who have reached the utmost in this are distressed by what happens to them of imperfection, even if it was not intentional. That is, if he misses an act of worship, he finds himself in distress and sadness, without being aware of it.

Let me illustrate this with the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. When he ended the prayer after two rak'ahs of the Zuhr prayer, what did he do? He turned from his prayer as if he were distressed. He stood, contrary to his custom, against a wooden post in the qiblah side of the mosque, leaned upon it, and placed his hands like this, as if he were angry. Why? Because his prayer was not complete, so his soul contracted without his being aware of it. But this is due to the perfection of his degree, peace and blessings be upon him, that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, places in a person's soul a contraction, even if he is not aware of it, because he did not complete the worship required of him. He leaned upon it and interlaced his fingers like this, the posture of one who is distressed, until he was reminded [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (482) and Muslim (573/97), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].

So whoever Allah has expanded his breast to Islam finds himself at ease and rejoicing in carrying out the laws of Islam, and conversely, if he neglects any of them or violates one of the prohibitions of Allah.

As for His saying: ﴿so he is upon a light from his Lord; then woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾ [Az-Zumar 22].

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, the commentator (al-Mufassir), said: "(﴿Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam﴾) so he was guided (﴿so he is upon a light from his Lord﴾) like one whose heart is sealed. This is indicated by His saying: (﴿so woe﴾)," and so on to the end.

This is what the author, may Allah have mercy on him, held in his tafsir: that is, he inferred the omitted element from what is mentioned afterward. If we wanted to infer the omitted element from what is mentioned after it, in strict correspondence, we would say: "like one whose heart has hardened," and we would not say "like one whose heart has been sealed," because Allah said: ﴿woe to those hardened﴾. And if you want to deduce the answer from what is mentioned, make it correspond to it, and then we say: "like one who has hardened." However, what we mentioned first is the correct view: that the equivalent is mentioned in contrast to what was stated, so the meaning is: "Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam like one whose breast Allah has constricted from Islam, or like one whose breast Allah has not expanded to Islam?"

﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾. The author said: "﴿So woe﴾." Here, perhaps we will explain or interpret according to what we have, and then return to the author's words, so that our discussion is not cut off.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾. ﴿Woe﴾ is the subject, and ﴿to those hardened﴾ is its predicate: ﴿so woe to those hardened﴾.

And "woe" (al-wayl), according to the preponderant view, is a word of warning (wa'id, threat). It was also said that it is a valley in Hell, but the more correct view is that it is a word of threat. What permitted beginning with it, though it is indefinite (nakirah), is that it is a threat. It may also be said that what permitted beginning with it, though it is indefinite, is that it indicates a severe attribute: meaning, "great woe," or "severe woe," to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah.

As for His saying: ﴿to those whose hearts are hardened﴾, al-qaswah means hardness, to such a degree that when you press something, it does not yield to your pressure, like a stone. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, struck the hardness of the heart with stones, saying: ﴿Then your hearts hardened after that, so they became like stones, or even harder in hardness﴾ [Al-Baqarah 74].

Here the questioner asks: why did He not say "like iron," since iron breaks stones, while stones do not break iron?

The answer to that: we say, iron softens, by what? By heating it in fire. Stones do not soften. Therefore the hardness of hearts was likened to stones.

"Those whose hearts are hardened" means: those that became hard and did not soften to the truth. We ask Allah for well-being.

As for His saying: ﴿against the remembrance of Allah﴾, the "min" (from) has been said to mean "'an" (away from); "hardened from" is like "hardened against". However, the more apparent view is that it retains its own meaning, and that the sense is: their hearts harden from the reminder, instead of what was expected, which is that they should soften. This meaning is supported by His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And when a surah is revealed, some of them say, "Which of you has this increased in faith?" As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice (124). But as for those in whose hearts is disease, it adds defilement to their defilement﴾ [At-Tawbah 124–125]; that is, it increased them in hardness and stiffness.

On this basis we say: "those whose hearts are hardened from the reminder," meaning: whenever Allah is remembered, their hearts harden, contrary to the believer, for whenever Allah is remembered his heart softens. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble before the remembrance of Allah?﴾ [Al-Hadid 16].

﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah; those are in manifest error﴾. ﴿Those﴾ refers to those whose hearts are hardened. He pointed to them with the demonstrative for the distant, to signal their lowliness and the debasement of their rank, because the distant demonstrative sometimes indicates elevation of rank and sometimes indicates debasement of rank.

Thus in His saying: ﴿That is the Book﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2], it indicates elevation of rank, while in His saying here: ﴿those are in manifest error﴾, it indicates debasement of rank.

If someone asks: these meanings differ while the wording is one; what determines which of the two meanings is intended?

We say: the context and the circumstances of the one spoken about determine it, because the context and the indicators each determine what is meant. ﴿Those are in manifest error﴾: ﴿in error﴾ (dalal): the meaning is bewilderment and failure to reach the truth. So these are in error, that is, they are bewildered and have not reached the truth.

And "manifest" (mubin) here may be derived from abana, intransitive, or from abana, transitive. Let us keep together: there are two verbs, bana and abana. Is bana intransitive or transitive?

* Students: Intransitive.
* The Shaykh: Intransitive. You say: "the matter became clear" (bana al-amr), "the morning appeared" (bana al-subh), "the meaning became evident" (bana al-ma'na).

With the hamza, it can be transitive or intransitive, depending on the context. For example, you say: "the dawn became clear" (abana al-fajr), meaning it appeared, that is, it became manifest. And you say: "the man made the truth clear" (abana al-rajul al-haqq), meaning he made it manifest.

So here, ﴿those are in manifest error﴾: is it intransitive or transitive?

* Student: Intransitive.
* The Shaykh: The apparent view is that it is intransitive, that is, in error that is clear and evident.

Let us return to the author's words, may Allah have mercy on him: "(﴿Is he whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam﴾) so he was guided (﴿so he is upon a light from his Lord﴾) like one whose heart is sealed, indicated by (﴿so woe﴾) a word of punishment," and so on to the end.

The author's statement regarding "like one whose heart is sealed" is open to question. If we want to say that the omitted element is indicated by what is mentioned, it must be estimated to correspond to what is mentioned, so we say: "like one whose heart has hardened." That is because the more correct view is what we previously established: that the equivalent is mentioned in meaning as the counterpart of what? Of what is mentioned. So it is said: "whoever Allah has expanded his breast is like one whose breast Allah has not expanded."

Then the author said: (﴿Woe, then, to those whose hearts are hardened﴾ is a word of punishment).

Had he said "a word of warning," it would have been better, because it is a threat. Even in our customary usage today you say "woe to you," meaning you threaten him with this, with whatever you wish.

And His saying: ﴿to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾, i.e., against accepting the Qur'an. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, took the word "dhikr" (remembrance) to mean the Qur'an, and took "min" (مِن, "from") to mean "'an" (عن, "against").

As for "dhikr" meaning the Qur'an, there is no doubt that the Qur'an is a remembrance. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾ [Yasin 69], and He the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and your people﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 44].

However, the better course is to interpret "the remembrance of Allah" here in a more general sense. We say: it certainly refers to the Qur'an, since it is part of the remembrance of Allah, and it also encompasses more than that, such that we say: whenever Allah is mentioned, their hearts harden, whether through the Qur'an or through other than the Qur'an. This is the more correct view.

As for "min" meaning "'an," we have already said that the correct view is that it retains its own meaning.

His saying that "min" replaces "'an" is based on a disputed question between the Kufan and Basran grammarians: when a particle comes in other than its proper place, is it a substitute for a particle that suits the context, or is the verb governing it understood with a meaning that suits the particle? Are you following? Good.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿a spring from which the servants of Allah drink﴾ [Al-Insan 6]. One does not drink *with* a spring; one drinks *from* a spring. Here the grammarians differed: is the "bi" (ب, "with") in the sense of "min" (from), so that one particle stands in for another; or is ﴿yashrabu﴾ (drink) in the sense of "yarwa" (to quench one's thirst), so that the servants of Allah quench their thirst with it, the drinking being implicitly given the meaning of quenching, and quenching includes drinking and something more, it includes drinking and more? On this there is a disagreement between the Kufan and Basran grammarians. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, favours the second view: that the verb is understood with a meaning that suits the particle. Because when we say the verb is understood with another meaning, we gain two benefits: we gain the meaning of what is stated, and the meaning of what is implied. For when you say "yarwa bihā" (they quench their thirst with it), we learn that they drink and also quench their thirst. But if we say "yashrabu bihā" (they drink from it), we gain only one meaning. So implication adds meaning, whereas replacing one particle with another adds no further meaning. Thus the preponderant view in this matter is what Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, held: that the verb is understood with a meaning that suits the particle. ﴿Woe, then, to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾.

The author said: Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Those are in clear error﴾ — "clear" is explanatory). So, is "mubin" (clear) here intransitive or transitive?
* Students: Intransitive.
* The Shaykh: Intransitive.

Then He said: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech, a Book﴾ [Az-Zumar 23]. The benefits, correct?
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: showing that people differ in their acceptance of the truth, and that some accept the truth with open hearts, while others do not.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever Allah has opened his breast to Islam, so that he accepts the truth, is upon a light from Allah.
* Branching from this: an increase in his knowledge, for knowledge is light, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O mankind, there has come to you a proof from your Lord, and We have sent down to you a clear light﴾ [An-Nisa 174].
* Also branching from it, from this same benefit: strength of insight (firasah). Allah the Exalted gives a person insight by which he knows what is in people's hearts from the glances of their faces, and more than that: he infers the unseen from the seen, and Allah gives him conclusions that others do not have. Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned in his book Madarij al-Salikin, in his discussion of insight, remarkable statements of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, concerning his own insight, though he mentioned some things that may not be accepted; but he mentioned much. He supports this with His saying: ﴿so he is upon a light from his Lord﴾.
* This noble verse also indicates that whoever Allah has opened his breast to Islam has a special lordship and special care from Allah. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿from his Lord﴾, for this special lordship is distinct from the general lordship. The lordship of Allah the Exalted over His creation is of two kinds: general and special.
The general is like His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [Al-Fatihah 2].
The special is like the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, about those of understanding who reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾ [Ali 'Imran 191], to the end.
Both kinds are combined in His saying about the magicians of Pharaoh's people: ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun"﴾ [Al-A'raf 121–122]. The first is general, the second is special.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the severe warning for whoever's heart is hardened against the remembrance of Allah, by His saying: ﴿Woe, then, to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾.
* Among its benefits: when you find in your heart a lack of softness toward the remembrance of Allah, then treat your soul, treat it, so that you may be spared this warning. People often complain of this, and we too complain of it. Sometimes the heart hardens and does not soften; it reads the mighty, deterrent verses but is not affected; and sometimes it reads the very same verses and is affected. So if you recognise hardness of heart in yourself, turn to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, ask Him to soften your heart to His remembrance, and prepare yourself for the warning if Allah does not overtake you with His kindness and forgiveness.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: hearts are divided into two kinds: hearts that soften at the remembrance of Allah, and hearts that harden against it.
If someone asks: how can one thing produce two opposite results? Is the question clear? One thing produces two contrary results. We say: this is possible, because the recipient of this thing differs. This is not strange, neither in matters of meaning nor in matters of the senses.
In matters of meaning, as you have seen with the speech of Allah the Mighty and Majestic: just as a person gives a lesson to a group, some of whom devour it, understand it completely, and find it delightful, while others are closed to it and do not understand it; and if one word closes off to them, the whole lesson becomes closed and they are unable to understand. The teacher is one, and the subject is one.
Likewise, we find dates, the well-known date of the palm, eaten by two men: for one it is a sickness, and for the other a nourishment, is that not so? A diabetic who eats dates is harmed by them, while a healthy person is not. We find water flowing over land: one land receives it, drinks it, and grows plants, while another land does not accept it, and the water pours over it without benefit. Likewise, the remembrance of Allah the Mighty and Majestic comes upon a soft heart, and it benefits from it, and upon a hard heart, and it grows harder, and we seek refuge in Allah.
* Among the benefits of this verse: those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah are the opposite of those whose breasts Allah has opened to Islam. Whoever Allah has opened his breast to Islam is upon light, and whoever's heart is hardened against the remembrance of Allah is in clear error.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah have plunged completely into error. From where is this taken?
* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: Because "fi" (في, "in") indicates enclosure, and the container surrounds what is contained. The contained is inside the container. So it is as if these people have been submerged in error, and it has encompassed them as a container encompasses what it holds: ﴿Those are in clear error﴾. We ask Allah for us and for you guidance and light (...).

**Student:** ﴿Those who fear their Lord, then their skins and their hearts soften at the remembrance of Allah. That is the guidance of Allah, by which He guides whom He wills; and whoever Allah sends astray, for him there is no guide. Is one who shields with his face from the evil of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection [like one who is safe]? It will be said to the wrongdoers, "Taste what you used to earn." Those before them denied, so the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive. So Allah made them taste disgrace in the life of this world, but the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew.﴾ [az-Zumar 23–26].

**Shaykh:** In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book consistent with itself, [and] oft-repeated﴾ [az-Zumar 23].

In discussing the previous lesson, what is the meaning of the hamza in His saying: ﴿Then is one whose breast Allah has opened to Islam...﴾?

**Student:** The hamza is the interrogative particle.

**Shaykh:** And the fa'?

**Student:** The fa' is conjunctive (ʿāṭifah).

**Shaykh:** And what is the thing conjoined to?

**Student:** It is said: it is conjoined to what came before. And it is said: it is conjoined to something implied after the hamza.

**Shaykh:** And according to the first view?

**Student:** It is conjoined to what came before.

**Shaykh:** Yes. The hamza is then considered to be placed after the conjunction. And what is the implied construction?

**Student:** Afa-man sharaḥa Allahu ṣadrahu lil-Islām (...).

**Shaykh:** No, that is not the counterpart (muʿādil) that I mean. If we say it is conjoined to what came before, how would the construction be?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** Fa-amman?

**Student:** Fa-amman sharaḥa.

**Shaykh:** Fa-amman sharaḥa Allahu ṣadrahu.

His saying: ﴿so he is upon a light from his Lord﴾. Is the intended light sensory or immaterial?

**Student:** Immaterial.

**Shaykh:** Immaterial. What does it include?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** What is this light? Is it knowledge, or knowledge and something else?

**Student:** Insight and guidance.

**Shaykh:** Good.

**Student:** It makes his breast expansive.

**Shaykh:** No.

**Student:** Knowledge.

**Shaykh:** Knowledge, and what else?

**Student:** Perceptiveness.

**Shaykh:** Perceptiveness and understanding of matters.

His saying: ﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾. What is (min) here?

**Student:** It is said that it means (ʿan), "away from." Or it retains its original meaning, that is, these hearts are hard because of the remembrance of Allah, meaning: due to the remembrance of Allah.

**Shaykh:** Can the remembrance of Allah be a cause of hardness?

**Student:** Yes. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And when a surah is revealed, some of them say, "Which of you has had his faith increased by this?" As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice. But as for those in whose hearts is disease, it has added to them defilement upon their defilement, and they die while they are disbelievers﴾ [at-Tawbah 124–125].

**Shaykh:** Yes.

His saying: ﴿in manifest error﴾. What is the meaning of ﴿mubīn﴾?

**Student:** Clear (bayyin).

**Shaykh:** That is, clear. We mentioned that the verb of mubīn is quadriliteral or triliteral. Which is it?

**Student:** Its verb could be (bāna) or (abāna).

**Shaykh:** Is its verb triliteral or quadriliteral?

**Student:** Triliteral.

**Shaykh:** Triliteral, meaning bāna: the letters bā', alif, nūn. Or quadriliteral?

**Student:** The quadriliteral abāna.

**Shaykh:** Now, is the verb of mubīn, the word we have here, triliteral or quadriliteral? Do you have no knowledge of grammar?

**Student:** Triliteral.

**Shaykh:** What is he saying?

**Students:** Triliteral.

**Shaykh:** Triliteral? Wrong.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** No, mubīn.

**Student:** From the triliteral.

**Shaykh:** From the triliteral? Wrong.

**Student:** From the triliteral and the quadriliteral.

**Shaykh:** Wrong.

**Student:** From the quadriliteral, but it came intransitive.

**Shaykh:** Yes, correct: from the quadriliteral, but it came intransitive. Mubīn is on the pattern mufʿil. It cannot be from the triliteral. Is mukrim (one who honours) from the triliteral or the quadriliteral?

**Student:** Quadriliteral.

**Shaykh:** Quadriliteral. It is the same thing, because mubīn originally was mubyin.

So mubīn is from the quadriliteral. But the quadriliteral comes both intransitive and transitive, unlike the triliteral, which comes only intransitive. Do you understand? Subhan Allah! I had assumed this was completely clear.

Mubīn is from abāna, the quadriliteral. But is abāna intransitive or transitive?

**Students:** Intransitive.

**Shaykh:** Intransitive? No, because abāna comes both intransitive and transitive. You say abāna al-ḥaqqa, meaning "he made the truth manifest," so it is transitive. And you say abāna al-ṣubḥ, meaning "the dawn appeared," so it is intransitive.

Then Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book consistent with itself, [and] oft-repeated﴾. This is the beginning of today's lesson.

﴿Allah has sent down﴾ is a declarative nominal sentence whose beginning is nominal and whose end is verbal.

﴿has sent down the best statement, a Book﴾: nazzala is from the doubled (intensive) form. The expression is sometimes given as anzala, from the quadriliteral with the added hamza.

The scholars differed over whether the two have the same meaning, that is, whether anzala and nazzala have one meaning or different meanings.

The correct view is that they have one meaning, except when there is a contextual indicator. With a contextual indicator, tanzīl (nazzala) refers to something sent down gradually, and inzāl (anzala) refers to something sent down all at once. But this distinction applies only with a contextual indicator. Without one, nazzala and anzala have the same meaning. For this reason Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And We sent down from the sky pure water﴾ [al-Furqan 48], and He says: ﴿And We sent down from the sky blessed water﴾ [Qaf 9]. Both have the same meaning. Similarly in the Qur'an, Allah sometimes says anzalnā and sometimes says nazzalnā, and both have the same meaning. But where there is a contextual indicator, tanzīl means gradual sending down, as in His saying: ﴿And a Qur'an that We have divided so that you may recite it to the people over time﴾, followed by: ﴿and We sent it down in stages﴾ [al-Isra' 106]. Here nazzalnā differs from anzalnā, and means gradual sending down, as shown by His saying: ﴿a Qur'an that We have divided﴾.

He says: ﴿has sent down the best statement, a Book﴾. ﴿Best statement﴾: ﴿aḥsan﴾ is an elative (ism al-tafḍīl) from ḥusn (goodness). Ḥusn includes the goodness of style and the goodness of subject matter.

His saying ﴿aḥsan﴾ includes both: it is best in its style and best in its subject matter.

As for style: it conforms to eloquence in its fullest sense: conciseness where conciseness is appropriate, elaboration where elaboration is appropriate, emphasis where emphasis is appropriate, and omission of emphasis where the context requires that, and so on.

Likewise it is best in subject matter. Its subject matter consists of reports and rulings. The best of reports are the most truthful and the most beneficial in lesson. The best of rulings are the most just and the most upright in serving the interests of the servants. The noble Qur'an includes both kinds of excellence.

What remains is the style. And the subject is ﴿the best statement﴾.

﴿a Book consistent with itself﴾: ﴿kitāban﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for ﴿aḥsan﴾ or an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān). If we treat ﴿kitāban mutashābihan﴾ as one unit, it is an explicative apposition. But if we treat ﴿kitāban﴾ as independent of ﴿mutashābihan﴾, then it is a substitute and not an explicative apposition.

﴿kitāban﴾ means "written," because the pattern fiʿāl often has the meaning of maf'ūl (passive participle). Examples include ghirās (planting, meaning "something planted"), binā' (building, meaning "something built"), kisā' (covering, meaning "something covered with"), firāsh (bedding, "something spread"), and ghiṭā' (covering, "something covered"). Examples of this pattern are numerous in the Arabic language, where fiʿāl comes in the sense of what? Of maf'ūl. Thus ghirās means maghrūs (planted), and binā' means mabnī (built).

﴿kitāban﴾ means "written." Written in what? It is written in three places: in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ), in the scrolls held by the angels, and in the pages in our hands. The noble Qur'an is written in all of these.

His saying ﴿a Book consistent with itself﴾ means that its parts resemble one another. In what respect? In perfection, excellence, and the goodness of its subject matter. You will never find it contradictory, and you will never find it inconsistent. Yet it varies according to the context: sometimes the context calls for brevity, and sometimes it calls for expansion. If we consider the surah "Qul Huwa Allahu Aḥad" and the surah before it, we find a resemblance between them in excellence, since each surah suits its theme or subject. "Qul Huwa Allahu Aḥad" speaks of the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and His names and attributes, so it came in the appropriate style. And "Tabbat Yada Abi Lahab" speaks of a disbelieving man, so it came in the appropriate style. No one should say: where is the resemblance between "Qul Huwa Allahu Aḥad" and "Tabbat Yada Abi Lahab"?

We say: resemblance means that every speech comes in the manner suited to its subject. This is the aspect of resemblance. Is it clear, everyone?

So it is "consistent with itself" in what? In perfection, excellence, and the goodness of its subject. And from perfection and excellence is that speech is suited to its subject: expansion where expansion is called for, summary where summary is called for, detail where detail is called for, and elaboration and lengthening where those are called for, according to what eloquence requires.

He, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿mutashābihan mathānī﴾. ﴿Mathānī﴾ comes from tathniyah (repetition by twos), meaning the Qur'an is ﴿mathānī﴾: twofold, that is, in pairs.

Mathānī means that it pairs a meaning with its opposite. Reflect on the noble verses and you will find that when the Fire is mentioned, the Garden is mentioned after it. When the people of the Fire are mentioned, the people of the Garden are mentioned after them, and so on. This is so that the listener does not become bored with one topic, and so that he moves from warning to encouragement, becoming eager to perform obligations and cautious about committing prohibitions. This is one of the methods of complete or perfect eloquence.

﴿mathānī, the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver at it﴾: ﴿taqshaʿirru﴾ means they tremble when they hear verses of threat and warning. They tremble, fear, and are agitated. Some of the early generation (salaf) would fall ill for days until people visited them when they heard certain verses. This happened to the Commander of the Believers, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him), when he recited His saying: ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is to occur, there is none to avert it﴾ [at-Tur 7–8]. He fell ill for days until the people visited him.

His saying: ﴿the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver at it﴾. ﴿Those who fear﴾ means they fear Him while knowing His greatness and majesty, because khashyah (awe-fear) occurs only with knowledge. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge truly fear Allah﴾ [Fatir 28]. The scholars distinguished between khashyah and khawf (fear) in several respects:

First: khashyah is accompanied by knowledge.

Second: khashyah arises from the greatness of the one feared, even if the one who fears is himself great.

Khawf, on the other hand, arises from the weakness of the one who fears, even if the thing feared is not great. These are two differences between khashyah and khawf: khashyah is with knowledge, while khawf may be with delusion. A person may see a shadow from afar and fear it, though it is nothing. And the second difference: khashyah arises from what? From the greatness of the one feared, even if the one who fears is great. But the one feared is greater. Khawf arises from the weakness of the one who fears, even if the thing feared is not great.

﴿those who fear their Lord﴾: His saying ﴿yakhshawna rabbahum﴾ refers to this lordship, which is a special lordship. Allah has bestowed favour upon them through the khashyah He placed in their hearts.

﴿those who fear their Lord, then their skins and their hearts soften at the remembrance of Allah﴾: ﴿talīnu﴾ comes after the shivering or trembling. ﴿talīnu﴾ means they become calm and tranquil. ﴿ilā dhikri Allah﴾ means they are submissive toward His remembrance, so this softening has as its aim the remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿That is the guidance of Allah, by which He guides whom He wills﴾: it is possible that the referent of "that" is what they experience of khashyah. In this case the guidance intended is the guidance of tawfīq (divine enablement), because khashyah is an action. It is also possible that the referent of "that" is ﴿the guidance of Allah﴾, namely the Book which is the best statement. In this case the guidance is the guidance of indication (dalālah), because the Book guides, meaning indicates. And enablement is in whose hand? In the hand of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿That is the guidance of Allah, by which He guides whom He wills, and whoever Allah sends astray, for him there is no guide﴾. In this conditional sentence Allah makes clear that whoever He decrees to be astray, no one can guide him.

His saying ﴿fa-mā lahu min hād﴾: its original form is hādī, with a yā'. But the yā' was dropped because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters. Where are the two unvocalized letters? The tanwīn on the dāl and the unvocalized yā' that was dropped. It is permissible to retain it, so one could say hādī, but it is often dropped for lightness and to avoid the meeting of two unvocalized letters.

Let us return to the words of the author, may Allah have mercy on him. He says: (﴿Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book﴾ is a substitute for ﴿the best﴾, that is, the Qur'an.)

His saying: (a substitute for ﴿the best﴾). We have already passed that it may be a substitute or an explicative apposition, on condition that what follows is connected to it: ﴿a Book consistent with itself﴾. This is because an explicative apposition clarifies what it is attached to, which is why it is called ʿaṭf bayān. It can only clarify if we treat ﴿mutashābihan﴾ as a necessary (lāzimah) attribute.

His saying: (i.e., the Qur'an). Is this explanation verbal or meaningful?

**Student:** Verbal.

**Shaykh:** When we want to explain verbally, we bring the same word. When we explain by meaning, we bring the meaning. Here, did he give the same word, saying "kitāban, i.e., maktūban," or did he give the meaning?

**Students:** The meaning.

**Shaykh:** The meaning. So what is intended by "book" here is the Qur'an. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, explained it by meaning, that is, he explained it by what is intended.

﴿consistent with itself﴾: he said: (i.e., resembling one another in arrangement and other respects). By arrangement is not meant what is opposed to prose, since the Qur'an is not poetry. Rather, it means the composition and organization of speech, such that its parts resemble one another.

He says: ﴿mathānī﴾ ("it is repeated in it with promise and threat and other things"). That is, promise is mentioned and then followed by threat. The Fire is mentioned and then followed by the Garden. The attributes of the believers are mentioned and then the attributes of others. Consider His saying: ﴿Allah is the ally of those who believe﴾ [al-Baqarah 257]. Who is their opposite? Those who disbelieve: ﴿and those who disbelieve, their allies are the tāghūt﴾ [al-Baqarah 257]. And consider His saying: ﴿Among them are the wretched and the blessed﴾ [Hud 105]. And consider His saying: ﴿On the Day when some faces will be brightened and some faces will be darkened﴾ [Ali ʿImran 106]. And consider His saying in Surat al-Kahf, when He mentioned the reward of the believers in the Garden, He mentioned the punishment of the disbelievers in the Fire. Examples of this are very numerous.

﴿the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver﴾: the author said: (﴿taqshaʿirru﴾ means they tremble when His threat is mentioned).

﴿the skins of those who fear their Lord﴾: (who fear their Lord).

His saying: ﴿the skins shiver at it﴾ means at the mention of the threat, or the mention of the Fire, or whatever causes fear and alarm, such as the mention of what befell the people of Noah, the people of Lot, and others.

Then he says: (﴿yakhshawna﴾ means they fear). This explanation is weak, because it explains the meaning by something less than it. We have said that khashyah is fear accompanied by knowledge, and we cited as evidence His saying: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge truly fear Allah﴾ [Fatir 28]. If the author had said: "They fear their Lord with a fear founded on knowledge of His greatness," the explanation would have been correct. But as it stands, we consider the explanation deficient.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verse 23 (part 2 of 3):**

(﴿ثُمَّ تَلِينُ﴾: tatma'inn), i.e. they become calm. Yet there is no doubt that mentioning softness (*lin*) is more eloquent than mentioning tranquillity (*tuma'ninah*), because goosebumps (*qash'a'rirah*) entail the skin rising, lifting and becoming rigid, and what is opposite to that is softness, calm and tranquillity. So the author's explanation of softness as tranquillity is, in reality, an explanation by a necessary consequence. Otherwise, softness is not the same as tranquillity, because when the skin rises in goosebumps it becomes stiff. This is why you find that a person's extremities become cold, as the blood recedes from them to some extent. When the fright subsides, the skin softens and that stiffness goes away.

﴿ثُمَّ تَلِينُ جُلُودُهُمْ وَقُلُوبُهُمْ إِلَى ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ﴾. The softening of the heart is the opposite of its hardness. That is, when they hear the threat, the skins shiver and the hearts recoil; then afterwards the skins and hearts soften ﴿إِلَى ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ﴾ (towards the remembrance of God). The author said: (i.e., at the mention of His promise). However, the correct view is that it refers to the remembrance of God in general, including the threat: when a person reflects and his soul calms down after something that frightened him has come upon him, he softens even at the threat.

So the author's restriction of this to the mention of the promise has some weakness in it. Nevertheless, it has a basis if the Qur'an is (*mathani*, oft-repeated), so that when the mention of Hell comes and is followed by the mention of Paradise, the hearts soften; or when the mention of the people of Hell is followed by the mention of the people of Paradise, the hearts also soften.

As for His words ﴿إِلَى ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ﴾, He did not say ﴿لِذِكْرِ اللَّهِ﴾ (for the remembrance of God) but rather ﴿إِلَى﴾ (towards). It is as if this softening has reached a refuge, namely the remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

As for His words ﴿إِلَى ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ﴾, is it an idafah of the verbal noun to its subject, meaning towards what God has reminded them of; or an idafah of the verbal noun to its object, meaning towards their remembrance of God?

The answer: it is both. The expression is suitable for both: towards their remembrance of God, or towards what God has reminded them of, which is the Qur'an that God has made oft-repeated.

﴿ذَلِكَ هُدَى اللَّهِ﴾: ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ means (the Book). ﴿هُدَى اللَّهِ يَهْدِي بِهِ مَنْ يَشَاءُ﴾ (This is the guidance of God; He guides thereby whomever He wills). The author, may God have mercy on him, informed us that the demonstrative in His words ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ refers to the Book. On this basis, the guidance meant here is the guidance of indication (*hidayat al-dalalah*), for the Qur'an is guidance in the sense that it indicates every good, indeed every thing, as He, Exalted, says: ﴿وَنَزَّلْنَا عَلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ تِبْيَانًا لِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ (And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things) [al-Nahl 89].

As for His words ﴿يَهْدِي بِهِ﴾, here the guidance is the guidance of indication and of divine enabling (*tawfiq*), because it is attributed to God, Exalted, and God, Glorified and Exalted, holds both kinds of guidance. The *ba'* in His words ﴿يَهْدِي بِهِ﴾ the author did not explain, but its meaning is causation, i.e., by means of ﴿مَنْ يَشَاءُ﴾ (whomever He wills).

﴿وَمَنْ يُضْلِلِ اللَّهُ فَمَا لَهُ مِنْ هَادٍ﴾ (And whomever God leaves to stray, for him there is no guide). * In this verse there are benefits:
* First: affirmation that the Qur'an was sent down from God; by His words ﴿اللَّهُ نَزَّلَ أَحْسَنَ الْحَدِيثِ﴾ (God has sent down the best of speech).
* Second: affirmation of God's exaltedness. Its basis: since the Qur'an is His speech, and the description of the Qur'an as sent down indicates that the one who speaks it is exalted. God's exaltedness is divided into two types: exaltedness of essence (*'uluw al-dhat*) and exaltedness of attributes (*'uluw al-sifat*). As for exaltedness of attributes, it is agreed upon among the People of the Sunnah and the People of innovation. As for exaltedness of essence, it is disputed. The People of the Sunnah believe that God, Exalted, is high above His creation in His essence, while the people of negation (*ta'til*) deny this, and they then divided into two groups:
One group said: He is in every place in His essence, and He is not above the heavens. Rather He is above the heavens, in the heavens, on the earth, in houses, in mosques, in markets, and in everything. The situation reached some of them to the point that they said He indwells even bodies, even humans, even dogs, even donkeys, may God protect us. These are the indwelling (*hululiyyah*) of the Jahmiyyah, who opened the door to the doctrine of incarnation and unity of existence (*hulul al-ittihad*).
The second group said: God is not described with height or descent. He is neither above the world nor below it, neither connected to the world nor separated from it, neither inside the world nor outside it. This is pure negation (*ta'til mahd*). Isn't it so?

For this reason some scholars said: If we were told, "Describe for us non-existence," we would find no more precise description than this: non-existence is that which is neither inside the world nor outside it, neither above nor below, neither connected nor separated.

For this reason Mahmud ibn Subuktakin, may God have mercy on him, said to Ibn Furak, saying to him: "Explain to us your Lord, if you describe Him with this description. Where is the Lord you worship?" And he spoke truly. So those who deny the exaltedness of essence have divided into two groups, to what?
* Students: Two groups.
* The Shaykh: The indwellers (*hululiyyah*), and the pure negators (*mu'attilah ta'til mahd*).
* A student: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (52), and Muslim (1599/107), from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir.]] Here the text mentioned the softening of the skins and the softening of the hearts. What is the benefit of the softening of the skins?
* The Shaykh: I say: there is no objection to saying that my heart and my deeds have become sound.
* The student: There is no objection, but...
* The Shaykh: This too is not objectionable. Also, because God described the skins themselves, saying ﴿تَقْشَعِرُّ مِنْهُ جُلُودُ﴾ (the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver therefrom). The shivering of the skins is based on the fear of the heart. So God mentioned that this shivering goes away and turns into softness, and likewise the heart, which is its origin.
* A student: The words of the Exalted: ﴿تَقْشَعِرُّ مِنْهُ جُلُودُ الَّذِينَ يَخْشَوْنَ رَبَّهُمْ﴾. Shaykh al-Islam blamed those who, i.e., swoon upon hearing the verses.
* The Shaykh: He blamed them?
* The student: And he mentioned that the Companions, may God be pleased with them, were not like that.
* The Shaykh: Yes. There is a difference between the shivering of the skin and the one who swoons. The one who swoons loses consciousness.
* The student: The desired fear.
* The Shaykh: No. The desired fear is that which a person has through knowledge of God, His greatness, and fear of Him. As for one who is unable to bear what has come upon his heart until he swoons and dies, or acts like a madman, there are also people who are the opposite: their skins do not shiver, but you find him saying, "Allah, Allah, Allah," sitting and jerking about. Is that correct or not? I say: is this action good?
* Students: No.
* The Shaykh: Not at all. This contradicts what the early generations (*salaf*) followed. For this reason, among the Sufis there is a litany they call the *Ghubayrah*. They come with whips, then sit in circles. Then the one who remembers God speaks, and when he shouts "There is no god but God" and "Glory be to God," they strike the ground with the whips. The best of them is the one who raises the most dust, because he has strong and intense emotion. They call this the *Ghubayrah*. I think some of them say to one another: "Have you raised dust today?"
* A student: Shaykh, does ﴿مَثَانِيَ﴾ not allow that it means that by it the mention of threat, the mention of tawhid, the narratives, and the prophets are repeated?
* The Shaykh: No, it is general.
* A student: The words ﴿ثُمَّ تَلِينُ جُلُودُهُمْ وَقُلُوبُهُمْ﴾: O Shaykh, is there a metaphor (*majaz*) in the softening of the hearts, I mean according to those who say so?
* The Shaykh: Not at all, there is no metaphor in it.
* The student: But is the matter sensory or non-sensory?
* The Shaykh: No, it is non-sensory.
* The student: Then the non-sensory matter was taken from the sensory matter.
* The Shaykh: No, it was not taken from it, because the softness of the heart, which is the softness of texture, is not intended here. The apparent heart does not stand and become rigid like the skin. Apparently. If it does stand and become rigid, this should be asked of the anatomists. If they say that under fear it becomes rigid, then the softness becomes sensory (...).
* * *
* A student: ﴿أَفَمَنْ يَتَّقِي بِوَجْهِهِ سُوءَ الْعَذَابِ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ وَقِيلَ لِلظَّالِمِينَ ذُوقُوا مَا كُنْتُمْ تَكْسِبُونَ (٢٤) كَذَّبَ الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ فَأَتَاهُمُ الْعَذَابُ مِنْ حَيْثُ لَا يَشْعُرُونَ (٢٥) فإذاقَهُمُ اللَّهُ الْخِزْيَ فِي الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا وَلَعَذَابُ الْآخِرَةِ أَكْبَرُ لَوْ كَانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ (٢٦) وَلَقَدْ ضَرَبْنَا لِلنَّاسِ فِي هَذَا الْقُرْآنِ مِنْ كُلِّ مَثَلٍ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَذَكَّرُونَ﴾ [al-Zumar 24-27] (Is one who shields his face from the terrible punishment on the Day of Resurrection [like one who is secure]? And it will be said to the wrongdoers: "Taste what you used to earn." Those before them denied, and the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive. So God made them taste disgrace in the life of this world, but the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew. And We have certainly presented for mankind in this Qur'an every kind of example, that they might remember).
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in God from Satan the accursed. God, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿اللَّهُ نَزَّلَ أَحْسَنَ الْحَدِيثِ كِتَابًا مُتَشَابِهًا مَثَانِيَ﴾ (God has sent down the best statement, a Book consistent and repeated).
What is the meaning of His words ﴿مُتَشَابِهًا﴾?
* A student: It resembles its parts to one another.
* The Shaykh: In what?
* The student: It resembles its parts to one another in style and (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, in perfection and excellence. All of it is perfect, all of it is excellent, all of it is eloquent.
What is the meaning of ﴿مَثَانِيَ﴾?
* A student: When Paradise is mentioned, Hell is mentioned, a repetition.
* The Shaykh: Matters and things are repeated in it: when Paradise is mentioned, Hell is mentioned; the promise and the threat; the believer and the disbeliever.
What is the meaning of His words ﴿تَقْشَعِرُّ مِنْهُ جُلُودُ الَّذِينَ يَخْشَوْنَ رَبَّهُمْ﴾?
* A student: The skins of those who believed recoil and rise.
* The Shaykh: From what? From joy or from something else?
* The student: At the mention of the threat.
* The Shaykh: That is, out of fear and awe.
His words ﴿ذَلِكَ هُدَى اللَّهِ﴾: what is meant by it?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The shivering of the skins, then the softening of the hearts and skins towards the remembrance of God, is the guidance of divine enabling.
His words ﴿مَنْ يُضْلِلِ اللَّهُ فَمَا لَهُ مِنْ هَادٍ﴾: what is its meaning?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Whoever is astray in God's knowledge, no one can guide him.
* We will take the benefits of this verse, since we have not taken them yet. God, Exalted, said: ﴿اللَّهُ نَزَّلَ أَحْسَنَ الْحَدِيثِ﴾. Its explanation has already been given, I think one or two benefits: that the Qur'an...?
* A student: Was sent down from God.
* The Shaykh: Was sent down from God.
* A student: Affirmation of exaltedness.
* The Shaykh: And affirmation of exaltedness.
It is known that * there branches from the first benefit: that the Qur'an is the speech of God, if it is sent down from Him. The Qur'an is the speech of God, Mighty and Majestic, in wording and meaning. He spoke it in wording and meaning, and it is with Him, Mighty and Majestic. This is contrary to the Ash'ariyyah, who say: speech is the meaning subsisting in the soul, not a sound that is heard nor letters that are seen, but a meaning subsisting in itself.
What is written in the mushafs or heard by ears is an expression of God's speech, not God's speech itself. The truth is that their statement implies the denial of speech to God, Mighty and Majestic, because they say: this Qur'an that we hear now is created, an expression of God's speech, and it is not God's speech. God's speech is only the meaning subsisting in Himself.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that this Qur'an is the best speech, by His words ﴿أَحْسَنَ الْحَدِيثِ﴾. Likewise, God's speech is the best speech. God, Exalted, said: ﴿وَمَنْ أَصْدَقُ مِنَ اللَّهِ حَدِيثًا﴾ (And who is more truthful in statement than God?) [al-Nisa' 87].
* Among the benefits of this verse: that the Qur'an is written, by His word ﴿كِتَابًا﴾ (a Book). It has already been mentioned that it is written in?
* Students: In three places.
* The Shaykh: In three places: the Preserved Tablet, the scrolls in the hands of the angels, and the scrolls in our hands.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Qur'an is consistent (*mutashabih*), by His words ﴿مُتَشَابِهًا﴾. Then one must reconcile this verse with His words: ﴿هُوَ الَّذِي أَنْزَلَ عَلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ مِنْهُ آيَاتٌ مُحْكَمَاتٌ هُنَّ أُمُّ الْكِتَابِ وَأُخَرُ مُتَشَابِهَاتٌ﴾ (It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are precise, which are the foundation of the Book, and others that are allegorical) [Al 'Imran 7]. That is this verse. God made the Qur'an of two kinds: precise (*muhkam*) and consistent (*mutashabih*). In the verse in al-Zumar He made it one kind, consistent.
The reconciliation between them is to say: the consistency mentioned in al-Zumar is not the consistency mentioned in Al 'Imran. The consistency in al-Zumar is that its parts resemble one another in perfection and excellence. The consistency mentioned in Al 'Imran is the ambiguity and obscurity of meaning. In this respect the Qur'an divides into two kinds: precise, i.e., clear in meaning; and consistent, i.e., obscure in meaning. Have you understood?
So the reconciliation is that we say: the consistency in Al 'Imran is other than the consistency in al-Zumar. The consistency in al-Zumar is that some of it resembles some of it; all the Qur'an is consistent. As for Al 'Imran, it is obscurity: ﴿مُتَشَابِهَاتٌ﴾ means obscure in meaning. So the Qur'an is partly precise, clear, and partly consistent, which none knows except those firm in knowledge.
In some verses the Qur'an is described as wise, without mention of consistency, such as His words: ﴿الر تِلْكَ آيَاتُ الْكِتَابِ الْحَكِيمِ﴾ (Alif. Lam. Ra. These are the verses of the wise Book) [Yunus 1]. This means precise and perfected, free of contradiction. It is the opposite of the consistent. The precise that is free of contradiction, pause on this. So the Qur'an is described as entirely precise, entirely consistent, and partly precise and partly consistent. Its description as entirely precise means that all of it is precise, perfected, free of contradiction: ﴿وَلَوْ كَانَ مِنْ عِنْدِ غَيْرِ اللَّهِ لَوَجَدُوا فِيهِ اخْتِلَافًا كَثِيرًا﴾ (Had it been from other than God, they would have found in it much contradiction) [al-Nisa' 82].
Its description as entirely consistent means that some of it resembles some of it in perfection and excellence. Its description as partly precise and partly consistent means that some of it is clear in meaning and some of it is obscure in meaning. Done.
An example of the clear in meaning: the heaven, the earth, the stars, the sun, the moon, man, and the like. This is clear.
An example of the consistent: there are two verses whose apparent meanings conflict, such as His words: ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ يَوَدُّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا وَعَصَوُا الرَّسُولَ لَوْ تُسَوَّى بِهِمُ الْأَرْضُ وَلَا يَكْتُمُونَ اللَّهَ حَدِيثًا﴾ (On that Day those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish the earth were leveled over them, and they will not conceal from God any statement) [al-Nisa' 42]. And in another verse: ﴿ثُمَّ لَمْ تَكُنْ فِتْنَتُهُمْ إِلَّا أَنْ قَالُوا وَاللَّهِ رَبِّنَا مَا كُنَّا مُشْرِكِينَ﴾ (Then their trial will be only that they will say: "By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists") [al-An'am 23]. How do you reconcile them? In the latter they deny, and in the former they do not conceal God any statement? Then a person comes and says: I do not know the point of contradiction. But those firm in knowledge know how to reconcile this with that.
The reconciliation: the Day of Resurrection has states for people, for it is a day whose length is fifty thousand years. Sometimes they conceal, and sometimes they confess: ﴿وَلَا يَكْتُمُونَ اللَّهَ حَدِيثًا﴾.
Likewise God mentioned that He gathers the criminals on the Day of Resurrection blue-eyed (*zurqan*), and He said: ﴿يَوْمَ تَبْيَضُّ وُجُوهٌ وَتَسْوَدُّ وُجُوهٌ﴾ (On the Day when faces will turn white and faces will turn black) [Al 'Imran 106]. How do we reconcile this? Once He says "blackened" and once "blue" [Ta-Ha 102]?
The answer: some of them are like this and some like that; or at one time they are blue and at another time black; or the dark blue tends toward black, so it is called black; or the blueness is in their eyes and the blackness is in the rest of the body; and similar things.
The point is that those firm in knowledge know how to reconcile, but others find it obscure.
For this reason the scholars say: the Qur'an is described as consistent in a general sense, and as precise in a general sense, and it is described as partly precise and partly consistent, and the reconciliation is as you have heard.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Qur'an has reached the utmost perfection of eloquence, by its coming in oft-repeated form.
* Branching from this benefit: whoever speaks to people in exhortation should not give only unrestricted encouragement (*targhib*), nor only unrestricted warning (*tarhib*). This is because if he gives only encouragement, he leads them to hope and they become careless; and if he gives only warning, he leads them to despair and they despair of God's mercy. So what is fitting for a person who speaks with people in exhortations is that he should always speak sometimes with this and sometimes with that, so as not to lead people to despair or to a hope that necessitates feeling secure from God's plan.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the believer is affected by the Qur'an; his skin shivers from it and he fears, then afterwards tranquillity and softness of heart return to him.
* Branching from this benefit: if you find yourself not in this state, know that your faith is weak, because this report is the report of whom? The report of God, Mighty and Majestic. Its report cannot fail. So every believer's skin shivers at what he hears of the noble Qur'an in its threats. If you are not like that, then your faith is weak.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: remembrance of Allah, mighty and majestic, is a cause of the softening of hearts and their tranquility; His saying: ﴿their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah﴾. The verse's support for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah. Verily, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest﴾ [Ar-Ra'd 28].

Another benefit of the noble verse: Allah, mighty and majestic, bestows favour upon these people with guidance; His saying: ﴿That is the guidance of Allah; He guides thereby whom He wills﴾.

Another of its benefits: the affirmation of causes (asbab); His saying: ﴿He guides thereby﴾, where the particle bi (ب) indicates causation, as has passed with us in the exegesis. And the affirmation of causes is what agrees with both transmitted proof (al-manqul) and reason (al-ma'qul). As for transmitted proof, there are many verses affirming causes: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky, and the earth becomes green?﴾ [Al-Hajj 63]; ﴿He sends down water from the sky, and the valleys flow according to their measure﴾ [Ar-Ra'd 17]; ﴿And We send down from the sky blessed water, and We produce thereby gardens and grain of harvest﴾ [Qaf 9]; and the verses on this are numerous.

Reason likewise indicates the affirmation of causes, and that they have an effect upon their effects. We all know that striking glass with a stone breaks it, and that the glass broke by the striking of the stone. This is in contrast to those who deny causes and say: there is no effect of causes upon their effects. Their statement contradicts the Sharia and contradicts reason, to the extent that it was said to them: Does paper not burn by fire? They said: No, it burns at the fire, not by the fire. And it was said to them: Does glass not break when a stone is thrown at it? They said: No, it breaks at the stone, not by the stone. Why? They said: Because if we affirm the effect of causes on their causes, we would be associating partners with Allah and making with Him an agent with effect, and no one is content to associate anything with Allah.

Our answer to this doubt is to say: causes do not have effect by their own essence; rather, they have effect by the powers Allah has placed in them.

The evidence for this is that Allah said to the fire of Ibrahim: ﴿O fire, be cool and safe﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 69]; and it became cool and safe and did not burn. So when we say that these effects that follow causes are only by the effective powers Allah has placed in these causes, we have not associated partners with Allah.

Others went to extremes from another direction, saying: causes have effect by their own essence. We know that if a stone is hurled at glass, it breaks it by itself. But these are the ones who made partners with Allah. We say: if Allah willed that this stone not break the glass, it would not break it, just as when Allah willed that the fire not burn Ibrahim, it did not burn him. So the People of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah are a middle path between these two extremist groups: the one that exaggerates causes, and the one that exaggerates the will of Allah. We say: causes are effective, but by the will of Allah.

Another benefit of this noble verse: the affirmation that guidance is by the will of Allah; His saying: ﴿He guides thereby whom He wills﴾. This verse is one instance of many proofs showing that the act of the servant occurs by the will of Allah. Among them is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for whoever among you wills to be upright. And you do not will except that Allah wills﴾ [At-Takwir 28-29]. On this matter there has occurred a great and very intense conflict among three groups: two extremist groups and one moderate group.

The two extremist groups: one said: man wills his deed and Allah has no connection with it; man is free and acts as he wills, and Allah has no intervention in it at all. He guides himself and he misguides himself. They said: Were it not so, Allah's punishment of the disobedient would be injustice, and His reward to the obedient would be pointless; for if you say man is not free, then he is managed, and the one who is managed is not praised for good nor blamed for evil. And it is known that Allah, exalted is He, ordained blame for the disobedient and praise for the obedient, so this shows that the act of the servant is an independent act.

As for the other extremists, they said: man has no will, no power, and no choice in his act; rather he is compelled to it, unable to oppose it. He is forced, he eats by compulsion, drinks by compulsion, advances by compulsion, and delays by compulsion, and he has no choice in any state. Allah's punishment of the wrongdoer is not injustice even though the wrongdoer acts without his choice, because Allah's punishment of him is a disposal in His own dominion, and Allah, mighty and majestic, does what He wills, with none to repel His judgment.

Thus the argument of the first party does not confront us, which said: if man were not fully free, then punishing the disobedient would be injustice and rewarding the obedient would be futile.

We say: punishing the wrongdoer is not injustice even if he is compelled, why? Because Allah is its owner, and He does in it what He wills, just as you do in your property what you will: you demolish the house, you build the house, you sell the car and buy its replacement, and the like. These latter are the Jabriyya (Compulsionists), and the first party are called the Qadariyya (Predestinarians). The first party was named Qadariyya because they deny the decree (qadar) of Allah concerning the act of the servant, and these were named Jabriyya because they hold that the servant is compelled in his deed.

To these people, the one who descends the ladder slowly and calmly step by step is equal to the one who is pushed from the top of the ladder until he falls on his face. They say: all are equal, all are compelled.

As for the People of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah, they took a middle position on this and said: we affirm the evidences showing that everything occurs by the will of Allah, and we affirm the evidences showing that man has choice and will, and thereby we reconcile the evidences.

So we say: the act of the servant occurs by his will, but his will is under the will of Allah. When I will something, I know that Allah willed it. When I will something, I know that Allah willed it, and I cannot know that Allah willed something except after it occurs, since the decree of Allah is hidden, a secret hidden from us, but when it occurs we know that Allah willed it. I do not will except what Allah wills, yet at the same time I have the freedom to will what I will, except that I believe that this will of mine was by the will of Allah.

This is supported by the fact that a person sometimes resolves to do something, and while he is inclined toward it, his resolve is diverted to another direction, or to cancelling the act. Do you not perceive this? So there is an authority above my authority, but this authority is not known; it is known only by its effects.

It was said to a Bedouin: By what did you know your Lord? He said: By the breaking of resolutions and the turning of aspirations. A Bedouin answered with this wondrous answer: I knew my Lord by the breaking of resolutions, meaning: I resolve upon a thing, then my resolve breaks without cause; and the turning of aspirations: I am intent on something to the right, then I find myself turned to the left without cause except from Allah, mighty and majestic.

However, I believe that this will of mine was by the will of Allah. This is supported by the fact that a person sometimes resolves to do something, and while he is inclined toward it, his resolve is diverted to another direction or to cancelling the act. Do you not perceive this? So there is an authority above my authority, but this authority is not known; it is known only by its effects.

It was said to a Bedouin: By what did you know your Lord? He said: By the breaking of resolutions and the turning of aspirations. A Bedouin answered with this wondrous answer: I knew my Lord by the breaking of resolutions; I resolve upon a thing, then my resolve breaks without cause, and the turning of aspirations: I am intent on something to the right, then I find myself turned to the left without cause except from Allah, mighty and majestic.

So the People of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah say: man wills and chooses, and is not compelled, but whatever he wills is after the will of Allah. We know that this is by the will of Allah, and this is what the soul is at rest with, and what the evidences agree upon.

If someone says: then the saying of the polytheists would be: ﴿Had Allah willed, we would not have worshipped besides Him anything, neither we nor our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything besides Him﴾ [An-Nahl 35]; for when we worshipped other than Allah, we knew that Allah willed that, and we have no power to oppose the will. What do you say about this argument? It is a fallacious argument, refuted by Allah, mighty and majestic, and refuted by reason. Allah refuted it by His saying: ﴿Thus did those before them deny until they tasted Our might﴾ [Al-An'am 148]; and in another verse: ﴿Thus did those before them act; so is there upon the messengers except clear delivery?﴾ [An-Nahl 35]. Allah refuted it.

Since Allah refuted it by the Sharia, we look: is it also false by reason? We say: it is also false by reason, because you did not know that Allah had decreed upon you the worship of idols except after the worship. Why did you not turn away from worshipping idols and estimate that Allah had decreed upon you the abandonment of idol worship? Why did you not do so? Your proceeding to worship idols while you did not know that Allah had written that is from you, and you are the one who willed it. And if you had estimated the better and the best, and that Allah had decreed for you to be a monotheist avoiding idol worship, that would have come about for you. Is it clear?

Then we say: there is also a sensory proof: if a person is given a choice between two things, one of which is better than the other, what does he choose? He chooses the better. Could a person choose the worse and say: this is what was decreed for me? Never. If it were said to him: there are two roads to Makkah, one safe and one dangerous, and he said: we will take the dangerous road because Allah has written this for us, is that possible or not? It is impossible, never; he will certainly take the safe road.

If two jobs were offered to him, for example, one of the two jobs is arduous and its wage is small, and the second is light and its wage is large, what does he choose?

* A student: The second.

* The Shaykh: He chooses the second without doubt. These are sensory proofs showing that invoking divine decree (al-qadar) as an excuse for sins or for abandoning obligations is an invalid argument that does not hold, neither by the Sharia, nor by reason, nor by the senses. This is the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah. They say: we act by our choice, but our choice, we know that Allah has chosen it for us before we chose it ourselves; yet we have no argument in saying: this is what Allah chose for us, so we cannot escape it. For at the time of the act we do not know what was decreed, and no person can know that Allah decreed something except after it occurs. This is why Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [As-Saff 5], making them the cause of that.

* Also among the benefits of the verse: a person should, and this is a benefit of conduct, turn to Allah alone in seeking guidance; His saying: ﴿He guides thereby whom He wills﴾ [Az-Zumar 23]. So do not rely on yourself and perish; rely on your Lord, and always turn to Him in asking for guidance until Allah guides you. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, who was the guide and the guided, used to begin his prayer, saying: "O Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You judge between Your servants concerning that in which they differed; guide me to the truth in what they differed about, by Your permission, for You guide whom You will to a straight path"[[Recorded by Muslim (770/200) from the hadith of 'A'isha.]]. This is the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, so how about us? So turn to your Lord in seeking guidance; do not rely on yourself, rely on Allah, mighty and majestic, for Allah, exalted is He, is your final return.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: whomever Allah misguides, there is no guide for him; His saying: ﴿And whomever Allah misguides, for him there is no guide﴾ [Az-Zumar 23]; and in another verse: ﴿And whomever Allah guides, for him there is no misleader﴾ [Az-Zumar 37].

If someone says: does this ruling not oblige us to cease calling people to the truth, since Allah said: ﴿And whomever Allah misguides, for him there is no guide﴾ [Az-Zumar 23]?

The answer: it does not oblige this; the benefit of it is that when we call someone to the truth and he does not accept, we do not destroy ourselves on his account. Rather we say: Allah has decreed misguidance upon him, and we have no responsibility for his affair. This is why we find Allah, mighty and majestic, saying to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 3], meaning: destroying.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 3].

* The student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: No, ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 3] in (Ta-Sin-Mim), ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers﴾, meaning: destroying yourself that they do not become believers. Do not destroy yourself. Allah sent down consolation to him when he called his uncle Abu Talib and he was not guided. He said: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [Al-Qasas 56].

Thus such a ruling should not prevent us from calling to Allah; but when we call to Allah and do not find people guided, we do not burden ourselves, and we do not destroy ourselves with worry and grief, because when a person looks at things from this perspective, his worldly life will be clouded for him, and indeed his good deeds will be lost, since people are not guided as he wishes. If he exhausts himself chasing after people and pants behind them, he becomes weary. He gives what is incumbent upon him, and the rest is up to whom? Up to Allah, mighty and majestic.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse also: the name (al-Hadi, the Guide) is applied to other than Allah; His saying: ﴿And whomever Allah misguides, for him there is no guide﴾ [Az-Zumar 23]; and as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾ [Ar-Ra'd 7]. So "al-hadi" (guide) is applied both to Allah and to others, but what is prohibited to apply to others is the guidance of tawfiq (divine enabling), for the guidance of tawfiq is only for Allah alone. As for the guidance of direction (hidayat al-dalala), it is for Allah and for others.

* A student: (...) do they continue?

* The Shaykh: No, they continue, because Allah, glorified and exalted is He, may postpone their guidance until a appointed term.

* A student: (...) that a person is given a choice between two paths, either good or evil, but there are disbelievers who never reached Islam and know nothing of Islam; if they die, they did not see good but saw evil. Are these disbelievers?

* The Shaykh: Yes, these are disbelievers, these are disbelievers..

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, these are disbelievers, but because of their excuse, that the message did not reach them, Allah will task them on the Day of Resurrection with whatever kinds of obligation He wills. Then if they are guided at that time they are among the people of Paradise, and if they go astray they are among the people of the Fire. This is the most correct thing said in answer regarding these people.

That is, the people of the interval (ahl al-fatra) and those after the message who were not reached by the correct message, that they will be tested on the Day of Resurrection with whatever obligations Allah wills, which we do not know. Then if they are guided they are saved, and otherwise (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verses 24–31 (part 1 of 3):

The one who guards against punishment tries to be saved from it, but the one who encounters a thing may encounter it with glad tidings, joy and happiness. So the interpretation of ﴿يَتَّقِي﴾ [Az-Zumar 24] as (yalqa, "meets") is without doubt deficient. However, at times the author interprets the Qur'an with something close to it.
