* Shaykh: ﴿لَا تَدْرِي لَعَلَّ اللَّهَ يُحْدِثُ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ أَمْرًا﴾ [At-Talaq 1], "You do not know; perhaps Allah will bring about after that some matter." This may be for expectation (tawaqquʿ).
* Student: ﴿لَعَلَّكَ بَاخِعٌ نَفْسَكَ﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿لَعَلَّكَ بَاخِعٌ﴾ [Ash-Shuʿara 3], "Perhaps you will destroy yourself," also for expectation. It occurs often in the Qur'an.
* Student: ﴿لَعَلِّي أَبْلُغُ الْأَسْبَابَ﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿لَعَلِّي أَبْلُغُ الْأَسْبَابَ﴾ [Ghafir 36], "Perhaps I may reach the ways," is for hope, and it may be for causation. Laʿalla occurs much in the Qur'an. Some people think it means hope everywhere, and say: how would Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, hope for something when He is capable of all things? We say: when laʿalla comes in the speech of Allah, it is for causation.

His statement: (﴿يَتَذَكَّرُونَ﴾ [Az-Zumar 27], i.e., they take admonition), because this is the purpose of setting forth examples.

﴿قُرْآنًا عَرَبِيًّا غَيْرَ ذِي عِوَجٍ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَّقُونَ﴾ [Az-Zumar 28], "A Qur'an in Arabic, without any crookedness, that they may be mindful of Allah." ﴿قُرْآنًا﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), and ﴿عَرَبِيًّا﴾ is another ḥāl. I.e., this Qur'an in which is every example is a Qur'an. Qur'ān comes as a masdar (verbal noun) and as an ism al-fāʿil or ism al-mafʿūl (active or passive participle). From its use as a masdar: al-Ghufrān and al-Shukrān; by this I mean the pattern fuʿlān, which comes as a masdar, such as al-Ghufrān, al-Shukrān, al-Qur'ān. This masdar in the word Qur'an may be understood as an ism al-mafʿūl, so Qur'an means maqrū' (recited), and on this it means matlūw (read). It may also be an ism al-fāʿil, meaning qāri' (reciter), from qara'a al-māʾ, when he gathers water in the pool. If you reflect, you will find both descriptions apply to it: it is recited and it gathers. For this reason the scholars of the principles of tafsir said: it is valid for it to be in the sense of an ism al-fāʿil and valid for it to be in the sense of an ism al-mafʿūl.

His statement ﴿عَرَبِيًّا﴾: i.e., in the Arabic language, which is the tongue of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the tongue of the people among whom he was sent.

Arabic is the best of tongues, the most eloquent, the most articulate and the clearest. For this reason Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, chose it for the message of Muhammad (ﷺ). If someone says: Are there not words in the Qur'an whose origin is non-Arabic? Yes, there are. But these words whose origin is not Arabic, when the Arabs spoke them, they Arabized them and they became Arabic. For this reason these Arabized words are not free of some change; in general there must be some change in them. When the Arabs speak them and use them and they become prevalent on their tongues, they become Arabic. Are they 'arabah (pure Arabic) or musta'rabah (Arabized)?

* Student: Musta'rabah.
* Shaykh: Musta'rabah. So they are Arabized words from people who were also Arabized; i.e., the origin of the Arabs was Arabized, because they were not Arabs originally. Ismāʿīl is the son of Ibrāhīm, and his language was not Arabic. But when the Jurhum came to the mother of Ismāʿīl and settled with her, he became Arabic, and Arabness has continued until this day.

He says: ﴿قُرْآنًا عَرَبِيًّا غَيْرَ ذِي عِوَجٍ﴾ [Az-Zumar 28]. This description is negative, not affirmative: ﴿غَيْرَ ذِي عِوَجٍ﴾. Know that there is no pure negative among the descriptions of the Qur'an, because a pure negative contains no praise. Rather, everything described to the Qur'an by way of negation indicates the perfection of its opposite. So when He says ﴿غَيْرَ ذِي عِوَجٍ﴾, it means for the perfection of its straightness. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ﴾ [Al-Isra' 9], "Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright." The Qur'an guides to what is most upright in matters of religion and matters of the world, in a manner that has no crookedness in any respect. For this reason He said: ﴿غَيْرَ ذِي عِوَجٍ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَّقُونَ﴾, i.e., so that they may be mindful of Allah. Allah made it clear to us in this Qur'an and made it without crookedness for the sake of His piety, the Mighty and Majestic.

The commentator, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (﴿وَلَقَدْ ضَرَبْنَا لِلنَّاسِ فِي هَذَا الْقُرْآنِ مِنْ كُلِّ مَثَلٍ﴾ [Az-Zumar 27], i.e., We made). This interpretation is a general one, because striking an example is not merely making it; rather, striking an example is for taking lesson from it. So "I struck it as an example" means I made it a likeness so that it may be taken as a lesson.

His statement: ﴿لِلنَّاسِ﴾ and ﴿مِنْ كُلِّ مَثَلٍ﴾ include all people, believer and disbeliever, so that these and those may be reminded.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, the humiliation, the disgrace, the shame, the scandal, all of it.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: I.e., do not humiliate us and do not disgrace us.
* Student: (...) Is the Arabic language the best of languages (...)?
* Shaykh: No. Which is better: the message of Muhammad (peace be upon him) and his nation, or the other messages and their communities?
* Student: The message of the Prophet (ﷺ).
* Shaykh: Then it is without doubt the best. For this reason there are reports, but there is scrutiny in them, that the Arabic language is the language of the people of Paradise.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. That Allah chose this great message in the Arabic language is sufficient, by His saying: ﴿اللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ حَيْثُ يَجْعَلُ رِسَالَتَهُ﴾ [Al-An'am 124], "Allah knows best where to place His message." Thus this place became suitable for this great message, because it is great.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It is known for its clarity. If it had come in other than Arabic, it would not have been clear. But that He chose that it be among these Arabs and in their language is evidence of its excellence.
* Student: (...). Someone says: the Messenger (ﷺ) is specific to the Arabs, because the Qur'an is Arabic. Do we answer with this same answer?
* Shaykh: No. If he says he is specific to the Arabs, we say: yes, he was sent to the unlettered, but to all people. As if someone were in the East or in the West and was a ruler over all the continent where he is. So Muhammad (peace be upon him) was sent to these people, but to all people. And it is known that he must be sent to his own people. Suppose he was sent to non-Arabs and was a messenger to the people: it is the same thing.
* Student: Does punishment have a color and a taste?
* Shaykh: Yes. The thing that strikes a person directly is said to be "tasted" (dhāqahu), but not with the tongue. Rather, because it struck him directly, it became like the food that a person puts into his stomach.
* Student: We said: negative description does not indicate praise, like the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted (...).
* Shaykh: Yes. If we say it must include perfection, then "He neither begets nor is begotten" indicates the perfection of His oneness.
* Student: (...) the evil of punishment on the Day of Resurrection (...). Does it indicate the face? The punishment reaches the face more severely than the rest of the body?
* Shaykh: In any case, the face's feeling of punishment is more intense than the body's feeling of the rest.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: If it is the worst punishment, and it is in the face, it becomes harder on a person than if it were in another part. But what appears to us, as we said, is that "sū' al-ʿadhāb" (evil punishment) is not an elative; rather it is of the type of attributing a quality to its described noun, i.e., "the evil punishment."
* Student: (...) good and evil. Is it not from the category of "good and evil"?
* Shaykh: "Good and evil" are also used as elatives, when you say: this is better than this, and this is worse than this. And they may be used to mean only the description of evil, as you say: this is evil, this is good.

* * *

* Student: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. ﴿Allah presents an example: a man in whom are partners disputing with one another, and a man belonging exclusively to one man. Are they equal in comparison? Praise be to Allah! But most of them do not know. Indeed, you will die, and indeed, they will die. Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, you will dispute.﴾ [Az-Zumar 29–31]

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿Allah presents an example: a man in whom are partners disputing with one another, and a man belonging exclusively to one man﴾ [Az-Zumar 29]. When Allah said: ﴿And We have certainly set forth for people in this Qur'an every kind of example﴾ [Az-Zumar 27], He mentioned this example, and He struck an example.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, clarified this great example, saying: ﴿Allah presents an example: a man in whom are partners disputing with one another﴾. ﴿A man in whom are partners disputing with one another﴾: ﴿in whom are partners disputing with one another﴾ means quarrelling and disagreeing. Each of them says: I am his master, I am the one who wants to use him, and similar things. So they are always in dispute and contention, because each of them wants to have him exclusively. The second man, ﴿a man belonging exclusively to one man﴾: salaman means belonging exclusively to this man, with no one sharing him.

If someone says: How do you know that salaman means "exclusively belonging" and free of partners?

We say: We know this from mentioning the opposite, which is His saying ﴿in whom are partners disputing with one another﴾; because a word is known from its context and from mentioning its opposite. Among the most prominent examples of this is the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿So go forth in separate groups or go forth all together﴾ [An-Nisa' 71].

If someone asks you: what is the meaning of thubāt? You would understand its meaning from what follows: ﴿or go forth all together﴾. So thubāt is the opposite of "gathered together," i.e., individually: go forth individually, or go forth all together. This is one of the rules of tafsir: the meaning of a word is known by mentioning what is opposed to it. Here we say: "a man belonging exclusively" (salaman), i.e., purely belonging to its owner, with no one sharing it with him. If someone asks: how do you know this? We say: by the rule we mentioned, that the counterpart of a thing, i.e., what is set as its equivalent, is its opposite in meaning. This man who belonged exclusively to one man: does anyone share with him in his ownership? No. Does anyone dispute with him? No.

So we must know the difference between the owned thing in which there are disputing partners, and the owned thing in which there are no partners, and then measure against it the one who is sincere to Allah, who worships Allah alone, and the one who worships others along with Allah. For this reason He said: ﴿Are they equal in comparison?﴾ [Az-Zumar 29], i.e., are these two men equal: one in whom there are disputing partners, and the other belonging exclusively to one man? Are these two equal? The answer is no. So the interrogative then means negation; i.e., the two are not equal.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verse 24–31 (part 2 of 3):

The interrogative (istifham) comes with many meanings, as is well known in the science of rhetoric (balaghah). But when it occurs in a context of negation, it carries the sense of a challenge (tahaddi). For if it were said: "They are not equal" (la yastawiyan), we would understand the negation of their equality. But when it is said: "Are they equal?" (hal yastawiyan), there are two matters:
The first matter: the negation of equality.
The second matter: the challenge. We say: "Do you have anything that proves that they are equal?" So converting the negation into an interrogative is more emphatic in negation and clearer. ﴿Are they equal in description?﴾ The answer is: No.
Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾ [az-Zumar 29]: He praises Himself, Mighty and Majestic, for the perfection of His attributes and the perfection of His bounty. Among His bounties is that He sets forth parables for people in the Qur'an, so that they may take heed, although He, Mighty and Majestic, is free of need from them. ﴿And whoever disbelieves - indeed, Allah is free from need of the worlds﴾ [Ali 'Imran 97]. Nevertheless, His mercy refuses except that He make clear to His servants what they need in the matters of their religion and their worldly life. For this reason, after this complete clarification in the parable, He said: ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾.
Then He said: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ [az-Zumar 29]. "Bal" (but, rather) here is for idrab (a shift or turning away), and idrab has two meanings:
The first meaning: idrab intiqal (a shift that moves from one thing to another).
The second meaning: idrab ibtal (a shift that nullifies), which cancels the first and affirms the second. When you say: "Zayd did not stand, but 'Amr did," this is idrab ibtal: you have nullified the first and affirmed the second.
In the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Rather, their knowledge has failed concerning the Hereafter; rather, they are in doubt about it; rather, they are blind to it﴾ [an-Naml 66], this is a shift from one meaning to a stronger meaning.
In this verse: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, is it idrab ibtal or idrab intiqal? It is idrab intiqal, because nothing preceded that it nullifies. And the saying ﴿But most of them do not know﴾: the intended meaning of ﴿most of them﴾ here is most of mankind, as occurs in other verses: ﴿But most of mankind do not know﴾ [al-A'raf 187].
The negation of knowledge here is due to the negation of its necessary consequence, which is action and compliance. Most people are in ignorance, and most people are in deviation. In ignorance, they do not recognize the truth; in deviation, they do not accept the truth nor act upon it. It is correct to negate knowledge from all of them. As for the one who is in ignorance, the negation of knowledge from him is evident. As for the one who is in deviation despite having knowledge, the negation of knowledge from him is because he has not benefited from it and has not acted upon it.
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed, they will die. Then indeed, you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, will dispute﴾ [az-Zumar 30-31]. ﴿Indeed, you﴾ is addressed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
﴿Will die﴾ is a description of him in the future.
﴿And indeed, they will die﴾ likewise. Death is emphasized even though it is known with certainty, because the deeds of those who denied the Prophet ﷺ are the deeds of one who has not been certain of death. For one who truly believes in death must prepare for it, but they do not prepare for it, so their not preparing for it is like denial, or is in the position of denial. Therefore it was emphasized.
His saying ﴿mayyit﴾ with a shaddah on the ya is said of one who will die while still alive. As for (mayt), it is said of one upon whom death has fallen, i.e., after the departure of life, one says (mayt). And sometimes (mayyit) is said, but the more common is (mayt). Accordingly, a distinction is made between describing a living person as dying, where one says (mayyit), and describing a dead person with death, where one says (mayt).
﴿Indeed, you﴾: the address is to the Prophet ﷺ and to whoever opposed him and disbelieved in him.
﴿On the Day of Resurrection﴾: its explanation has already passed.
﴿Before your Lord, you will dispute﴾: before your Lord who created you the first time and returned you a second time, you will dispute before Him as to which of you is upon the truth. Now we know the outcome of this dispute, who will prevail?
* Students: The believers.
* Shaykh: The believers, without doubt. Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿And never will Allah give the disbelievers over the believers a way﴾ [an-Nisa' 141]. So the disbeliever has no way over the believer. Thus the outcome, praise be to Allah, is known: the believers are the victorious on the Day of Resurrection, and they are the ones who prevail over their enemies.
Now let us return to the words of the author, and then we will take all the benefits, God willing.
The author, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (Allah struck a parable for the polytheist and the monotheist). The author's restriction to the polytheist and the monotheist is clear, because the parable struck, namely the servant owned by several partners and the servant wholly devoted to one master, applies exactly to the polytheist and the monotheist.
He says: (Allah struck a parable for the polytheist and the monotheist: ﴿a man﴾ [az-Zumar 29]), a substitute (badal) for ﴿a parable﴾. Concerning the badal, Imam Ibn Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, says:
"The follower intended by the ruling without an intermediary..."
This is the badal.
His saying "the follower intended by the ruling" excludes the rest of the followers (tawabi'). His saying "without an intermediary" excludes the conjunctive introduced by (bal), for the conjunctive introduced by (bal), when it is for idrab ibtal, is the one intended by the ruling, but through an intermediary, so it is not called a badal.
Here He said: ﴿a parable, a man﴾. If ﴿a parable﴾ were removed and He said: "Allah struck a man," would the statement be correct or not? It is correct, because the intended word is "man." If you say: "I saw Muhammad, 'Ali," 'Ali is a badal, because the intended is 'Ali. If a speaker says: "I saw 'Ali Muhammad," you understand that he meant Muhammad and did not mean 'Ali, because Muhammad is a badal from 'Ali. The badal is what is intended by the ruling, but its cause may be error, forgetfulness, or other causes. The point is that the badal is what Ibn Malik defined by his saying:
"The follower intended by the ruling without an intermediary is what is named a badal."
He says: (﴿in it are partners in dispute﴾ disputing, bad of character). From where did he derive bad character? From His saying ﴿in dispute﴾, because mutual contention indicates bad character, since good character yields its right even if that causes harm or loss to oneself, because the goodness of his character prevails over taking his right. Thus it is fitting for a person to be of good character, and to overlook some of his right even if that harms himself. And let him know that if his soul says: "Your humility and your pardon of your right is humiliation for you," let him know that this is from the whisperings of Satan. For the Prophet ﷺ said: «Allah does not increase a servant in pardon except in honor, and whoever humbles himself for Allah, Allah raises him» [narrated by Muslim (2588/69) from Abu Hurayrah]. So do not let your soul overcome you and pride take you into sin, saying: "I cannot remain silent about this man; who am I, that he should transgress against me? I am so-and-so, son of so-and-so!" This is from Satan. ﴿So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is upon Allah﴾ [ash-Shura 40]. ﴿And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel [evil] with that which is better, and thereupon the one who is between you and him is [as if he were] a devoted friend﴾ [Fussilat 34]. ﴿But none receives it except those who are patient, and none receives it except one of great fortune﴾ [Fussilat 35], meaning: none is granted success in it except those who are patient, and none receives it except one of great fortune.
He says: (disputing, bad of character; ﴿and a man wholly devoted﴾). In my copy it is ﴿saliman﴾, a reading, and the commentator explained it accordingly. Salim means pure, as he explained it (pure, ﴿to a man﴾). ﴿Are they equal in description?﴾ He says: (﴿mathalan﴾ is a tamyiz). What is the tamyiz? From mayyaza, meaning to clarify. Ibn Malik defined it in the Alfiyyah, saying:
"A noun with the meaning of (min), clarifying and indefinite, is put in the accusative as a tamyiz, by what it explains."
This is the tamyiz: an indefinite noun that clarifies the ambiguous term it explains, and it has the meaning of (min). Its example is the saying: "Zayd perspired sweat" (tassabba Zaydun 'araqan). ''Araqan'' is a tamyiz. Apply the definition to it and you find it is a noun with the meaning of (min), since you say: "he perspired from sweat." Clarifying: i.e., explaining the verb "perspired," since "perspired" can mean perspired blood, perspired water, perspired sweat, so it clarified the one who perspired. Is it indefinite or definite?
Indefinite. This is the tamyiz:
"A noun with the meaning of (min), clarifying and indefinite, is put in the accusative as a tamyiz, by what it explains."
Now I have dictated to you two verses from the Alfiyyah of Ibn Malik. Whoever has memorized them now, let him recite the first verse of them. [Student:]
"The follower intended by the ruling without an intermediary is what is named a badal."
* Shaykh: Yes, the badal:
"The follower intended by the ruling without an intermediary is what is named a badal."
And this second one, the tamyiz?
* Student:
"A noun with the meaning of (min), clarifying and indefinite, is put in the accusative as a tamyiz, by what it explains."
* Shaykh: He says: (﴿mathalan﴾ is a tamyiz, meaning: a servant belonging to a group is not equal to a servant belonging to one, for the first, when all his owners demand his service at one time, is perplexed about whom among them to serve.)
He says: (is not equal), and thereby, may Allah have mercy on him, clarified that the interrogative in His saying ﴿Are they equal?﴾ is for negation, since he explained it as a negation.
His saying: (a servant belonging to a group is not equal to a servant belonging to one) is correct: they are not equal. The servant belonging to one may be dealt with as he wishes: whenever he wishes, he says "Serve me," and whenever he wishes, he says "Rest." Whenever he wishes, he sells him; whenever he wishes, he rents him out. But a servant belonging to a group, with a group who are contentious, of bad character, in constant dispute: are they equal? Never. If one says, "Come and serve me," and the second says, "Serve me," and the third says, "Serve me," and the fourth says, "Serve me," then one takes him by the right hand, the second by the left, the third by the right foot, and the fourth by the left foot, and then they tear the servant apart, because each wants him to be with him, to be the one he serves. Likewise in selling: if one wants to sell him, and the second says, "I do not want that," and the third says, "I want to rent him," and the fourth says, "I want to lend him," how can this be? Always in dispute and discord. The servant himself is in anxiety, perplexity, and affliction, and the partners too are always contentious. This cannot be equal to a man. This is undoubtedly a approximate parable; otherwise the difference between worshipping Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and worshipping others along with Him is great, meaning that it is greater. But Allah, the Exalted, brings this close to His servants, just as He brought the resurrection close by water sent down from the sky, by which the earth then brings forth plants. How long does it remain?
The plants of the earth after the rain falls? It remains for a period according to the goodness of the land, the abundance of rain, the suitable climate, and the season, but it remains.
Resurrection: ﴿It will be but one shout, and at once they will be on the surface﴾ [an-Nazi'at 13-14]. ﴿One shout, and at once they will be upon the surface﴾. Parables may not correspond exactly; the thing paralleled may be quicker than the parable, but it is mentioned by way of approximation. Undoubtedly, the difference between worshipping Allah alone and worshipping others with Him is greater than the difference between a man wholly devoted to one man and a man shared among contentious partners.
The author, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (This is a parable for the polytheist, and the second is a parable for the monotheist.) What is the second? A man wholly devoted to a man: this is for the monotheist, and the first is for the polytheist. And what is the purpose of striking this parable? The purpose is to warn against associating partners with Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
Then know that partners over a servant are in dispute, but with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, the matter is different. Allah says in the sacred hadith: «I am the most free of partners from partnership. Whoever does a deed in which he associates another with Me, I leave him and his partnership» [narrated by Muslim (2985/46) from Abu Hurayrah]. Contending partners cannot give up their share, but shirk with Allah: Allah leaves the polytheist and his partnership.
«Whoever does a deed in which he associates another with Me, I leave him and his partnership.» For this reason He said: (﴿Praise be to Allah﴾ [az-Zumar 29], alone). If praise belongs to Him alone, then worship must be to Him alone, because He is worthy of praise and worthy of worship, glorified and exalted; He alone deserves to be worshipped.
(﴿But most of them﴾, i.e., the people of Makkah, ﴿do not know﴾ what they will come to of punishment, so they associate partners.)
His saying: (﴿But most of them﴾, i.e., the people of Makkah). The author, may Allah have mercy on him, always, especially in the Meccan verses and surahs, makes such address specific to the people of Makkah. But what we should always do is take the indication of the Qur'an as general, except in cases of necessity, because the Qur'an was revealed for all creation until the Day of Resurrection. Restricting it to the people of Makkah would mean it does not include others except by analogy, whereas if we take its general wording, it includes the people of Makkah and others by explicit text.
There is a difference between a ruling being included by explicit text and its inclusion by analogy. The correct view is that the pronoun in ﴿most of them﴾ refers to all creation: most of creation do not know. This is why it is established in the authentic hadith that Allah says: «O Adam!» He says: «Here I am, at Your call and Your pleasure.» He says: «Bring forth from your progeny a group for the Fire,» or «the group of the Fire.» He says: «O Lord, what is the group of the Fire?» He says: «Of every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine» [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3348) and Muslim (222/379) from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri]. Are these the majority or the minority? The majority. So most of creation do not know, either because of their ignorance or their deviation. If it is due to ignorance, as I told you before, then knowledge is negated from them. If it is due to deviation, then knowledge is negated from them because it has no benefit, since they have not been guided by it.
He says: ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed, they will die.﴾
(﴿Indeed, you﴾ is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ; ﴿will die﴾ [az-Zumar 30], i.e., you will die.)
He says: (﴿And indeed, they will die﴾). He says: (So you will die and they will die), and as our common people say: "The promise is ahead" (qudda:m). (qudda:m) means the Day of Resurrection, because on the Day of Resurrection Allah judges between the servants; people will dispute over their deeds and religions, and dispute over their private rights, and Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection.
He says: (So there is no gloating over death), meaning that if you die, there is no gloating against you, because they too will die like you.
(It was revealed when they were slow to see his death ﷺ.) Thus the author said: the cause of its revelation was that Quraysh were slow to see the death of the Prophet ﷺ, so this verse was revealed informing him that he would die, and when he dies they too will die and dispute on the Day of Resurrection. But this claim requires evidence. Let us look at the occasion of revelation; we do not find this. If that is so, then one should not imagine a cause of revelation for the meaning of a verse of the Book of Allah, because the cause of revelation is pure report, and pure report has no room for reason in it. But we say: Allah mentioned this sentence as an indication that He will not waste your deed or theirs. He will not waste your deed in calling to monotheism, and He will not waste their deed of associating partners. For you have an appointed time in which you will be gathered and dispute before Allah, Mighty and Majestic. In this there is consolation for the Messenger ﷺ and a warning to the polytheists. It is, on one side, consolation and reassurance for the Messenger, peace be upon him, and on another side, a warning to the polytheists that they will die, and their death will also be near, and it will be certain with no doubt about it.

(﴿ثُمَّ إِنَّكُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ﴾ [الزمر ٣١] "Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection," ثم إنكم أيها الناس فيما بينكم من المظالم) This is a strange thing from the author, may God have mercy on him. The address in ﴿إِنَّكَ مَيِّتٌ وَإِنَّهُمْ مَيِّتُونَ (٣٠) ثُمَّ إِنَّكُمْ﴾ ["Indeed, you will die, and indeed they will die. Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord will dispute."] [Az-Zumar 30–31] is directed to the Prophet, but the author turned it to the general people, saying: "O people." ﴿ثُمَّ إِنَّكُمْ﴾ he explains as: "O people, among yourselves regarding wrongs." The context rejects this interpretation. Rather, the address is to the Prophet ﷺ and to whoever disbelieved in him, and this is the required reading. "And you will dispute..." regarding the wrongs between you, or regarding what is between you of truth and falsehood? The second: truth and falsehood. You call to monotheism while they deny it, and you have an appointment in which you will dispute. ﴿ثُمَّ إِنَّكُمْ﴾ means: the Messenger ﷺ and those who denied him, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, will dispute.

In His saying ﴿عِنْدَ رَبِّكُمْ﴾ ["before your Lord"] there is an indication that this dispute follows from His lordship, glorified and exalted be He, because He is the Just Judge, and of His justice is that He will decide between the disputants on the Day of Resurrection, just as He decides between disputants over private rights.

* A student: (...) on the proof of qiyas (analogical reasoning) from the verse.
* The Shaykh: Indeed, may God bless you, every parable in the Qur'an contains evidence for establishing qiyas.
* A student: A person who takes his right (...).
* The Shaykh: No. If he leaves it to be settled before God, then he has not left it. But if he leaves it for the reward from God, then he has left it.
* The student: (...) trusting in God.
* The Shaykh: Yes, but trusting that he will dispute with his opponent? Let me ask you.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Has he pardoned him in this case?
* The student: (...) lordship.
* The Shaykh: No, I am asking you now: is his leaving it for the dispute before God on the Day of Resurrection, or not? Has he pardoned him in this case?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That is fine. In this case I see that he should demand his right in this world, or leave it to God, because if he demands it in this world and his right is taken, the good deeds of the one who wronged him are spared on the Day of Resurrection, so the punishment of this world is lighter than the punishment of the Hereafter, and he thereby does good to him. Or he leaves it for what is better, which is pardon and awaiting the reward from Allah, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿فَمَنْ عَفَا وَأَصْلَحَ فَأَجْرُهُ عَلَى اللَّهِ﴾ ["So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah."] [Ash-Shura 40]. Do you understand now?

So the states are three: either he takes his right in this world, or he postpones his right to the Hereafter, or he pardons.

Ranking them from the most severe to the mildest, we say: the most severe is to postpone it to the Hereafter, then to take it in this world, then to pardon. However, pardon must have a condition: that there be reform in it. If there is corruption in the pardon, such that if we pardon this man he will increase in his evil and transgression, then here taking the right is better than pardon. But if we know that this man will regard the pardon with esteem and his conduct will improve afterwards, then there is no doubt that pardon is better.

* A student: If a strong wrongdoer exists and no one can take his right from him, do we say: pardon him, or say: postpone your matter to the Hereafter?
* The Shaykh: No. That means that if we pardoned this man he would not reform, so postpone his right to the Hereafter, because Allah has restricted it: ﴿فَمَنْ عَفَا وَأَصْلَحَ﴾ ["whoever pardons and makes reconciliation"]. But inform him, tell him: "You have now wronged me in such and such, and such and such, and I will postpone my claim until the Day of Resurrection," so that he does not think you have pardoned.
* A student: Pardon is with ability.
* The Shaykh: Yes. No, and also without ability. But the praiseworthy pardon is pardon with ability.
* A student: (...) I will not pardon the man until I take from his good deeds on the Day of Resurrection.
* The Shaykh: Yes, we say: that is your right.
* The student: Which is better, O Shaykh: that he not pardon him?
* The Shaykh: No. The better course is that he pardon him, but as Allah, glorified and exalted be He, said: ﴿فَمَنْ عَفَا وَأَصْلَحَ﴾ ["whoever pardons and makes reconciliation"], if there is reform in the pardon. But if this man, when you pardon him, for example for killing your son, goes tomorrow to kill the son of others...
* * *
* The student: I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed: ﴿فَمَنْ أَظْلَمُ مِمَّنْ كَذَبَ عَلَى اللَّهِ وَكَذَّبَ بِالصِّدْقِ إِذْ جَاءَهُ أَلَيْسَ فِي جَهَنَّمَ مَثْوًى لِلْكَافِرِينَ (٣٢) وَالَّذِي جَاءَ بِالصِّدْقِ وَصَدَّقَ بِهِ أُولَئِكَ هُمُ الْمُتَّقُونَ (٣٣) لَهُمْ مَا يَشَاءُونَ عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ ذَلِكَ جَزَاءُ الْمُحْسِنِينَ (٣٤) لِيُكَفِّرَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ أَسْوَأَ الَّذِي عَمِلُوا وَيَجْزِيَهُمْ أَجْرَهُمْ بِأَحْسَنِ الَّذِي كَانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ ["So who is more unjust than one who lies about Allah and denies the truth when it comes to him? Is there not in Hell a residence for the disbelievers? And the one who brings the truth and confirms it — those are the righteous. For them is whatever they wish with their Lord. That is the reward of the good-doers. That Allah may remove from them the worst of what they did and reward them with their best deeds."] [Az-Zumar 32–35].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَلَقَدْ ضَرَبْنَا لِلنَّاسِ فِي هَذَا الْقُرْآنِ مِنْ كُلِّ مَثَلٍ﴾ ["And We have certainly presented for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example"] [Az-Zumar 27].

* From the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, glorified and exalted be He, revealed this Qur'an as a clarification of everything, and of that clarification is the coining of parables, because they bring the meaning close and place the intelligible in the form of the perceptible. Among that is His saying: ﴿مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ اتَّخَذُوا مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ أَوْلِيَاءَ كَمَثَلِ الْعَنْكَبُوتِ اتَّخَذَتْ بَيْتًا وَإِنَّ أَوْهَنَ الْبُيُوتِ لَبَيْتُ الْعَنْكَبُوتِ لَوْ كَانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ["The example of those who take protectors other than Allah is like the spider, which takes a home; and indeed, the weakest of homes is the home of the spider, if only they knew."] [Al-Ankabut 41].
* From the benefits of this noble verse: the mercy of Allah, glorified and exalted be He, toward His servants, in that He made this complete clarification for them.
* From its benefits: the teacher should use many parables for others that help them understand the meaning, because this is the method of the Qur'an.
* From the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of causes (ʿilal) and wisdoms (ḥikam) in Allah's actions and legislation, from His saying: ﴿لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَذَكَّرُونَ﴾ ["so that they may remember"] [Az-Zumar 27].
* From the benefits of this noble verse: a refutation of the Jahmiyyah (a heterodox sect) and those like them who denied the wisdom of Allah and said: Allah does a thing not for a cause or wisdom, but merely by will. The proof of this is that ﴿لَعَلَّ﴾ ["so that"] here indicates causation, and causation means affirming wisdom.

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿قُرْآنًا عَرَبِيًّا غَيْرَ ذِي عِوَجٍ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَّقُونَ﴾ ["An Arabic Qur'an, without any crookedness, that they may fear Allah."] [Az-Zumar 28].

* From this noble verse it is derived: that the Qur'an is Arabic, that is, revealed in the language of the Arabs.
* From its benefits: there is no non-Arabic (ʿajami) word in the Qur'an, because Allah described the whole Qur'an as Arabic, and this requires that it contain nothing of the language of non-Arabs. There is no doubt that this is the reality, so there is no non-Arabic word in the Qur'an. However, the scholars of tafsir and others differed on whether there is in the Qur'an a word whose origin is non-Arabic which was then Arabized. Some say yes, and some say no. Those who said yes argued that there are words in the noble Qur'an to which the rules of the Arabic language do not apply, and this means they are non-Arabic. This does not contradict the Qur'an being Arabic, because when the Arabs Arabized them they became Arabic through arabization (istiʿrab), just as the Arabs themselves were originally "Arabized" (mustaʿribah), since the language of their forefather Ismail was not Arabic.
Others said: these words which are non-Arabic came into the language of the Arabs by the coincidence of two languages (tawārud al-lughatayn), and there is no objection to two languages coinciding on one word. The dispute here is close to being verbal, because they all agree that there is no word in the Qur'an that is non-Arabic at the time of its revelation, never.
* From the benefits of this noble verse: the clarification of the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in revealing the Qur'an in the Arabic tongue, because the Prophet ﷺ was sent to an Arab people, so the wisdom was that his language be Arabic, as is the case with all the messengers. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَمَا أَرْسَلْنَا مِنْ رَسُولٍ إِلَّا بِلِسَانِ قَوْمِهِ لِيُبَيِّنَ لَهُمْ﴾ ["And We did not send any messenger except with the language of his people, to make clear to them."] [Ibrahim 4].
* From the benefits of this noble verse: understanding the meaning helps one toward righteousness, from His saying: ﴿قُرْآنًا عَرَبِيًّا﴾ ["an Arabic Qur'an"] ﴿لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَّقُونَ﴾ ["that they may fear Allah"]. This is a clear matter: understanding the meaning is among the causes of righteousness, because if someone speaks to you in words whose meaning you do not understand, nothing affects you; only what you understand the meaning of affects you. For this reason He said: ﴿لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَّقُونَ﴾.
* From this sentence we derive what we derived from the preceding sentence, His saying: ﴿لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَذَكَّرُونَ﴾ [Az-Zumar 27].

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿ضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا رَجُلًا فِيهِ شُرَكَاءُ مُتَشَاكِسُونَ﴾ ["Allah presents an example: a man in whom are partners in dispute..."] to the end [Az-Zumar 29].

* From the benefits of this noble verse: this verse is an application of His saying: ﴿وَلَقَدْ ضَرَبْنَا لِلنَّاسِ فِي هَذَا الْقُرْآنِ مِنْ كُلِّ مَثَلٍ﴾ [Az-Zumar 27], since this is a parable.
* From its benefits: the example of one who worships others along with Allah is like a servant in whom are partners who are quarrelsome, contending and disputing with one another. The reason is that this worshipper who associates others with Allah does not have a heart sincerely devoted to Allah; rather, partners pull at it from right and left until it is lost among them.
* From the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, the Exalted, brings a report or other matter and then establishes it for the addressee in the best manner. This is in His saying: ﴿هَلْ يَسْتَوِيَانِ مَثَلًا﴾ ["Are they equal in comparison?"] [Az-Zumar 29], because this interrogative, which is intended as a negation, serves to establish what was mentioned and to bind the addressee to it.
* From the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, the Exalted, deserves all praise for the perfection of His monotheism, from His saying: ﴿الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ﴾ ["All praise is due to Allah"].
* From its benefits: unrestricted praise belongs only to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. As for others, if they are praised, their praise is not absolute; rather, they are praised for a specific thing and a particular part of what is praiseworthy. Unrestricted praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds, the Mighty and Majestic, because He is the One praised in every state. The Prophet ﷺ, when something pleasing came to him, would say: "Praise be to Allah through whose blessing good things are completed." And when something displeasing came to him, he would say: "Praise be to Allah in every state."[[Narrated by Ibn Majah (3803) from the hadith of ʿAʾishah.]]
* From the benefits of this noble verse: most of the children of Adam do not know realities as they are, and even if they know them, they do not benefit from them, from His saying: ﴿بَلْ أَكْثَرُهُمْ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ["But most of them do not know"] [Az-Zumar 29].

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿إِنَّكَ مَيِّتٌ وَإِنَّهُمْ مَيِّتُونَ (٣٠) ثُمَّ إِنَّكُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ عِنْدَ رَبِّكُمْ تَخْتَصِمُونَ﴾ ["Indeed, you will die, and indeed they will die. Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord will dispute."] [Az-Zumar 30–31].

* From its benefits: our Prophet ﷺ will not live forever; rather, he will die, just as his opponents are dead. This is like His saying: ﴿وَمَا جَعَلْنَا لِبَشَرٍ مِنْ قَبْلِكَ الْخُلْدَ أَفَإِنْ مِتَّ فَهُمُ الْخَالِدُونَ﴾ ["And We did not grant eternity to any human before you. So if you die, would they be eternal?"] [Al-Anbiya 34].
* From its benefits: consolation for the Prophet ﷺ, from His saying: ﴿إِنَّكَ مَيِّتٌ وَإِنَّهُمْ مَيِّتُونَ (٣٠) ثُمَّ إِنَّكُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ عِنْدَ رَبِّكُمْ تَخْتَصِمُونَ﴾ [Az-Zumar 30–31].
* From its benefits: a warning to these deniers that they have an appointment with the Messenger ﷺ, which is the dispute on the Day of Resurrection.
* From its benefits: the people of polytheism and disbelief are adversaries of the people of monotheism and faith in the Hereafter, just as they are adversaries in this world. In this world there is no doubt about their enmity and the hostility of some toward others, and in the Hereafter it is greater and more severe.
* From its benefits: creatures will dispute before Allah on the Day of Resurrection. It is well known that when the dispute is between a believer and a disbeliever, the one who prevails is the believer, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿فَاللَّهُ يَحْكُمُ بَيْنَكُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ وَلَنْ يَجْعَلَ اللَّهُ لِلْكَافِرِينَ عَلَى الْمُؤْمِنِينَ سَبِيلًا﴾ ["Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection, and never will Allah give the disbelievers over the believers a way."] [An-Nisa 141].
* From the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of resurrection and reckoning, from His saying: ﴿ثُمَّ إِنَّكُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ عِنْدَ رَبِّكُمْ تَخْتَصِمُونَ﴾ ["Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord will dispute."] [Az-Zumar 31].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verses 24–31 (part 1 of 3):

The one who guards against punishment tries to be saved from it, but the one who encounters a thing may encounter it with glad tidings, joy and happiness. So the interpretation of ﴿يَتَّقِي﴾ [Az-Zumar 24] as (yalqa, "meets") is without doubt deficient. However, at times the author interprets the Qur'an with something close to it.

He says: (yalqa ﴿بِوَجْهِهِ سُوءَ الْعَذَابِ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ﴾ [Az-Zumar 24], i.e., ashaddahu, "the most severe of it"). So he interpreted (sū'a, "evil") as (aswa', "worst"). (Aswa') is without doubt an ism al-tafdil (elative noun, comparative/superlative form), whereas (sū') is not an ism al-tafdil. On this basis, the author has interpreted the Book with something higher than it. The interpreter should correspond exactly to what is interpreted. If the author, may Allah have mercy on him, had said "the evil punishment," it would have been a more precise correspondence to the Qur'an.

He says: (by being thrown into the Fire with his hand chained to his neck). It seems he took this from the fact that he guards against the punishment with his face, because if his hand were free he would have guarded against the punishment with his hand. But I say: it does not follow from guarding against the punishment with his face that his hand is shackled, because his hand may be free and unrestrained, yet he is unable [to use it], or he thinks that repelling it with his face is stronger, so he repels it with his face.

The author, in mentioning the counterpart, said: (like one who is secure from it by entering Paradise).

The answer is: no. In that case the interrogative is for negation; meaning, one who guards against the evil of the punishment with his face is not equal to one who is secure from the punishment and did not guard against it.

(﴿وَقِيلَ لِلظَّالِمِينَ﴾ [Az-Zumar 24], i.e., the disbelievers of Makkah, ﴿ذُوقُوا مَا كُنْتُمْ تَكْسِبُونَ﴾, i.e., its recompense.)

His statement: (﴿لِلظَّالِمِينَ﴾, i.e., the disbelievers of Makkah). It seems he took this from His saying: ﴿كَذَّبَ الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ﴾ [Az-Zumar 25]. Otherwise, (al-zālimīn, "the wrongdoers") here is general, a general term that includes the disbelievers of Makkah and others, and this is the preferable reading.

If it is said: ﴿كَذَّبَ الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ﴾ indicates that this refers to later people. We say: yes, it indicates that it refers to later people, but every messenger was preceded by a messenger.

So for ʿĀd, we say: those before them denied, the people of Nūḥ (Noah) denied; and Thamūd denied, those before them the people of ʿĀd denied; and so on. Thus (al-zālimūn, "the wrongdoers") is general, including the disbelievers of Makkah and others. But the first to be included among them, without doubt, are the disbelievers of Makkah, because the Qur'an was revealed as a rebuke, a denunciation and a call to them.

The author said: (﴿فَأَتَاهُمُ الْعَذَابُ مِنْ حَيْثُ لَا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ [Az-Zumar 25], from a direction that does not occur to their minds). And this, as we have said, is a more severe and more emphatic interpretation than that the punishment came upon them while they were prepared for it.

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿فَأَذَاقَهُمُ اللَّهُ الْخِزْيَ﴾ [Az-Zumar 26], the humiliation and disgrace, from transformation, killing and other things, ﴿فِي الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا وَلَعَذَابُ الْآخِرَةِ أَكْبَرُ لَوْ كَانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾).

﴿أَذَاقَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ means He made it reach them, as if they had tasted it and experienced it through their own tasting.

The author's statement, may Allah have mercy on him: (from transformation and killing and other things). Transformation, like the Jews to whom Allah said: ﴿كُونُوا قِرَدَةً خَاسِئِينَ﴾ [Al-Baqarah 65], "Be apes, despised." And killing: the fighting of the Children of Israel against whom?

* Student: Against themselves.
* Shaykh: They killed themselves when they were commanded to repent, and it was said to them: if you are truthful in repentance, then kill yourselves. But Allah the Exalted mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah Jalut and Talut, and in it there is fighting.

Likewise the author says: (and other things), such as destruction by thunderbolt, the earthquake, and what is similar. The point is that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, destroyed all who denied the messengers.

If someone says: Were not some messengers killed?

The answer: Yes. But those who were killed either were not commanded to fight, so whoever transgressed against them did so without fighting; or they were attacked unawares without openly being killed. Then, when they were killed, does that mean what they called to dies with their death? It may remain, and this will be a victory for them even after their death.

(﴿فَأَذَاقَهُمُ اللَّهُ الْخِزْيَ﴾, the humiliation and disgrace, from transformation, killing and other things, in the life of this world, ﴿وَلَعَذَابُ الْآخِرَةِ أَكْبَرُ لَوْ كَانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾. ﴿لَوْ كَانُوا﴾, i.e., the deniers, if they knew its punishment, they would not have denied.) His statement (they would not have denied) is the omitted answer of (law, "if").

Then the Exalted said: ﴿وَلَقَدْ ضَرَبْنَا لِلنَّاسِ فِي هَذَا الْقُرْآنِ مِنْ كُلِّ مَثَلٍ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَذَكَّرُونَ﴾ [Az-Zumar 27]. "We have certainly set forth for people in this Qur'an every kind of example, that they may be reminded."

﴿ضَرَبْنَا﴾ (We struck/set forth). The author says (jaʿalnā, "We made"). Perhaps (ḍarb, "striking/setting forth") is more specific than (jaʿl, "making"); i.e., We clarified for people in this Qur'an every example. The sentence here is emphasized by three emphatics: the lām, qad, and the implied oath, because the construction in such a structure is understood as: "By Allah, indeed..." so it is emphasized by three emphatics.

As for His saying ﴿وَلَقَدْ ضَرَبْنَا لِلنَّاسِ﴾: if someone says, how is this emphasized when it is a known matter, and generally emphasis is used only when there is need for it?

The answer: emphasis may be used when there is need for it, when the addressee is doubtful or denying. It may also be used for the importance of the emphasized matter even if there is no denial or hesitation. This verse is an example: Allah's setting forth of examples for people in the Qur'an is a perceptible, apprehensible matter, but because of its importance Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, emphasized it.

﴿لِلنَّاسِ فِي هَذَا الْقُرْآنِ مِنْ كُلِّ مَثَلٍ﴾ [Az-Zumar 27], i.e., from every likeness. Allah sets forth similitudes and parallels so that whoever is in the position of this parallel and this likeness is warned, so that he does not do what [the other] did.

﴿لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَذَكَّرُونَ﴾, i.e., they may take admonition. Here (laʿalla, "perhaps/so that") is for ta'līl (causation, "so that"), which is one of its meanings. Among its other meanings is tarajjī (hope), as in: perhaps the beloved is coming. Another is ishfāq (apprehension), as in: perhaps the beloved has perished. In the first, "perhaps the beloved is coming," it is hope; in the second, it is apprehension, meaning I fear he has perished. It also comes for causation, as in this verse, and as in His saying: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ الصِّيَامُ كَمَا كُتِبَ عَلَى الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِكُمْ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَّقُونَ﴾ [Al-Baqarah 183]. Is there a third example?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: ﴿لَعَلَّ اللَّهَ يُحْدِثُ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ أَمْرًا﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿لَا تَدْرِي لَعَلَّ اللَّهَ يُحْدِثُ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ أَمْرًا﴾ [At-Talaq 1], "You do not know; perhaps Allah will bring about after that some matter." This may be for expectation (tawaqquʿ).
* Student: ﴿لَعَلَّكَ بَاخِعٌ نَفْسَكَ﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿لَعَلَّكَ بَاخِعٌ﴾ [Ash-Shuʿara 3], "Perhaps you will destroy yourself," also for expectation. It occurs often in the Qur'an.
* Student: ﴿لَعَلِّي أَبْلُغُ الْأَسْبَابَ﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿لَعَلِّي أَبْلُغُ الْأَسْبَابَ﴾ [Ghafir 36], "Perhaps I may reach the ways," is for hope, and it may be for causation. Laʿalla occurs much in the Qur'an. Some people think it means hope everywhere, and say: how would Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, hope for something when He is capable of all things? We say: when laʿalla comes in the speech of Allah, it is for causation.

His statement: (﴿يَتَذَكَّرُونَ﴾ [Az-Zumar 27], i.e., they take admonition), because this is the purpose of setting forth examples.

﴿قُرْآنًا عَرَبِيًّا غَيْرَ ذِي عِوَجٍ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَّقُونَ﴾ [Az-Zumar 28], "A Qur'an in Arabic, without any crookedness, that they may be mindful of Allah." ﴿قُرْآنًا﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), and ﴿عَرَبِيًّا﴾ is another ḥāl. I.e., this Qur'an in which is every example is a Qur'an. Qur'ān comes as a masdar (verbal noun) and as an ism al-fāʿil or ism al-mafʿūl (active or passive participle). From its use as a masdar: al-Ghufrān and al-Shukrān; by this I mean the pattern fuʿlān, which comes as a masdar, such as al-Ghufrān, al-Shukrān, al-Qur'ān. This masdar in the word Qur'an may be understood as an ism al-mafʿūl, so Qur'an means maqrū' (recited), and on this it means matlūw (read). It may also be an ism al-fāʿil, meaning qāri' (reciter), from qara'a al-māʾ, when he gathers water in the pool. If you reflect, you will find both descriptions apply to it: it is recited and it gathers. For this reason the scholars of the principles of tafsir said: it is valid for it to be in the sense of an ism al-fāʿil and valid for it to be in the sense of an ism al-mafʿūl.

His statement ﴿عَرَبِيًّا﴾: i.e., in the Arabic language, which is the tongue of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the tongue of the people among whom he was sent.

Arabic is the best of tongues, the most eloquent, the most articulate and the clearest. For this reason Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, chose it for the message of Muhammad (ﷺ). If someone says: Are there not words in the Qur'an whose origin is non-Arabic? Yes, there are. But these words whose origin is not Arabic, when the Arabs spoke them, they Arabized them and they became Arabic. For this reason these Arabized words are not free of some change; in general there must be some change in them. When the Arabs speak them and use them and they become prevalent on their tongues, they become Arabic. Are they 'arabah (pure Arabic) or musta'rabah (Arabized)?

* Student: Musta'rabah.
* Shaykh: Musta'rabah. So they are Arabized words from people who were also Arabized; i.e., the origin of the Arabs was Arabized, because they were not Arabs originally. Ismāʿīl is the son of Ibrāhīm, and his language was not Arabic. But when the Jurhum came to the mother of Ismāʿīl and settled with her, he became Arabic, and Arabness has continued until this day.

He says: ﴿قُرْآنًا عَرَبِيًّا غَيْرَ ذِي عِوَجٍ﴾ [Az-Zumar 28]. This description is negative, not affirmative: ﴿غَيْرَ ذِي عِوَجٍ﴾. Know that there is no pure negative among the descriptions of the Qur'an, because a pure negative contains no praise. Rather, everything described to the Qur'an by way of negation indicates the perfection of its opposite. So when He says ﴿غَيْرَ ذِي عِوَجٍ﴾, it means for the perfection of its straightness. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ يَهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ﴾ [Al-Isra' 9], "Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright." The Qur'an guides to what is most upright in matters of religion and matters of the world, in a manner that has no crookedness in any respect. For this reason He said: ﴿غَيْرَ ذِي عِوَجٍ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَّقُونَ﴾, i.e., so that they may be mindful of Allah. Allah made it clear to us in this Qur'an and made it without crookedness for the sake of His piety, the Mighty and Majestic.

The commentator, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (﴿وَلَقَدْ ضَرَبْنَا لِلنَّاسِ فِي هَذَا الْقُرْآنِ مِنْ كُلِّ مَثَلٍ﴾ [Az-Zumar 27], i.e., We made). This interpretation is a general one, because striking an example is not merely making it; rather, striking an example is for taking lesson from it. So "I struck it as an example" means I made it a likeness so that it may be taken as a lesson.

His statement: ﴿لِلنَّاسِ﴾ and ﴿مِنْ كُلِّ مَثَلٍ﴾ include all people, believer and disbeliever, so that these and those may be reminded.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, the humiliation, the disgrace, the shame, the scandal, all of it.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: I.e., do not humiliate us and do not disgrace us.
* Student: (...) Is the Arabic language the best of languages (...)?
* Shaykh: No. Which is better: the message of Muhammad (peace be upon him) and his nation, or the other messages and their communities?
* Student: The message of the Prophet (ﷺ).
* Shaykh: Then it is without doubt the best. For this reason there are reports, but there is scrutiny in them, that the Arabic language is the language of the people of Paradise.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. That Allah chose this great message in the Arabic language is sufficient, by His saying: ﴿اللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ حَيْثُ يَجْعَلُ رِسَالَتَهُ﴾ [Al-An'am 124], "Allah knows best where to place His message." Thus this place became suitable for this great message, because it is great.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It is known for its clarity. If it had come in other than Arabic, it would not have been clear. But that He chose that it be among these Arabs and in their language is evidence of its excellence.
* Student: (...). Someone says: the Messenger (ﷺ) is specific to the Arabs, because the Qur'an is Arabic. Do we answer with this same answer?
* Shaykh: No. If he says he is specific to the Arabs, we say: yes, he was sent to the unlettered, but to all people. As if someone were in the East or in the West and was a ruler over all the continent where he is. So Muhammad (peace be upon him) was sent to these people, but to all people. And it is known that he must be sent to his own people. Suppose he was sent to non-Arabs and was a messenger to the people: it is the same thing.
* Student: Does punishment have a color and a taste?
* Shaykh: Yes. The thing that strikes a person directly is said to be "tasted" (dhāqahu), but not with the tongue. Rather, because it struck him directly, it became like the food that a person puts into his stomach.
* Student: We said: negative description does not indicate praise, like the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted (...).
* Shaykh: Yes. If we say it must include perfection, then "He neither begets nor is begotten" indicates the perfection of His oneness.
* Student: (...) the evil of punishment on the Day of Resurrection (...). Does it indicate the face? The punishment reaches the face more severely than the rest of the body?
* Shaykh: In any case, the face's feeling of punishment is more intense than the body's feeling of the rest.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: If it is the worst punishment, and it is in the face, it becomes harder on a person than if it were in another part. But what appears to us, as we said, is that "sū' al-ʿadhāb" (evil punishment) is not an elative; rather it is of the type of attributing a quality to its described noun, i.e., "the evil punishment."
* Student: (...) good and evil. Is it not from the category of "good and evil"?
* Shaykh: "Good and evil" are also used as elatives, when you say: this is better than this, and this is worse than this. And they may be used to mean only the description of evil, as you say: this is evil, this is good.

* * *

* Student: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. ﴿Allah presents an example: a man in whom are partners disputing with one another, and a man belonging exclusively to one man. Are they equal in comparison? Praise be to Allah! But most of them do not know. Indeed, you will die, and indeed, they will die. Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, you will dispute.﴾ [Az-Zumar 29–31]

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿Allah presents an example: a man in whom are partners disputing with one another, and a man belonging exclusively to one man﴾ [Az-Zumar 29]. When Allah said: ﴿And We have certainly set forth for people in this Qur'an every kind of example﴾ [Az-Zumar 27], He mentioned this example, and He struck an example.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, clarified this great example, saying: ﴿Allah presents an example: a man in whom are partners disputing with one another﴾. ﴿A man in whom are partners disputing with one another﴾: ﴿in whom are partners disputing with one another﴾ means quarrelling and disagreeing. Each of them says: I am his master, I am the one who wants to use him, and similar things. So they are always in dispute and contention, because each of them wants to have him exclusively. The second man, ﴿a man belonging exclusively to one man﴾: salaman means belonging exclusively to this man, with no one sharing him.

If someone says: How do you know that salaman means "exclusively belonging" and free of partners?

We say: We know this from mentioning the opposite, which is His saying ﴿in whom are partners disputing with one another﴾; because a word is known from its context and from mentioning its opposite. Among the most prominent examples of this is the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿So go forth in separate groups or go forth all together﴾ [An-Nisa' 71].

If someone asks you: what is the meaning of thubāt? You would understand its meaning from what follows: ﴿or go forth all together﴾. So thubāt is the opposite of "gathered together," i.e., individually: go forth individually, or go forth all together. This is one of the rules of tafsir: the meaning of a word is known by mentioning what is opposed to it. Here we say: "a man belonging exclusively" (salaman), i.e., purely belonging to its owner, with no one sharing it with him. If someone asks: how do you know this? We say: by the rule we mentioned, that the counterpart of a thing, i.e., what is set as its equivalent, is its opposite in meaning. This man who belonged exclusively to one man: does anyone share with him in his ownership? No. Does anyone dispute with him? No.

So we must know the difference between the owned thing in which there are disputing partners, and the owned thing in which there are no partners, and then measure against it the one who is sincere to Allah, who worships Allah alone, and the one who worships others along with Allah. For this reason He said: ﴿Are they equal in comparison?﴾ [Az-Zumar 29], i.e., are these two men equal: one in whom there are disputing partners, and the other belonging exclusively to one man? Are these two equal? The answer is no. So the interrogative then means negation; i.e., the two are not equal.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verse 24–31 (part 2 of 3):

The interrogative (istifham) comes with many meanings, as is well known in the science of rhetoric (balaghah). But when it occurs in a context of negation, it carries the sense of a challenge (tahaddi). For if it were said: "They are not equal" (la yastawiyan), we would understand the negation of their equality. But when it is said: "Are they equal?" (hal yastawiyan), there are two matters:
The first matter: the negation of equality.
The second matter: the challenge. We say: "Do you have anything that proves that they are equal?" So converting the negation into an interrogative is more emphatic in negation and clearer. ﴿Are they equal in description?﴾ The answer is: No.
Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾ [az-Zumar 29]: He praises Himself, Mighty and Majestic, for the perfection of His attributes and the perfection of His bounty. Among His bounties is that He sets forth parables for people in the Qur'an, so that they may take heed, although He, Mighty and Majestic, is free of need from them. ﴿And whoever disbelieves - indeed, Allah is free from need of the worlds﴾ [Ali 'Imran 97]. Nevertheless, His mercy refuses except that He make clear to His servants what they need in the matters of their religion and their worldly life. For this reason, after this complete clarification in the parable, He said: ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾.
Then He said: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ [az-Zumar 29]. "Bal" (but, rather) here is for idrab (a shift or turning away), and idrab has two meanings:
The first meaning: idrab intiqal (a shift that moves from one thing to another).
The second meaning: idrab ibtal (a shift that nullifies), which cancels the first and affirms the second. When you say: "Zayd did not stand, but 'Amr did," this is idrab ibtal: you have nullified the first and affirmed the second.
In the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Rather, their knowledge has failed concerning the Hereafter; rather, they are in doubt about it; rather, they are blind to it﴾ [an-Naml 66], this is a shift from one meaning to a stronger meaning.
In this verse: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, is it idrab ibtal or idrab intiqal? It is idrab intiqal, because nothing preceded that it nullifies. And the saying ﴿But most of them do not know﴾: the intended meaning of ﴿most of them﴾ here is most of mankind, as occurs in other verses: ﴿But most of mankind do not know﴾ [al-A'raf 187].
The negation of knowledge here is due to the negation of its necessary consequence, which is action and compliance. Most people are in ignorance, and most people are in deviation. In ignorance, they do not recognize the truth; in deviation, they do not accept the truth nor act upon it. It is correct to negate knowledge from all of them. As for the one who is in ignorance, the negation of knowledge from him is evident. As for the one who is in deviation despite having knowledge, the negation of knowledge from him is because he has not benefited from it and has not acted upon it.
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed, they will die. Then indeed, you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, will dispute﴾ [az-Zumar 30-31]. ﴿Indeed, you﴾ is addressed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
﴿Will die﴾ is a description of him in the future.
﴿And indeed, they will die﴾ likewise. Death is emphasized even though it is known with certainty, because the deeds of those who denied the Prophet ﷺ are the deeds of one who has not been certain of death. For one who truly believes in death must prepare for it, but they do not prepare for it, so their not preparing for it is like denial, or is in the position of denial. Therefore it was emphasized.
His saying ﴿mayyit﴾ with a shaddah on the ya is said of one who will die while still alive. As for (mayt), it is said of one upon whom death has fallen, i.e., after the departure of life, one says (mayt). And sometimes (mayyit) is said, but the more common is (mayt). Accordingly, a distinction is made between describing a living person as dying, where one says (mayyit), and describing a dead person with death, where one says (mayt).
﴿Indeed, you﴾: the address is to the Prophet ﷺ and to whoever opposed him and disbelieved in him.
﴿On the Day of Resurrection﴾: its explanation has already passed.
﴿Before your Lord, you will dispute﴾: before your Lord who created you the first time and returned you a second time, you will dispute before Him as to which of you is upon the truth. Now we know the outcome of this dispute, who will prevail?
* Students: The believers.
* Shaykh: The believers, without doubt. Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿And never will Allah give the disbelievers over the believers a way﴾ [an-Nisa' 141]. So the disbeliever has no way over the believer. Thus the outcome, praise be to Allah, is known: the believers are the victorious on the Day of Resurrection, and they are the ones who prevail over their enemies.
Now let us return to the words of the author, and then we will take all the benefits, God willing.
The author, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (Allah struck a parable for the polytheist and the monotheist). The author's restriction to the polytheist and the monotheist is clear, because the parable struck, namely the servant owned by several partners and the servant wholly devoted to one master, applies exactly to the polytheist and the monotheist.
He says: (Allah struck a parable for the polytheist and the monotheist: ﴿a man﴾ [az-Zumar 29]), a substitute (badal) for ﴿a parable﴾. Concerning the badal, Imam Ibn Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, says:
"The follower intended by the ruling without an intermediary..."
This is the badal.
His saying "the follower intended by the ruling" excludes the rest of the followers (tawabi'). His saying "without an intermediary" excludes the conjunctive introduced by (bal), for the conjunctive introduced by (bal), when it is for idrab ibtal, is the one intended by the ruling, but through an intermediary, so it is not called a badal.
Here He said: ﴿a parable, a man﴾. If ﴿a parable﴾ were removed and He said: "Allah struck a man," would the statement be correct or not? It is correct, because the intended word is "man." If you say: "I saw Muhammad, 'Ali," 'Ali is a badal, because the intended is 'Ali. If a speaker says: "I saw 'Ali Muhammad," you understand that he meant Muhammad and did not mean 'Ali, because Muhammad is a badal from 'Ali. The badal is what is intended by the ruling, but its cause may be error, forgetfulness, or other causes. The point is that the badal is what Ibn Malik defined by his saying:
"The follower intended by the ruling without an intermediary is what is named a badal."
He says: (﴿in it are partners in dispute﴾ disputing, bad of character). From where did he derive bad character? From His saying ﴿in dispute﴾, because mutual contention indicates bad character, since good character yields its right even if that causes harm or loss to oneself, because the goodness of his character prevails over taking his right. Thus it is fitting for a person to be of good character, and to overlook some of his right even if that harms himself. And let him know that if his soul says: "Your humility and your pardon of your right is humiliation for you," let him know that this is from the whisperings of Satan. For the Prophet ﷺ said: «Allah does not increase a servant in pardon except in honor, and whoever humbles himself for Allah, Allah raises him» [narrated by Muslim (2588/69) from Abu Hurayrah]. So do not let your soul overcome you and pride take you into sin, saying: "I cannot remain silent about this man; who am I, that he should transgress against me? I am so-and-so, son of so-and-so!" This is from Satan. ﴿So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is upon Allah﴾ [ash-Shura 40]. ﴿And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel [evil] with that which is better, and thereupon the one who is between you and him is [as if he were] a devoted friend﴾ [Fussilat 34]. ﴿But none receives it except those who are patient, and none receives it except one of great fortune﴾ [Fussilat 35], meaning: none is granted success in it except those who are patient, and none receives it except one of great fortune.
He says: (disputing, bad of character; ﴿and a man wholly devoted﴾). In my copy it is ﴿saliman﴾, a reading, and the commentator explained it accordingly. Salim means pure, as he explained it (pure, ﴿to a man﴾). ﴿Are they equal in description?﴾ He says: (﴿mathalan﴾ is a tamyiz). What is the tamyiz? From mayyaza, meaning to clarify. Ibn Malik defined it in the Alfiyyah, saying:
"A noun with the meaning of (min), clarifying and indefinite, is put in the accusative as a tamyiz, by what it explains."
This is the tamyiz: an indefinite noun that clarifies the ambiguous term it explains, and it has the meaning of (min). Its example is the saying: "Zayd perspired sweat" (tassabba Zaydun 'araqan). ''Araqan'' is a tamyiz. Apply the definition to it and you find it is a noun with the meaning of (min), since you say: "he perspired from sweat." Clarifying: i.e., explaining the verb "perspired," since "perspired" can mean perspired blood, perspired water, perspired sweat, so it clarified the one who perspired. Is it indefinite or definite?
Indefinite. This is the tamyiz:
"A noun with the meaning of (min), clarifying and indefinite, is put in the accusative as a tamyiz, by what it explains."
Now I have dictated to you two verses from the Alfiyyah of Ibn Malik. Whoever has memorized them now, let him recite the first verse of them. [Student:]
"The follower intended by the ruling without an intermediary is what is named a badal."
* Shaykh: Yes, the badal:
"The follower intended by the ruling without an intermediary is what is named a badal."
And this second one, the tamyiz?
* Student:
"A noun with the meaning of (min), clarifying and indefinite, is put in the accusative as a tamyiz, by what it explains."
* Shaykh: He says: (﴿mathalan﴾ is a tamyiz, meaning: a servant belonging to a group is not equal to a servant belonging to one, for the first, when all his owners demand his service at one time, is perplexed about whom among them to serve.)
He says: (is not equal), and thereby, may Allah have mercy on him, clarified that the interrogative in His saying ﴿Are they equal?﴾ is for negation, since he explained it as a negation.
His saying: (a servant belonging to a group is not equal to a servant belonging to one) is correct: they are not equal. The servant belonging to one may be dealt with as he wishes: whenever he wishes, he says "Serve me," and whenever he wishes, he says "Rest." Whenever he wishes, he sells him; whenever he wishes, he rents him out. But a servant belonging to a group, with a group who are contentious, of bad character, in constant dispute: are they equal? Never. If one says, "Come and serve me," and the second says, "Serve me," and the third says, "Serve me," and the fourth says, "Serve me," then one takes him by the right hand, the second by the left, the third by the right foot, and the fourth by the left foot, and then they tear the servant apart, because each wants him to be with him, to be the one he serves. Likewise in selling: if one wants to sell him, and the second says, "I do not want that," and the third says, "I want to rent him," and the fourth says, "I want to lend him," how can this be? Always in dispute and discord. The servant himself is in anxiety, perplexity, and affliction, and the partners too are always contentious. This cannot be equal to a man. This is undoubtedly a approximate parable; otherwise the difference between worshipping Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and worshipping others along with Him is great, meaning that it is greater. But Allah, the Exalted, brings this close to His servants, just as He brought the resurrection close by water sent down from the sky, by which the earth then brings forth plants. How long does it remain?
The plants of the earth after the rain falls? It remains for a period according to the goodness of the land, the abundance of rain, the suitable climate, and the season, but it remains.
Resurrection: ﴿It will be but one shout, and at once they will be on the surface﴾ [an-Nazi'at 13-14]. ﴿One shout, and at once they will be upon the surface﴾. Parables may not correspond exactly; the thing paralleled may be quicker than the parable, but it is mentioned by way of approximation. Undoubtedly, the difference between worshipping Allah alone and worshipping others with Him is greater than the difference between a man wholly devoted to one man and a man shared among contentious partners.
The author, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (This is a parable for the polytheist, and the second is a parable for the monotheist.) What is the second? A man wholly devoted to a man: this is for the monotheist, and the first is for the polytheist. And what is the purpose of striking this parable? The purpose is to warn against associating partners with Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
Then know that partners over a servant are in dispute, but with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, the matter is different. Allah says in the sacred hadith: «I am the most free of partners from partnership. Whoever does a deed in which he associates another with Me, I leave him and his partnership» [narrated by Muslim (2985/46) from Abu Hurayrah]. Contending partners cannot give up their share, but shirk with Allah: Allah leaves the polytheist and his partnership.
«Whoever does a deed in which he associates another with Me, I leave him and his partnership.» For this reason He said: (﴿Praise be to Allah﴾ [az-Zumar 29], alone). If praise belongs to Him alone, then worship must be to Him alone, because He is worthy of praise and worthy of worship, glorified and exalted; He alone deserves to be worshipped.
(﴿But most of them﴾, i.e., the people of Makkah, ﴿do not know﴾ what they will come to of punishment, so they associate partners.)
His saying: (﴿But most of them﴾, i.e., the people of Makkah). The author, may Allah have mercy on him, always, especially in the Meccan verses and surahs, makes such address specific to the people of Makkah. But what we should always do is take the indication of the Qur'an as general, except in cases of necessity, because the Qur'an was revealed for all creation until the Day of Resurrection. Restricting it to the people of Makkah would mean it does not include others except by analogy, whereas if we take its general wording, it includes the people of Makkah and others by explicit text.
There is a difference between a ruling being included by explicit text and its inclusion by analogy. The correct view is that the pronoun in ﴿most of them﴾ refers to all creation: most of creation do not know. This is why it is established in the authentic hadith that Allah says: «O Adam!» He says: «Here I am, at Your call and Your pleasure.» He says: «Bring forth from your progeny a group for the Fire,» or «the group of the Fire.» He says: «O Lord, what is the group of the Fire?» He says: «Of every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine» [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3348) and Muslim (222/379) from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri]. Are these the majority or the minority? The majority. So most of creation do not know, either because of their ignorance or their deviation. If it is due to ignorance, as I told you before, then knowledge is negated from them. If it is due to deviation, then knowledge is negated from them because it has no benefit, since they have not been guided by it.
He says: ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed, they will die.﴾
(﴿Indeed, you﴾ is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ; ﴿will die﴾ [az-Zumar 30], i.e., you will die.)
He says: (﴿And indeed, they will die﴾). He says: (So you will die and they will die), and as our common people say: "The promise is ahead" (qudda:m). (qudda:m) means the Day of Resurrection, because on the Day of Resurrection Allah judges between the servants; people will dispute over their deeds and religions, and dispute over their private rights, and Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection.
He says: (So there is no gloating over death), meaning that if you die, there is no gloating against you, because they too will die like you.
(It was revealed when they were slow to see his death ﷺ.) Thus the author said: the cause of its revelation was that Quraysh were slow to see the death of the Prophet ﷺ, so this verse was revealed informing him that he would die, and when he dies they too will die and dispute on the Day of Resurrection. But this claim requires evidence. Let us look at the occasion of revelation; we do not find this. If that is so, then one should not imagine a cause of revelation for the meaning of a verse of the Book of Allah, because the cause of revelation is pure report, and pure report has no room for reason in it. But we say: Allah mentioned this sentence as an indication that He will not waste your deed or theirs. He will not waste your deed in calling to monotheism, and He will not waste their deed of associating partners. For you have an appointed time in which you will be gathered and dispute before Allah, Mighty and Majestic. In this there is consolation for the Messenger ﷺ and a warning to the polytheists. It is, on one side, consolation and reassurance for the Messenger, peace be upon him, and on another side, a warning to the polytheists that they will die, and their death will also be near, and it will be certain with no doubt about it.

(﴿ثُمَّ إِنَّكُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ﴾ [الزمر ٣١] "Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection," ثم إنكم أيها الناس فيما بينكم من المظالم) This is a strange thing from the author, may God have mercy on him.
