The proof of this is that ﴿لَعَلَّ﴾ ["so that"] here indicates causation, and causation means affirming wisdom.

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿قُرْآنًا عَرَبِيًّا غَيْرَ ذِي عِوَجٍ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَّقُونَ﴾ ["An Arabic Qur'an, without any crookedness, that they may fear Allah."] [Az-Zumar 28].

* From this noble verse it is derived: that the Qur'an is Arabic, that is, revealed in the language of the Arabs.
* From its benefits: there is no non-Arabic (ʿajami) word in the Qur'an, because Allah described the whole Qur'an as Arabic, and this requires that it contain nothing of the language of non-Arabs. There is no doubt that this is the reality, so there is no non-Arabic word in the Qur'an. However, the scholars of tafsir and others differed on whether there is in the Qur'an a word whose origin is non-Arabic which was then Arabized. Some say yes, and some say no. Those who said yes argued that there are words in the noble Qur'an to which the rules of the Arabic language do not apply, and this means they are non-Arabic. This does not contradict the Qur'an being Arabic, because when the Arabs Arabized them they became Arabic through arabization (istiʿrab), just as the Arabs themselves were originally "Arabized" (mustaʿribah), since the language of their forefather Ismail was not Arabic.
Others said: these words which are non-Arabic came into the language of the Arabs by the coincidence of two languages (tawārud al-lughatayn), and there is no objection to two languages coinciding on one word. The dispute here is close to being verbal, because they all agree that there is no word in the Qur'an that is non-Arabic at the time of its revelation, never.
* From the benefits of this noble verse: the clarification of the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in revealing the Qur'an in the Arabic tongue, because the Prophet ﷺ was sent to an Arab people, so the wisdom was that his language be Arabic, as is the case with all the messengers. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَمَا أَرْسَلْنَا مِنْ رَسُولٍ إِلَّا بِلِسَانِ قَوْمِهِ لِيُبَيِّنَ لَهُمْ﴾ ["And We did not send any messenger except with the language of his people, to make clear to them."] [Ibrahim 4].
* From the benefits of this noble verse: understanding the meaning helps one toward righteousness, from His saying: ﴿قُرْآنًا عَرَبِيًّا﴾ ["an Arabic Qur'an"] ﴿لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَّقُونَ﴾ ["that they may fear Allah"]. This is a clear matter: understanding the meaning is among the causes of righteousness, because if someone speaks to you in words whose meaning you do not understand, nothing affects you; only what you understand the meaning of affects you. For this reason He said: ﴿لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَّقُونَ﴾.
* From this sentence we derive what we derived from the preceding sentence, His saying: ﴿لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَذَكَّرُونَ﴾ [Az-Zumar 27].

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿ضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا رَجُلًا فِيهِ شُرَكَاءُ مُتَشَاكِسُونَ﴾ ["Allah presents an example: a man in whom are partners in dispute..."] to the end [Az-Zumar 29].

* From the benefits of this noble verse: this verse is an application of His saying: ﴿وَلَقَدْ ضَرَبْنَا لِلنَّاسِ فِي هَذَا الْقُرْآنِ مِنْ كُلِّ مَثَلٍ﴾ [Az-Zumar 27], since this is a parable.
* From its benefits: the example of one who worships others along with Allah is like a servant in whom are partners who are quarrelsome, contending and disputing with one another. The reason is that this worshipper who associates others with Allah does not have a heart sincerely devoted to Allah; rather, partners pull at it from right and left until it is lost among them.
* From the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, the Exalted, brings a report or other matter and then establishes it for the addressee in the best manner. This is in His saying: ﴿هَلْ يَسْتَوِيَانِ مَثَلًا﴾ ["Are they equal in comparison?"] [Az-Zumar 29], because this interrogative, which is intended as a negation, serves to establish what was mentioned and to bind the addressee to it.
* From the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, the Exalted, deserves all praise for the perfection of His monotheism, from His saying: ﴿الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ﴾ ["All praise is due to Allah"].
* From its benefits: unrestricted praise belongs only to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. As for others, if they are praised, their praise is not absolute; rather, they are praised for a specific thing and a particular part of what is praiseworthy. Unrestricted praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds, the Mighty and Majestic, because He is the One praised in every state. The Prophet ﷺ, when something pleasing came to him, would say: "Praise be to Allah through whose blessing good things are completed." And when something displeasing came to him, he would say: "Praise be to Allah in every state."[[Narrated by Ibn Majah (3803) from the hadith of ʿAʾishah.]]
* From the benefits of this noble verse: most of the children of Adam do not know realities as they are, and even if they know them, they do not benefit from them, from His saying: ﴿بَلْ أَكْثَرُهُمْ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ["But most of them do not know"] [Az-Zumar 29].

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿إِنَّكَ مَيِّتٌ وَإِنَّهُمْ مَيِّتُونَ (٣٠) ثُمَّ إِنَّكُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ عِنْدَ رَبِّكُمْ تَخْتَصِمُونَ﴾ ["Indeed, you will die, and indeed they will die. Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord will dispute."] [Az-Zumar 30–31].

* From its benefits: our Prophet ﷺ will not live forever; rather, he will die, just as his opponents are dead. This is like His saying: ﴿وَمَا جَعَلْنَا لِبَشَرٍ مِنْ قَبْلِكَ الْخُلْدَ أَفَإِنْ مِتَّ فَهُمُ الْخَالِدُونَ﴾ ["And We did not grant eternity to any human before you. So if you die, would they be eternal?"] [Al-Anbiya 34].
* From its benefits: consolation for the Prophet ﷺ, from His saying: ﴿إِنَّكَ مَيِّتٌ وَإِنَّهُمْ مَيِّتُونَ (٣٠) ثُمَّ إِنَّكُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ عِنْدَ رَبِّكُمْ تَخْتَصِمُونَ﴾ [Az-Zumar 30–31].
* From its benefits: a warning to these deniers that they have an appointment with the Messenger ﷺ, which is the dispute on the Day of Resurrection.
* From its benefits: the people of polytheism and disbelief are adversaries of the people of monotheism and faith in the Hereafter, just as they are adversaries in this world. In this world there is no doubt about their enmity and the hostility of some toward others, and in the Hereafter it is greater and more severe.
* From its benefits: creatures will dispute before Allah on the Day of Resurrection. It is well known that when the dispute is between a believer and a disbeliever, the one who prevails is the believer, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿فَاللَّهُ يَحْكُمُ بَيْنَكُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ وَلَنْ يَجْعَلَ اللَّهُ لِلْكَافِرِينَ عَلَى الْمُؤْمِنِينَ سَبِيلًا﴾ ["Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection, and never will Allah give the disbelievers over the believers a way."] [An-Nisa 141].
* From the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of resurrection and reckoning, from His saying: ﴿ثُمَّ إِنَّكُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ عِنْدَ رَبِّكُمْ تَخْتَصِمُونَ﴾ ["Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord will dispute."] [Az-Zumar 31].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verse 32 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So who is more unjust than one who lies against Allah and denies the truth when it has come to him?﴾ [Az-Zumar 32] (man) here is interrogative, and His saying ﴿when it has come to him﴾: ﴿idh﴾ is an adverb meaning "when", and the interrogation in His saying ﴿Is not...﴾ is for affirmation (taqrir).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So who is more unjust than one who lies against Allah﴾. This interrogation here carries the meaning of negation; that is, no one is more unjust than one who lies against Allah. His saying ﴿lies against Allah﴾ means he fabricates falsehood against Him: either by attributing a partner to Him, or by declaring something forbidden which He has not forbidden, or making lawful something which He has not made lawful, or making obligatory something which He has not made obligatory, or denying one of His attributes, or affirming for Him what He has not described Himself with, or other things in which there is lying against Allah. So no one is more unjust than one who lies against Allah. Lying against Allah is not like lying against people, and lying against the Messenger ﷺ is not like lying against others among mankind. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, lying against me is not like lying against anyone else. Whoever lies against me deliberately, let him take his seat in the Fire"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1291), and Muslim (4/4), from the hadith of al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba.]].

As for His saying ﴿and denies the truth when it has come to him﴾ [Az-Zumar 32], He combined the two matters. ﴿denies the truth﴾ means he attributes falsehood to the truth and says: "This is a lie." Among this is the denial of the Messenger ﷺ by the Quraysh when they said: "He is a sorcerer, a liar."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?﴾ This interrogation is for affirmation (taqrir). The general rule is that when the interrogative hamza enters upon something that implies negation, it is generally for affirmation, and its answer is (bala), its answer in the affirmative is (bala), like: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [Ash-Sharh 1]. The interrogation here is for affirmation, and its meaning is: We have indeed expanded your breast.

﴿Has there not come to you the news of those who disbelieved before?﴾ [At-Taghabun 5], meaning: (indeed it has come to you). Examples of this in the Qur'an are many.

As for His saying ﴿Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?﴾ [Az-Zumar 32], it has used the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, and the context would have required him to say: "Is there not in Hell an abode for them?" Using the apparent noun in place of the pronoun has benefits, which we mentioned to you earlier. So who recalls them? Using the apparent noun in place of the pronoun?

* Student: It benefits generality.
* Shaykh: That is one; the benefit of generality, meaning an abode for them and for other disbelievers.
* Student: Reproach.
* Shaykh: No, because the matter may not contain reproach.
* Student: Drawing attention.
* Shaykh: No, that belongs to iltifat (shift of grammatical person), and perhaps this too increases attention.
* Student: Recording the description upon these disbelievers.
* Shaykh: Yes, recording the description upon these, that they are disbelievers; meaning, establishing that these are disbelievers. The third?
* Student: Emphasis.
* Shaykh: No, the third is causation (ta'lil). It conveys causation. If he had said: "Is there not in Hell an abode for them?" we would not have learned what the reason is for their abode being Hell. But when he says: ﴿Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?﴾ [Az-Zumar 32], we know that the cause is their disbelief. So it contains an explanation of the cause. Thus the use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun has three benefits. What is the first benefit?

Glory be to Allah the Mighty, how strange is the sleep of one who is awake!!

* Student: Causation, O Shaykh.
* Shaykh: The Nile flows, even if you were here.
* Student: Causation.
* Another student: We mentioned that it conveys generality, conveying generality.
* Shaykh: Yes, that is one. The second?
* Student: The second: the establishment of the attribute upon these described persons, and conveying causation.
* Shaykh: The third: conveying causation, this is among the benefits of using the apparent noun in place of the pronoun.

﴿Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?﴾ [Az-Zumar 32]. So these disbelievers who lied against Allah and denied the truth are disbelievers, and their abode is Hell, we seek refuge with Allah. And (Jahannam) has been said to be among the Arabicized foreign words, and its origin in the Persian language is (jahannam). It has also been said that it is an Arabic word, derived from (al-juhmah), meaning darkness.

The Fire, due to the depth of its bottom, may Allah protect me and you from it, is blackened and dark. Allah knows best. Whether this or that, the point is that in the Arabic language it is used for a great fire that is blackened.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (﴿So who is more unjust﴾ ﴿so who﴾ meaning no one). The author's conversion of the interrogation into negation indicates that the meaning of the interrogation is what, O people?

* Students: Affirmation.
* Shaykh: No, negation. No one is more unjust than one who lies against Allah; that is, who fabricates falsehood against Him. The author said: (by attributing a partner and a son to Him), and this is by way of example, not restriction. So whoever says that Allah has a son has lied against Allah; whoever says that Allah has a partner has lied against Allah; whoever says that Allah is not described by these attributes with which He described Himself has lied against Allah; whoever says that Allah resembles His creation has lied against Allah; whoever says that Allah prohibited the sa'iba, the wasila and the ham has lied against Allah.

The point is that the author, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned only these two matters as an example, not as a restriction. Lying against Allah is numerous, and some of it is worse than others.

He said: (﴿and denies the truth﴾ [Az-Zumar 32] with the Qur'an when it has come to him). There is no doubt that the Qur'an is truth; indeed it is truth and justice, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [Al-An'am 115]. It is truth in terms of its reports and just in terms of its rulings. But the matter is more general than what the author said: ﴿the truth﴾ means whatever is true, whether in the Qur'an or in the Sunnah, for it is included in His saying ﴿and denies the truth﴾.

As for His saying ﴿when it has come to him﴾, it means when it reached him. It is not something transmitted to him; rather it reached him directly, and was reported to him on the tongue of the truthful one, so he denies it. If someone related to us from his shaykh, and his shaykh from his shaykh, and his shaykh from his shaykh, until it reached the Messenger ﷺ, could we deny this if one of the narrators was accused of lying?

* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes, it is possible. But if the report came to us directly from the Messenger, then denying it is disbelief. For this reason, if one of the people denied a hadith in one of the books of hadith, and denied it, we would say to him: Why did you deny it? Do you have doubt that the Messenger ﷺ said it? He says: I have no doubt that he said it, but it is a lie. What do we say to him? We say: This one is a disbeliever, because the truth came to him by his own acknowledgment. But if he says: This is a lie, because one of the narrators is a liar or a great liar, so I reject it for this reason, what do we say? Does he become a disbeliever or not? He does not become a disbeliever; rather this may be what is obligatory upon him if this is the result of his ijtihad.

The benefit of His saying ﴿when it has come to him﴾ [Az-Zumar 32] is that there is no intermediary between him and the one who brought the truth, so that it might be said: "Perhaps she has an excuse, while you blame her." There is no intermediary there.

He said: (﴿Is there not in Hell an abode﴾ a dwelling ﴿for the disbelievers﴾ [Az-Zumar 32]) He said: Yes (bala). This is the answer to "Is there not" and similar expressions. When the interrogative hamza enters upon something that implies negation, the answer for affirmation is (bala). Had you said (na'am), it would have been negation. So if you say: "Did Zayd not stand?" and the addressee says: "Na'am," it means he did not stand; and if you say: "Did Zayd not stand?" and the addressee says: "Bala," meaning he did stand. For this reason it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, regarding His saying ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ "They said: Bala" [Al-A'raf 172], that he said: If they had said "Na'am," they would have disbelieved; meaning, if they had said "Na'am," it would mean "You are not our Lord." This is well known in the Arabic language. However, sometimes the answer comes with (na'am) intended as affirmation, and from it is the saying of the poet:

Is not the night gathering Umm 'Amr
and us, so that is what brings us close?
Na'am, and you see the crescent as I see it,
and the day rises over it as it rose over me.

Are you with us? Who will recite the verse for me? Did you not memorize it before?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Repeat it a second and third time:
Is not the night gathering Umm 'Amr
and us, so that is what brings us close?
Na'am, and you see the crescent as I see it,
and the day rises over it as it rose over me.
A third time:
Is not the night gathering Umm 'Amr
and us, so that is what brings us close?
Na'am, and you see the crescent as I see it,
and the day rises over it as it rose over me.
A man of the Arabs used to recite a qasida of fifty or sixty verses at one time and then depart, and people would have memorized it.

* Student:
Is not the night gathering Umm 'Amr
and us, so that is what brings us close?
Na'am, and you see the crescent as I see it,
and the day rises over it as it rose over me.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: Na'am, and you see the crescent .....
* Shaykh: As I see it.
* Student: As I see it.
* Shaykh: ......... and the day rises over it as it rose over me.
Poor fellow. It is enough for him with Umm 'Amr that the night gathers them, and that she sees the crescent as he sees it, and the day rises over her as it rose over him.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: If someone said: perhaps this is a poetic necessity, we say: No, because if he had used (bala) instead of (na'am), the verse would have been sound. If he had said:
Bala, and you see the crescent as I see it,
the verse would have been sound.

In any case, the author answered with (bala), meaning to affirm what was mentioned, that ﴿there is in Hell an abode for the disbelievers﴾ [Az-Zumar 32].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that no one is more unjust ﴿than one who lies against Allah and denies the truth﴾, because he combines two evils. The first evil: lying against others. The second evil: denying the truthful one. If one of them is alone, does he deserve this description of being the most unjust of people? If he lied against Allah but affirmed the truth, does he deserve this description? No, because a judgment or description built upon a combination of attributes is established only when they are all present. Nevertheless, if the attributes are separate, he has a share of this description. So His saying: ﴿Woe to those who pray, who are heedless of their prayer, who make show, and withhold small kindnesses﴾ [Al-Ma'un 4-7]: each of these attributes has a share of woe, but the full woe only occurs with the combination of the attributes: ﴿What has brought you into Saqar? They said: We were not of those who prayed, and we did not feed the poor, and we used to plunge with the plungers, and we used to deny the Day of Judgment﴾ [Al-Muddaththir 42-46]. Four attributes are the cause of their entering the Fire; if any one of them stood alone, their entry into the Fire would not be deserved, but it has a share of this threat.

Here: ﴿So who is more unjust than one who lies against Allah and denies the truth﴾ [Az-Zumar 32]: how many attributes are there?

* Student: Two attributes.
* Shaykh: What are they?
* Student: He fabricated against Allah, and denied the truth.
* Shaykh: And denied the truth. If he fabricated without denying the truth?
* Student: It does not apply to him.
* Shaykh: The description of being most unjust does not apply to him, but he is still unjust. And if he denied the truth without lying against Allah, likewise.

If someone said: this verse indicates that whoever is characterized by these two attributes is the most unjust of people, so how do we reconcile it with other texts that indicate the same meaning, such as: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mention of His name in the mosques of Allah and strives for their ruin?﴾ [Al-Baqarah 114], and in the hadith: "And who is more unjust than one who goes to create as I create" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5953), and Muslim (2111/101), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah], and many other texts?

The answer is that we say: all of these share the attribute of being most unjust. We say these matters share the attribute of being most unjust, and there is no objection to their sharing it. You say, for example: So-and-so is the most truthful of people; and the second also: So-and-so is the most truthful of people; and the third: So-and-so is the most truthful of people, meaning they share this highest rank, since the superlative indicates perfection in this attribute.

Or we say: the being most unjust is considered in terms of the kind of this sin. For example: who is the most unjust of people in lying against others? One who lies against Allah. Who is the most unjust of people in denying others? One who denies the truth. This second way is closer, because sharing in being most unjust may prevent the superlative in the other category; that is, a person cannot fully conceive that sharing in being most unjust requires that none of them be more unjust than the others. So if we say the being most unjust here is considered in terms of the kind of the one compared against: that is, "who is more unjust than one who lies against Allah among those who lie against others," then the one who lies against Allah is more unjust than the one who lies against Zayd and 'Amr, is it not so?

And the one who denies what may be true or false is not like the one who denies what is known to be the truth: ﴿denies the truth when it has come to him﴾ [Az-Zumar 32].

﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mention of His name in the mosques of Allah?﴾ [Al-Baqarah 114]: whoever prevents the mosques of Allah is more unjust than whoever prevents another person his right. If you prevented a man from entering his own house, your prevention of this man from entering the mosques of Allah and mentioning His name there would be greater. "Who is more unjust than one who goes to create as I create?" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5953), and Muslim (2111/101), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. If someone went to create like the creation of so-and-so, of those whose craft he is forbidden to compete with, the one who went to create like the creation of Allah would be more unjust, and so on. This answer, as you see, is sound, and no objection can be raised against it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that lying against Allah is the most unjust type of lying, because of His saying: ﴿So who is more unjust than one who lies against Allah?﴾ And if the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, lying against me is not like lying against any of you" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1291), and Muslim (4/4), from the hadith of al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba], then what of lying against Allah, who sent him? If lying against the Messenger is of this standing, then what of one who lies against Allah?!

Commentary of Ibn ʿUthaymin (Tafsir al-Qur'an al-Karim) on Surah 39, verse 32 (part 2 of 2):

* Among the benefits of this noble verse is the obligation of caution in explaining the Qur'an (tafsir, explanation of the Qur'an), because the one who explains the Qur'an is bearing witness about Allah that He meant such-and-such. The matter may be otherwise, in which case he has lied about Allah. For this reason, the eminent Companions were cautious about explaining the Qur'an, even though it was revealed in their language, in their era, and in their presence. Yet they were still cautious. Abu Bakr was asked about the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And fruit and pasture﴾ [ʿAbasa 31]: "What is al-abb?" He said: "What earth would bear me, and what sky would shade me, if I were to say about the Book of Allah what I do not know?"[[Narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf (30609).]] He meant that he did not know it, and he said: "What earth would bear me, and what sky would shade me." Today, by the will of Allah, there are people who explain verses as if they were Ibn ʿAbbas, though he was among the most ignorant of Allah's servants, and they do not care about explaining. If he explained the words of Zayd or ʿAmr, we would not care, and why would we care? But when he explains the words of Allah, he bears witness about Allah that He meant such-and-such. Therefore, among the gravest things is to interpret the words of Allah away from their apparent meaning toward a meaning that contradicts the apparent sense without clear evidence. By this we recognize the misguidance of the people of taʿtil (those who deny Allah's attributes), who say: "He istawa ʿala al-ʿarsh" means "He seized control of the Throne." Do you bear witness that Allah meant this? ﴿That which I created with My two hands﴾ [Sad 75]: "with My power" or "with My blessing" or something similar. This is a lie against Allah, because Allah addressed us in the Qur'an in the Arabic tongue, so it is obligatory that we interpret this Qur'an according to the Arabic language without distorting it.

* Student: Sometimes, O Shaykh, a verse passes and a person is asked about it, and its meaning is very clear to him, even though he has never read a tafsir of it. May he say its apparent meaning like this? Or should he say: "By Allah, I do not know, because I have not read a tafsir of this verse"?

* Shaykh: If the clear thing whose explanation is required by the language, there is no harm in it. If someone asked: "What is the meaning of Allah's words ﴿Establish the prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah 43]?" and a layman said: "Aqim al-salah," meaning: "Say: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, the prayer has been established," and so on, this is forbidden. But if ﴿Establish the prayer﴾ were asked about of a student of knowledge who knows the meaning of iqamah (establishing), which is doing a thing in a upright manner, and he said: "The meaning of ﴿establish﴾ is: bring it complete," there is no objection to this.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah pardon you. The Prophet ﷺ said: "You are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your worldly life,"[[Narrated by Muslim (2363/141) from the hadith of ʿAʾishah and Anas ibn Malik.]] concerning the matter of pollinating palm trees. If someone said: "When the Prophet ﷺ speaks about worldly matters, such as medicine and others, we may take it or reject it according to whether it agrees with experience, so is this rejecting the ruling of the Prophet ﷺ or not?"

* Shaykh: If the Prophet ﷺ said a statement and it is not established during his lifetime that he retracted it, then his statement remains, and it is not permissible for us to oppose it, even if it concerns matters of medicine. For this reason, when he said: "If a fly falls into the drink of one of you, let him immerse it, then remove it, for in one of its wings is a disease and in the other is a cure,"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (3320) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] or he said "healing," it is not permissible for us to say: "By Allah, this contradicts medicine." Rather, it is obligatory for us to say: "This is true," and then we know that medicine has not reached this knowledge. As for a statement made during his lifetime that he himself later retracted, there is no harm in that.
Now, for example, carpenters know more about carpentry than we do, do they not? They know more about carpentry than us; they know how to work wood and we do not. The engineers who build cars, those who build (...), and those who make watches know more about them than we do. So his saying: "You are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your worldly life"[[Narrated by Muslim (2363/141) from the hadith of ʿAʾishah and Anas ibn Malik.]] means: what you make and handle in a tangible way, you know better. But the rulings of our religious life belong to Allah and His Messenger, and they know best about these.

* Student: O Shaykh, the report of Abu Bakr: "What sky would shade me." Is this authentic?

* Shaykh: This is well known among the exegetes and others. Even Shaykh al-Islam quoted it in the introduction.

* Student: The author's words: (﴿Without any crookedness﴾ [al-Zumar 28], meaning: without confusion or contradiction) (...)?

* Shaykh: That was in yesterday's lesson.

* Student: Yes, indeed, we did not mention it.

* Shaykh: No, we mentioned it, we explained it. Did we not explain it yesterday? And we said that it guides to that which is most upright.

* Student: No, I mean the author's statement (...).

* Shaykh: No, it is ﴿without any crookedness﴾, not just confusion and fabrication. ﴿Without any crookedness﴾ in its rulings and its reports (...).

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed: ﴿And he who brings the truth and confirms it—those are the righteous. For them is whatever they will in their Lord's presence. That is the reward of the doers of good, that Allah may remove from them the worst of what they did and reward them their due for the best of what they used to do. Is not Allah sufficient for His servant? Yet they frighten you with those other than Him, and whom Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide. And whom Allah guides, for him there is no misleader. Is not Allah Almighty, Owner of Retribution?﴾ [al-Zumar 33–37].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿So who is more unjust than one who lies about Allah and denies the truth when it has come to him? Is there not in Hell a residence for the disbelievers?﴾. What is the meaning of the interrogative here?

* Student: Negation.

* Shaykh: It means negation.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes. And what is the benefit of expressing a negation in the form of a question?

* Student: Emphasis (...).

* Another student: Approximation.

* Shaykh: Approximation? Does expressing negation in the form of a question mean approximation?

* Student: Affirmation (taqrir).

* Shaykh: Or affirmation.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes. Its benefit is that it includes a challenge, because saying "no one is more unjust" without ﴿so who is more unjust﴾ would not carry the sense of challenge. So it is negation plus something more.

What is the meaning of ﴿lies about Allah﴾?

* Student: ﴿Lies about Allah﴾ means: fabricates against Allah.

* Shaykh: Fabricates against Allah in what?

* Student: By attributing a partner (...).

* Shaykh: And what else?

* Student: And other than that.

* Shaykh: Other than what, like what?

* Student: Attributing falsehood to His speech (...).

* Shaykh: And what else?

* Shaykh: No, what is denial? Denial is other than lying.

* Student: Negating the names and attributes of Allah, the Exalted, ta'til (nullifying them).

* Shaykh: Like taʿtil, nullifying His names and attributes.

* Student: ﴿So woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands, then say: "This is from Allah"﴾ [al-Baqarah 79].

* Shaykh: Yes. Lying against the Sharia is to say: "This is lawful and this is unlawful."

And His words ﴿denies the truth when it has come to him﴾: what is the benefit of His words ﴿when it has come to him﴾?

* Student: That he did not merely hear it, but verified it.

* Shaykh: That is, it came to him directly without an intermediary. Well done.

His words ﴿Is there not in Hell a residence for the disbelievers?﴾: does this sentence contain a rhetorical nuance?

* Student: Using an explicit noun in place of a pronoun.

* Shaykh: Using an explicit noun in place of a pronoun. What is the benefit of using an explicit noun in place of a pronoun?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: (...) We have only heard two answers.

* Student: It indicates generality.

* Shaykh: Yes, it indicates generality.

* Student: It indicates causation.

* Shaykh: Causation.

* Student: It indicates (...) the description according to what was described (...).

* Shaykh: The interrogative in His words ﴿Is there not﴾: what is meant by it?

* Student: ﴿Is there not﴾ is interrogative.

* Shaykh: Yes. What is meant by it?

* Student: What is meant (...).

* Shaykh: ﴿Is there not﴾?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: What is meant here is affirmation (taqrir). Why?

* Student: Because (...).

What is the reconciliation between this verse and His words, the Exalted: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned in them﴾ [al-Baqarah 114]?

* Student: (...) the most unjust thing (...), for the most unjust thing is to lie about Allah and deny the truth when it has come to him.

* Shaykh: That is, the comparative form (af'al al-tafdil) with respect to this type of what?

* Student: Injustice.

* Shaykh: So lying about people is not like lying about Allah. ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah﴾.

* Student: ﴿More unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah﴾ in preventing people from their rights.

* Shaykh: That the most unjust of what is withheld from rights is to prevent the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned in them. This is one aspect. What is the second aspect?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes. Is it that all these rulings of being most unjust are shared by everything mentioned? Which of the two is more likely?

* Student: The first is more likely.

* Shaykh: The first is more likely, because it is less forced and further from ambiguity.

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And he who brings the truth and confirms it—those are...﴾ [al-Zumar 33]...

* Student: We have not completed the benefits.

* Shaykh: We have not completed them?

* From the benefits: Lying about Allah is the greatest kind of lying.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of caution in explaining the Qur'an, because the explanation of the Qur'an is a translation of what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said. If one explains it contrary to Allah's intended meaning, he becomes a liar against Allah.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the differing ranks of sins. Sins have ranks that vary in severity, just as good deeds have ranks that vary.

* Among its benefits: Based on this benefit, faith increases and decreases, because the greater the sin, the greater the decrease in faith caused by it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation to believe the one whose truthfulness is established by evidence, from His words ﴿and denies the truth when it has come to him﴾. This indicates that whoever denies the truth falls under this description, the one who is most unjust among those who commit this act.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: praise of the truthful. The reason is that whoever denies them falls under this grave wrong, which is the most unjust of wrongs.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever denies something directly experienced is worse than whoever denies something only heard, because an intermediary between him and the reality may weaken the standing of truthfulness in his heart, as His words indicate: ﴿when it has come to him﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation that the Fire is the residence of the disbelievers.

* Among its benefits: clarifying what many people say today when a person dies: "He has gone..."?

* Students: "To his final residence."

* Shaykh: "To his final residence." If we took this phrase at face value, it would imply denial of resurrection, if the grave is made the final residence, and then there is no resurrection. The final residence is either Paradise or Hell. Therefore it is obligatory to be attentive to this expression and to alert others to it, and to say that this is a phrase borrowed from those who deny resurrection. But many common people take up words without reflecting on their meaning.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the believer will not be eternally in the Fire, because of His words ﴿a residence﴾ for whom? ﴿for the disbelievers﴾. The believer does not have the Fire as his residence. Rather, if he is punished in the Fire according to his sin, his final destination is Paradise.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verse 33:

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And he who brings the truth and believes in it—those are the righteous (al-muttaqun)﴾. ﴿Alladhi (he who)﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is the clause ﴿those are the righteous﴾. This clause therefore contains two clauses: a major clause (jumlah kubra) and a minor clause (jumlah sughra). The major clause is the one made up of the subject and predicate, and the minor clause is the predicate that consists of a subject and predicate. The clause that falls as a predicate is called a minor clause (jumlah sughra) because it occupies the position of a single word (mufrad). The major clause is that which is made up of a subject and predicate, or of a verb and its object.

His saying: ﴿And he who brings the truth and believes in it—those are the righteous﴾ contains a difficulty that comes to mind, namely that he has given a predicate about ﴿alladhi (he who)﴾, which is a singular noun, in the plural, namely his saying ﴿those are the righteous﴾, and he did not say "that is the righteous one." The reason for this is that ﴿alladhi﴾ is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul), and a relative pronoun conveys generality even when it is singular. For this reason it is correct to make a predicate about it in the plural despite its being singular.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And he who brings the truth and believes in it﴾. ﴿He who brings the truth﴾ is general, encompassing everyone who brings the truth: the messengers, peace be upon them, the prophets, and the truthful among others. Everyone who brings the truth is included. Among them, for example, is Ka'b ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him), who brought the truth when he remained behind from the expedition of Tabuk and reported the truth. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded us to be with them when He mentioned their story, saying: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and be with the truthful﴾ [al-Tawbah 119].

His saying: ﴿and believes in it﴾, i.e., believes in the truth whose truthfulness has been established by evidence. I think we do not need to explain the meaning of truth and falsehood: truth is the conformity of the reality to the report, and falsehood is its opposition to it. That is, whoever reports what conforms to reality is truthful, and whoever reports what contradicts reality is a liar. His saying "believes in it" means believes in what the evidence has established as true. ﴿Those are the righteous (al-muttaqun)﴾ means those who fear Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so they do not speak falsehood, and who fear Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so they do not reject the truth.

The commentator, may Allah have mercy on him, says: "(﴿And he who brings the truth﴾ refers to the Prophet ﷺ)." As you see, this is a restriction of a general term without any evidence. When the Qur'an uses a general term, the proper course is to leave it general, indeed it is obligatory to leave it general unless there is evidence. Here there is no evidence making this specific to the Prophet ﷺ, so it is obligatory that we take it as general, because restricting it to the specific without evidence is a deficiency in the meaning of the Qur'an. Therefore it includes the Prophet ﷺ and others.

("﴿And believes in it﴾ refers to the believers.") Glory be to Allah, this too is an error, because if we interpreted the verse as the author did, it would lead to a scattering of pronouns and a lack of coherence in the speech. ﴿And he who brings the truth and believes in it﴾: ﴿and believes in it﴾ is coordinated with the clause that is the relative clause (silat al-mawsul). When it is coordinated with the clause that is the relative clause, the one characterized by it must be the relative pronoun. Since it is coordinated with the relative clause, it is part of the relative clause, and the relative clause is a description of the relative pronoun. The author, may Allah have mercy on him and pardon him, scattered the pronouns: he made the first pronoun refer to the Messenger ﷺ and the second to the believers. The truth is that both refer to one thing, namely the relative pronoun, since the relative clause is its description, and what is coordinated with the relative clause is also a description of it.

So, ﴿and believes in it﴾: who? It includes everyone, even the Prophet, peace be upon him. He believed that he was the Messenger of Allah, and he would sometimes say: "I testify that there is no god but Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah" [narrated by al-Bukhari (2484) from Salamah ibn al-Akwa']. He believed that he was the Messenger of Allah, and that what was sent down to him from his Lord is the truth. The first to enter this verse after the Messenger ﷺ is Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, for Abu Bakr al-Siddiq brought the truth and believed in it, may Allah be pleased with him, even in the most difficult circumstance of the Messenger, peace be upon him, on the night of the Isra', when the Quraysh spread the claim that the Messenger, peace be upon him, had lied and was talking nonsense and saying what is impossible. When the news reached him, he said: "If he said that, then he is truthful" [narrated by 'Abd al-Razzaq in al-Musannaf (9719) from al-Zuhri]. From that day he was called al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him.

He said: ("those who believe": alladhi here means alladhina), meaning that it is a singular noun but with the meaning of the plural, because it indicates generality.

(﴿Those are the righteous (al-muttaqun)﴾: polytheism (al-shirk).) ﴿Those are the righteous﴾ uses the demonstrative for the distant (ulaika) to indicate their high rank. He did not say "these" (haa'ula'), but said "those" (ulaika), and "ulaika" is used for the distant. They were indicated with the distant demonstrative, despite the closeness in speaking about them, because of their high rank.

The author's saying: ("al-muttaqun": polytheism (al-shirk)) is among the strangest things. The discussion now is about truth and believing in truth, so where is polytheism? It has not been mentioned before. If we wished to restrict it, we would say: "those are the ones who fear lying and rejecting the truth," and we would say so. However, the evidence indicates that the meaning is: "those are the ones who fear Allah." This is because when taqwa is used without qualification, it means the fear of Allah; when it is qualified, it is according to what it is qualified by.

So His saying ﴿And fear a day in which you will be returned to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 281] refers to the Day, and His saying ﴿And fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ [Al 'Imran 131] refers to the Fire, and His saying "and fear Allah" refers to Allah. When unqualified, to whom does it refer? To Allah, because Allah is most worthy of being feared, Mighty and Majestic. Here we say: "those are the ones who fear Allah," and for this reason they brought the truth and believed in it; they feared Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

* Benefits drawn from this noble verse: praise for the one who speaks the truth. Truthfulness is obligatory and lying is forbidden. Someone may say it is among the major sins, because the Prophet ﷺ made it one of the signs of hypocrisy [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (33) and Muslim (59/107) from Abu Hurayrah], and the hypocrite is not among the believers. So if someone says that lying is a major sin, his statement is not far-fetched.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: praise for the one who believes in what has been established as true by evidence. As for one who does not believe what he doubts, there is no blame on him. The reports that reach a person are divided into three categories:

The first: what evidence has shown to be true, so it is believed.

The second: what evidence has shown to be false, either because its transmitter is known for lying, or because it is impossible, or the like. This is rejected, and there is no blame on one who rejects it.

The third: what may be true and may be false. This is withheld from judgment: it is not rejected since no evidence requires its rejection, and it is not accepted since no evidence requires its acceptance. The evidence for this category is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O you who believe, if a defiant one comes to you with news, verify it, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and become regretful for what you have done﴾ [al-Hujurat 6]. For this reason, in the verse before this one He said ﴿and denied the truth﴾, and here He said ﴿And he who brings the truth and believes in it﴾, so He censured the first and praised the latter.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: truthfulness is part of taqwa, and believing in one whose truthfulness has been established by evidence is also part of taqwa, by His saying ﴿those are the righteous﴾.

* Among its benefits for the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) regarding legal rulings: the relative pronoun is among the forms of generality, by His saying ﴿And he who brings the truth and believes in it, those are the righteous﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verse 34–35 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They will have whatever they wish with their Lord. That is the reward of the doers of good﴾. ﴿They will have﴾, i.e., these God-fearing people (al-muttaqun) will have ﴿whatever they wish with their Lord﴾, i.e., whatever they desire from their Lord, who is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He attributed Lordship (rububiyyah) to them specifically, because the Lordship given to the God-fearing is a special Lordship, not like the general Lordship that encompasses the disbeliever and the believer, the righteous and the wicked. Rather, it is a special Lordship.
﴿They will have whatever they wish with their Lord. That is the reward of the doers of good﴾. ﴿That﴾, i.e., that their reward is whatever they wish, ﴿is the reward of the doers of good﴾, the doers of good who did good in worshipping Allah and did good to the servants of Allah. Doing good in worshipping Allah is explained by what the Prophet (ﷺ) explained it as: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50) and Muslim (9/5) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. Doing good in dealing with people is that you treat them with what you love to be treated with, you love for them what you love for yourself. What is doing good in worshipping Allah?
* Student: As the Prophet (ﷺ) defined it: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you."
* Shaykh: And in dealing with people?
* Student: That you treat them with what you love to be treated with.
* Shaykh: With what you love to be treated with, well done.
﴿So that Allah may remove from them the worst of what they did and reward them their due with the best of what they used to do﴾ [az-Zumar 35]. The lam here appears to be for consequence (lam al-'aqibah), because the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil) sometimes indicates cause and sometimes indicates consequence. If what precedes it is the cause of what follows, it is for causation; if what follows is a consequence of what precedes and is not intended, it is for consequence. This is the difference between them. So if you say: "I came to read." Here, the lam is what?
* Students: For causation.
* Shaykh: For causation. And if someone says: "I traveled so that the accident happened to me."
* Students: For consequence.
* Shaykh: This is for consequence. ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas 8].
* Students: For consequence.
* Shaykh: This is for consequence. So the difference: if what precedes it is the cause of what follows, it is for causation; and if what follows is a consequence of what precedes and not intended, it is for consequence. He, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿So that Allah may remove from them the worst of what they did﴾, meaning the consequence of piety is that Allah removes from them the worst of what they did. It may also be for causation, meaning that they feared Allah for the sake of expiation: ﴿So that Allah may remove from them the worst of what they did﴾, and that is by Him bestowing forgiveness upon them.
Expiation usually comes by way of corresponding deeds: bad deeds are expiated by good deeds. Look at zihar: when a person commits zihar, he expiates it with what Allah the Mighty and Majestic mentioned, meaning he performs good deeds that cover the sins he committed. For an oath, when broken, one makes expiation. So expiation generally takes the form of good deeds covering bad deeds. But it is also permissible that expiation be purely a bounty from Allah the Mighty and Majestic, by which Allah conceals the sin of His servant out of His grace.
As for His saying ﴿the worst of what they did﴾: ﴿worst﴾ is a superlative form (ism tafdil), and it retains its proper meaning. So if Allah expiates for them the worst of what they did, then what is less than it is all the more so. The expression with "the worst" serves as good news for them.
﴿And reward them their due﴾, i.e., their reward for the good deeds they did, ﴿with the best of what they used to do﴾, i.e., with the best of the reward for what they used to do. The meaning of ﴿with the best of what they used to do﴾ is: with the best reward for what they used to do. This is because a good deed is rewarded with ten times its like, up to seven hundred times, up to many multiples. And "best" here retains its proper meaning, i.e., it is a superlative; He does not reward them a good deed with a good deed, but with something better than it, as you have heard: a good deed is rewarded with ten times its like, up to seven hundred times, up to many multiples.
As for His saying ﴿with the best of what they used to do﴾, it is not hidden that His saying ﴿what they used to do﴾ is the relative clause (silah) of the relative pronoun ﴿alladhi﴾, and a relative clause requires a returning pronoun (a'id) to link the clause to the relative pronoun. So what is the returning pronoun here? It is omitted, and the estimated form is: "they used to do it."
The author said: ("worst" and "best" mean "bad" and "good"). That is, ("worst") means "bad" and ("best") means "good." The author said this, but it is an incorrect statement, because it amounts to distorting the Qur'an. Everyone knows that "worst" is a superlative, while "bad" is a descriptive adjective without comparison, and likewise "best" is a superlative while "good" is a descriptive adjective without comparison. Why then do we lower the degree of comparison to what is lower? This is an error and a distortion. The correct view is what we explained to you earlier: that the superlative here retains its proper meaning, and that Allah gives them the good news that He expiates the worst, and whoever has the worst expiated has what is less than it expiated as well, and He gives them the good news that He rewards them with the best of what they used to do, not that He rewards a good deed with its like, but with better. This is a great difference between good and better, and bad and worst.
* Among the benefits of this verse, these two verses: First: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They will have whatever they wish with their Lord﴾.
* Among its benefits: that these God-fearing people have whatever they wish with Allah. When? In the Hereafter, in Paradise. Allah has explained in another verse that they have more than that, when He said: ﴿They will have therein whatever they wish, and with Us is more﴾ [Qaf 35]. The increase has been explained as looking upon the Face of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and what appears is that looking is part of that; otherwise the increase is more comprehensive than this.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah's care for these people, by attributing Lordship to them.
* Among the benefits of this verse: that piety is part of doing good, due to His saying ﴿That is the reward of the doers of good﴾, and He did not say "the God-fearing," though what is meant is the God-fearing; but the God-fearing person is a doer of good, because the God-fearing, when used unrestrictedly, is one who performs what is commanded and abandons what is forbidden, and this is doing good.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: encouragement to doing good, due to His saying ﴿That is the reward of the doers of good﴾. Encouragement to doing good and commanding it is abundant in the Book and the Sunnah. Doing good includes, as I told you, doing good in worshipping Allah and doing good to the servants of Allah. Doing good to the servants of Allah is by speech, by action, by status, and other kinds of good. So do not spare any effort in extending good to your brothers, for that is among the causes of entering Paradise, and it is also a cause of Allah's help for you, for Allah is in the aid of His servant as long as the servant is in the aid of his brother.
* Among the benefits of the second verse: that by their piety Allah expiates for them the worst of their deeds, due to His saying ﴿So that Allah may remove from them the worst of what they did﴾.
* Among its benefits: that Allah rewards them with the best reward, and this has been made clear in the Book and the Sunnah: whoever brings a good deed has ten times its like, up to seven hundred times, up to many multiples.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the thoughts that pass through hearts have no ruling, due to His saying ﴿what they did﴾ and His saying ﴿what they used to do﴾. A hadith supports this, when the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah has overlooked for my Ummah what its souls whisper, so long as they do not act upon it or speak of it"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2528) and Muslim (127/201) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. But whoever has bad thoughts must resist them with what he can, and among resisting them is to seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan and desist, meaning turn away from these imaginings, and they will go away. But if he submits to them, yields to them, and persists, they will destroy him, because Satan tests the heart of a person: if he finds it soft and yielding, he gains power over it until he takes him out of his religion and his world, and we seek refuge with Allah. If it is hard and firm, Satan cannot penetrate it, and then it is strong, and Satan's bones break against it. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, advised his student Ibn al-Qayyim when some doubts were presented to him, saying: Do not make your heart like a sponge that soaks up water and does not release it except by squeezing. Make your heart like a clear glass, through which what is within can be seen, and nothing penetrates it.
That is, the heart should be clear and pure from these doubts, and nothing penetrates it. Thus a person should not yield to Satan in these whisperings that come to him. If someone asks: Is intention an act or not? What do you say? Intention is an act, but it is an act of the heart, unlike mere self-talk, because self-talk does not mean submitting to a thing or affirming it, whereas intention only occurs after that thing has been settled. For this reason, "the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding the two Muslims who meet with their swords, and one kills the other, said: Both are in the Fire. 'When two Muslims meet with their swords, the killer and the killed are in the Fire.' They said: O Messenger of Allah, this is the killer, but what about the killed? He said: 'Because he was eager to kill his companion'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (31) and Muslim (2888/14) from the hadith of Abu Bakrah.]]. And when he mentioned the four men, among them: "a man whom Allah, Glorified and Exalted, gave wealth, and he spends it in other than what pleases Allah. The poor man said: 'If only I had the wealth of so-and-so, I would act with it as so-and-so acts.' He said: 'Then he has according to his intention, and both are equal in sin'"[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2325) and Ibn Majah (4228) from the hadith of Abu Kabshah al-Anmari.]], even though he did not act, but he wished and intended. And Allah knows best.
* Student: If one reports (...) in agreement with reality, and it was contrary to reality, is it called a liar?
* Shaykh: It is called a liar, but he does not bear the sin of the liar.
* Student: The one who fears Allah so that He expiates his bad deeds, or do we say: he must fear Allah and please Allah, then (...).
* Shaykh: All of this is correct. As for the saying of the Sufis, "I worship Allah for Allah's sake," this is an error, but worship Allah for this and for that.
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿seeking bounty from their Lord and approval﴾ [al-Ma'idah 2], beginning with bounty. This is in the description of the Messenger (ﷺ) and his companions: ﴿You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from Allah and approval﴾ [al-Fath 29].
* Student: I am sincere in order to learn.
* Shaykh: Sincere in order to learn, or: learn while sincere?
* Student: No (...).
* Shaykh: What?
* Student: Be sincere to Allah and knowledge comes to you.
* Shaykh: Without doubt, sincerity to Allah means it is a help and a cause for obtaining knowledge and the blessing of knowledge. Sincerity is a cause for attaining what is lacking and for blessing in what is present (...).
* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant? Yet they frighten you with those other than Him. And whomever Allah leaves astray, there is for him no guide. (36) And whomever Allah guides, there is for him no misleader. Is not Allah Mighty, Owner of Retribution? (37) And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah." Say, "Have you considered that which you invoke other than Allah — if Allah intended me some harm, could they remove His harm? Or if He intended me mercy, could they withhold His mercy?" Say, "Sufficient for me is Allah; upon Him rely the reliant"﴾ [az-Zumar 36–38].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿And the one who brought the truth and confirmed it — those are the God-fearing﴾ [az-Zumar 33]. Who is meant by ﴿the one who brought the truth﴾?
* Student: ﴿The one who brought the truth﴾?
* Shaykh: Who is meant by it?
* Student: Everyone who was truthful.
* Shaykh: Everyone who brought the truth; everyone who was truthful in his speech, his deeds, and his intention is included in the verse.
What do you say about restricting that to the Messenger (ﷺ)?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: I say restricting it to the Messenger?
* Student: (...) ﴿brought the truth and confirmed it﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes, so this is a deficiency in explaining the verse.
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Does truthfulness here refer specifically to truthfulness of intention, speech, and action?
* Student: It includes all of them.
* Shaykh: It includes all. Truthfulness of intention is with what?
* Student: With sincerity.
* Shaykh: With sincerity to Allah. And speech?
* Student: Speech does not contradict reality.
* Shaykh: Reporting what agrees with reality, and action is that it conforms to the Sharia.
His saying ﴿those are the God-fearing﴾: how is the predicate plural when the subject is singular: ﴿And the one who brought the truth and confirmed it — those are the God-fearing﴾?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Because the relative pronoun, even if singular, conveys?
* Student: It conveys generality.
* Shaykh: It conveys generality. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They will have whatever they wish with their Lord﴾. Does the Qur'an contain anything indicating that they have more than that?
* Student: Yes, His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For those who did good is the best reward and an increase﴾ [Yunus 26].
* Shaykh: We do not want that; the matter is "whatever they wish."
* Student: ﴿They will have therein whatever they wish, and with Us is more﴾ [Qaf 35].
* Shaykh: Is there anything in the verse indicating encouragement to doing good?
* Student: His saying, Exalted is He (...).
* Shaykh: How many kinds of doing good are there?
* Student: Doing good to the servants and doing good to the Lord of the servants.
* Shaykh: Doing good in worshipping Allah and doing good in dealing with the servants of Allah. What is doing good in worshipping Allah?
* Student: Doing good in worshipping Allah is performing acts of worship in the most perfect manner.
* Shaykh: I do not want an explanation better than the explanation of the one by whom it was explained.
* Student: The Prophet (ﷺ) explained it: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50) and Muslim (9/5) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].
* Shaykh: Excellent. Is it clear? Hold on to the evidence.
Doing good in dealing with the servants?
* Student: Doing good in dealing with the servants is to treat them as you love to be treated.
* Shaykh: With which they are treated. Is there a warning for opposing this? That is, if you treat people contrary to this reality, is there a warning? Doing good in dealing with creation is that you treat them as you love to be treated by them. Is there a warning indicating that if you treated them otherwise...
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: After, the verse is complete.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Excellent. And in the Sunnah: "None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (13) and Muslim (45/71) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]]. The author explained His saying: ﴿So that Allah may remove from them the worst of what they did﴾ with an explanation contrary to its apparent meaning. What is the explanation he gave it?
* Student: He explained "worst" and "best," saying (...) good and bad.
* Shaykh: In the sense of bad and good. What is the difference between "worst" and "bad"?
* Student: "Worst" is a comparative form.
* Shaykh: And "bad"?
* Student: "Bad" is not a comparative form.
* Shaykh: Likewise "best" and "good": "best" is a comparative form, and "good" is not. Is what he said correct?
* Student: No, it is not correct.
* Shaykh: Not correct. Why?
* Student: O Shaykh, his explanation has a deficiency (...).
* Shaykh: First: because it contradicts the apparent wording. And second?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Correct; because expiating the worst and rewarding with the best is more eloquent than expiating the bad and rewarding with the good.
Regarding His saying ﴿with the best of what they used to do﴾, is there an omission in it?
* Student: That is, the omission of (...) which they used to do.
* Shaykh: The omitted element is the pronoun returning to the relative clause.

The author said: "(﴿The one who brought the truth﴾ is the Prophet, and ﴿those who affirmed it﴾ are the believers)." We mentioned that this interpretation completely contradicts the context of the verse. What is its reasoning?

*Student:* Its reasoning is that we said: indeed... we did not say this.

*Shaykh:* No, we said it. We said that this interpretation completely contradicts the verse.

*Student:* (...) the pious.

*Shaykh:* No, this.

*Student:* (...) the context of the verse is that the one who brought the truth and affirmed it (...).

*Shaykh:* The verse is ﴿And the one who brought the truth and affirmed it﴾. ﴿Affirmed﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ﴿brought﴾ within the relative clause (silat al-mawsul, the clause that completes the relative pronoun). What is conjoined to the relative clause belongs to the relative clause. On this basis, the antecedent is one. The relative clause functions as a descriptive qualifier. If you say: "The one who honored me and gave me money is beloved to me," for example, do we say that the one who gave me money is different from the first, or is it the first?

*Student:* The first.

*Shaykh:* It is the same thing.

So the difference: if what precedes it is the cause of what follows, it is for causation; and if what follows is a consequence of what precedes and not intended, it is for consequence. He, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿So that Allah may remove from them the worst of what they did﴾, meaning the consequence of piety is that Allah removes from them the worst of what they did. It may also be for causation, meaning that they feared Allah for the sake of expiation: ﴿So that Allah may remove from them the worst of what they did﴾, and that is by Him bestowing forgiveness upon them.
Expiation usually comes by way of corresponding deeds: bad deeds are expiated by good deeds. Look at zihar: when a person commits zihar, he expiates it with what Allah the Mighty and Majestic mentioned, meaning he performs good deeds that cover the sins he committed. For an oath, when broken, one makes expiation. So expiation generally takes the form of good deeds covering bad deeds. But it is also permissible that expiation be purely a bounty from Allah the Mighty and Majestic, by which Allah conceals the sin of His servant out of His grace.
As for His saying ﴿the worst of what they did﴾: ﴿worst﴾ is a superlative form (ism tafdil), and it retains its proper meaning. So if Allah expiates for them the worst of what they did, then what is less than it is all the more so. The expression with "the worst" serves as good news for them.
﴿And reward them their due﴾, i.e., their reward for the good deeds they did, ﴿with the best of what they used to do﴾, i.e., with the best of the reward for what they used to do. The meaning of ﴿with the best of what they used to do﴾ is: with the best reward for what they used to do. This is because a good deed is rewarded with ten times its like, up to seven hundred times, up to many multiples. And "best" here retains its proper meaning, i.e., it is a superlative; He does not reward them a good deed with a good deed, but with something better than it, as you have heard: a good deed is rewarded with ten times its like, up to seven hundred times, up to many multiples.
As for His saying ﴿with the best of what they used to do﴾, it is not hidden that His saying ﴿what they used to do﴾ is the relative clause (silah) of the relative pronoun ﴿alladhi﴾, and a relative clause requires a returning pronoun (a'id) to link the clause to the relative pronoun. So what is the returning pronoun here? It is omitted, and the estimated form is: "they used to do it."
The author said: ("worst" and "best" mean "bad" and "good"). That is, ("worst") means "bad" and ("best") means "good." The author said this, but it is an incorrect statement, because it amounts to distorting the Qur'an. Everyone knows that "worst" is a superlative, while "bad" is a descriptive adjective without comparison, and likewise "best" is a superlative while "good" is a descriptive adjective without comparison. Why then do we lower the degree of comparison to what is lower? This is an error and a distortion. The correct view is what we explained to you earlier: that the superlative here retains its proper meaning, and that Allah gives them the good news that He expiates the worst, and whoever has the worst expiated has what is less than it expiated as well, and He gives them the good news that He rewards them with the best of what they used to do, not that He rewards a good deed with its like, but with better. This is a great difference between good and better, and bad and worst.
* Among the benefits of this verse, these two verses: First: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They will have whatever they wish with their Lord﴾.
* Among its benefits: that these God-fearing people have whatever they wish with Allah. When? In the Hereafter, in Paradise. Allah has explained in another verse that they have more than that, when He said: ﴿They will have therein whatever they wish, and with Us is more﴾ [Qaf 35]. The increase has been explained as looking upon the Face of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and what appears is that looking is part of that; otherwise the increase is more comprehensive than this.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah's care for these people, by attributing Lordship to them.
* Among the benefits of this verse: that piety is part of doing good, due to His saying ﴿That is the reward of the doers of good﴾, and He did not say "the God-fearing," though what is meant is the God-fearing; but the God-fearing person is a doer of good, because the God-fearing, when used unrestrictedly, is one who performs what is commanded and abandons what is forbidden, and this is doing good.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: encouragement to doing good, due to His saying ﴿That is the reward of the doers of good﴾. Encouragement to doing good and commanding it is abundant in the Book and the Sunnah. Doing good includes, as I told you, doing good in worshipping Allah and doing good to the servants of Allah. Doing good to the servants of Allah is by speech, by action, by status, and other kinds of good. So do not spare any effort in extending good to your brothers, for that is among the causes of entering Paradise, and it is also a cause of Allah's help for you, for Allah is in the aid of His servant as long as the servant is in the aid of his brother.
* Among the benefits of the second verse: that by their piety Allah expiates for them the worst of their deeds, due to His saying ﴿So that Allah may remove from them the worst of what they did﴾.
* Among its benefits: that Allah rewards them with the best reward, and this has been made clear in the Book and the Sunnah: whoever brings a good deed has ten times its like, up to seven hundred times, up to many multiples.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the thoughts that pass through hearts have no ruling, due to His saying ﴿what they did﴾ and His saying ﴿what they used to do﴾. A hadith supports this, when the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah has overlooked for my Ummah what its souls whisper, so long as they do not act upon it or speak of it"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2528) and Muslim (127/201) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. But whoever has bad thoughts must resist them with what he can, and among resisting them is to seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan and desist, meaning turn away from these imaginings, and they will go away. But if he submits to them, yields to them, and persists, they will destroy him, because Satan tests the heart of a person: if he finds it soft and yielding, he gains power over it until he takes him out of his religion and his world, and we seek refuge with Allah. If it is hard and firm, Satan cannot penetrate it, and then it is strong, and Satan's bones break against it. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, advised his student Ibn al-Qayyim when some doubts were presented to him, saying: Do not make your heart like a sponge that soaks up water and does not release it except by squeezing. Make your heart like a clear glass, through which what is within can be seen, and nothing penetrates it.
That is, the heart should be clear and pure from these doubts, and nothing penetrates it. Thus a person should not yield to Satan in these whisperings that come to him. If someone asks: Is intention an act or not? What do you say? Intention is an act, but it is an act of the heart, unlike mere self-talk, because self-talk does not mean submitting to a thing or affirming it, whereas intention only occurs after that thing has been settled. For this reason, "the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding the two Muslims who meet with their swords, and one kills the other, said: Both are in the Fire. 'When two Muslims meet with their swords, the killer and the killed are in the Fire.' They said: O Messenger of Allah, this is the killer, but what about the killed? He said: 'Because he was eager to kill his companion'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (31) and Muslim (2888/14) from the hadith of Abu Bakrah.]]. And when he mentioned the four men, among them: "a man whom Allah, Glorified and Exalted, gave wealth, and he spends it in other than what pleases Allah. The poor man said: 'If only I had the wealth of so-and-so, I would act with it as so-and-so acts.' He said: 'Then he has according to his intention, and both are equal in sin'"[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2325) and Ibn Majah (4228) from the hadith of Abu Kabshah al-Anmari.]], even though he did not act, but he wished and intended. And Allah knows best.
* Student: If one reports (...) in agreement with reality, and it was contrary to reality, is it called a liar?

* Student: The one who fears Allah so that He expiates his bad deeds, or do we say: he must fear Allah and please Allah, then (...).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿seeking bounty from their Lord and approval﴾ [al-Ma'idah 2], beginning with bounty. This is in the description of the Messenger (ﷺ) and his companions: ﴿You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from Allah and approval﴾ [al-Fath 29].

And whomever Allah leaves astray, there is for him no guide. (36) And whomever Allah guides, there is for him no misleader. Is not Allah Mighty, Owner of Retribution? (37) And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah." Say, "Sufficient for me is Allah; upon Him rely the reliant"﴾ [az-Zumar 36–38].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿And the one who brought the truth and confirmed it — those are the God-fearing﴾ [az-Zumar 33]. Who is meant by ﴿the one who brought the truth﴾?

What do you say about restricting that to the Messenger (ﷺ)?

His saying ﴿those are the God-fearing﴾: how is the predicate plural when the subject is singular: ﴿And the one who brought the truth and confirmed it — those are the God-fearing﴾?
* Student: (...).
