The author said: "(﴿The one who brought the truth﴾ is the Prophet, and ﴿those who affirmed it﴾ are the believers)." We mentioned that this interpretation completely contradicts the context of the verse. What is its reasoning?

*Student:* Its reasoning is that we said: indeed... we did not say this.

*Shaykh:* No, we said it. We said that this interpretation completely contradicts the verse.

*Student:* (...) the pious.

*Shaykh:* No, this.

*Student:* (...) the context of the verse is that the one who brought the truth and affirmed it (...).

*Shaykh:* The verse is ﴿And the one who brought the truth and affirmed it﴾. ﴿Affirmed﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ﴿brought﴾ within the relative clause (silat al-mawsul, the clause that completes the relative pronoun). What is conjoined to the relative clause belongs to the relative clause. On this basis, the antecedent is one. The relative clause functions as a descriptive qualifier. If you say: "The one who honored me and gave me money is beloved to me," for example, do we say that the one who gave me money is different from the first, or is it the first?

*Student:* The first.

*Shaykh:* It is the same thing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verses 36–37 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ The interrogative (istifham) here is for affirmation (taqrir), based on the rule we mentioned earlier: when the interrogative hamzah enters upon a negative statement, it conveys affirmation. Examples include ﴿Did We not expand your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh 1], meaning: We have indeed expanded your breast; and ﴿Were not My verses recited to you?﴾ [al-Mu'minun 105], meaning: they indeed were.

So also ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ means: Allah has indeed sufficed His servant. As for His words ﴿bi-kafin 'abdahu﴾, the word that governs the object ('abdahu) is ﴿kafin﴾, because ﴿kafin﴾ is an active participle (ism fa'il), its subject is a hidden pronoun, and ﴿'abdahu﴾ is its direct object. The word ('abd) is a singular noun in the construct state (mufrad mudaf), so it is general (ʿamm), including everyone who is characterized by this attribute. Whoever is truly a servant of Allah, Allah suffices him. A similar statement is His saying: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, He is sufficient for him﴾ [al-Talaq 3], and His saying: ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah 137]. Thus, "servant" here is an inclusive attribute, not restricted to one individual over another. Whoever truly fulfills servitude, Allah the Exalted suffices him. ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ The answer to this sentence is to say: Yes (bala).

Then He says: ﴿And they frighten you with those other than Him.﴾ Here the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿They frighten you﴾ is addressed specifically to the Messenger. The conjunction of the specific ﴿they frighten you﴾ with the general statement before it does not require restricting the general wording. Similar cases have come up often: a general term is mentioned, and then a ruling is mentioned that applies to some of its members. We have said that this does not require specification (takhsis). What is the closest example we have covered in this regard? We have covered examples; which is the closest?

* Student: ﴿Those who brought the truth﴾.

* Shaykh: No, that is general. We covered it in a hadith. How quickly you forget! These rules should not be forgotten, brothers, they should not be forgotten. If you now memorize the rule, for example: when a general term is followed by a ruling that applies to some of its members, this does not require specification. This is a clear rule. But if someone says to you, "Give me an example that fits this," and you forget the example, he will say, "This rule is not acceptable." Rather, I say: when a ruling applying to some members comes, it indicates that the intended meaning of the first general term is the specific. So he will turn the rule against you.

The seeker of knowledge should record the scattered benefits. Benefits that slip from the mind should be cared for and recorded by the student of knowledge, otherwise they will be lost to him.

* Student: If there is no hadith (...)?

* Shaykh: No, those are two separate texts. We want them in one context. We covered an example in the Qur'an and an example in the Sunnah. The closer one is what we covered in the Qur'an, or all of them have been covered.

* Student: The hadith of Ibn 'Abbas (...).

* Shaykh: No. "The Prophet (ﷺ) ruled concerning pre-emption (shuf'ah) in everything that has not been divided." This is general, isn't it? Answer, brothers: "He ruled concerning everything that has not been divided." Everything not divided is general. "But when the boundaries are set and the roads are arranged, there is no pre-emption." [Narrated by al-Bukhari (2214).] This is a ruling that applies to some members of the general term. To what does it apply? To immovable property, to lands. So do we say that the first general term means the specific? Or do we say the first is general, and a ruling that applies to some of its members does not require specification? This is the second view.

In the Qur'an: ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾ up to His saying: ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back during that period﴾ [al-Baqarah 228]. ﴿Divorced women﴾ is general, and ﴿their husbands have more right﴾ is a ruling that applies to some members of this general term. Which member does it apply to? To the revocable divorcee (raj'iyyah). So do we say that His saying ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾ is specific to revocable divorcees? Or do we say it is general? It is well known among the scholars that it is general, covering women divorced irrevocably (ba'in) and women divorced revocably (raj'i).

Have you now taken two examples? Does this example in the Qur'an that we have here apply or not? ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant? And they frighten you with those other than Him.﴾

* Student: It applies.

* Shaykh: It applies to it? The first, ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾, is general. He did not say, "Is not Allah sufficient for you?" It is general. ﴿And they frighten you﴾ is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ). But one of you may say to me: why is it not valid for the address to be directed to everyone who can be addressed, i.e., "they frighten you, O addressee"? One of you may say this, as is customary in many texts. The answer is that it is not valid for it to be directed to every addressee, because not every addressee can be described this way. Is every addressee frightened with those other than Allah? No. Only the Prophet (ﷺ) was frightened with those other than Allah, because they threatened him with their gods.

In any case, this example fits the rule we mentioned: when a general term occurs and is followed by a ruling that applies to some of its members, this does not require specification. Rather, the general term remains general and the ruling is established for this member.

He says: (﴿And they frighten you﴾: the address is to him), meaning to the Prophet (ﷺ), (﴿with those other than Him﴾: that is, the idols; i.e., they would kill him or derange him). This is like His saying: ﴿That is only Satan frightening you of his allies. So fear them not, but fear Me, if you should be believers﴾ [Al 'Imran 175]. They frighten the Prophet (ﷺ) with those other than Allah. Restricting this to idols, as the author (al-Mu'allif) did, is open to question. Rather, they frighten him with those other than Allah, including idols and non-idols, even rulers. For example, one says, "So-and-so will do such-and-such to you," or "the jinn will do such-and-such to you," or "he will do this or that to you." So we should understand ﴿those other than Him﴾ in its generality, not restricted to idols, because frightening is broader than that.

Now, for example in our time, if someone says to a person, "If you forbid this evil, I will report you to so-and-so, one whose evil is feared," is this frightening with those other than Allah? Yes, this is frightening with those other than Allah. So the verse is general, and one should not restrict it as the author, may Allah have mercy on him, did.

﴿And they frighten you with those other than Him.﴾ Allah says: ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾. The word ﴿man﴾ is conditional (shartiyyah), so it conveys generality: whoever Allah leaves astray, there is no guide for him. His saying ﴿fa-ma lahu min hadin﴾ is a nominal sentence consisting of a subject and a predicate. It is strange to say that it consists of a subject and a predicate when we find in it neither a subject nor a predicate. Where is the nominative noun? It is known that the subject and predicate are nominative, but here nothing is nominative. The answer is to say: ﴿ma﴾ is a negation particle, ﴿lahu﴾ is a prepositional phrase functioning as a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), and ﴿min hadin﴾ is a delayed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar). How do we analyze ﴿min hadin﴾? We say: ﴿min﴾ is a superfluous (za'idah) preposition, and ﴿hadin﴾ is a noun in the genitive governed by ﴿min﴾. Correct?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: ﴿Hadin﴾ is a subject in the nominative, marked by a presumed damma on the deleted ya', prevented from appearance by...?

* Student: Occupation of the place by a vowel (ishtighal al-mahall bi-harakah)...

* Shaykh: There is no vowel here. The ya' is not vowelled here, because it does not take a vowel in the genitive. It is the deleted ya', for the meeting of two unvowelled letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn), and the kasrah is presumed on it for harmony with the superfluous preposition. This is if we want to strain the i'rab to fit the grammatical rules. Otherwise, it is enough to say: ﴿min﴾ is a superfluous preposition, and ﴿hadin﴾ is a subject in the nominative, marked by a presumed damma on the deleted ya' for the meeting of two unvowelled letters, and we stop there, because the vowel of a superfluous preposition in a word like this does not appear.

His saying: ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾ means: whoever Allah decrees misguidance for, no one can guide him, however much the community gathers against him. Here is the greatest of creation in guidance and in calling to it, Muhammad (ﷺ). He strove with the utmost effort to guide his uncle Abu Talib until his last breath, but he was not guided, because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, had decreed misguidance for him. The last thing he said was to testify to the creed of disbelief. He said: "He is upon the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1360) and Muslim (24/39), from the hadith of al-Musayyab ibn Hazn.] "But the Prophet (ﷺ), because of his good character, and because his uncle stood up in support that helped Islam, interceded for him with Allah, so he is in a shallow fire, and upon him are two sandals of fire that make his brain boil." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3885) and Muslim (210/360), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.] This is the highest part of him, while the sandals are at the lowest part of him, and the brain is boiling. How much more intensely boils what is below it of the body! And indeed he is the least punished of the people of the Fire [narrated by Muslim (212/362), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas]. And he thinks that he is the most punished. Why does Allah show him that he is the most punished? So that he is not consoled by others, because if the one in the Fire knew that someone else was worse than him or equal to him, he would be consoled and the matter would be easier for him. Allah alluded to this in His saying: ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you have wronged, that you are sharing in the punishment﴾ [al-Zukhruf 39]. Even though if you shared in punishment in this world, it would be easier for you. Consider Ka'b ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him: when it was said to him that so-and-so and so-and-so had stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk, the matter became easy for him. [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4418) and Muslim (2769/53), from the hadith of Ka'b ibn Malik.] This is a known matter. And al-Khansa' laments her brother Sakhr and says:

Were it not for the abundance of those weeping around me over their brothers, I would have killed myself.
They do not weep like my brother, but I console myself for him with consolation.

So we say: whoever Allah has decreed misguidance for, no one will guide him, however many signs he is given, for: ﴿Signs and warnings avail not people who do not believe﴾ [Yunus 101].

* From the benefits of this noble verse, first: Allah's sufficiency for His servant.

* Among its benefits: encouragement to realize servitude to Allah. For when you realize servitude, sufficiency is realized for you, since a ruling tied to an attribute grows stronger with the strength of that attribute and weaker with its weakness. When sufficiency is ordered upon servitude, the worshipper obtains from this sufficiency in proportion to his servitude, following the rule that a ruling tied to an attribute grows stronger with its strength and weaker with its weakness.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah the Mighty and Majestic defends the believers, because if Allah is sufficient for him, He will defend him. This is confirmed by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah defends those who have believed﴾ [al-Hajj 38].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the enemies of Allah frighten the servants of Allah with what is other than Allah, as in His saying: ﴿And they frighten you with those other than Him﴾.

* Among the benefits of this verse: that Satan, who is the leader of the enemies of Allah, frightens the believing worshipper of Allah with what is other than Allah. You find him coming to a person who wants to enjoin good and forbid evil, and saying: "Do not do it. The people hate you. The people will accuse you of extremism. The ruler may discipline you," and similar things. But the believer is not afraid of this at all, because he holds fast to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. He is a servant of Allah, certain that Allah will support him, so these people do not concern him. But does that mean that a person should rush into matters with a stormy emotion, or should he use wisdom and proceed in the truth?

* Student: The second.

* Shaykh: The second. That is why we criticize some people who have zeal for the religion of Allah but do not enter houses through their doors. They want to approach matters with violence and force, even though they have no strength. We say: proceed with what Allah has commanded you, but use wisdom in doing so.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that everything other than Allah is "other than Allah," as His saying shows: ﴿They frighten you with those other than Him﴾. There is nothing here except Allah or what is other than Allah.

* A branch of this benefit: everything other than Allah is subdued (maghlub). If Allah suffices His servant and everything other than Allah is subdued, this means that a person will prevail if he realizes servitude. But one may raise an objection: Allah the Exalted mentioned that some people killed the prophets. How can this verse be reconciled with what is established about the killing of some prophets?

The answer to this, or its response, is that the killing of the prophets does not mean the killing of the truth they brought. The prophets spoke to establish the truth, not to establish their own personalities. They spoke to establish the truth. Furthermore, if they missed victory in this world, the victory you witness, they did not miss it in the Hereafter, based on Allah's saying: ﴿Indeed, We will surely support Our messengers and those who believe in the life of this world and on the day when the witnesses stand﴾ [Ghafir 51]. And Allah knows best.

* Student: (...) the definition of (...)?

* Shaykh: No, its definition, the definition of ihsan.

* Student: Regarding the address ﴿And they frighten you with those other than Him﴾, why does (...) the fear of other than Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

* Shaykh: We said that this is not for everyone, if we say it is general for every person.

* Student: (...) fear, Shaykh.

* Shaykh: Yes, we can make it for everyone who is frightened. We can do that, but it appears that it is specific to the Messenger.

* Student: The Messenger (ﷺ) interceded for his uncle Abu Talib, and he said: "Were it not for me, he would be in the lowest level of the Fire." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3883) and Muslim (209/357), from the hadith of al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib.] And he sees himself as the most punished of people. Because if he saw himself as the least punished, he would be consoled by that. Does this mean that he did not know of the Prophet's (ﷺ) intercession for him, that he was in this shallow fire? Or did he know, but still see himself as the most punished?

* Shaykh: Whether he knew or did not know, he sees himself as the most punished of people. That Allah informed him that he deserved the lowest level of the Fire, but through the intercession of the Messenger, may be that Allah informed him of this so that he would know that Allah had rewarded him for what he did for the Messenger (peace be upon him). Or perhaps not. And Allah knows best.

* Student: The saying of Allah, glory be to Him, ﴿And they frighten you with those other than Him﴾: does its context match that the earlier people said ﴿We only say that some of our gods have struck you with evil﴾ [Hud 54]?

* Shaykh: Who transmitted this?

* Student: The people of Shu'ayb.

* Shaykh: No. Those who said it were 'Ad, to Hud.

* Student: Yes. Is it the same...? That is, the polytheists frightened the Prophet (ﷺ) that evil from the gods would befall him if he opposed them...

* Shaykh: No. Those people said: ﴿We only say that some of our gods have struck you with evil﴾ [Hud 54], meaning: they have driven you mad and made you insane. But these people said: our gods will drive you mad, and they threatened him for the future (...).

* * *

* Student: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿And whoever Allah guides, for him there is no misleader. Is not Allah Exalted in Might, Owner of Retribution? (37) And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah." Say, "Have you considered that which you invoke other than Allah? If Allah intended to harm me, could they remove His harm? Or if He intended for me mercy, could they withhold His mercy?" Say, "Sufficient for me is Allah. On Him rely the reliant." (38) Say, "O my people, work according to your position; indeed, I am working, so you will know (39) on whom will come a punishment that will disgrace him and upon him will descend a lasting punishment."﴾ [al-Zumar 37–40].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant? Yet they frighten you with those other than Him.﴾ We mentioned that the interrogative in His words ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ is what?
* Student: That the interrogative hamza (hamzat al-istifham), when it occurs in a context of negation, conveys affirmation (taqrir).
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is for affirmation. The interrogative in His words ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ is for affirmation, based on the rule that when the interrogative hamza is followed by something that conveys negation, it is for affirmation. There are many examples of this in the Qur'an. We also mentioned the meaning of ﴿His servant﴾.
* Student: The Prophet ﷺ (...).
* The Shaykh: And what does the author see?
* Student: (...) the Prophet ﷺ.
* The Shaykh: What led the author to make it refer to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him?
* Student: His words after it: ﴿and they frighten you with those other than Him.﴾
* The Shaykh: Yes. The correct view is the general meaning. What is the meaning of ﴿they frighten you (yukhawwifunaka)﴾?
* Student: They threaten you.
* Another student: They frighten you. The author mentioned that it refers to the idols, but it conveys generality.
* The Shaykh: No. That is an explanation of ﴿those other than Him (alladhina min dunihi)﴾. But what is the meaning of the word ﴿yukhawwifunaka﴾? They cast fear into your heart concerning them, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It is only Satan who frightens his allies﴾ [Al 'Imran 175]. In His words ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾, what is this ﴿min﴾?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Where is the response of the condition (jawab al-shart)?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What is the meaning of His words ﴿whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾?
* Student: It means the one whom Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, did not want to guide.
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: ﴿Whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾?
* Student: (...) Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for misguidance. Whatever effort a person exerts in guiding him, he cannot do it, as the Prophet ﷺ did with his uncle.
* The Shaykh: Correct. What is meant by guidance in His words ﴿for him there is no guide﴾?
* Student: Guidance of indication (hidayat al-dalalah), guidance of direction (hidayat al-irshad), guidance of divine success (hidayat al-tawfiq).
* The Shaykh: Guidance of indication, guidance of direction, and guidance of divine success.
* Student: The last one, O Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: The last one is guidance of divine success. What is the evidence that the meaning of guidance here is guidance of divine success?
* Student: Because the guidance of divine success (...) except Allah.
* The Shaykh: But what is the evidence that the meaning of ﴿for him there is no guide﴾ is: for him there is no one who grants him success in guidance? One might say: ﴿for him there is no guide﴾ means: there is no one who points to the truth?
* Student: (...) ﴿for him there is no guide﴾ (...).
* The Shaykh: A word from which one understands it is not sufficient; there must be evidence.
* Student: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [al-Qasas 56], which shows that the Prophet ﷺ guides only (...).
* Another student: (...) that the servants do not possess this thing which Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, possesses.
* The Shaykh: Yes, there is no doubt about that. But what is the evidence that this is the intended meaning? Because guidance is of two kinds: guidance of divine success and guidance of indication.
* Student: His words ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray﴾, where He attributed misguidance to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
* Another student: Because Allah, glorified and exalted, guided them with the guidance of indication; that is, He showed them the guidance of indication.
* The Shaykh: Because those whom Allah has led astray had already been guided with the guidance of indication: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat 17]. The messengers were sent to disbelieving peoples against whom the word of punishment had come into effect. Therefore it is necessary here that the meaning of the Guide is guidance of divine success: ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide.﴾
* From the benefits of this noble verse: whoever Allah has decreed to be astray, no one can guide him, because of His words: ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide.﴾
* And from its benefits: a person should seek guidance only from Allah, because He alone leads astray and guides, so guidance is sought from Him. This verse is not meant to despair of guiding creation, but the intended meaning is returning to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in guiding creation.
* And from the benefits of the noble verse: a refutation of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school), who say that a person is independent in his actions, guiding himself and misguiding himself, and that Allah's will has no connection to his action, because of His words: ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide.﴾
* And from its benefits: affirming that guidance, in the sense of guidance of indication, can be attributed to other than Allah, whereas divine success belongs to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
Then Allah, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿And whomever Allah guides, for him there is no misleader﴾. We have taken this, I think.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It was not explained. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whomever Allah guides, for him there is no misleader﴾, meaning: whoever Allah has decreed guidance for, there is no misleader for him.
A person should seek guidance only from Allah, because He alone leads astray and guides, so guidance is sought from Him. This verse is not meant to despair of guiding creation, but the intended meaning is returning to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in guiding creation.
* And from the benefits of the noble verse: a refutation of the Mu'tazilah, who say: a person is independent in his actions, guiding himself and misguiding himself, and Allah's will has no connection to his action; because of His words: ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾ [al-Zumar 36].
* And from its benefits: affirming that guidance, in the sense of guidance of indication, belongs to others, whereas divine success belongs to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
Then He said: ﴿And whomever Allah guides, for him there is no misleader﴾ [al-Zumar 37]. We have taken this. Was it explained?
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whomever Allah guides, for him there is no misleader﴾, meaning: whoever Allah decrees guidance for, there is no misleader for him. No one can mislead him, however many doubts and however many desires there are. If Allah decrees guidance for a servant, no desire and no doubt will lead him astray, because at the time of desire reason overcomes and he refrains from it, and at the time of doubt knowledge overcomes and he is guided by it away from it. This is the one whom Allah guides; for him there is no misleader.
In this statement there is clearly an encouragement for a person to persist in guidance. So this is one of the benefits of the verse: encouraging the one who is guided to remain on guidance, because Allah is the One who guided him, and no one can mislead him.
* And from its benefits: seeking refuge in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in asking Him for guidance and persevering in it.
Then He said: ﴿Is not Allah the Almighty, Possessor of retribution?﴾ [al-Zumar 37]. The answer is: Yes. His words ﴿Almighty (bi-'azizin)﴾: this is the predicate of "laysa," to which the particle bi has been added, extra in form and extra in meaning. It is extra in form, but it conveys the emphasis of generality in negation, since negation conveys generality when it is followed by an indefinite noun. But when the bi is added, the particles of emphasis are among those additional particles, as the scholars of rhetoric have mentioned.
As for His words ﴿'Azīz﴾, the exegetes said regarding the Most Beautiful Names of Allah that al-'Aziz has three meanings. The first meaning: might of rank (izzat al-qadr). The second meaning: might of subjugation (izzat al-qahr). The third meaning: might of inaccessibility (izzat al-imtina').
As for might of rank, its meaning is that Allah has a great rank and a lofty honor; no one is like Him, and no one equals Him or comes near Him. As for might of subjugation, its meaning is that Allah, the Exalted, subdues everything and overcomes everything. As for might of inaccessibility, its meaning is that every defect and deficiency is impossible for Allah, the Exalted. This is well known in the Arabic language. The second meaning, which is domination, the poet said regarding it:
Where is the escape, when the Seeker is God? ∗∗∗ And the Ashram, the vanquished, is not the victor.
As for the first, which is might of rank, it is said: "This is 'aziz," meaning rare and not found, because of its nobility and generosity. As for the third, there is the saying: "Land 'azzaz," meaning firm and solid, which cannot be dug by pickaxes. So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is 'Aziz in these three meanings. The first, brother?
* Student: The first is might of domination, might of...
* The Shaykh: Might of domination and subjugation.
* Student: The first is might of domination, the second is might of subjugation, and the third is might of inaccessibility.
* The Shaykh: Inaccessibility, good.
As for His words ﴿Is not Allah the Almighty, Possessor of retribution?﴾ [al-Zumar 37]: "Dhū" means "possessor," and "intiqam" is indefinite. An indefinite noun in an affirmative context does not convey generality, but here it is in what context? ﴿Is not Allah the Almighty, Possessor of retribution?﴾, meaning: possessor of retribution. Whenever wisdom requires retribution, He takes retribution. Reflect on His words ﴿Possessor of retribution﴾, and He did not say "Muntaqim" (the Avenger), because "al-Muntaqim" is not among the Names of Allah, and "al-Muntaqim" did not come as a Name of Allah in any authentic hadith. Rather, it came only in the form of a qualified active participle, as He said: ﴿Indeed, We will take retribution from the criminals﴾ [al-Sajdah 22], and He did not say "Indeed, We are avengers." He said "Possessor of retribution," meaning: possessor of retribution in its proper place. So "al-Muntaqim" is not among the Names of Allah, even if it is paired with "al-'Afu" (the Pardoner), in contrast to what some scholars held, that if it is paired with pardon there is no harm. Rather we say: "al-Muntaqim" is not among the Names of Allah, neither paired with pardon nor alone. But He is described with retribution in a qualified form: ﴿Indeed, We will take retribution from the criminals﴾, and it is described as proceeding from Him, not that He is "Muntaqim," as in His words: ﴿Almighty, Possessor of retribution﴾.
* From the benefits of this verse: affirming the might of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in all its meanings.
* And from its benefits: threatening those who deny the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, with these two attributes: the attribute of might, derived from "'Azīz," and the attribute of retribution, derived from His words ﴿Possessor of retribution﴾. It is as if Allah threatens them with His might and His retribution against those who deny the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him.
We take up the explanation of the author, may Allah have mercy on him. He said: ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide (36). And whomever Allah guides, for him there is no misleader. Is not Allah the Almighty﴾ [al-Zumar 36–37] (the Dominant over His affair). His explanation of "al-'Aziz" as "the Dominant over His affair" is considered deficient, because might has three meanings, as we have explained.
He said: ﴿Possessor of retribution﴾ (against His enemies). Retribution is taking the criminal for his crime. His words "(Yes)" are the answer to the interrogative in His words: ﴿Is not Allah the Almighty, Possessor of retribution?﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verses 36–37 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ The interrogative (istifham) here is for affirmation (taqrir), based on the rule we mentioned earlier: when the interrogative hamzah enters upon a negative statement, it conveys affirmation. Examples include ﴿Did We not expand your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh 1], meaning: We have indeed expanded your breast; and ﴿Were not My verses recited to you?﴾ [al-Mu'minun 105], meaning: they indeed were.

So also ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ means: Allah has indeed sufficed His servant. As for His words ﴿bi-kafin 'abdahu﴾, the word that governs the object ('abdahu) is ﴿kafin﴾, because ﴿kafin﴾ is an active participle (ism fa'il), its subject is a hidden pronoun, and ﴿'abdahu﴾ is its direct object. The word ('abd) is a singular noun in the construct state (mufrad mudaf), so it is general (ʿamm), including everyone who is characterized by this attribute. Whoever is truly a servant of Allah, Allah suffices him. A similar statement is His saying: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, He is sufficient for him﴾ [al-Talaq 3], and His saying: ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah 137]. Thus, "servant" here is an inclusive attribute, not restricted to one individual over another. Whoever truly fulfills servitude, Allah the Exalted suffices him. ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ The answer to this sentence is to say: Yes (bala).

Then He says: ﴿And they frighten you with those other than Him.﴾ Here the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿They frighten you﴾ is addressed specifically to the Messenger. The conjunction of the specific ﴿they frighten you﴾ with the general statement before it does not require restricting the general wording. Similar cases have come up often: a general term is mentioned, and then a ruling is mentioned that applies to some of its members. We have said that this does not require specification (takhsis). What is the closest example we have covered in this regard? We have covered examples; which is the closest?

* Student: ﴿Those who brought the truth﴾.

* Shaykh: No, that is general. We covered it in a hadith. How quickly you forget! These rules should not be forgotten, brothers, they should not be forgotten. If you now memorize the rule, for example: when a general term is followed by a ruling that applies to some of its members, this does not require specification. This is a clear rule. But if someone says to you, "Give me an example that fits this," and you forget the example, he will say, "This rule is not acceptable." Rather, I say: when a ruling applying to some members comes, it indicates that the intended meaning of the first general term is the specific. So he will turn the rule against you.

The seeker of knowledge should record the scattered benefits. Benefits that slip from the mind should be cared for and recorded by the student of knowledge, otherwise they will be lost to him.

* Student: If there is no hadith (...)?

* Shaykh: No, those are two separate texts. We want them in one context. We covered an example in the Qur'an and an example in the Sunnah. The closer one is what we covered in the Qur'an, or all of them have been covered.

* Student: The hadith of Ibn 'Abbas (...).

* Shaykh: No. "The Prophet (ﷺ) ruled concerning pre-emption (shuf'ah) in everything that has not been divided." This is general, isn't it? Answer, brothers: "He ruled concerning everything that has not been divided." Everything not divided is general. "But when the boundaries are set and the roads are arranged, there is no pre-emption." [Narrated by al-Bukhari (2214).] This is a ruling that applies to some members of the general term. To what does it apply? To immovable property, to lands. So do we say that the first general term means the specific? Or do we say the first is general, and a ruling that applies to some of its members does not require specification? This is the second view.

In the Qur'an: ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾ up to His saying: ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back during that period﴾ [al-Baqarah 228]. ﴿Divorced women﴾ is general, and ﴿their husbands have more right﴾ is a ruling that applies to some members of this general term. Which member does it apply to? To the revocable divorcee (raj'iyyah). So do we say that His saying ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾ is specific to revocable divorcees? Or do we say it is general? It is well known among the scholars that it is general, covering women divorced irrevocably (ba'in) and women divorced revocably (raj'i).

Have you now taken two examples? Does this example in the Qur'an that we have here apply or not? ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant? And they frighten you with those other than Him.﴾

* Student: It applies.

* Shaykh: It applies to it? The first, ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾, is general. He did not say, "Is not Allah sufficient for you?" It is general. ﴿And they frighten you﴾ is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ). But one of you may say to me: why is it not valid for the address to be directed to everyone who can be addressed, i.e., "they frighten you, O addressee"? One of you may say this, as is customary in many texts. The answer is that it is not valid for it to be directed to every addressee, because not every addressee can be described this way. Is every addressee frightened with those other than Allah? No. Only the Prophet (ﷺ) was frightened with those other than Allah, because they threatened him with their gods.

In any case, this example fits the rule we mentioned: when a general term occurs and is followed by a ruling that applies to some of its members, this does not require specification. Rather, the general term remains general and the ruling is established for this member.

He says: (﴿And they frighten you﴾: the address is to him), meaning to the Prophet (ﷺ), (﴿with those other than Him﴾: that is, the idols; i.e., they would kill him or derange him). This is like His saying: ﴿That is only Satan frightening you of his allies. So fear them not, but fear Me, if you should be believers﴾ [Al 'Imran 175]. They frighten the Prophet (ﷺ) with those other than Allah. Restricting this to idols, as the author (al-Mu'allif) did, is open to question. Rather, they frighten him with those other than Allah, including idols and non-idols, even rulers. For example, one says, "So-and-so will do such-and-such to you," or "the jinn will do such-and-such to you," or "he will do this or that to you." So we should understand ﴿those other than Him﴾ in its generality, not restricted to idols, because frightening is broader than that.

Now, for example in our time, if someone says to a person, "If you forbid this evil, I will report you to so-and-so, one whose evil is feared," is this frightening with those other than Allah? Yes, this is frightening with those other than Allah. So the verse is general, and one should not restrict it as the author, may Allah have mercy on him, did.

﴿And they frighten you with those other than Him.﴾ Allah says: ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾. The word ﴿man﴾ is conditional (shartiyyah), so it conveys generality: whoever Allah leaves astray, there is no guide for him. His saying ﴿fa-ma lahu min hadin﴾ is a nominal sentence consisting of a subject and a predicate. It is strange to say that it consists of a subject and a predicate when we find in it neither a subject nor a predicate. Where is the nominative noun? It is known that the subject and predicate are nominative, but here nothing is nominative. The answer is to say: ﴿ma﴾ is a negation particle, ﴿lahu﴾ is a prepositional phrase functioning as a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), and ﴿min hadin﴾ is a delayed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar). How do we analyze ﴿min hadin﴾? We say: ﴿min﴾ is a superfluous (za'idah) preposition, and ﴿hadin﴾ is a noun in the genitive governed by ﴿min﴾. Correct?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: ﴿Hadin﴾ is a subject in the nominative, marked by a presumed damma on the deleted ya', prevented from appearance by...?

* Student: Occupation of the place by a vowel (ishtighal al-mahall bi-harakah)...

* Shaykh: There is no vowel here. The ya' is not vowelled here, because it does not take a vowel in the genitive. It is the deleted ya', for the meeting of two unvowelled letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn), and the kasrah is presumed on it for harmony with the superfluous preposition. This is if we want to strain the i'rab to fit the grammatical rules. Otherwise, it is enough to say: ﴿min﴾ is a superfluous preposition, and ﴿hadin﴾ is a subject in the nominative, marked by a presumed damma on the deleted ya' for the meeting of two unvowelled letters, and we stop there, because the vowel of a superfluous preposition in a word like this does not appear.

His saying: ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾ means: whoever Allah decrees misguidance for, no one can guide him, however much the community gathers against him. Here is the greatest of creation in guidance and in calling to it, Muhammad (ﷺ). He strove with the utmost effort to guide his uncle Abu Talib until his last breath, but he was not guided, because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, had decreed misguidance for him. The last thing he said was to testify to the creed of disbelief. He said: "He is upon the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1360) and Muslim (24/39), from the hadith of al-Musayyab ibn Hazn.] "But the Prophet (ﷺ), because of his good character, and because his uncle stood up in support that helped Islam, interceded for him with Allah, so he is in a shallow fire, and upon him are two sandals of fire that make his brain boil." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3885) and Muslim (210/360), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.] This is the highest part of him, while the sandals are at the lowest part of him, and the brain is boiling. How much more intensely boils what is below it of the body! And indeed he is the least punished of the people of the Fire [narrated by Muslim (212/362), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas]. And he thinks that he is the most punished. Why does Allah show him that he is the most punished? So that he is not consoled by others, because if the one in the Fire knew that someone else was worse than him or equal to him, he would be consoled and the matter would be easier for him. Allah alluded to this in His saying: ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you have wronged, that you are sharing in the punishment﴾ [al-Zukhruf 39]. Even though if you shared in punishment in this world, it would be easier for you. Consider Ka'b ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him: when it was said to him that so-and-so and so-and-so had stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk, the matter became easy for him. [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4418) and Muslim (2769/53), from the hadith of Ka'b ibn Malik.] This is a known matter. And al-Khansa' laments her brother Sakhr and says:

Were it not for the abundance of those weeping around me over their brothers, I would have killed myself.
They do not weep like my brother, but I console myself for him with consolation.

So we say: whoever Allah has decreed misguidance for, no one will guide him, however many signs he is given, for: ﴿Signs and warnings avail not people who do not believe﴾ [Yunus 101].

* From the benefits of this noble verse, first: Allah's sufficiency for His servant.

* Among its benefits: encouragement to realize servitude to Allah. For when you realize servitude, sufficiency is realized for you, since a ruling tied to an attribute grows stronger with the strength of that attribute and weaker with its weakness. When sufficiency is ordered upon servitude, the worshipper obtains from this sufficiency in proportion to his servitude, following the rule that a ruling tied to an attribute grows stronger with its strength and weaker with its weakness.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah the Mighty and Majestic defends the believers, because if Allah is sufficient for him, He will defend him. This is confirmed by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah defends those who have believed﴾ [al-Hajj 38].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the enemies of Allah frighten the servants of Allah with what is other than Allah, as in His saying: ﴿And they frighten you with those other than Him﴾.

* Among the benefits of this verse: that Satan, who is the leader of the enemies of Allah, frightens the believing worshipper of Allah with what is other than Allah. You find him coming to a person who wants to enjoin good and forbid evil, and saying: "Do not do it. The people hate you. The people will accuse you of extremism. The ruler may discipline you," and similar things. But the believer is not afraid of this at all, because he holds fast to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. He is a servant of Allah, certain that Allah will support him, so these people do not concern him. But does that mean that a person should rush into matters with a stormy emotion, or should he use wisdom and proceed in the truth?

* Student: The second.

* Shaykh: The second. That is why we criticize some people who have zeal for the religion of Allah but do not enter houses through their doors. They want to approach matters with violence and force, even though they have no strength. We say: proceed with what Allah has commanded you, but use wisdom in doing so.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that everything other than Allah is "other than Allah," as His saying shows: ﴿They frighten you with those other than Him﴾. There is nothing here except Allah or what is other than Allah.

* A branch of this benefit: everything other than Allah is subdued (maghlub). If Allah suffices His servant and everything other than Allah is subdued, this means that a person will prevail if he realizes servitude. But one may raise an objection: Allah the Exalted mentioned that some people killed the prophets. How can this verse be reconciled with what is established about the killing of some prophets?

The answer to this, or its response, is that the killing of the prophets does not mean the killing of the truth they brought. The prophets spoke to establish the truth, not to establish their own personalities. They spoke to establish the truth. Furthermore, if they missed victory in this world, the victory you witness, they did not miss it in the Hereafter, based on Allah's saying: ﴿Indeed, We will surely support Our messengers and those who believe in the life of this world and on the day when the witnesses stand﴾ [Ghafir 51]. And Allah knows best.

* Student: (...) the definition of (...)?

* Shaykh: No, its definition, the definition of ihsan.

* Student: Regarding the address ﴿And they frighten you with those other than Him﴾, why does (...) the fear of other than Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

* Shaykh: We said that this is not for everyone, if we say it is general for every person.

* Student: (...) fear, Shaykh.

* Shaykh: Yes, we can make it for everyone who is frightened. We can do that, but it appears that it is specific to the Messenger.

* Student: The Messenger (ﷺ) interceded for his uncle Abu Talib, and he said: "Were it not for me, he would be in the lowest level of the Fire." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3883) and Muslim (209/357), from the hadith of al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib.] And he sees himself as the most punished of people. Because if he saw himself as the least punished, he would be consoled by that. Does this mean that he did not know of the Prophet's (ﷺ) intercession for him, that he was in this shallow fire? Or did he know, but still see himself as the most punished?

* Shaykh: Whether he knew or did not know, he sees himself as the most punished of people. That Allah informed him that he deserved the lowest level of the Fire, but through the intercession of the Messenger, may be that Allah informed him of this so that he would know that Allah had rewarded him for what he did for the Messenger (peace be upon him). Or perhaps not. And Allah knows best.

* Student: The saying of Allah, glory be to Him, ﴿And they frighten you with those other than Him﴾: does its context match that the earlier people said ﴿We only say that some of our gods have struck you with evil﴾ [Hud 54]?

* Shaykh: Who transmitted this?

* Student: The people of Shu'ayb.

* Shaykh: No. Those who said it were 'Ad, to Hud.

* Student: Yes. Is it the same...? That is, the polytheists frightened the Prophet (ﷺ) that evil from the gods would befall him if he opposed them...

* Shaykh: No. Those people said: ﴿We only say that some of our gods have struck you with evil﴾ [Hud 54], meaning: they have driven you mad and made you insane. But these people said: our gods will drive you mad, and they threatened him for the future (...).

* * *

* Student: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿And whoever Allah guides, for him there is no misleader. Is not Allah Exalted in Might, Owner of Retribution? (37) And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah." Say, "Have you considered that which you invoke other than Allah? If Allah intended to harm me, could they remove His harm? Or if He intended for me mercy, could they withhold His mercy?" Say, "Sufficient for me is Allah. On Him rely the reliant." (38) Say, "O my people, work according to your position; indeed, I am working, so you will know (39) on whom will come a punishment that will disgrace him and upon him will descend a lasting punishment."﴾ [al-Zumar 37–40].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant? Yet they frighten you with those other than Him.﴾ We mentioned that the interrogative in His words ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ is what?
* Student: That the interrogative hamza (hamzat al-istifham), when it occurs in a context of negation, conveys affirmation (taqrir).
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is for affirmation. The interrogative in His words ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ is for affirmation, based on the rule that when the interrogative hamza is followed by something that conveys negation, it is for affirmation. There are many examples of this in the Qur'an. We also mentioned the meaning of ﴿His servant﴾.
* Student: The Prophet ﷺ (...).
* The Shaykh: And what does the author see?
* Student: (...) the Prophet ﷺ.
* The Shaykh: What led the author to make it refer to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him?
* Student: His words after it: ﴿and they frighten you with those other than Him.﴾
* The Shaykh: Yes. The correct view is the general meaning. What is the meaning of ﴿they frighten you (yukhawwifunaka)﴾?
* Student: They threaten you.
* Another student: They frighten you. The author mentioned that it refers to the idols, but it conveys generality.
* The Shaykh: No. That is an explanation of ﴿those other than Him (alladhina min dunihi)﴾. But what is the meaning of the word ﴿yukhawwifunaka﴾? They cast fear into your heart concerning them, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It is only Satan who frightens his allies﴾ [Al 'Imran 175]. In His words ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾, what is this ﴿min﴾?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Where is the response of the condition (jawab al-shart)?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What is the meaning of His words ﴿whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾?
* Student: It means the one whom Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, did not want to guide.
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: ﴿Whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾?
* Student: (...) Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for misguidance. Whatever effort a person exerts in guiding him, he cannot do it, as the Prophet ﷺ did with his uncle.
* The Shaykh: Correct. What is meant by guidance in His words ﴿for him there is no guide﴾?
* Student: Guidance of indication (hidayat al-dalalah), guidance of direction (hidayat al-irshad), guidance of divine success (hidayat al-tawfiq).
* The Shaykh: Guidance of indication, guidance of direction, and guidance of divine success.
* Student: The last one, O Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: The last one is guidance of divine success. What is the evidence that the meaning of guidance here is guidance of divine success?
* Student: Because the guidance of divine success (...) except Allah.
* The Shaykh: But what is the evidence that the meaning of ﴿for him there is no guide﴾ is: for him there is no one who grants him success in guidance? One might say: ﴿for him there is no guide﴾ means: there is no one who points to the truth?
* Student: (...) ﴿for him there is no guide﴾ (...).
* The Shaykh: A word from which one understands it is not sufficient; there must be evidence.
* Student: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [al-Qasas 56], which shows that the Prophet ﷺ guides only (...).
* Another student: (...) that the servants do not possess this thing which Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, possesses.
* The Shaykh: Yes, there is no doubt about that. But what is the evidence that this is the intended meaning? Because guidance is of two kinds: guidance of divine success and guidance of indication.
* Student: His words ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray﴾, where He attributed misguidance to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
* Another student: Because Allah, glorified and exalted, guided them with the guidance of indication; that is, He showed them the guidance of indication.
* The Shaykh: Because those whom Allah has led astray had already been guided with the guidance of indication: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat 17]. The messengers were sent to disbelieving peoples against whom the word of punishment had come into effect. Therefore it is necessary here that the meaning of the Guide is guidance of divine success: ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide.﴾
* From the benefits of this noble verse: whoever Allah has decreed to be astray, no one can guide him, because of His words: ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide.﴾
* And from its benefits: a person should seek guidance only from Allah, because He alone leads astray and guides, so guidance is sought from Him. This verse is not meant to despair of guiding creation, but the intended meaning is returning to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in guiding creation.
* And from the benefits of the noble verse: a refutation of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school), who say that a person is independent in his actions, guiding himself and misguiding himself, and that Allah's will has no connection to his action, because of His words: ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide.﴾
* And from its benefits: affirming that guidance, in the sense of guidance of indication, can be attributed to other than Allah, whereas divine success belongs to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
Then Allah, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿And whomever Allah guides, for him there is no misleader﴾. We have taken this, I think.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It was not explained. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whomever Allah guides, for him there is no misleader﴾, meaning: whoever Allah has decreed guidance for, there is no misleader for him.
A person should seek guidance only from Allah, because He alone leads astray and guides, so guidance is sought from Him. This verse is not meant to despair of guiding creation, but the intended meaning is returning to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in guiding creation.
* And from the benefits of the noble verse: a refutation of the Mu'tazilah, who say: a person is independent in his actions, guiding himself and misguiding himself, and Allah's will has no connection to his action; because of His words: ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾ [al-Zumar 36].
* And from its benefits: affirming that guidance, in the sense of guidance of indication, belongs to others, whereas divine success belongs to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
Then He said: ﴿And whomever Allah guides, for him there is no misleader﴾ [al-Zumar 37]. We have taken this. Was it explained?
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whomever Allah guides, for him there is no misleader﴾, meaning: whoever Allah decrees guidance for, there is no misleader for him. No one can mislead him, however many doubts and however many desires there are. If Allah decrees guidance for a servant, no desire and no doubt will lead him astray, because at the time of desire reason overcomes and he refrains from it, and at the time of doubt knowledge overcomes and he is guided by it away from it. This is the one whom Allah guides; for him there is no misleader.
In this statement there is clearly an encouragement for a person to persist in guidance. So this is one of the benefits of the verse: encouraging the one who is guided to remain on guidance, because Allah is the One who guided him, and no one can mislead him.
* And from its benefits: seeking refuge in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in asking Him for guidance and persevering in it.
Then He said: ﴿Is not Allah the Almighty, Possessor of retribution?﴾ [al-Zumar 37]. The answer is: Yes. His words ﴿Almighty (bi-'azizin)﴾: this is the predicate of "laysa," to which the particle bi has been added, extra in form and extra in meaning. It is extra in form, but it conveys the emphasis of generality in negation, since negation conveys generality when it is followed by an indefinite noun. But when the bi is added, the particles of emphasis are among those additional particles, as the scholars of rhetoric have mentioned.
As for His words ﴿'Azīz﴾, the exegetes said regarding the Most Beautiful Names of Allah that al-'Aziz has three meanings. The first meaning: might of rank (izzat al-qadr). The second meaning: might of subjugation (izzat al-qahr). The third meaning: might of inaccessibility (izzat al-imtina').
As for might of rank, its meaning is that Allah has a great rank and a lofty honor; no one is like Him, and no one equals Him or comes near Him. As for might of subjugation, its meaning is that Allah, the Exalted, subdues everything and overcomes everything. As for might of inaccessibility, its meaning is that every defect and deficiency is impossible for Allah, the Exalted. This is well known in the Arabic language. The second meaning, which is domination, the poet said regarding it:
Where is the escape, when the Seeker is God? ∗∗∗ And the Ashram, the vanquished, is not the victor.
As for the first, which is might of rank, it is said: "This is 'aziz," meaning rare and not found, because of its nobility and generosity. As for the third, there is the saying: "Land 'azzaz," meaning firm and solid, which cannot be dug by pickaxes. So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is 'Aziz in these three meanings. The first, brother?
* Student: The first is might of domination, might of...
* The Shaykh: Might of domination and subjugation.
* Student: The first is might of domination, the second is might of subjugation, and the third is might of inaccessibility.
* The Shaykh: Inaccessibility, good.
As for His words ﴿Is not Allah the Almighty, Possessor of retribution?﴾ [al-Zumar 37]: "Dhū" means "possessor," and "intiqam" is indefinite. An indefinite noun in an affirmative context does not convey generality, but here it is in what context? ﴿Is not Allah the Almighty, Possessor of retribution?﴾, meaning: possessor of retribution. Whenever wisdom requires retribution, He takes retribution. Reflect on His words ﴿Possessor of retribution﴾, and He did not say "Muntaqim" (the Avenger), because "al-Muntaqim" is not among the Names of Allah, and "al-Muntaqim" did not come as a Name of Allah in any authentic hadith. Rather, it came only in the form of a qualified active participle, as He said: ﴿Indeed, We will take retribution from the criminals﴾ [al-Sajdah 22], and He did not say "Indeed, We are avengers." He said "Possessor of retribution," meaning: possessor of retribution in its proper place. So "al-Muntaqim" is not among the Names of Allah, even if it is paired with "al-'Afu" (the Pardoner), in contrast to what some scholars held, that if it is paired with pardon there is no harm. Rather we say: "al-Muntaqim" is not among the Names of Allah, neither paired with pardon nor alone. But He is described with retribution in a qualified form: ﴿Indeed, We will take retribution from the criminals﴾, and it is described as proceeding from Him, not that He is "Muntaqim," as in His words: ﴿Almighty, Possessor of retribution﴾.
* From the benefits of this verse: affirming the might of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in all its meanings.
* And from its benefits: threatening those who deny the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, with these two attributes: the attribute of might, derived from "'Azīz," and the attribute of retribution, derived from His words ﴿Possessor of retribution﴾. It is as if Allah threatens them with His might and His retribution against those who deny the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him.
We take up the explanation of the author, may Allah have mercy on him. He said: ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide (36). And whomever Allah guides, for him there is no misleader. Is not Allah the Almighty﴾ [al-Zumar 36–37] (the Dominant over His affair). His explanation of "al-'Aziz" as "the Dominant over His affair" is considered deficient, because might has three meanings, as we have explained.
He said: ﴿Possessor of retribution﴾ (against His enemies). Retribution is taking the criminal for his crime. His words "(Yes)" are the answer to the interrogative in His words: ﴿Is not Allah the Almighty, Possessor of retribution?﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verse 38 (part 1 of 3):

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ [Az-Zumar 38] As for ﴿And if you asked them﴾, the address is either to the Messenger (ﷺ), or to everyone to whom the address is directed. The lam in His words ﴿And if﴾ is the lam that prepares for an oath (lam al-muwatti'ah lil-qasam), and "in" (in) is a conditional particle. Is the answer in His words ﴿they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ the answer to the condition or the answer to the oath? It is the answer to the oath, because it is preceded by the lam, and what takes the lam as its answer is the oath, not the condition. The rule is that when a condition and an oath come together, the answer belongs to whichever of the two comes first. Ibn Malik said in the Alfiyyah:
"Omit, when a condition and an oath come together, the answer of whichever you placed later; that is obligatory."
Here, which is the one placed later: the oath or the condition?
* Student: The condition.
* Shaykh: The condition. So its answer is omitted, and its answer is understood from the answer of the oath.
His words ﴿And if you asked them﴾ are an interrogative question: "Who created the heavens and the earth?" That is, who brought them into being in this wondrous form? The words "heavens" (as-samawat) and "earth" (al-ard) are derived from "sumuw," which means height, because of their elevation and loftiness. The heavens are in the plural because they are seven heavens, layered one upon another, each above the other. Accordingly, the second is wider than the first, the third is wider than the second, the fourth is wider than the third, and so on. If the distance between them is a journey of five hundred years, you will understand the width of each heaven in relation to what is beneath it, and that its vastness is great. Yet despite this great vastness, these heavens are, in relation to the Kursi (Footstool), like a ring thrown into a desert of the earth. The ring is the small ring of a coat of mail, thrown into a desert of the earth. The superiority of the Throne (al-'Arsh) over the Kursi is like the superiority of the desert over that ring. And the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, none can measure His measure except Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

So the heavens are seven, layered, and the earth is one, because He said ﴿al-ard﴾ and did not say "al-aradin" (the earths). We say: what is meant by it is the genus; the word "earth" here refers to the category, so it does not contradict its being seven. Allah, the Exalted, has indicated in the Qur'an that it is seven, in His words: ﴿Allah is the One who created seven heavens and of the earth their like﴾ [At-Talaq 12]. The Sunnah is also explicit on this, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever seizes a span of land unjustly, Allah will encircle him with it on the Day of Resurrection from seven earths."[[Recorded by Muslim (1610/137) from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd.]]

﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ This is the answer to a question: they would say, "Allah is the One who created the heavens and the earth." The polytheists did not claim that the heavens and the earth were eternal and not originated, nor did they claim that anyone created them besides Allah. Rather, they acknowledged that the Creator is Allah alone. Likewise, if they were asked, "Who created you?" they would say, "Allah." Whenever they were asked about something related to lordship, they attributed it to whom? To Allah, Mighty and Majestic, without any partner. Thus they affirm the Tawhid of Lordship (tawhid ar-rububiyyah) to the utmost affirmation; they know that Allah is the Creator.

His words ﴿they would surely say, "Allah"﴾: I will raise a difficulty for you regarding the vowelling of this verb together with the attached emphatic nun. It is well known that the imperfect verb is built (mabni) in two situations: when the emphatic nun is attached to it, it is built on fatha, and when the nun of the feminine plural is attached, it is built on sukun. So why is it here vowelled with damma?
* Student: (...) O Shaykh, it was deleted and the damma was given in its place (...).
* Shaykh: The damma was given in its place?
* Student: (...) omitted.
* Shaykh: Just that? Good, complete it.
* Student: The nun of the verb, in "liyaqulunna."
* Shaykh: So the nun is not directly attached to the verb. On this analysis, between it and the verb there is the waw of the plural and the nun of the nominative. So it is not directly attached in reality; it is directly attached in form. The verb is built with the emphatic nun when it is directly attached both in form and in estimation. But this one is not directly attached in estimation, and for this reason the verb remained inflected (mu'rab). It is said: it is in the nominative by the deleted nun, due to the succession of like letters, and by the deleted waw, due to the meeting of two sukuns, as subject. This is how it is parsed.
﴿liyaqulunna Allah﴾: "Allah" is in the nominative as the predicate of a deleted subject, meaning "He is Allah." It may also be the subject of a deleted verb, meaning "Allah created them both." It may also be the subject with the predicate deleted, the estimate being "Allah is their Creator." The matter here is broad; the chapter of i'rab (grammatical parsing) has many aspects.

﴿liyaqulunna Allah. Say: "Have you considered what you invoke besides Allah? If Allah should intend for me some harm, could they remove His harm? Or if He should intend for me some mercy, could they withhold His mercy?"﴾ [Az-Zumar 38] That is: ask them another question. When they have acknowledged that the Creator is Allah, say to them: Tell me what you invoke besides Allah. As for ﴿tad'un﴾ (you invoke), the author says: (you worship). It may also be meant as supplication of request (du'a al-mas'alah), because "du'a" (supplication) is applied to two meanings: the first meaning is supplication of request, and the second is supplication of worship (du'a al-'ibadah).

From the first is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Is there anyone asking, that I may give to him? Is there anyone calling, that I may respond to him?"[[Recorded by Muslim (758/170) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] And His words: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the caller when he calls upon Me﴾ [Al-Baqarah 186]; this is supplication of request. From the second, which is supplication of worship, is His words: ﴿And your Lord says, "Call upon Me; I will respond to you. Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, humbled."﴾ [Ghafir 60]. These people invoke besides Allah. Do they invoke besides Allah with supplication of request or supplication of worship?
* Student: General.
* Shaykh: Yes, general: they invoke besides Allah both with supplication of request and with supplication of worship. Tell us about these idols that you invoke besides Allah: do they benefit the one who invokes them? Do they bring benefit or ward off harm? ﴿If Allah should intend for me some harm, could they remove His harm?﴾ [Az-Zumar 38] If Allah intends harm for me, can they remove it? The answer: No, they cannot ward off harm when Allah wills it. ﴿Or if He should intend for me some mercy, could they withhold His mercy?﴾ [Az-Zumar 38] The answer: No.
So how can you worship besides Allah? How can you invoke besides Allah? When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, intends harm for me, they cannot repel it, and when He intends mercy for me, they cannot withhold that mercy. The answer: He says, "No."

﴿Say: "Sufficient for me is Allah. In Him rely those who rely."﴾ [Az-Zumar 38] That is: it does not concern me that you threaten me with these idols, for "sufficient for me is Allah," that is, He suffices me against whatever else there is.

In the phrase "hasbiya Allah" it is permissible to have inversion (taqdim and ta'khir). We may parse "hasbi" as a fronted predicate and "Allah" as a postponed subject, or we may say "hasbi" is the subject and "Allah" the predicate, and the meaning differs as the parsing differs. If you wish to inform about the sufficiency that it is Allah, make "hasbi" the subject. If you wish to inform about Allah that He is the sufficiency, make "hasbi" a fronted predicate. The verse, in meaning, is suitable for both: Allah is the sufficiency, and the sufficiency is Allah; we have no sufficiency other than Allah, and Allah, glorified and exalted, is our sufficiency and our sufficer.

﴿Say: "Sufficient for me is Allah. In Him rely those who rely."﴾ [Az-Zumar 38] Tawakkul (reliance): it is depending upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in bringing benefit and warding off harm, together with trust in Allah, glorified and exalted. This is tawakkul: depending upon Allah with true and sincere dependence in bringing benefit and warding off harm, together with trust in Him.

It is among the worship specific to Allah, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾ [Ali 'Imran 122], that is, upon Allah alone. As for reliance in matters other than worship, it is permissible for a person to rely upon another in what he has entrusted to him, as when you say to so-and-so, "I have appointed you to buy such-and-such for me," and so you rely on him in the purchase. This is not reliance of worship, because the one relying in this case does not feel that he is of lower rank than the agent; he may even feel he is of higher rank, since he has made that one a servant to him, executing what he says. But reliance upon Allah is that you rely upon Allah while believing in yourself that you are in need of Him, and that He, glorified and exalted, is the One in whose hand is the management of your affairs, so you rely upon Him out of hope, fear, and drawing near to Him.

Hence we say: may I say, "I have relied upon so-and-so"?
The answer: If it is in the manner of worship, this is forbidden, it is shirk. If it is in the manner of substitution (inabah), meaning you have made him your substitute in what you have entrusted to him, there is no harm or fault in it. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to appoint his companions as agents for collecting and distributing the zakat and other matters.

Returning to the words of the author, may Allah have mercy on him. The author says: (﴿And if you asked them﴾: the lam is the lam of oath. ﴿"Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah." Say:﴾ [Az-Zumar 38]) That is, if they acknowledge this acknowledgment, (﴿"Have you considered what you invoke﴾: worship ﴿besides Allah﴾, that is, the idols) meaning, tell us about them (﴿If Allah should intend for me some harm, could they remove His harm?﴾). He says: (The answer is: no. ﴿Or if He should intend for me some mercy, could they withhold His mercy?﴾ No. And in one reading, with the genitive (iḍafah) in both places.) That is, in His words ﴿kashifat﴾ (removers).
And in His words ﴿mumsikat﴾ (withholders). So on this reading we read: ﴿could they remove His harm?﴾ and ﴿could they withhold His mercy?﴾. Both readings are canonical (sab'iyyah). It is a principle of the author in this book that when he says "and it was read" (wa-qurii), it is a shadhdh (irregular) reading; and when he says "and in a reading" (wa-fi qira'ah), it is canonical (sab'iyyah). Let this terminology be known so that it is not confused: when he says "it was read," it is an irregular reading not to be recited with; when he says "and in a reading," it is canonical and recited with.
He said: ﴿Say: "Sufficient for me is Allah. In Him rely those who rely."﴾ [Az-Zumar 38]. He said: (those who trust will trust).

* There are benefits in this verse. First: the acknowledgment of these polytheists of Lordship, from His words ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ [Az-Zumar 38].
* And among its benefits: acknowledgment of Lordship does not benefit the servant nor bring him into Islam. The proof of this is that the Prophet (ﷺ) fought these people who acknowledged Lordship, and made lawful their blood, their women, and their property. Had their acknowledgment of Lordship been beneficial, their blood would have been protected, their property protected, and their families protected.
* And among the benefits of this verse: the refutation, indeed the nullification, of what the theologians (mutakallimun) understood by Tawhid. For the common theologians, when they explain Tawhid, say that it has three types: Tawhid in His essence, in His attributes, and in His actions. Thus they say, Allah's Tawhid is of three types: His Tawhid in His essence, His Tawhid in His attributes, and His Tawhid in His actions. They say He is one in His essence, without any counterpart (qasim), and by this they mean that He has no face, no hand, no eye, and similar things.
They say: if we affirmed these attributes for Him, it would follow that He has parts, and He, glorified and exalted, is not divisible. So He is one in His essence without counterpart, one in His actions without partner. Then they make this type of Tawhid the Tawhid of Divinity (tawhid al-uluhiyyah), and they say: the meaning of the saying "There is no god but Allah" is: there is no one capable of creating and originating except Allah.
The third: He is one in His attributes, without any likeness. A statement whose outward meaning is mercy and whose inward is punishment from its source. What do they mean by their saying "without any likeness"? They mean: He has no attributes, because they believe that whoever affirms an attribute for Allah is an anthropomorphist (mushabbih). So He is one in His attributes without likeness. If you recited this classification to a layman, what would he say about it? He would say, "How good, how beautiful!"
One in His essence without counterpart, glorified and exalted, and He glorifies and declares His oneness; one in His actions without partner, likewise; one in His attributes without likeness, likewise. But one does not know what lies behind the hill. They mean by "one in His essence without counterpart" that He has no attributes which, relative to us, would be like organs, such as hand, face, eye, foot, and shin.
"One in His actions without partner": they mean by this that this is the meaning of "There is no god but Allah." Had this been the meaning of "There is no god but Allah," the polytheists whom the Messenger (ﷺ) fought would have been believers and monotheists. Yet when it was said to them, "There is no god but Allah," they became arrogant and would not accept it, saying, "Has he made the gods one god?" So consider how the polytheists in the Jahiliyyah understood Tawhid better than these theologians understood it. The scholars, such as Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah and others, have mentioned this meaning and said: the polytheists were better in understanding Tawhid than these theologians, because these theologians made Tawhid only the Tawhid of Lordship, which the polytheists do not deny; they affirm it, and they deny the Tawhid of Divinity, because they know that the meaning of "There is no god but Allah" is: there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah. They know this. As for those theologians, they give no weight to Divinity; they regard it as a trivial matter and do not include it among the types of Tawhid.
"One in His attributes without likeness": what do they mean? They mean the negation of the attributes, because they claim that whoever affirms an attribute for Allah is an anthropomorphist. Thus this verse makes clear the refutation of those theologians who make the Tawhid of Divinity the same as the Tawhid of Lordship. The rest of the discussion of it will come, God willing.
* Student: (...) O Shaykh, that the evidence for the Tawhid of Lordship does not benefit anything, that the fighting of the Prophet (ﷺ) (...) that it is permissible to make lawful the blood of a Muslim..
* Shaykh: No. Fighting a Muslim is not like fighting a disbeliever. You fight a Muslim because he has neglected one of the rites of Islam, and you do not take his women, his offspring, and his land. But you fight a disbeliever because he has abandoned Islam entirely, and therefore you take his women, his offspring, and his land.
* Student: We said: the names of Allah are tawqifi (restricted to revelation) (...) this principle, is it applied so that Allah, glorified and exalted, is called "al-Muntaqim" (the Avenger)?
* Shaykh: "Al-Muntaqim" no, because Allah restricted the avenging. When He described Himself with the active participle, He restricted it. Here we say: the names of Allah, all of them, include attributes; every name includes one or more attributes. Does every attribute include a name? No. Then the attributes are broader than the names. This is one point.
Second: among the attributes are those by which Allah described Himself, and there is no doubt that these are permissible. But we describe Allah with them according to how He described Himself. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Almighty, Owner of retribution﴾ [Ibrahim 47]. Here we do not say "Allah is Muntaqim," but we say "Dhu intiqam" (Owner of retribution), meaning He has retribution. There is a difference between calling a man "carpenter" because his profession is carpentry, and saying that he has carpentry, meaning he does carpentry when the need arises. Is that not so? Good.
What Allah described Himself with among attributes is described according to how He described Himself. What He did not describe Himself with: if it indicates a meaning befitting Allah, it is permissible to report it about Allah; and if it indicates a meaning not befitting Allah, it is forbidden to describe Allah with it, neither as a report nor as a permanent description. This is an important matter: what is not befitting Allah may not be ascribed to Him, neither as an act nor as a permanent attribute. What does not contradict what is befitting Allah may be reported about Him. Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned this division, I think in the book al-Fatawa in the section on Tawhid.
