Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of will for Allah in His saying: ﴿If Allah intends me﴾ and ﴿or if He intends me﴾. Allah's will is divided into two kinds: legislative will (*al-irādah al-shar'iyyah*), and universal, decreed will (*al-irādah al-kawniyyah al-qadariyyah*).

I ask the brothers not to comment on the book of tafsīr itself, because commentary on the book spoils the book. Sometimes the commentary may be longer than the tafsīr itself, especially when we want to speak about the division of will and similar matters. But if we want to explain a word, and write it in the margin, that is easier. However, you spoil your books with things that contain detail. No one will read them after you, and perhaps even you will not benefit from them over time. So we hope that whoever wants to write such lengthy material writes it outside the book, which is better.

Alright. We said the will is universal and legislative. The universal will is that which means decree (*mashī'ah*), and the legislative will is that which means love (*maḥabbah*). If "*yurīd*" means "*yashā'*" (wills), then it is universal will. If "*yurīd*" means "*yuḥibb*" (loves), then it is legislative will.

The difference between them is that universal will necessarily entails the occurrence of what is willed, because it is universal. No one can overturn Allah's decree. Legislative will does not necessarily entail the occurrence of what is willed.

Second: legislative will occurs only in what Allah loves, while universal will encompasses what Allah loves and what He does not love. We will take some exercises on this. If someone says to you: "Does Allah will sins?" If you say "yes," you are wrong. If you say "no," you are also wrong. So what do you say? We say: by universal will, yes, He wills them, and sins happen only by His will. By legislative will, no, because Allah dislikes sins. Have you understood? With this detail, many difficulties about sins disappear: are they willed by Allah or not willed? We say: they are willed by universal will and not willed by legislative will. If someone says: "How does Allah will them when He dislikes them?" We say: yes, they are willed for the sake of something else, meaning loved for something else, that is, for the great benefits that result from them. Alright, so they are not willed by legislative will, but they are willed by universal will.

If someone objects to us: "How does Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will them while He dislikes them?" The answer is: He wills them and dislikes them, because they are willed for something else. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, brings about sins, and wills sins for the sake of much good for the one who commits them if he repents to Allah. For a sinner who repents to Allah becomes better than he was before the sin. The evidence for this is that Adam disobeyed his Lord and erred, then repented to Allah, and after his repentance He chose him and guided him. Without this sin he would not have attained the election and guidance that he attained after the sin. So the sin became good for Adam. Furthermore, there is another good in it: when a person who sins against Allah knows his own worth, he feels shame before his Lord and considers every good deed he does small, because he always keeps his sin before his eyes. But if he does not sin, he may become arrogant, lift his nose high, be pleased with himself, and say: "I have never disobeyed Allah," and so on, and then his deeds are nullified without his realizing it.

Now, these two benefits are for whom? For the sinner. There is a third benefit for ordinary people. Were it not for disobedience, enjoining good and forbidding evil would not be established, because if people were all upon righteousness and good, what would we command, and what would we forbid? So enjoining good and forbidding evil is established only when its causes exist, and its causes are sins.

Fourth: were it not for sins, a person would not know the worth of the faith that Allah has bestowed upon him, nor its sweetness. If people were all on one level, a person would not know the worth of Allah's blessing upon him. This is why no one knows the worth of health except one who has been afflicted with illness, isn't that so? Likewise, a servant does not know the worth of Allah's blessing of obedience unless he knows the effects of sins on those who commit them.

Five; have we taken five?

The fifth: were it not for sins, the greatest of which is disbelief, the market of jihad would not have been established, because if we were all Muslims, whom would we fight? No one. But when there is a disbeliever and a believer, the market of jihad is established. The great good and merit of jihad is not hidden from you.

Sixth: were it not for sins, the wisdom behind the creation of all creatures would be lost. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one community﴾, meaning upon guidance, ﴿and they will not cease to differ, except those upon whom your Lord has mercy. And for that He created them. And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together"﴾ [Hūd 118–119].

Seventh: were it not for sins, there would be no wisdom in creating Paradise and Hell, because Hell is for those who disobey. If there were no disobedient ones, the creation of Hell would be pointless. This is why He said: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together"﴾ [Hūd 119].

So it becomes clear now that what Allah decrees, which He dislikes, has great and enormous benefits, and then it is willed by Allah for something else, and from this aspect it is loved by Allah. Thus the objection we raised first is dismissed, namely how Allah wills sins while He dislikes them. Do you understand? You may not find such benefits in a book, so I urge you to preserve them and write them down. Alright, a parallel in tangible matters: a father or mother comes to a sick son and cauterizes him with fire, which causes him pain and burns his skin. But why? To seek healing. So the cautery is disliked by him and not loved by him, yet it is loved for something else, namely for the benefits that result from it. This shows that there is nothing wrong with a thing being disliked in one respect and loved in another. Alright, let us return to the difference between the two wills, legislative and universal. Which of them necessarily entails the occurrence of what is willed?

* **The Shaykh:** Universal, legislative.

* **The Shaykh:** Universal, legislative. Which do we settle on?

* **Students:** Universal.

* **The Shaykh:** Universal?

* **Students:** Legislative.

* **The Shaykh:** He is willed to disbelieve by universal will. So the disbelief of a believer who believed is willed from him to believe by legislative will, and is willed from him to believe by universal will, because he did believe. Accordingly, both universal and legislative wills converge in respect of the believer. Correct? Are you sure?

* **Students:** Correct.

* **Students:** Universal.

* **The Shaykh:** Universal will.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, tests a person with harm and with mercy, yes. He tests them with harm and tests them with mercy. Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿And when harm touches mankind, they call upon their Lord, turning to Him in repentance. Then when He gives them a taste of mercy from Him, behold, a party of them associates others with their Lord﴾ [Ar-Rūm 33]. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, tests with harm and tests with mercy.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the difference between harm and mercy. He said of mercy: ﴿Are they withholders of His mercy?﴾ [Az-Zumar 38], and of harm: ﴿Are they removers of His harm?﴾ [Az-Zumar 38], because mercy needs continuation. If Allah maintains mercy, are these idols the ones who hold back the mercy, or Allah? Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Allah is the one who holds back mercy, not these idols.

The verse may also have another meaning: "Are they withholders of His mercy from reaching the one who is shown mercy?" Then "*mumsikāt*" would mean "preventers of mercy," so that it corresponds to ﴿Are they removers of His harm?﴾ [Az-Zumar 38].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation for a person to rely upon Allah, from His saying: ﴿Say: "Allah is sufficient for me"﴾ [Az-Zumar 38], meaning: say it with your tongue while believing it in your heart.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the one most deserving of reliance is Allah, from His saying: ﴿In Him let those who trust put their trust﴾ [Az-Zumar 38].

If someone says: "Does realizing reliance on Allah contradict taking the means?"

If there is no way out, then the answer is no, unless the means have been cut off and nothing remains but reliance (tawakkul). In that case, reliance itself becomes the means behind all means. A person is commanded to take the means. If he takes it and it does not benefit him, or if the means does not exist or is beyond his power, then nothing remains but reliance. If someone says: what is the evidence that taking the means does not contradict reliance? We say: it is the practice of the master of those who rely upon God, Muhammad (ﷺ). He would take the means: he ate so that hunger would be driven away from him, he drank so that thirst would be driven away from him, and he wore armour in battle to protect himself from arrows. Indeed, at Uhud he (ﷺ) wore two coats of mail[[Narrated by Ibn Majah (2806) and Ahmad (15722) from the hadith of al-Sa'ib ibn Yazid.]], because that is stronger in protection and defence. He (ﷺ) also dug the trench around Madinah in the Battle of the Confederates (al-Ahzab) to prevent the enemy from entering Madinah. The evidence for this is abundant. However, we restrict the means to those whose causation is established either by the Law (shar') or by sense perception (hiss). It must be established that a thing is a cause either through the Law or through sense and experience. As for mere supposition that something is a cause, that is shirk.

Pay attention to this point. Among the indications that a thing is a cause by the Law is that the Qur'an is a healing for what is in the hearts, which is the disease of doubts and desires, and a healing for what is in the bodies. This is based on the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to the one who recited al-Fatihah over a person bitten by a scorpion (or snake): "How did you know that it is a ruqyah?"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2276) and Muslim (2201/65) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]] How do we know that the Qur'an is a healing? From the Law. It may also be known through experience, such as our knowledge that senna (al-sanna') is a laxative. How did we know that? Is it in the Qur'an and the Sunnah that senna is a laxative?
* Student: Through experience.
* Shaykh: But through experience. In our language, senna is called... I don't know whether you in Qassim call it that: al-sanawin, the dual form, though it is one senna. It is a kind of leaf, the leaves of a well-known tree resembling the lote tree (sidr). When it is crushed and soaked in water for about twenty hours or so, and a person drinks it, it cleanses what is in his stomach of harm and acts as a laxative. It has an unpleasant smell, so people add onion to it to mask its smell, although onion is itself foul, but less so.
* Student: The lesser of two harms.
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed, the lesser of two harms. In any case, how do we know that this is a laxative? From experience. Most of the medicines available today are of this kind of experiential knowledge. As for something merely imagined, it is not permissible to rely on it, and it is a kind of shirk. Tiwalah (a love charm) is shirk. Why? Because it has not been established as a cause of a man's love for his wife or a woman's love for her husband, neither by the Law nor by sense. So affirming it as a cause is shirk, because you have affirmed what God has not affirmed, as though you made yourself like God in establishing causes and their effects.

Therefore, the words of the Most High: ﴿Upon Him let those who rely [upon Him] rely﴾ [Yusuf 67] do not contradict taking means; rather, means are in reality part of reliance. For this reason, "'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said to Abu 'Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah when he said: 'Are you fleeing from the decree of Allah?' He said: 'We flee from the decree of Allah to the decree of Allah.'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5729) and Muslim (2219/98) from the hadith of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf.]] And Allah knows best.
* Student: Is the sinner who repents to Allah better, or the one who has never disobeyed Allah, the Mighty and Majestic?
* Shaykh: No, the one who has not disobeyed Allah is better, because the sinner may not be granted the success of repentance. I say: may not be granted success in repentance. Yet a person senses within himself that when he sins and then repents, he finds in himself shame before Allah, he returns to Him and feels modesty before Him. But if he continues in obedience without ever experiencing the sweetness of repentance, this is something tested and observed.
* Student: Are the medicines available now proven (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, there is no doubt.
* Student: But the patient does not know that they are proven, as evidenced by the fact that he uses many of them...
* Shaykh: How does he not know? No, because he trusts the medical people, and he knows that they are beneficial. They cannot now release medicines to the market except after extensive trials. They test them on mice, rabbits, and dogs. They conduct trials, especially for incurable diseases. Do not think that one of them mixes these pills and gives them to you straight away.
* Student: But sometimes a person does not find a result from using it...
* Shaykh: Yes, well said. The principle is that medicine must reach a receptive place. If it does not reach a receptive place, it does not benefit. Even recitation, which is established as a cause beyond doubt, is often recited over a patient who does not benefit, because the place is not receptive. You find someone reciting over him, and he says: "Well, why keep going? He has no knowledge, he does not benefit."
* Student: In this case, is it forbidden to use it, O Shaykh?
* Shaykh: No, using it is not forbidden. But if it leads to harm, such as some antibiotics which may harm a person more than they benefit him, then if he finds no benefit, it is obligatory for him to stop, even if the doctor tells him to continue, and he has found no benefit. These are among the antibiotic medicines called antibiotics, and they are dangerous to a person.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verses 39–41 (part 1 of 2):

Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: ﴿Say, "O my people, act according to your position; indeed I am acting."﴾ [39:39] The address here is to the Prophet (ﷺ). His saying "Say, O my people" refers to those who denied him and opposed him. "O my people" is a vocative (munada). Its original form is "yā qawmī" (O my people), but the yā' was dropped for lightness and the kasra was left as an indication of it. Accordingly, in its i'rab (grammatical analysis) we say: qawm is a vocative in the accusative, marked by a presumed fatha on the letter before the elided yā' of the speaker, which was dropped for lightness. ﴿O my people, act according to your position; indeed I am acting.﴾ "Act according to your position" means: act according to what you are upon of disbelief, enmity and harm, for that does not concern me and will not prevent me from continuing in my work. For this reason he emphasized his statement, "indeed I am acting," meaning: I am acting according to what I am upon. So you act, and we will act. This is like His saying: ﴿And wait; indeed we are waiting﴾ [11:122].

﴿Indeed I am acting; so you will know﴾ [39:39–40]. "You will know" (sawfa ta'lamūn) is a clause affirmed by the entry of sawfa upon it. Sawfa affirms the clause just as the sīn does, but the difference is that the sīn indicates this for the near future, while sawfa indicates it after a delay. For this reason it is said: the sīn is for tanfīs, and sawfa is for taswīf, meaning postponement and delay; and tanfīs means nearness. ﴿So you will know who﴾ [39:39–40]: "man" (who) here is the object of "you will know." The knowledge here means recognition (ma'rifa), and therefore it takes only one object, as Ibn Mālik said:

*Knowledge in the sense of recognition, and assumption in the sense of suspicion, are transitive to one object, as is required.*

He says: "tā'lamūn" means "you will recognize." ﴿who there will come to him a punishment that will disgrace him﴾: that is, you will know the one to whom a punishment will come that disgraces him. "Punishment" here means retribution, and "disgrace" means humiliation and shame. ﴿And there will descend upon him a lasting punishment﴾ [40]: that is, there will descend upon him a lasting punishment that will never leave him. You will know this, whether it is us or you. But they will know it at a time when they cannot be saved, and they will only be calling out with "woe" and "destruction." We seek refuge with Allah.

So, do we parse "man" as the first or the second object of "you will know"? There is no first or second object here, because "ya'lamūn" in this context means "ya'rifūn" (they recognize). ﴿So you will know who there will come to him a punishment that will disgrace him, and there will descend upon him a lasting punishment﴾ [39:39–40].

Then He, the Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed We have sent down to you the Book for mankind in truth﴾ [39:41]. Reflect on "innā anzalnā 'alayka" (We have sent down upon you), and in another verse "anzalnā ilayka" (We have sent down to you) [2]. Are the two particles the same in meaning, or do they differ?

The answer: the basic principle is that what differs in wording differs in meaning, since wording stands to meanings as a garment stands to bodies. So when we find two expressions with the same transitive construction but different wording, the basic presumption is that their meanings differ. Thus ﴿We have sent down to you﴾ (anzalnā ilayka) indicates that the ultimate destination of the revelation is the Messenger (ﷺ) and does not go beyond him to anyone else. And ﴿upon you﴾ ('alayka) indicates that the revelation rose above the Prophet (ﷺ) until it penetrated him, as though it descended into the very heart of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him). Have you not read the saying of Allah: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down, upon your heart﴾ [26:193–194], where He did not say "to your heart"? This is the difference.

As for His saying ﴿the Book﴾ (al-kitāb), the Book here is the Noble Qur'an. It is called a "kitāb" (book) because it is written in the Preserved Tablet, in the scriptures in the hands of the angels, and in the scriptures that are among us. On this basis, fi'āl (the form fi'āl) carries the meaning of maf'ūl (passive), and this pattern, fi'āl in the sense of maf'ūl, occurs frequently in the Arabic language. Among its examples:

* Student: *firāsh* in the sense of *mafrūsh* (spread out).
* Shaykh: *firāsh* in the sense of *mafrūsh*. *Kisā'*?
* Student: In the sense of *maksī* (clothed).
* Shaykh: And *binā'* in the sense of *mabnī* (built), and *ghirās* in the sense of *maghrūs* (planted). There are many examples.

Now, He says: ﴿the Book for mankind in truth﴾. The lām in "lil-nās" (for mankind) may indicate exclusivity (ikhtiṣāṣ) or transitivity (ta'diya); both are permissible. The meaning is that Allah sent down the Book upon Muhammad (ﷺ) so that people might be guided by it and benefit from it, and that is indeed the case. People have benefited from this Qur'an in a way that no other benefit can match. The Qurayshi nation was worth nothing in the eyes of other nations; they were humble and poor, with journeys to Sham in summer and to Yemen in winter, because they had no movement, no trade and no wealth. With the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ) and this Qur'an, they became the masters of the nations. ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?﴾ [93:6]. "Āwā" means "He sheltered you" and "He sheltered [people] through you." So you became a father to people after you had been an orphan without a father. This is why we say that the direct object is omitted in "āwā" for the sake of generality, meaning He sheltered you and sheltered [others] through you. ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾ [93:7]: He guided whom? He guided you and guided [others] through you. ﴿And He found you poor and made you rich﴾ [93:8]: He enriched you and enriched [others] through you. For this reason the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said to the Ansār: "You were in need, and Allah enriched you through me" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (4330) and Muslim (1061/139), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Zayd ibn 'Āṣim]. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) brought blessing to his community, and this is why He said: ﴿upon you the Book for mankind﴾.

As for His saying ﴿in truth﴾ (bil-ḥaqq), it has two meanings. First: that what this Qur'an brings is true, and truth is sincerity in reports and justice in rulings. Allah said: ﴿The word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [6:115]. The meaning is that this Qur'an was sent down in truth and came with truth, and what is truth? Truthfulness of reports and justice of rulings. The second meaning: "bil-ḥaqq" means that it is accompanied by truth, that is, its descent is true and contains no falsehood, as in His saying: ﴿The devils did not bring it down. It is not befitting for them, nor are they able to. Indeed, they are removed from hearing it﴾ [26:210–212]. So "bil-ḥaqq" has two meanings: the first…

* Student: Truthfulness of reports and justice of rulings.
* Shaykh: That is, what he brought is the truth. And the second…
* Student: Accompanied by truth.
* Shaykh: That is…
* Student: That it was sent down with it (...).
* Shaykh: No, this returns to the first meaning.
* Student: Its descent is true.
* Shaykh: That is, its descent is true, not false, for falsehood does not reach it: ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or behind it﴾ [41:42]. I have recited to you His saying: ﴿The devils did not bring it down. It is not befitting for them, nor are they able to. Indeed, they are removed from hearing it﴾. Unlike the reports of soothsayers, whose reports all come from the devils.

﴿Indeed We have sent down to you the Book for mankind in truth. So whoever is guided, it is for his own self﴾ [39:41]. The "fa" here follows from what came before. That is, after the descent of this Qur'an, people divided into two groups: a group that was guided by it and benefited, and a group that turned away from it and perished.

His saying ﴿So whoever is guided﴾: "man" here is conditional (sharṭiyya). Its conditional clause is "ihtadā" (is guided), and its response is a nominal clause, "fa-li-nafsihi" (it is for his own self). Because the response is nominal, it is preceded by "fa." His saying "ihtadā" (is guided) means guidance of knowledge and guidance of action. Guidance of knowledge is that he is eager for this Qur'an, memorizes it, reflects on it and contemplates it. Guidance of action is that he applies this Qur'an and acts upon it in belief, speech and deed. ﴿Whoever is guided, it is for his own self﴾ means: his guidance benefits his own self, or: he is for his own self. The point is that the omitted element here must be the subject (mubtada'), necessarily. Why do we say "necessarily"? Because what is mentioned is a prepositional phrase (jār wa-majrūr), and a prepositional phrase can never be a subject. So the omitted element is the subject. If you wish, estimate: "for his own self is his guidance," or if you wish, estimate: "he is for his own self."

Now we ask: why was the response clause preceded by "fa"?

* Student: (...) nominal.
* Shaykh: Because it is nominal, and when the response clause is nominal, it must be preceded by "fa." Sometimes the "fa" may be omitted, but rarely. Among that is the poet's saying:

*Whoever does good deeds, Allah will reward them* (...........................)

He did not say "then Allah will reward them," but this is rare.

Now let us address what must be preceded by "fa" among clauses when it is a response, which is mentioned in a verse.

* Student: The five nouns (al-asmā' al-khamsa).
* Shaykh: Good.
* Student: A rigid noun, and "sawfa," and "sīn," and a nominal clause; and if it is an imperative (...) a verbal clause whose verb is imperative (...).
* Shaykh: Good. That makes five, but complete the verse so you can finish.
* Student: The poet said:

*Nominal, imperative, with a rigid noun, with mā, qad, lan and the tanfīs*

* Shaykh:

*Nominal, imperative, and with a rigid noun, and with mā, qad, lan and with tanfīs.*

﴿So whoever is guided, it is for his own self; and whoever goes astray, he only goes astray to his own detriment﴾ [39:41]. "Whoever goes astray" means he is not guided, neither in knowledge nor in action. ﴿He only goes astray to his own detriment﴾: that is, to his own self, and he does not harm Allah at all, nor does he harm anyone else. ﴿And you are not a guardian over them﴾ [39:41]. The "mā" here is Ḥijāzī, meaning that only the people of the Ḥijāz pronounce it this way. (If I am wrong, say: "wrong.") This "mā" is Ḥijāzī, meaning only the people of the Ḥijāz pronounce it this way?

* Student: Wrong.
* Shaykh: Wrong, because the people of the Ḥijāz and others both pronounce it, but it functions like "laysa" (is not) only according to the people of the Ḥijāz, and that is why it is called Ḥijāzī. According to the people of the Ḥijāz, it functions like "laysa": it raises the subject and puts the predicate in the accusative. Among that is Allah's saying: ﴿This is not a human being﴾ [12:31]. According to the Banū Tamīm, it does not function like "laysa"; it is inactive (muhmala), so they say in His saying ﴿This is not a human being﴾, outside the Qur'an: "mā hādhā basharun." Now I will speak, so say: are you Ḥijāzī or Tamīmī? "Mā Zaydun qā'imun."

* Students: Tamīmī.
* Shaykh: Tamīmī. "Mā Zaydun qā'iman."
* Students: Ḥijāzī.
* Shaykh: Ḥijāzī. So it is the language of Quraysh, who are the people of the Ḥijāz. They say "mā hādhā basharan," and the Banū Tamīm say "mā hādhā basharun." They used to recite the Qur'an as "mā hādhā basharun" before it was unified in the dialect of Quraysh, because the Qur'an was revealed in seven ahruf (modes). There is a witty verse in which the poet said:

*A slender-waisted one, I said to her: "Tell me your lineage," and she replied: "The killing of the lover is not forbidden."*

(A slender-waisted one, I said to her: "Tell me your lineage," meaning: where are you from? She answered without naming her tribe, saying: "The killing of the lover is not forbidden." What do you think this woman is? A Tamīmiyya, because she said "the killing of the lover is not forbidden" with the Tamīmī construction, so he knew she was Tamīmī.) Nowadays, can we tell the Tamīmī from the Qurayshī? All Tamīmīs and all Qurayshīs have now mixed together. You find one saying "mā hādhā basharun" and another saying "mā hādhā basharun," and they all differ. They have intermingled.

Now, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And you are not a guardian over them﴾ [39:41]. Do we now parse "mā" according to the dialect of the Banū Tamīm or the dialect of Quraysh? According to the dialect of Quraysh, even though the wording in this structure does not differ. The wording does not differ, because the Banū Tamīm say "mā anta 'alayhim bi-wakīl" and so do the Quraysh, but since we know that the Qur'an is in the dialect of Quraysh, we say: "mā" here is Ḥijāzī, "anna" is its subject, the "tā'" is for address, the "bā'" is a superfluous prepositional particle (ḥarf jarr zā'id), and "wakīl" is its predicate in the accusative, marked by a presumed fatḥa on its last letter, prevented from appearing by the occupation of the position by the kasra of the superfluous preposition.

If someone says: "You said the bā' is a superfluous preposition, and we know that the Noble Qur'an contains no nonsense (laghw), and superfluity is nonsense."

The answer to this is: superfluity is nonsense only if it does not convey a meaning. If it conveys a meaning, it is not nonsense. The meaning it conveys here is the emphasis of negation. On this basis, it is not nonsense, but rather superfluous in form and not superfluous in meaning; it adds to the meaning.

But someone may say: "How is it superfluous?" We say: it is superfluous. The first (zāda) is from intransitive "zād," and the second superfluous one is from transitive "zād," because "zād" (to increase) is like "naqasa" (to decrease): it is used intransitively and it is used transitively with an object. Allah said: ﴿So it increased them in faith﴾ [3:173], transitive; ﴿then they did not diminish anything from you﴾ [9:4], transitive. And you say: "zāda īmānu al-rajul" (the man's faith increased), intransitive; and you say: "naqaṣa al-mā'" (the water decreased), intransitive. ﴿And you are not a guardian over them﴾ [39:41]: that is, you are not a watcher over them, observing them and protecting them. That is for Allah. You are only responsible for conveying the message, and the reckoning rests with the Lord of the worlds, Mighty and Majestic.

Now let us return to the words of the exegete, may Allah have mercy on him. He says: ﴿Say, "O my people, act according to your position"﴾ [39:39]: "according to your state." So "makāna" means "ḥāla" (state). As we mentioned in the tafsir, "al-makāna" means what you were upon, and it is in the sense of "ḥāla" in the words of the exegete. ﴿Indeed I am acting﴾: "according to my state." From where did he understand that the implied meaning is "according to my state"? Because it corresponds to His saying: ﴿act according to your position﴾, meaning: indeed I am acting according to my position. Fine. ﴿Indeed I am acting; so you will know who there will come to him a punishment that will disgrace him﴾ [39:39–40].

* Student: (...)
* Shaykh: How?
* Student: Indeed I am acting according to my position.
* Shaykh: No, it is "according to my state."
* Student: The implied meaning is...
* Shaykh: The implied meaning is "according to my position." ﴿So you will know who﴾: he says "man" is a relative pronoun, the object of knowledge. How?
* Student: Object of (...).
* Shaykh: No, the object of knowledge with the "tā'" you have it that way.
* Student: (...) knowledge (...).
* Shaykh: Good. And what did I say?
* Student: For knowledge.
* Shaykh: I said: the object of knowledge, and you have it.
* Student: The object of knowledge.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. No, I assumed it was the relative pronoun for knowledge, the object of knowledge. Where is the knowledge? If the author had said "the object of 'you will know'" it would have been clearer, because what is in the verse is not the verbal noun but the verb, and he should have said "the object of 'you will know'." But the book is in fact written for students of knowledge, and for this reason we do not advise beginners to read this book, because although it is small, it is beyond the understanding of beginners. Good...

* Student: What should one read, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: One moment. The answer is memorized, God willing. "Man" is a relative pronoun and the object of "'alima" (knew). ﴿There comes to him a punishment that will disgrace him﴾: when "man" is a relative pronoun, the clause "yātīhi" (comes to him) has no place in the i'rab; it is the relative clause. ﴿A punishment that will disgrace him﴾: what did we say about "'adhāb"? Retribution. The clause "yukhzīhi" (disgraces him) is an attribute of "'adhāb," and not a response to "man," because "man" is a relative pronoun and does not require a response.

﴿Who there comes to him a punishment that will disgrace him, and there will descend upon him a lasting punishment﴾ [39:40] (there will descend upon him a lasting punishment, permanent, and it is the punishment of the Fire, and Allah disgraced them at Badr).

"Man" is a relative pronoun, the object of "'alima." When "man" is a relative pronoun, the clause "yātīhi" [39:40] has no place in the i'rab; it is the relative clause.

﴿A punishment that will disgrace him﴾: what did we say about "'adhāb"? Retribution. The clause "yukhzīhi" is an attribute of "'adhāb," and not a response to "man," because "man" is a relative pronoun and does not require a response.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verses 39–41 (part 2 of 2):

(﴿Upon him will come a punishment that will disgrace him, and upon him will descend a lasting punishment﴾ [al-Zumar 40]: constant, which is the punishment of the Fire. Allah disgraced them at Badr.) This means that the greatest humiliation that befell the Quraysh was what happened at Badr. Allah, glorified and exalted, gathered their leaders, their elders and their nobles, and they went out on that day. These nobles and elders were killed; they were killed, dragged away, and thrown into a well among the wells of Badr, a foul and stinking well. So their recompense, may Allah protect us, was this recompense, and this is among the greatest disgrace. The Prophet (ﷺ) stood over them, rebuking them and making them regret, and he said: "O so-and-so, son of so-and-so," naming them and their fathers, "O so-and-so, son of so-and-so, did you find what your Lord promised to be true? For I have found what my Lord promised me to be true." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, you are speaking to corpses that have rotted; how can you speak to bodies?" He said: "You are no more able to hear what I say than they are, but they are unable to answer." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3976) and Muslim (2875/78), from the hadith of Abu Talha.] The Messenger (ﷺ) spoke the truth. They hear the speech of the Messenger, and this speech only increases them in anguish and remorse.

For this reason, one of them said to 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who was Abu Jahl, when he came to him while there was still a breath of life in him. He said to him: "Who are you?" He said: "Ibn Mas'ud." He said: "You have climbed a difficult height, O little shepherd of the goats! How dare you tread on the head of a noble of the nobles of Quraysh?" Then he said: "To whom does the victory belong today?" He said: "To Allah and His Messenger." [Related by al-Bayhaqi in Dala'il al-Nubuwwah (1020), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.] The point is that the Messenger rebuked them for what had happened.

Then He said: (﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book for mankind in truth﴾ [al-Zumar 41]): the phrase "bil-haqq" (in truth) is connected to "anzalna" (We sent down).

Why did He not say "bi-anzalna"? Because the governing element (ʿamil) is the verb, and "nā" (We) is a pronoun that is detached from the verb. This is a lesson from the author to you: when you want to say that something is connected (muta'allaq), mention only the governing word, and do not mention the subject with it, nor the object if the object is attached to it. So this is connected to "anzal" (sent down).

In fact, in our i'rab (grammatical analysis) of the Qur'an we are lax; we say in such a case: connected to "anzalna." This is not precise. The correct form is to say: connected to "anzal," which is the governing word alone, without what is attached to it of subject or object.

(﴿So whoever is guided, it is for his own self﴾ [al-Zumar 41]: his guidance benefits him. ﴿And whoever goes astray, only to its detriment does he stray. And you are not over them a guardian﴾ [al-Zumar 41]: that you would compel them to guidance.) This is like His saying: ﴿And you are not over them a compeller﴾ [Qaf 45]. The Messenger (ﷺ) is not one who compels them to guidance, nor is he a guardian over them, watching them and watching over them.

Now let us return to the benefits. (﴿Say, O my people, act according to your position﴾ and so on [al-Zumar 39].)

* Among the benefits of this verse: the one who holds the truth should be strong and confront his opponent, not stand in a position of weakness. From where is this derived? From ﴿Act﴾ and ﴿Indeed, I am acting﴾ [al-Zumar 39], meaning: do not worry about me.
* Among its benefits: consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ), for Allah commanded him to say this as good news and consolation, that the final outcome will be his.
* Among its benefits: there is no harm in leaving the disbelievers in their disbelief as a threat. This is a method commonly used even in a father's discipline of his son. What does he say to him if he disobeys? He says: "Continue in your disobedience, continue in your play, do not come to receive the guests," for example. What does he mean? He means it as a threat.

I think we cannot cover all of them today, so we will leave them for tomorrow, God willing.

(...)

* * *

* Student: (﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died during their sleep. Then He keeps those for which He has decreed death and releases the others until a specified term. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾ [42]. ﴿Or have they taken intercessors besides Allah? Say: "Even though they possess nothing and do not reason?"﴾ [43]. ﴿Say: "To Allah belongs intercession entirely. His is the dominion of the heavens and the earth. Then to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-Zumar 42–44].)
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say, O my people, act according to your position; indeed, I am acting, so you will soon know﴾ [al-An'am 135], and so on to the end.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, glorified and exalted, wants His Prophet to be elevated above his people, speaking to them or with them from a position of height. This is shown by His saying: ﴿O my people, act according to your position, indeed I am acting﴾. This resembles a challenge to them: I do not care whether you do what you know; I will do what is contrary to it.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: I think we have already mentioned this benefit, that the one who holds the truth should be strong against his opponent and rise above him.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a threat to those deniers of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and that they will soon know who is more deserving of punishment and upon whom the punishment will come.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the punishment of disbelief is a humiliating punishment, a shame in the Hereafter and a degradation in this world; indeed, a degradation in both this world and the Hereafter, may Allah protect us. This is based on His saying: ﴿Upon whom will come a punishment that will disgrace him﴾ [al-Zumar 40].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the punishment of the people of the Fire is lasting and does not cease for them. From this verse follows what the Qur'an and the Sunnah indicate: that the people of the Fire will abide in it forever, and that it will not perish. The view that it will perish is a weak view, indeed a false one, because it contradicts the Book and the Sunnah.

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book for mankind in truth﴾ and so on to the end [al-Zumar 41].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a clarification that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, because Allah sent it down. It is speech, not a specific substance, like the iron about which Allah said: ﴿And We sent down iron, in which is great might﴾ [al-Hadid 25], or like livestock: ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [al-Zumar 6]. The Qur'an is speech, and if it is speech, then it is not created, because speech is an attribute of the speaker, and the One who speaks it, who is Allah, is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's elevation. From where?
* Student: ﴿We sent down﴾.
* Shaykh: And sending down cannot occur except from what?
* Student: Only from above.
* Shaykh: Only from above. This is what the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus, reason and innate nature (fitrah) indicate.

The elevation of Allah, mighty and majestic, is indicated by the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus, reason and innate nature. The Book's indications of Allah's elevation are of many varieties, and the Sunnah likewise agrees, in its sayings, its actions and its tacit approvals, that Allah, glorified and exalted, is high above His Throne, above His creation.

As for consensus (ijma'): the Salaf (early pious generations) agreed on this, and none of them ever held a contrary view. The principle in this matter is that when the Book and the Sunnah indicate something, and it is not known that any of the Salaf, the Companions or the Successors (tabi'un) held a contrary view, then they did not say anything other than it. This is an important point. A questioner might say: where is the evidence that the Companions held that Allah established Himself upon the Throne, meaning that He rose above it? Did anyone interpret it that way? What do we say?

We say: since the Qur'an says it and nothing contrary to it is reported from them, then they held it, because they took by the indication of the Qur'an, which they were commanded to follow. So from this we derive the consensus of the Companions on the elevation of Allah. Likewise the Successors who followed them in excellence, and the imams after them. Not a single letter has come from any of them saying otherwise.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the virtue of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), where He said what?
The rational proofs for Allah's elevation are that it is said: elevation is either an attribute of deficiency or of perfection, and no one doubts that it is an attribute of perfection, so it must be affirmed for Allah, for the Lord is necessarily described by the attributes of perfection by reason.

As for innate nature: people are created with the disposition that when they ask Allah for something, their hearts rise toward the sky. No one denies this.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in that this magnificent Qur'an was sent down to him. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am 124].
* Among its benefits: the Qur'an was sent down for the benefit of creation, because of His saying: ﴿for mankind﴾. The Qur'an was not sent down against the interests of creation; it was sent down for their interests. This is why He said: "We sent it down to you for mankind."
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the generality of the Prophet's (ﷺ) mission, because of His saying: ﴿for mankind﴾. He did not say "for your people," for example. It is for mankind in general.
* Among its benefits: the Qur'an was sent down in truth in both senses of the interpretation mentioned earlier. It is true, and it comes with truth. It is true in what it brings, since its rulings are just and its reports are truthful, and it is itself true, not false.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Qur'an is a proof, because of His saying: ﴿So whoever is guided, it is for his own self, and whoever goes astray, only to its detriment does he stray﴾ [al-Zumar 41].
* Among its benefits: people divide, in their response to this Qur'an, into those who are guided and those who go astray, because of His saying: ﴿So whoever is guided, it is for his own self, and whoever goes astray, only to its detriment does he stray﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a refutation of the Jabriyyah (determinists) who say that a person is compelled in his actions. The basis of this is that He attributed guidance and misguidance to the servant, which shows that it is his own act, which he chose.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the evil consequence of sins, and that they fall back upon the servant, not in his favor.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the blessing of guidance, and that it is an acquisition of the servant, because of His saying: ﴿for his own self﴾.
* Among its benefits: consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) when those among mankind go astray, because of His saying: ﴿And you are not over them a guardian﴾. Allah alone is the Guardian over them. As for you, you are a conveyer of the message. If you have fulfilled the duty of conveying it, then the reckoning is with Allah.
* Among its benefits: a refutation of those who attached themselves to the Prophet (ﷺ) out of fear, hope, desire and dread, to the point that they called upon him besides Allah, because of His saying: ﴿And you are not over them a guardian﴾.
* Among its benefits: that the caller who conveys the law of Allah, when he has conveyed it in the manner he was commanded, has cleared his responsibility, and nothing further is required of him. The indication is that if Muhammad (ﷺ), the leader of all callers and conveyers, was not a guardian over people and not a watcher over them, then those below him are even more so.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verses 39–41 (part 1 of 2):

Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: ﴿Say, "O my people, act according to your position; indeed I am acting."﴾ [39:39] The address here is to the Prophet (ﷺ). His saying "Say, O my people" refers to those who denied him and opposed him. "O my people" is a vocative (munada). Its original form is "yā qawmī" (O my people), but the yā' was dropped for lightness and the kasra was left as an indication of it. Accordingly, in its i'rab (grammatical analysis) we say: qawm is a vocative in the accusative, marked by a presumed fatha on the letter before the elided yā' of the speaker, which was dropped for lightness. ﴿O my people, act according to your position; indeed I am acting.﴾ "Act according to your position" means: act according to what you are upon of disbelief, enmity and harm, for that does not concern me and will not prevent me from continuing in my work. For this reason he emphasized his statement, "indeed I am acting," meaning: I am acting according to what I am upon. So you act, and we will act. This is like His saying: ﴿And wait; indeed we are waiting﴾ [11:122].

﴿Indeed I am acting; so you will know﴾ [39:39–40]. "You will know" (sawfa ta'lamūn) is a clause affirmed by the entry of sawfa upon it. Sawfa affirms the clause just as the sīn does, but the difference is that the sīn indicates this for the near future, while sawfa indicates it after a delay. For this reason it is said: the sīn is for tanfīs, and sawfa is for taswīf, meaning postponement and delay; and tanfīs means nearness. ﴿So you will know who﴾ [39:39–40]: "man" (who) here is the object of "you will know." The knowledge here means recognition (ma'rifa), and therefore it takes only one object, as Ibn Mālik said:

*Knowledge in the sense of recognition, and assumption in the sense of suspicion, are transitive to one object, as is required.*

He says: "tā'lamūn" means "you will recognize." ﴿who there will come to him a punishment that will disgrace him﴾: that is, you will know the one to whom a punishment will come that disgraces him. "Punishment" here means retribution, and "disgrace" means humiliation and shame. ﴿And there will descend upon him a lasting punishment﴾ [40]: that is, there will descend upon him a lasting punishment that will never leave him. You will know this, whether it is us or you. But they will know it at a time when they cannot be saved, and they will only be calling out with "woe" and "destruction." We seek refuge with Allah.

So, do we parse "man" as the first or the second object of "you will know"? There is no first or second object here, because "ya'lamūn" in this context means "ya'rifūn" (they recognize). ﴿So you will know who there will come to him a punishment that will disgrace him, and there will descend upon him a lasting punishment﴾ [39:39–40].

Then He, the Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed We have sent down to you the Book for mankind in truth﴾ [39:41]. Reflect on "innā anzalnā 'alayka" (We have sent down upon you), and in another verse "anzalnā ilayka" (We have sent down to you) [2]. Are the two particles the same in meaning, or do they differ?

The answer: the basic principle is that what differs in wording differs in meaning, since wording stands to meanings as a garment stands to bodies. So when we find two expressions with the same transitive construction but different wording, the basic presumption is that their meanings differ. Thus ﴿We have sent down to you﴾ (anzalnā ilayka) indicates that the ultimate destination of the revelation is the Messenger (ﷺ) and does not go beyond him to anyone else. And ﴿upon you﴾ ('alayka) indicates that the revelation rose above the Prophet (ﷺ) until it penetrated him, as though it descended into the very heart of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him). Have you not read the saying of Allah: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down, upon your heart﴾ [26:193–194], where He did not say "to your heart"? This is the difference.

As for His saying ﴿the Book﴾ (al-kitāb), the Book here is the Noble Qur'an. It is called a "kitāb" (book) because it is written in the Preserved Tablet, in the scriptures in the hands of the angels, and in the scriptures that are among us. On this basis, fi'āl (the form fi'āl) carries the meaning of maf'ūl (passive), and this pattern, fi'āl in the sense of maf'ūl, occurs frequently in the Arabic language. Among its examples:

* Student: *firāsh* in the sense of *mafrūsh* (spread out).
* Shaykh: *firāsh* in the sense of *mafrūsh*. *Kisā'*?
* Student: In the sense of *maksī* (clothed).
* Shaykh: And *binā'* in the sense of *mabnī* (built), and *ghirās* in the sense of *maghrūs* (planted). There are many examples.

Now, He says: ﴿the Book for mankind in truth﴾. The lām in "lil-nās" (for mankind) may indicate exclusivity (ikhtiṣāṣ) or transitivity (ta'diya); both are permissible. The meaning is that Allah sent down the Book upon Muhammad (ﷺ) so that people might be guided by it and benefit from it, and that is indeed the case. People have benefited from this Qur'an in a way that no other benefit can match. The Qurayshi nation was worth nothing in the eyes of other nations; they were humble and poor, with journeys to Sham in summer and to Yemen in winter, because they had no movement, no trade and no wealth. With the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ) and this Qur'an, they became the masters of the nations. ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?﴾ [93:6]. "Āwā" means "He sheltered you" and "He sheltered [people] through you." So you became a father to people after you had been an orphan without a father. This is why we say that the direct object is omitted in "āwā" for the sake of generality, meaning He sheltered you and sheltered [others] through you. ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾ [93:7]: He guided whom? He guided you and guided [others] through you. ﴿And He found you poor and made you rich﴾ [93:8]: He enriched you and enriched [others] through you. For this reason the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said to the Ansār: "You were in need, and Allah enriched you through me" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (4330) and Muslim (1061/139), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Zayd ibn 'Āṣim]. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) brought blessing to his community, and this is why He said: ﴿upon you the Book for mankind﴾.

As for His saying ﴿in truth﴾ (bil-ḥaqq), it has two meanings. First: that what this Qur'an brings is true, and truth is sincerity in reports and justice in rulings. Allah said: ﴿The word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [6:115]. The meaning is that this Qur'an was sent down in truth and came with truth, and what is truth? Truthfulness of reports and justice of rulings. The second meaning: "bil-ḥaqq" means that it is accompanied by truth, that is, its descent is true and contains no falsehood, as in His saying: ﴿The devils did not bring it down. It is not befitting for them, nor are they able to. Indeed, they are removed from hearing it﴾ [26:210–212]. So "bil-ḥaqq" has two meanings: the first…

* Student: Truthfulness of reports and justice of rulings.
* Shaykh: That is, what he brought is the truth. And the second…
* Student: Accompanied by truth.
* Shaykh: That is…
* Student: That it was sent down with it (...).
* Shaykh: No, this returns to the first meaning.
* Student: Its descent is true.
* Shaykh: That is, its descent is true, not false, for falsehood does not reach it: ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or behind it﴾ [41:42]. I have recited to you His saying: ﴿The devils did not bring it down. It is not befitting for them, nor are they able to. Indeed, they are removed from hearing it﴾. Unlike the reports of soothsayers, whose reports all come from the devils.

﴿Indeed We have sent down to you the Book for mankind in truth. So whoever is guided, it is for his own self﴾ [39:41]. The "fa" here follows from what came before. That is, after the descent of this Qur'an, people divided into two groups: a group that was guided by it and benefited, and a group that turned away from it and perished.

His saying ﴿So whoever is guided﴾: "man" here is conditional (sharṭiyya). Its conditional clause is "ihtadā" (is guided), and its response is a nominal clause, "fa-li-nafsihi" (it is for his own self). Because the response is nominal, it is preceded by "fa." His saying "ihtadā" (is guided) means guidance of knowledge and guidance of action. Guidance of knowledge is that he is eager for this Qur'an, memorizes it, reflects on it and contemplates it. Guidance of action is that he applies this Qur'an and acts upon it in belief, speech and deed. ﴿Whoever is guided, it is for his own self﴾ means: his guidance benefits his own self, or: he is for his own self. The point is that the omitted element here must be the subject (mubtada'), necessarily. Why do we say "necessarily"? Because what is mentioned is a prepositional phrase (jār wa-majrūr), and a prepositional phrase can never be a subject. So the omitted element is the subject. If you wish, estimate: "for his own self is his guidance," or if you wish, estimate: "he is for his own self."

Now we ask: why was the response clause preceded by "fa"?

* Student: (...) nominal.
* Shaykh: Because it is nominal, and when the response clause is nominal, it must be preceded by "fa." Sometimes the "fa" may be omitted, but rarely. Among that is the poet's saying:

*Whoever does good deeds, Allah will reward them* (...........................)

He did not say "then Allah will reward them," but this is rare.

Now let us address what must be preceded by "fa" among clauses when it is a response, which is mentioned in a verse.

* Student: The five nouns (al-asmā' al-khamsa).
* Shaykh: Good.
* Student: A rigid noun, and "sawfa," and "sīn," and a nominal clause; and if it is an imperative (...) a verbal clause whose verb is imperative (...).
* Shaykh: Good. That makes five, but complete the verse so you can finish.
* Student: The poet said:

*Nominal, imperative, with a rigid noun, with mā, qad, lan and the tanfīs*

* Shaykh:

*Nominal, imperative, and with a rigid noun, and with mā, qad, lan and with tanfīs.*

﴿So whoever is guided, it is for his own self; and whoever goes astray, he only goes astray to his own detriment﴾ [39:41]. "Whoever goes astray" means he is not guided, neither in knowledge nor in action. ﴿He only goes astray to his own detriment﴾: that is, to his own self, and he does not harm Allah at all, nor does he harm anyone else. ﴿And you are not a guardian over them﴾ [39:41]. The "mā" here is Ḥijāzī, meaning that only the people of the Ḥijāz pronounce it this way. (If I am wrong, say: "wrong.") This "mā" is Ḥijāzī, meaning only the people of the Ḥijāz pronounce it this way?

* Student: Wrong.
* Shaykh: Wrong, because the people of the Ḥijāz and others both pronounce it, but it functions like "laysa" (is not) only according to the people of the Ḥijāz, and that is why it is called Ḥijāzī. According to the people of the Ḥijāz, it functions like "laysa": it raises the subject and puts the predicate in the accusative. Among that is Allah's saying: ﴿This is not a human being﴾ [12:31]. According to the Banū Tamīm, it does not function like "laysa"; it is inactive (muhmala), so they say in His saying ﴿This is not a human being﴾, outside the Qur'an: "mā hādhā basharun." Now I will speak, so say: are you Ḥijāzī or Tamīmī? "Mā Zaydun qā'imun."

* Students: Tamīmī.
* Shaykh: Tamīmī. "Mā Zaydun qā'iman."
* Students: Ḥijāzī.
* Shaykh: Ḥijāzī. So it is the language of Quraysh, who are the people of the Ḥijāz. They say "mā hādhā basharan," and the Banū Tamīm say "mā hādhā basharun." They used to recite the Qur'an as "mā hādhā basharun" before it was unified in the dialect of Quraysh, because the Qur'an was revealed in seven ahruf (modes). There is a witty verse in which the poet said:

*A slender-waisted one, I said to her: "Tell me your lineage," and she replied: "The killing of the lover is not forbidden."*

(A slender-waisted one, I said to her: "Tell me your lineage," meaning: where are you from? She answered without naming her tribe, saying: "The killing of the lover is not forbidden." What do you think this woman is? A Tamīmiyya, because she said "the killing of the lover is not forbidden" with the Tamīmī construction, so he knew she was Tamīmī.) Nowadays, can we tell the Tamīmī from the Qurayshī? All Tamīmīs and all Qurayshīs have now mixed together. You find one saying "mā hādhā basharun" and another saying "mā hādhā basharun," and they all differ. They have intermingled.

Now, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And you are not a guardian over them﴾ [39:41]. Do we now parse "mā" according to the dialect of the Banū Tamīm or the dialect of Quraysh? According to the dialect of Quraysh, even though the wording in this structure does not differ. The wording does not differ, because the Banū Tamīm say "mā anta 'alayhim bi-wakīl" and so do the Quraysh, but since we know that the Qur'an is in the dialect of Quraysh, we say: "mā" here is Ḥijāzī, "anna" is its subject, the "tā'" is for address, the "bā'" is a superfluous prepositional particle (ḥarf jarr zā'id), and "wakīl" is its predicate in the accusative, marked by a presumed fatḥa on its last letter, prevented from appearing by the occupation of the position by the kasra of the superfluous preposition.

If someone says: "You said the bā' is a superfluous preposition, and we know that the Noble Qur'an contains no nonsense (laghw), and superfluity is nonsense."

The answer to this is: superfluity is nonsense only if it does not convey a meaning. If it conveys a meaning, it is not nonsense. The meaning it conveys here is the emphasis of negation. On this basis, it is not nonsense, but rather superfluous in form and not superfluous in meaning; it adds to the meaning.

But someone may say: "How is it superfluous?" We say: it is superfluous. The first (zāda) is from intransitive "zād," and the second superfluous one is from transitive "zād," because "zād" (to increase) is like "naqasa" (to decrease): it is used intransitively and it is used transitively with an object. Allah said: ﴿So it increased them in faith﴾ [3:173], transitive; ﴿then they did not diminish anything from you﴾ [9:4], transitive. And you say: "zāda īmānu al-rajul" (the man's faith increased), intransitive; and you say: "naqaṣa al-mā'" (the water decreased), intransitive. ﴿And you are not a guardian over them﴾ [39:41]: that is, you are not a watcher over them, observing them and protecting them. That is for Allah. You are only responsible for conveying the message, and the reckoning rests with the Lord of the worlds, Mighty and Majestic.

Now let us return to the words of the exegete, may Allah have mercy on him. He says: ﴿Say, "O my people, act according to your position"﴾ [39:39]: "according to your state." So "makāna" means "ḥāla" (state). As we mentioned in the tafsir, "al-makāna" means what you were upon, and it is in the sense of "ḥāla" in the words of the exegete. ﴿Indeed I am acting﴾: "according to my state." From where did he understand that the implied meaning is "according to my state"? Because it corresponds to His saying: ﴿act according to your position﴾, meaning: indeed I am acting according to my position. Fine. ﴿Indeed I am acting; so you will know who there will come to him a punishment that will disgrace him﴾ [39:39–40].

* Student: (...)
* Shaykh: How?
* Student: Indeed I am acting according to my position.
* Shaykh: No, it is "according to my state."
* Student: The implied meaning is...
* Shaykh: The implied meaning is "according to my position." ﴿So you will know who﴾: he says "man" is a relative pronoun, the object of knowledge. How?
* Student: Object of (...).
* Shaykh: No, the object of knowledge with the "tā'" you have it that way.
* Student: (...) knowledge (...).
* Shaykh: Good. And what did I say?
* Student: For knowledge.
* Shaykh: I said: the object of knowledge, and you have it.
* Student: The object of knowledge.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. No, I assumed it was the relative pronoun for knowledge, the object of knowledge. Where is the knowledge? If the author had said "the object of 'you will know'" it would have been clearer, because what is in the verse is not the verbal noun but the verb, and he should have said "the object of 'you will know'." But the book is in fact written for students of knowledge, and for this reason we do not advise beginners to read this book, because although it is small, it is beyond the understanding of beginners. Good...

* Student: What should one read, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: One moment. The answer is memorized, God willing. "Man" is a relative pronoun and the object of "'alima" (knew). ﴿There comes to him a punishment that will disgrace him﴾: when "man" is a relative pronoun, the clause "yātīhi" (comes to him) has no place in the i'rab; it is the relative clause. ﴿A punishment that will disgrace him﴾: what did we say about "'adhāb"? Retribution. The clause "yukhzīhi" (disgraces him) is an attribute of "'adhāb," and not a response to "man," because "man" is a relative pronoun and does not require a response.

﴿Who there comes to him a punishment that will disgrace him, and there will descend upon him a lasting punishment﴾ [39:40] (there will descend upon him a lasting punishment, permanent, and it is the punishment of the Fire, and Allah disgraced them at Badr).

"Man" is a relative pronoun, the object of "'alima." When "man" is a relative pronoun, the clause "yātīhi" [39:40] has no place in the i'rab; it is the relative clause.

﴿A punishment that will disgrace him﴾: what did we say about "'adhāb"? Retribution. The clause "yukhzīhi" is an attribute of "'adhāb," and not a response to "man," because "man" is a relative pronoun and does not require a response.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verses 39–41 (part 2 of 2):

(﴿Upon him will come a punishment that will disgrace him, and upon him will descend a lasting punishment﴾ [al-Zumar 40]: constant, which is the punishment of the Fire. Allah disgraced them at Badr.) This means that the greatest humiliation that befell the Quraysh was what happened at Badr. Allah, glorified and exalted, gathered their leaders, their elders and their nobles, and they went out on that day. These nobles and elders were killed; they were killed, dragged away, and thrown into a well among the wells of Badr, a foul and stinking well. So their recompense, may Allah protect us, was this recompense, and this is among the greatest disgrace. The Prophet (ﷺ) stood over them, rebuking them and making them regret, and he said: "O so-and-so, son of so-and-so," naming them and their fathers, "O so-and-so, son of so-and-so, did you find what your Lord promised to be true? For I have found what my Lord promised me to be true." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, you are speaking to corpses that have rotted; how can you speak to bodies?" He said: "You are no more able to hear what I say than they are, but they are unable to answer." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3976) and Muslim (2875/78), from the hadith of Abu Talha.] The Messenger (ﷺ) spoke the truth. They hear the speech of the Messenger, and this speech only increases them in anguish and remorse.

For this reason, one of them said to 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who was Abu Jahl, when he came to him while there was still a breath of life in him. He said to him: "Who are you?" He said: "Ibn Mas'ud." He said: "You have climbed a difficult height, O little shepherd of the goats! How dare you tread on the head of a noble of the nobles of Quraysh?" Then he said: "To whom does the victory belong today?" He said: "To Allah and His Messenger." [Related by al-Bayhaqi in Dala'il al-Nubuwwah (1020), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.] The point is that the Messenger rebuked them for what had happened.

Then He said: (﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book for mankind in truth﴾ [al-Zumar 41]): the phrase "bil-haqq" (in truth) is connected to "anzalna" (We sent down).

Why did He not say "bi-anzalna"? Because the governing element (ʿamil) is the verb, and "nā" (We) is a pronoun that is detached from the verb. This is a lesson from the author to you: when you want to say that something is connected (muta'allaq), mention only the governing word, and do not mention the subject with it, nor the object if the object is attached to it. So this is connected to "anzal" (sent down).

In fact, in our i'rab (grammatical analysis) of the Qur'an we are lax; we say in such a case: connected to "anzalna." This is not precise. The correct form is to say: connected to "anzal," which is the governing word alone, without what is attached to it of subject or object.

(﴿So whoever is guided, it is for his own self﴾ [al-Zumar 41]: his guidance benefits him. ﴿And whoever goes astray, only to its detriment does he stray. And you are not over them a guardian﴾ [al-Zumar 41]: that you would compel them to guidance.) This is like His saying: ﴿And you are not over them a compeller﴾ [Qaf 45]. The Messenger (ﷺ) is not one who compels them to guidance, nor is he a guardian over them, watching them and watching over them.

Now let us return to the benefits. (﴿Say, O my people, act according to your position﴾ and so on [al-Zumar 39].)

* Among the benefits of this verse: the one who holds the truth should be strong and confront his opponent, not stand in a position of weakness. From where is this derived? From ﴿Act﴾ and ﴿Indeed, I am acting﴾ [al-Zumar 39], meaning: do not worry about me.
* Among its benefits: consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ), for Allah commanded him to say this as good news and consolation, that the final outcome will be his.
* Among its benefits: there is no harm in leaving the disbelievers in their disbelief as a threat. This is a method commonly used even in a father's discipline of his son. What does he say to him if he disobeys? He says: "Continue in your disobedience, continue in your play, do not come to receive the guests," for example. What does he mean? He means it as a threat.

I think we cannot cover all of them today, so we will leave them for tomorrow, God willing.

(...)

* * *

* Student: (﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died during their sleep. Then He keeps those for which He has decreed death and releases the others until a specified term. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾ [42]. ﴿Or have they taken intercessors besides Allah? Say: "Even though they possess nothing and do not reason?"﴾ [43]. ﴿Say: "To Allah belongs intercession entirely. His is the dominion of the heavens and the earth. Then to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-Zumar 42–44].)
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say, O my people, act according to your position; indeed, I am acting, so you will soon know﴾ [al-An'am 135], and so on to the end.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, glorified and exalted, wants His Prophet to be elevated above his people, speaking to them or with them from a position of height. This is shown by His saying: ﴿O my people, act according to your position, indeed I am acting﴾. This resembles a challenge to them: I do not care whether you do what you know; I will do what is contrary to it.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: I think we have already mentioned this benefit, that the one who holds the truth should be strong against his opponent and rise above him.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a threat to those deniers of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and that they will soon know who is more deserving of punishment and upon whom the punishment will come.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the punishment of disbelief is a humiliating punishment, a shame in the Hereafter and a degradation in this world; indeed, a degradation in both this world and the Hereafter, may Allah protect us. This is based on His saying: ﴿Upon whom will come a punishment that will disgrace him﴾ [al-Zumar 40].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the punishment of the people of the Fire is lasting and does not cease for them. From this verse follows what the Qur'an and the Sunnah indicate: that the people of the Fire will abide in it forever, and that it will not perish. The view that it will perish is a weak view, indeed a false one, because it contradicts the Book and the Sunnah.

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book for mankind in truth﴾ and so on to the end [al-Zumar 41].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a clarification that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, because Allah sent it down. It is speech, not a specific substance, like the iron about which Allah said: ﴿And We sent down iron, in which is great might﴾ [al-Hadid 25], or like livestock: ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [al-Zumar 6]. The Qur'an is speech, and if it is speech, then it is not created, because speech is an attribute of the speaker, and the One who speaks it, who is Allah, is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's elevation. From where?
* Student: ﴿We sent down﴾.
* Shaykh: And sending down cannot occur except from what?
* Student: Only from above.
* Shaykh: Only from above. This is what the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus, reason and innate nature (fitrah) indicate.

The elevation of Allah, mighty and majestic, is indicated by the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus, reason and innate nature. The Book's indications of Allah's elevation are of many varieties, and the Sunnah likewise agrees, in its sayings, its actions and its tacit approvals, that Allah, glorified and exalted, is high above His Throne, above His creation.

As for consensus (ijma'): the Salaf (early pious generations) agreed on this, and none of them ever held a contrary view. The principle in this matter is that when the Book and the Sunnah indicate something, and it is not known that any of the Salaf, the Companions or the Successors (tabi'un) held a contrary view, then they did not say anything other than it. This is an important point. A questioner might say: where is the evidence that the Companions held that Allah established Himself upon the Throne, meaning that He rose above it? Did anyone interpret it that way? What do we say?

We say: since the Qur'an says it and nothing contrary to it is reported from them, then they held it, because they took by the indication of the Qur'an, which they were commanded to follow. So from this we derive the consensus of the Companions on the elevation of Allah. Likewise the Successors who followed them in excellence, and the imams after them. Not a single letter has come from any of them saying otherwise.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the virtue of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), where He said what?
The rational proofs for Allah's elevation are that it is said: elevation is either an attribute of deficiency or of perfection, and no one doubts that it is an attribute of perfection, so it must be affirmed for Allah, for the Lord is necessarily described by the attributes of perfection by reason.

As for innate nature: people are created with the disposition that when they ask Allah for something, their hearts rise toward the sky. No one denies this.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in that this magnificent Qur'an was sent down to him. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am 124].
* Among its benefits: the Qur'an was sent down for the benefit of creation, because of His saying: ﴿for mankind﴾. The Qur'an was not sent down against the interests of creation; it was sent down for their interests. This is why He said: "We sent it down to you for mankind."
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the generality of the Prophet's (ﷺ) mission, because of His saying: ﴿for mankind﴾. He did not say "for your people," for example. It is for mankind in general.
* Among its benefits: the Qur'an was sent down in truth in both senses of the interpretation mentioned earlier. It is true, and it comes with truth. It is true in what it brings, since its rulings are just and its reports are truthful, and it is itself true, not false.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Qur'an is a proof, because of His saying: ﴿So whoever is guided, it is for his own self, and whoever goes astray, only to its detriment does he stray﴾ [al-Zumar 41].
* Among its benefits: people divide, in their response to this Qur'an, into those who are guided and those who go astray, because of His saying: ﴿So whoever is guided, it is for his own self, and whoever goes astray, only to its detriment does he stray﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a refutation of the Jabriyyah (determinists) who say that a person is compelled in his actions. The basis of this is that He attributed guidance and misguidance to the servant, which shows that it is his own act, which he chose.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the evil consequence of sins, and that they fall back upon the servant, not in his favor.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the blessing of guidance, and that it is an acquisition of the servant, because of His saying: ﴿for his own self﴾.
* Among its benefits: consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) when those among mankind go astray, because of His saying: ﴿And you are not over them a guardian﴾. Allah alone is the Guardian over them. As for you, you are a conveyer of the message. If you have fulfilled the duty of conveying it, then the reckoning is with Allah.
* Among its benefits: a refutation of those who attached themselves to the Prophet (ﷺ) out of fear, hope, desire and dread, to the point that they called upon him besides Allah, because of His saying: ﴿And you are not over them a guardian﴾.
* Among its benefits: that the caller who conveys the law of Allah, when he has conveyed it in the manner he was commanded, has cleared his responsibility, and nothing further is required of him. The indication is that if Muhammad (ﷺ), the leader of all callers and conveyers, was not a guardian over people and not a watcher over them, then those below him are even more so.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verses 39–41 (part 1 of 2):

Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: ﴿Say, "O my people, act according to your position; indeed I am acting."﴾ [39:39] The address here is to the Prophet (ﷺ). His saying "Say, O my people" refers to those who denied him and opposed him. "O my people" is a vocative (munada). Its original form is "yā qawmī" (O my people), but the yā' was dropped for lightness and the kasra was left as an indication of it. Accordingly, in its i'rab (grammatical analysis) we say: qawm is a vocative in the accusative, marked by a presumed fatha on the letter before the elided yā' of the speaker, which was dropped for lightness. ﴿O my people, act according to your position; indeed I am acting.﴾ "Act according to your position" means: act according to what you are upon of disbelief, enmity and harm, for that does not concern me and will not prevent me from continuing in my work. For this reason he emphasized his statement, "indeed I am acting," meaning: I am acting according to what I am upon. So you act, and we will act. This is like His saying: ﴿And wait; indeed we are waiting﴾ [11:122].

﴿Indeed I am acting; so you will know﴾ [39:39–40]. "You will know" (sawfa ta'lamūn) is a clause affirmed by the entry of sawfa upon it. Sawfa affirms the clause just as the sīn does, but the difference is that the sīn indicates this for the near future, while sawfa indicates it after a delay. For this reason it is said: the sīn is for tanfīs, and sawfa is for taswīf, meaning postponement and delay; and tanfīs means nearness. ﴿So you will know who﴾ [39:39–40]: "man" (who) here is the object of "you will know." The knowledge here means recognition (ma'rifa), and therefore it takes only one object, as Ibn Mālik said:

*Knowledge in the sense of recognition, and assumption in the sense of suspicion, are transitive to one object, as is required.*

He says: "tā'lamūn" means "you will recognize." ﴿who there will come to him a punishment that will disgrace him﴾: that is, you will know the one to whom a punishment will come that disgraces him. "Punishment" here means retribution, and "disgrace" means humiliation and shame. ﴿And there will descend upon him a lasting punishment﴾ [40]: that is, there will descend upon him a lasting punishment that will never leave him. You will know this, whether it is us or you. But they will know it at a time when they cannot be saved, and they will only be calling out with "woe" and "destruction." We seek refuge with Allah.

So, do we parse "man" as the first or the second object of "you will know"? There is no first or second object here, because "ya'lamūn" in this context means "ya'rifūn" (they recognize). ﴿So you will know who there will come to him a punishment that will disgrace him, and there will descend upon him a lasting punishment﴾ [39:39–40].

Then He, the Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed We have sent down to you the Book for mankind in truth﴾ [39:41]. Reflect on "innā anzalnā 'alayka" (We have sent down upon you), and in another verse "anzalnā ilayka" (We have sent down to you) [2]. Are the two particles the same in meaning, or do they differ?

The answer: the basic principle is that what differs in wording differs in meaning, since wording stands to meanings as a garment stands to bodies. So when we find two expressions with the same transitive construction but different wording, the basic presumption is that their meanings differ. Thus ﴿We have sent down to you﴾ (anzalnā ilayka) indicates that the ultimate destination of the revelation is the Messenger (ﷺ) and does not go beyond him to anyone else. And ﴿upon you﴾ ('alayka) indicates that the revelation rose above the Prophet (ﷺ) until it penetrated him, as though it descended into the very heart of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him). Have you not read the saying of Allah: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down, upon your heart﴾ [26:193–194], where He did not say "to your heart"? This is the difference.

As for His saying ﴿the Book﴾ (al-kitāb), the Book here is the Noble Qur'an. It is called a "kitāb" (book) because it is written in the Preserved Tablet, in the scriptures in the hands of the angels, and in the scriptures that are among us.
