On this basis, fi'āl (the form fi'āl) carries the meaning of maf'ūl (passive), and this pattern, fi'āl in the sense of maf'ūl, occurs frequently in the Arabic language. Among its examples:

* Student: *firāsh* in the sense of *mafrūsh* (spread out).
* Shaykh: *firāsh* in the sense of *mafrūsh*. *Kisā'*?
* Student: In the sense of *maksī* (clothed).
* Shaykh: And *binā'* in the sense of *mabnī* (built), and *ghirās* in the sense of *maghrūs* (planted). There are many examples.

Now, He says: ﴿the Book for mankind in truth﴾. The lām in "lil-nās" (for mankind) may indicate exclusivity (ikhtiṣāṣ) or transitivity (ta'diya); both are permissible. The meaning is that Allah sent down the Book upon Muhammad (ﷺ) so that people might be guided by it and benefit from it, and that is indeed the case. People have benefited from this Qur'an in a way that no other benefit can match. The Qurayshi nation was worth nothing in the eyes of other nations; they were humble and poor, with journeys to Sham in summer and to Yemen in winter, because they had no movement, no trade and no wealth. With the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ) and this Qur'an, they became the masters of the nations. ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?﴾ [93:6]. "Āwā" means "He sheltered you" and "He sheltered [people] through you." So you became a father to people after you had been an orphan without a father. This is why we say that the direct object is omitted in "āwā" for the sake of generality, meaning He sheltered you and sheltered [others] through you. ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾ [93:7]: He guided whom? He guided you and guided [others] through you. ﴿And He found you poor and made you rich﴾ [93:8]: He enriched you and enriched [others] through you. For this reason the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said to the Ansār: "You were in need, and Allah enriched you through me" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (4330) and Muslim (1061/139), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Zayd ibn 'Āṣim]. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) brought blessing to his community, and this is why He said: ﴿upon you the Book for mankind﴾.

As for His saying ﴿in truth﴾ (bil-ḥaqq), it has two meanings. First: that what this Qur'an brings is true, and truth is sincerity in reports and justice in rulings. Allah said: ﴿The word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [6:115]. The meaning is that this Qur'an was sent down in truth and came with truth, and what is truth? Truthfulness of reports and justice of rulings. The second meaning: "bil-ḥaqq" means that it is accompanied by truth, that is, its descent is true and contains no falsehood, as in His saying: ﴿The devils did not bring it down. It is not befitting for them, nor are they able to. Indeed, they are removed from hearing it﴾ [26:210–212]. So "bil-ḥaqq" has two meanings: the first…

* Student: Truthfulness of reports and justice of rulings.
* Shaykh: That is, what he brought is the truth. And the second…
* Student: Accompanied by truth.
* Shaykh: That is…
* Student: That it was sent down with it (...).
* Shaykh: No, this returns to the first meaning.
* Student: Its descent is true.
* Shaykh: That is, its descent is true, not false, for falsehood does not reach it: ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or behind it﴾ [41:42]. I have recited to you His saying: ﴿The devils did not bring it down. It is not befitting for them, nor are they able to. Indeed, they are removed from hearing it﴾. Unlike the reports of soothsayers, whose reports all come from the devils.

﴿Indeed We have sent down to you the Book for mankind in truth. So whoever is guided, it is for his own self﴾ [39:41]. The "fa" here follows from what came before. That is, after the descent of this Qur'an, people divided into two groups: a group that was guided by it and benefited, and a group that turned away from it and perished.

His saying ﴿So whoever is guided﴾: "man" here is conditional (sharṭiyya). Its conditional clause is "ihtadā" (is guided), and its response is a nominal clause, "fa-li-nafsihi" (it is for his own self). Because the response is nominal, it is preceded by "fa." His saying "ihtadā" (is guided) means guidance of knowledge and guidance of action. Guidance of knowledge is that he is eager for this Qur'an, memorizes it, reflects on it and contemplates it. Guidance of action is that he applies this Qur'an and acts upon it in belief, speech and deed. ﴿Whoever is guided, it is for his own self﴾ means: his guidance benefits his own self, or: he is for his own self. The point is that the omitted element here must be the subject (mubtada'), necessarily. Why do we say "necessarily"? Because what is mentioned is a prepositional phrase (jār wa-majrūr), and a prepositional phrase can never be a subject. So the omitted element is the subject. If you wish, estimate: "for his own self is his guidance," or if you wish, estimate: "he is for his own self."

Now we ask: why was the response clause preceded by "fa"?

* Student: (...) nominal.
* Shaykh: Because it is nominal, and when the response clause is nominal, it must be preceded by "fa." Sometimes the "fa" may be omitted, but rarely. Among that is the poet's saying:

*Whoever does good deeds, Allah will reward them* (...........................)

He did not say "then Allah will reward them," but this is rare.

Now let us address what must be preceded by "fa" among clauses when it is a response, which is mentioned in a verse.

* Student: The five nouns (al-asmā' al-khamsa).
* Shaykh: Good.
* Student: A rigid noun, and "sawfa," and "sīn," and a nominal clause; and if it is an imperative (...) a verbal clause whose verb is imperative (...).
* Shaykh: Good. That makes five, but complete the verse so you can finish.
* Student: The poet said:

*Nominal, imperative, with a rigid noun, with mā, qad, lan and the tanfīs*

* Shaykh:

*Nominal, imperative, and with a rigid noun, and with mā, qad, lan and with tanfīs.*

﴿So whoever is guided, it is for his own self; and whoever goes astray, he only goes astray to his own detriment﴾ [39:41]. "Whoever goes astray" means he is not guided, neither in knowledge nor in action. ﴿He only goes astray to his own detriment﴾: that is, to his own self, and he does not harm Allah at all, nor does he harm anyone else. ﴿And you are not a guardian over them﴾ [39:41]. The "mā" here is Ḥijāzī, meaning that only the people of the Ḥijāz pronounce it this way. (If I am wrong, say: "wrong.") This "mā" is Ḥijāzī, meaning only the people of the Ḥijāz pronounce it this way?

* Student: Wrong.
* Shaykh: Wrong, because the people of the Ḥijāz and others both pronounce it, but it functions like "laysa" (is not) only according to the people of the Ḥijāz, and that is why it is called Ḥijāzī. According to the people of the Ḥijāz, it functions like "laysa": it raises the subject and puts the predicate in the accusative. Among that is Allah's saying: ﴿This is not a human being﴾ [12:31]. According to the Banū Tamīm, it does not function like "laysa"; it is inactive (muhmala), so they say in His saying ﴿This is not a human being﴾, outside the Qur'an: "mā hādhā basharun." Now I will speak, so say: are you Ḥijāzī or Tamīmī? "Mā Zaydun qā'imun."

* Students: Tamīmī.
* Shaykh: Tamīmī. "Mā Zaydun qā'iman."
* Students: Ḥijāzī.
* Shaykh: Ḥijāzī. So it is the language of Quraysh, who are the people of the Ḥijāz. They say "mā hādhā basharan," and the Banū Tamīm say "mā hādhā basharun." They used to recite the Qur'an as "mā hādhā basharun" before it was unified in the dialect of Quraysh, because the Qur'an was revealed in seven ahruf (modes). There is a witty verse in which the poet said:

*A slender-waisted one, I said to her: "Tell me your lineage," and she replied: "The killing of the lover is not forbidden."*

(A slender-waisted one, I said to her: "Tell me your lineage," meaning: where are you from? She answered without naming her tribe, saying: "The killing of the lover is not forbidden." What do you think this woman is? A Tamīmiyya, because she said "the killing of the lover is not forbidden" with the Tamīmī construction, so he knew she was Tamīmī.) Nowadays, can we tell the Tamīmī from the Qurayshī? All Tamīmīs and all Qurayshīs have now mixed together. You find one saying "mā hādhā basharun" and another saying "mā hādhā basharun," and they all differ. They have intermingled.

Now, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And you are not a guardian over them﴾ [39:41]. Do we now parse "mā" according to the dialect of the Banū Tamīm or the dialect of Quraysh? According to the dialect of Quraysh, even though the wording in this structure does not differ. The wording does not differ, because the Banū Tamīm say "mā anta 'alayhim bi-wakīl" and so do the Quraysh, but since we know that the Qur'an is in the dialect of Quraysh, we say: "mā" here is Ḥijāzī, "anna" is its subject, the "tā'" is for address, the "bā'" is a superfluous prepositional particle (ḥarf jarr zā'id), and "wakīl" is its predicate in the accusative, marked by a presumed fatḥa on its last letter, prevented from appearing by the occupation of the position by the kasra of the superfluous preposition.

If someone says: "You said the bā' is a superfluous preposition, and we know that the Noble Qur'an contains no nonsense (laghw), and superfluity is nonsense."

The answer to this is: superfluity is nonsense only if it does not convey a meaning. If it conveys a meaning, it is not nonsense. The meaning it conveys here is the emphasis of negation. On this basis, it is not nonsense, but rather superfluous in form and not superfluous in meaning; it adds to the meaning.

But someone may say: "How is it superfluous?" We say: it is superfluous. The first (zāda) is from intransitive "zād," and the second superfluous one is from transitive "zād," because "zād" (to increase) is like "naqasa" (to decrease): it is used intransitively and it is used transitively with an object. Allah said: ﴿So it increased them in faith﴾ [3:173], transitive; ﴿then they did not diminish anything from you﴾ [9:4], transitive. And you say: "zāda īmānu al-rajul" (the man's faith increased), intransitive; and you say: "naqaṣa al-mā'" (the water decreased), intransitive. ﴿And you are not a guardian over them﴾ [39:41]: that is, you are not a watcher over them, observing them and protecting them. That is for Allah. You are only responsible for conveying the message, and the reckoning rests with the Lord of the worlds, Mighty and Majestic.

Now let us return to the words of the exegete, may Allah have mercy on him. He says: ﴿Say, "O my people, act according to your position"﴾ [39:39]: "according to your state." So "makāna" means "ḥāla" (state). As we mentioned in the tafsir, "al-makāna" means what you were upon, and it is in the sense of "ḥāla" in the words of the exegete. ﴿Indeed I am acting﴾: "according to my state." From where did he understand that the implied meaning is "according to my state"? Because it corresponds to His saying: ﴿act according to your position﴾, meaning: indeed I am acting according to my position. Fine. ﴿Indeed I am acting; so you will know who there will come to him a punishment that will disgrace him﴾ [39:39–40].

* Student: (...)
* Shaykh: How?
* Student: Indeed I am acting according to my position.
* Shaykh: No, it is "according to my state."
* Student: The implied meaning is...
* Shaykh: The implied meaning is "according to my position." ﴿So you will know who﴾: he says "man" is a relative pronoun, the object of knowledge. How?
* Student: Object of (...).
* Shaykh: No, the object of knowledge with the "tā'" you have it that way.
* Student: (...) knowledge (...).
* Shaykh: Good. And what did I say?
* Student: For knowledge.
* Shaykh: I said: the object of knowledge, and you have it.
* Student: The object of knowledge.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. No, I assumed it was the relative pronoun for knowledge, the object of knowledge. Where is the knowledge? If the author had said "the object of 'you will know'" it would have been clearer, because what is in the verse is not the verbal noun but the verb, and he should have said "the object of 'you will know'." But the book is in fact written for students of knowledge, and for this reason we do not advise beginners to read this book, because although it is small, it is beyond the understanding of beginners. Good...

* Student: What should one read, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: One moment. The answer is memorized, God willing. "Man" is a relative pronoun and the object of "'alima" (knew). ﴿There comes to him a punishment that will disgrace him﴾: when "man" is a relative pronoun, the clause "yātīhi" (comes to him) has no place in the i'rab; it is the relative clause. ﴿A punishment that will disgrace him﴾: what did we say about "'adhāb"? Retribution. The clause "yukhzīhi" (disgraces him) is an attribute of "'adhāb," and not a response to "man," because "man" is a relative pronoun and does not require a response.

﴿Who there comes to him a punishment that will disgrace him, and there will descend upon him a lasting punishment﴾ [39:40] (there will descend upon him a lasting punishment, permanent, and it is the punishment of the Fire, and Allah disgraced them at Badr).

"Man" is a relative pronoun, the object of "'alima." When "man" is a relative pronoun, the clause "yātīhi" [39:40] has no place in the i'rab; it is the relative clause.

﴿A punishment that will disgrace him﴾: what did we say about "'adhāb"? Retribution. The clause "yukhzīhi" is an attribute of "'adhāb," and not a response to "man," because "man" is a relative pronoun and does not require a response.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verses 39–41 (part 2 of 2):

(﴿Upon him will come a punishment that will disgrace him, and upon him will descend a lasting punishment﴾ [al-Zumar 40]: constant, which is the punishment of the Fire. Allah disgraced them at Badr.) This means that the greatest humiliation that befell the Quraysh was what happened at Badr. Allah, glorified and exalted, gathered their leaders, their elders and their nobles, and they went out on that day. These nobles and elders were killed; they were killed, dragged away, and thrown into a well among the wells of Badr, a foul and stinking well. So their recompense, may Allah protect us, was this recompense, and this is among the greatest disgrace. The Prophet (ﷺ) stood over them, rebuking them and making them regret, and he said: "O so-and-so, son of so-and-so," naming them and their fathers, "O so-and-so, son of so-and-so, did you find what your Lord promised to be true? For I have found what my Lord promised me to be true." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, you are speaking to corpses that have rotted; how can you speak to bodies?" He said: "You are no more able to hear what I say than they are, but they are unable to answer." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3976) and Muslim (2875/78), from the hadith of Abu Talha.] The Messenger (ﷺ) spoke the truth. They hear the speech of the Messenger, and this speech only increases them in anguish and remorse.

For this reason, one of them said to 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who was Abu Jahl, when he came to him while there was still a breath of life in him. He said to him: "Who are you?" He said: "Ibn Mas'ud." He said: "You have climbed a difficult height, O little shepherd of the goats! How dare you tread on the head of a noble of the nobles of Quraysh?" Then he said: "To whom does the victory belong today?" He said: "To Allah and His Messenger." [Related by al-Bayhaqi in Dala'il al-Nubuwwah (1020), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.] The point is that the Messenger rebuked them for what had happened.

Then He said: (﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book for mankind in truth﴾ [al-Zumar 41]): the phrase "bil-haqq" (in truth) is connected to "anzalna" (We sent down).

Why did He not say "bi-anzalna"? Because the governing element (ʿamil) is the verb, and "nā" (We) is a pronoun that is detached from the verb. This is a lesson from the author to you: when you want to say that something is connected (muta'allaq), mention only the governing word, and do not mention the subject with it, nor the object if the object is attached to it. So this is connected to "anzal" (sent down).

In fact, in our i'rab (grammatical analysis) of the Qur'an we are lax; we say in such a case: connected to "anzalna." This is not precise. The correct form is to say: connected to "anzal," which is the governing word alone, without what is attached to it of subject or object.

(﴿So whoever is guided, it is for his own self﴾ [al-Zumar 41]: his guidance benefits him. ﴿And whoever goes astray, only to its detriment does he stray. And you are not over them a guardian﴾ [al-Zumar 41]: that you would compel them to guidance.) This is like His saying: ﴿And you are not over them a compeller﴾ [Qaf 45]. The Messenger (ﷺ) is not one who compels them to guidance, nor is he a guardian over them, watching them and watching over them.

Now let us return to the benefits. (﴿Say, O my people, act according to your position﴾ and so on [al-Zumar 39].)

* Among the benefits of this verse: the one who holds the truth should be strong and confront his opponent, not stand in a position of weakness. From where is this derived? From ﴿Act﴾ and ﴿Indeed, I am acting﴾ [al-Zumar 39], meaning: do not worry about me.
* Among its benefits: consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ), for Allah commanded him to say this as good news and consolation, that the final outcome will be his.
* Among its benefits: there is no harm in leaving the disbelievers in their disbelief as a threat. This is a method commonly used even in a father's discipline of his son. What does he say to him if he disobeys? He says: "Continue in your disobedience, continue in your play, do not come to receive the guests," for example. What does he mean? He means it as a threat.

I think we cannot cover all of them today, so we will leave them for tomorrow, God willing.

(...)

* * *

* Student: (﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died during their sleep. Then He keeps those for which He has decreed death and releases the others until a specified term. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾ [42]. ﴿Or have they taken intercessors besides Allah? Say: "Even though they possess nothing and do not reason?"﴾ [43]. ﴿Say: "To Allah belongs intercession entirely. His is the dominion of the heavens and the earth. Then to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-Zumar 42–44].)
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say, O my people, act according to your position; indeed, I am acting, so you will soon know﴾ [al-An'am 135], and so on to the end.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, glorified and exalted, wants His Prophet to be elevated above his people, speaking to them or with them from a position of height. This is shown by His saying: ﴿O my people, act according to your position, indeed I am acting﴾. This resembles a challenge to them: I do not care whether you do what you know; I will do what is contrary to it.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: I think we have already mentioned this benefit, that the one who holds the truth should be strong against his opponent and rise above him.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a threat to those deniers of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and that they will soon know who is more deserving of punishment and upon whom the punishment will come.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the punishment of disbelief is a humiliating punishment, a shame in the Hereafter and a degradation in this world; indeed, a degradation in both this world and the Hereafter, may Allah protect us. This is based on His saying: ﴿Upon whom will come a punishment that will disgrace him﴾ [al-Zumar 40].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the punishment of the people of the Fire is lasting and does not cease for them. From this verse follows what the Qur'an and the Sunnah indicate: that the people of the Fire will abide in it forever, and that it will not perish. The view that it will perish is a weak view, indeed a false one, because it contradicts the Book and the Sunnah.

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book for mankind in truth﴾ and so on to the end [al-Zumar 41].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a clarification that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, because Allah sent it down. It is speech, not a specific substance, like the iron about which Allah said: ﴿And We sent down iron, in which is great might﴾ [al-Hadid 25], or like livestock: ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [al-Zumar 6]. The Qur'an is speech, and if it is speech, then it is not created, because speech is an attribute of the speaker, and the One who speaks it, who is Allah, is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's elevation. From where?
* Student: ﴿We sent down﴾.
* Shaykh: And sending down cannot occur except from what?
* Student: Only from above.
* Shaykh: Only from above. This is what the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus, reason and innate nature (fitrah) indicate.

The elevation of Allah, mighty and majestic, is indicated by the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus, reason and innate nature. The Book's indications of Allah's elevation are of many varieties, and the Sunnah likewise agrees, in its sayings, its actions and its tacit approvals, that Allah, glorified and exalted, is high above His Throne, above His creation.

As for consensus (ijma'): the Salaf (early pious generations) agreed on this, and none of them ever held a contrary view. The principle in this matter is that when the Book and the Sunnah indicate something, and it is not known that any of the Salaf, the Companions or the Successors (tabi'un) held a contrary view, then they did not say anything other than it. This is an important point. A questioner might say: where is the evidence that the Companions held that Allah established Himself upon the Throne, meaning that He rose above it? Did anyone interpret it that way? What do we say?

We say: since the Qur'an says it and nothing contrary to it is reported from them, then they held it, because they took by the indication of the Qur'an, which they were commanded to follow. So from this we derive the consensus of the Companions on the elevation of Allah. Likewise the Successors who followed them in excellence, and the imams after them. Not a single letter has come from any of them saying otherwise.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the virtue of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), where He said what?
The rational proofs for Allah's elevation are that it is said: elevation is either an attribute of deficiency or of perfection, and no one doubts that it is an attribute of perfection, so it must be affirmed for Allah, for the Lord is necessarily described by the attributes of perfection by reason.

As for innate nature: people are created with the disposition that when they ask Allah for something, their hearts rise toward the sky. No one denies this.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in that this magnificent Qur'an was sent down to him. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am 124].
* Among its benefits: the Qur'an was sent down for the benefit of creation, because of His saying: ﴿for mankind﴾. The Qur'an was not sent down against the interests of creation; it was sent down for their interests. This is why He said: "We sent it down to you for mankind."
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the generality of the Prophet's (ﷺ) mission, because of His saying: ﴿for mankind﴾. He did not say "for your people," for example. It is for mankind in general.
* Among its benefits: the Qur'an was sent down in truth in both senses of the interpretation mentioned earlier. It is true, and it comes with truth. It is true in what it brings, since its rulings are just and its reports are truthful, and it is itself true, not false.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Qur'an is a proof, because of His saying: ﴿So whoever is guided, it is for his own self, and whoever goes astray, only to its detriment does he stray﴾ [al-Zumar 41].
* Among its benefits: people divide, in their response to this Qur'an, into those who are guided and those who go astray, because of His saying: ﴿So whoever is guided, it is for his own self, and whoever goes astray, only to its detriment does he stray﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a refutation of the Jabriyyah (determinists) who say that a person is compelled in his actions. The basis of this is that He attributed guidance and misguidance to the servant, which shows that it is his own act, which he chose.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the evil consequence of sins, and that they fall back upon the servant, not in his favor.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the blessing of guidance, and that it is an acquisition of the servant, because of His saying: ﴿for his own self﴾.
* Among its benefits: consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) when those among mankind go astray, because of His saying: ﴿And you are not over them a guardian﴾. Allah alone is the Guardian over them. As for you, you are a conveyer of the message. If you have fulfilled the duty of conveying it, then the reckoning is with Allah.
* Among its benefits: a refutation of those who attached themselves to the Prophet (ﷺ) out of fear, hope, desire and dread, to the point that they called upon him besides Allah, because of His saying: ﴿And you are not over them a guardian﴾.
* Among its benefits: that the caller who conveys the law of Allah, when he has conveyed it in the manner he was commanded, has cleared his responsibility, and nothing further is required of him. The indication is that if Muhammad (ﷺ), the leader of all callers and conveyers, was not a guardian over people and not a watcher over them, then those below him are even more so.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verse 42 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [Az-Zumar 42]. ﴿Allah﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and the clause ﴿yatawaffa﴾ (takes) is its predicate (khabar). At-tawaffi (taking in full) means qabd (seizing), as one says: "tawaffa al-rajul haqqahu min gharimihi," meaning he received his right in full from his debtor, i.e. seized it from him. Al-anfus is the plural of nafs (soul, self), and it refers to the spirits, the spirits by which bodies are alive. The word nafs is used in the Quran with several meanings, and among them here is that it is the spirit by which a person's life exists. So He seizes the spirits ﴿at the time of their death﴾, meaning at the time of death, which is the departure of the spirit from the body, the departure by which life ceases.

﴿And those that have not died in their sleep﴾ [Az-Zumar 42]. Here ﴿wa-allati﴾ (and those): the waw is a conjunction particle, and ﴿allati﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) with ﴿al-anfus﴾. The meaning is: and He takes those that have not died. In such a construction you have the choice of saying: the waw is a conjunction particle, and ﴿allati﴾ is an attribute (sifah) of a coordinated noun, the estimate being: "wa-al-anfus allati lam tamut" (and the souls which have not died). You may also coordinate the attribute directly on what precedes, saying: ﴿allati lam tamut﴾ is coordinated on His saying ﴿al-anfus hina mawtiha﴾. ﴿Those that have not died﴾ He takes ﴿in their sleep﴾, meaning He seizes them, but not a complete seizing; rather it is a restricted seizing. This is why you find that the sleeper has awareness in one respect and no awareness in another. In terms of the outward faculties he has no awareness: he does not see and does not hear. In terms of the inward faculties, and that if he is woken he would wake up, he is alive. So the connection of the spirit to the sleeper is different from its connection to the one who is awake, and different from its connection to the dead. It is thus intermediate between the living who is awake and the dead.

He says: ﴿And those that have not died in their sleep﴾. Allah the Exalted has named sleep a tawaffi (taking), saying: ﴿It is He who takes you in the night and knows what you have committed by day; then He revives you therein until a specified term is fulfilled﴾ [Al-An'am 60].

﴿Then He keeps those on whom He has decreed death and releases the others until a specified term﴾ [Az-Zumar 42]. He keeps the one on whom death has been decreed, so it does not return to its body; He keeps it until the resurrection comes. His saying ﴿qada﴾ (decreed) means hukm (ordained), like His saying: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [Al-Isra 23], meaning He ordained that you worship none but Him. The qada' here is qada' kawni (decree of creation), and I say it is qada' kawni because the decree of Allah is divided into two parts: shar'i (legislative) and kawni (cosmic).

The shar'i is what He commanded, such as His saying: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [Al-Isra 23], and His saying: ﴿And Allah judges with truth﴾ [Ghafir 20], meaning He rules by it.

The kawni is such as His saying: ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book that you will surely cause corruption in the land﴾ [Al-Isra 4]. Allah does not decree corruption in the land in the legislative sense; it is a cosmic decree. Here He says: ﴿decreed death upon it﴾ [Az-Zumar 42], a cosmic decree. Good. ﴿He decreed death upon it and releases the other﴾ [Az-Zumar 42], meaning the one whose tawaffi happened during its sleep He releases. ﴿Until a specified term﴾ means until a determined appointed time. What is the specified term? It is death: He releases it to go back to its body and remain in it until a specified, determined term.

﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who give thought﴾ [Az-Zumar 42]. ﴿In that﴾ means the taking of the two kinds of souls, the release of one of them, and the keeping of the other, contains signs. The signs that are before us now are very clear, four of them: the taking at death, the taking in sleep, the keeping of the dead, the release of the sleeper. All four are from the signs of Allah the Mighty and Majestic. You may come to a group of people asleep and say: "Glory be to Allah," ﴿And among His signs is your sleep by night and day﴾ [Ar-Rum 23]. People who are like corpses, not hearing, except one who is a light sleeper. But the principle is that they are like corpses. So you say: "Glory be to Him who caused them to die and then revived them after they had been like the dead." These are signs, and it is also a sign of the resurrection, for sleep is a minor death in which Allah revives the sleeper until he wakes up completely. Likewise, revival after death is decreed by Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and He is capable of it. The intelligent person measures the unseen by the seen and the future by the present, and the matter becomes clear to him.

His saying ﴿for a people who give thought﴾ [Az-Zumar 42]. Tafakkur (giving thought) is the exercise of reflection, exercising it so that it turns back and forth, right and left, until what is to be made clear through reflection becomes clear to him. The opposite of tafakkur is heedlessness, and that the heart be a smooth stone on which nothing settles: if a grain of dust settled on it, the winds would blow it away and the waters would carry it off. So the person who gives thought is one who is not heedless; rather he turns his thought right and left, going and returning, until the matter becomes clear to him.

Now let us return to the words of the commentator, may Allah have mercy on him. He says: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [Az-Zumar 42], (and takes) ﴿those that have not died in their sleep﴾ [Az-Zumar 42]. He estimated the verb after the conjunction particle, indicating that it is coordinated with what has this as its governing word. And what is its governing word? The souls. He takes the souls ﴿that have not died in their sleep﴾ (meaning He takes them at the time of sleep). Thus it becomes clear that sleep is a tawaffi.

﴿He decreed death upon it and releases the other until a specified term﴾ [Az-Zumar 42] (meaning the time of its death). This is the specified term. (The released soul is the soul of discernment; the life-soul remains without it, unlike the reverse.) It is as if the author is saying: the souls are of two kinds: the soul of discernment and the soul of life. The soul of discernment is the one released ﴿and releases the other until a specified term﴾, and does life remain without it or not? It remains. The sleeper certainly has life, so the soul of discernment remains and life remains after it, but not the reverse. This is why he said: (unlike the reverse). For when the soul of life is seized, the soul of discernment does not remain after it. So the commentator, may Allah have mercy on him, has informed us that the souls in His saying ﴿the souls at the time of their death﴾ are which souls? They are the souls of life, followed by the souls of discernment. ﴿And those that have not died in their sleep﴾ are the souls of discernment.

He says: (﴿Indeed in that﴾, the mentioned, ﴿are signs﴾, proofs, ﴿for a people who give thought﴾ [Az-Zumar 42], so that they know that the One who is able to do that is able to resurrect, and the Quraysh did not give thought to this.)

In what has been mentioned there are signs, and we have mentioned four apparent ones. If we reflect, we will find far more than that, but they require thought, contemplation and reflection in order to become clear.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: showing the strength of the authority of Allah the Mighty and Majestic and its comprehensiveness. From where is this derived? From His disposing in this way even over the souls: He takes all of them, releases this one and keeps that one. This is evidence of perfect dominion and authority.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the one who takes the souls at the time of their death is Allah the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [Az-Zumar 42]. Is this not the reality? Yes. This is what the verse indicates.

But this indication may be opposed by some verses, in His saying: ﴿until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not neglect﴾ [Al-An'am 61], and ﴿then they are returned to Allah, their true Master﴾ [Al-An'am 62], and His saying: ﴿Say: The angel of death who has been charged with you will take you; then to your Lord you will be returned﴾ [As-Sajdah 11]. We find that in the surah of Az-Zumar He attributed the taking to whom? To Himself, the Mighty and Majestic. In the surah As-Sajdah to the angel of death, and in the surah Al-An'am to the messengers: ﴿Our messengers take him﴾. So how do we reconcile these verses?

The answer is that we must know a very important principle: two definitive proofs can never conflict, never, neither from the Quran, nor the Sunnah, nor reason; for if they conflicted, one of them would be established and the other negated, and if we say the other is negated, it loses the name of definitive. This principle will benefit you in many matters.

For example, if someone says to you: "The Quran indicates such-and-such, but it has been established by sense perception that the actual matter is contrary to this indication." Sensory evidence cannot be denied, but we say: your understanding of the Quran is wrong. For example, if someone says: "The earth is not spherical, because of the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿And at the earth, how it was spread out?﴾ [Al-Ghashiyah 20]," and he believes it is spherical, which contradicts the indication of the verse. The Quran is definite in its authenticity (qat'i al-thubut). What is meant by qat'i al-thubut?

That is, it is established definitively, without any problem. Allah says: ﴿And at the earth, how it was spread out?﴾ [Al-Ghashiyah 20]. And is the sphericity of the earth established by sense perception or not?

* Students: Established.

* Shaykh: Definitively, or not definitively?

* Students: Not definitively.

* Shaykh: No, definitively. The sphericity of the earth is established definitively, with no doubt.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: By sense perception, yes. Now, if a plane leaves Jeddah airport heading west on a straight line, it returns to its airport, nothing turning it back. So it is spherical, with no problem. The verse? We say: its wording is definitive and established, but its indication that it is one flat surface is not correct. It is not explicit. And if the indication is not explicit, it is not definitive. Then we say: the conflict now is between an indication that is speculative (zanni) and a sensory matter that is definitive. What is the speculative indication? That the verse indicates the earth is one surface. And the definitive sensory matter is that the earth is spherical. We say: praise be to Allah, the conflict now is between the speculative and the definitive. And when the speculative conflicts with the definitive, what is given precedence? The definitive. We say: the surface of the earth, with respect to the part facing us, is a surface, is it not? But at a distance there is curvature. The evidence for that is that if a ship sails on the sea and has tall masts, as it moves away from you, it disappears, passes out of sight. What makes it vanish? Because the earth is round. The earth is round, so it disappears. If it were a flat surface, you would see it even to its hulls, if it has hulls, yes, you would see it from afar as you see it from near on a surface. The matter is evident, there is no problem with it. The summary now: two proofs that are definitive in authenticity and indication cannot conflict, do you understand? And a definitive and a speculative cannot conflict.

* Students: It is possible.

* Shaykh: O people, how long were you in your mothers' wombs? Give me nine minutes. It is not possible, because the speculative cannot withstand the definitive. The speculative cannot withstand the definitive, and if it cannot withstand it, it falls, so there is no opponent. Right? Then the conflict remains between speculative and speculative, and if a conflict arises between two speculative indications, then seek preponderance (tarjih), or if abrogation (naskh, the replacement of one ruling by a later one) is possible, apply abrogation. This principle was mentioned by Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, in his great book Dar' Ta'arud al-'Aql wa-al-Naql (Refuting the Conflict Between Reason and Revelation). Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, praised this book in his Nuniyyah, saying:

"And he has the book of Reason and Transmission, which has no second equal in existence."

He means that among what he refuted the philosophers with is this book, in which he mentioned this beneficial principle. A conflict between two definitive proofs is impossible, right?

* Students: Right.

* Shaykh: Right?

* Students: Yes.

* Shaykh: Why?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes; because if a conflict occurred, one of them would not be definitive, which is not possible. Good. Second: a conflict between the definitive and the speculative is impossible.

* Student: It occurs.

* Shaykh: It occurs, but it cannot withstand it; meaning we drop the conflict, and we say the ruling is? By the definitive. The conflict between two speculative proofs does occur, and it must be examined, and preponderance applied, or abrogation applied if it is of a kind that can be abrogated. Clear? Good. Now what are we talking about? About reconciling the taking attributed to Allah, the taking attributed to the messengers, and the taking attributed to the angel of death.

We say: there is no conflict in the indication; they differ. In these verses of Az-Zumar, Allah attributed the taking to Himself because it occurs by His command, and a thing may be attributed to another because it occurs by his command. As you say: "The king built a palace." Have you seen the king working with his hands with cement and sand, saying: "Boy, bring the basket, bring this, bring that"? The answer is no, but he ordered it. From this is the famous proverb in rhetoric: "'Amr ibn al-'As built the city of Fustat." Where is the city of Fustat located?

* Student: In Egypt.

* Shaykh: In Egypt?

* Student: Cairo.

* Shaykh: Good. Did 'Amr ibn al-'As build it with his own hand?

* Student: No.

* Shaykh: No, he ordered it. So the attribution of the taking to Allah is because it occurs by His command. Good. There remain now the attribution to the angel of death and to the messengers. The reconciliation is that we say: either the messengers are meant in the generic sense: ﴿Our messengers took him﴾ [Al-An'am 61], meaning the angel of death, because the angel of death is a messenger, and from the hadith: "Soon the messenger of my Lord will come to me and I will respond." Good. Or we say: the taking by the angel of death is different from the taking by the messengers, because of what came in the hadith: "The angel of death sits beside the dying person and commands his spirit to come out, and he takes it in his hand, then immediately hands it over to the angels who came down from heaven, with them the spices and the shroud suitable for it. If it was a believing soul" (and I ask Allah to make my spirit and your spirits believing), "it is placed in a shroud from Paradise and spices from Paradise. If it was the other, then a shroud of fire and spices of fire." We seek refuge in Allah from that.

(...) This shroud, and the ascent with it to heaven, is undertaken by the angels. This is why He said: ﴿Our messengers took him, and they do not neglect. Then they are returned to Allah, their true Master﴾ [Al-An'am 61, 62]. They carry it to Allah the Mighty and Majestic. If it is a believer's soul, it passes beyond the heavens to Allah, because Allah is the ultimate goal of the believer's soul in life and after death. The believer's heart and soul are attached to Allah the Mighty and Majestic; he always looks to Allah the Mighty and Majestic with the eye of insight. If he stands, it is by Allah, for Allah, and in Allah; if he sits, it is by Allah, for Allah, and in Allah. Likewise, if he goes and comes, it is for Allah, by Allah, and in Allah. We want the brother to distinguish between these three words: li-Allah, bi-Allah, and fi-Allah.

* Student: li-Allah means for the sake of Allah...

* Shaykh: Sincerity, good.

* Student: And bi-Allah means with the help of Allah.

* Shaykh: Seeking help.

* Student: Seeking help, and li-Allah.

* Shaykh: And fi-Allah?

* Student: Fi-Allah means in the way of Allah.

* Shaykh: That is, in His law and His judgment, and so on. Look at al-Fatihah, which includes the three in sequence: ﴿You alone we worship﴾ [Al-Fatihah 5]. What is this?

* Students: For Allah.

* Shaykh: For Allah, sincerity. ﴿You alone we ask for help﴾ [Al-Fatihah 5]?

* Students: By Allah.

* Shaykh: By Allah. ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [Al-Fatihah 6]?

* Students: In Allah.

* Shaykh: In Allah, in the law, that we be on the straight path and not transgress it (...).

* * *

* Student: ﴿And when those besides Him are mentioned, behold, they rejoice﴾ [Az-Zumar 45].

* Shaykh: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah's blessings and peace be upon our Prophet Muhammad and upon his family and all his companions. What remains for us is in the words of the author. Rather...

* Student: In the verses.

* Shaykh: In the verses, the explanation of the benefits from His saying: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [Az-Zumar 42], or the verse before it?

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, glory be to Him, takes the souls at the time of their death. We have mentioned that the apparent meaning of the verse seems to conflict with two verses in the Book of Allah: ﴿Say: The angel of death who has been charged with you will take you﴾ [As-Sajdah 11], and ﴿When death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not fail﴾ [Al-An'am 61]. We explained how these three verses are reconciled, saying: the attribution of the taking of souls to Allah is because He is the one who commands it, and the one who commands a thing is credited with it. We gave an example for this, saying: If it were said, "The king built a lofty palace," no one would understand that the king personally did the building, but he ordered it. As for reconciling His saying, ﴿When death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him﴾, with His saying, ﴿Say: The angel of death takes you﴾, there are two possibilities: either "the messengers" refers to the category (jins), and it is one, namely the angel of death; or the angel of death takes the soul from the body and then hands it over to the angels who are present, and they take it.

We also explained a useful principle on this subject: there is no contradiction between two definitive (qat'i) texts, nor between a definitive text and a speculative (zanni) text. As for two definitive texts, if they contradicted each other, one of them would not be definitive. As for a definitive and a speculative text, there is no contradiction, because the definitive text takes precedence. So, the contradiction remains between—?
* Student: Between the speculative and the definitive.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: Between the speculative and the speculative.
* Shaykh: Between two speculative texts only. We also explained that definiteness (qat') may pertain to authenticity of transmission (thubut) and may pertain to indication (dalalah). Among the evidences, some are definitive in transmission but speculative in indication, some are definitive in both transmission and indication, and some are definitive in indication but speculative in transmission.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: sleep is called a death (wafah), by His saying: ﴿And the one who has not died during her sleep﴾ [Az-Zumar 42]. This is supported by the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿It is He who takes you in death at night, and knows what you have committed by day﴾ [Al-An'am 60].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: time passes quickly for the dead, even if the days and ages are long. For if we measure the lesser death (sleep), or if we consider the lesser death and the swiftness with which time passes in it, then the greater death is even more so. However, there is no doubt that whoever is punished in his grave will find the time lengthened, while whoever is blessed will find the time short for him. Nevertheless, the one who is blessed says: "My Lord, establish the Hour so that I may return to my family and my wealth," while the one who is punished says: "My Lord, do not establish the Hour," because he sees that the punishment of the grave is lighter than the punishment of the Day of Resurrection. We ask Allah for well-being.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the sleeper is not held accountable for his deeds, neither for good nor for evil. From where is this derived? Because when Allah called sleep a death, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «When a person dies, his deeds are cut off except for three»[[Recorded by Muslim (1631/14) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]]. Accordingly, if the sleeper sees that he is praying, is a reward for the prayer written for him? No. And if he sees that he is being killed, the sin of killing is not written upon him, because he is not legally accountable (mukallaf).

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the description of Allah with withholding and releasing; He withholds and He releases. We have explained earlier that the attributes of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, are divided into categories. One category is what is known from His names, such as forgiveness from "the Forgiving" and mercy from "the Merciful." The second is what is stated concerning Him in His essence but is not among the names, such as—?
* Student: Istiwa' (settling) over the Throne.
* Shaykh: Like istiwa', the Throne. This is stated, but it is not among His names; it is an attribute and not one of Allah's names: ﴿Then He settled upon the Throne﴾ [Al-A'raf 54]. And like "creating" (sun') ﴿the handiwork of Allah, who perfected everything﴾ [An-Naml 88], and "doing" (fi'l): ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the Doer of what He intends﴾ [Hud 107], and what is similar to these. And among them is what is reported about Him even if it is not mentioned in the Book and the Sunnah; but it is reported about Him. The scholars say that this too is divided into two categories:
One category does not befit Allah, and reporting it about Him is not permissible.
The other category does not contradict His perfection, and there is no harm in it, because the scope of reporting (khabar) is broader than the scope of creating a description (insha'). For example, if someone says, "Allah is Willing," we say: Yes, you may describe Allah with it. First, because Allah described Himself with willing in His saying: ﴿Allah intends for you ease﴾ [Al-Baqarah 185], and ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 82]. Second, because willing is an attribute that does not contradict the perfection of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the perfection of Allah's acts, since they are orderly and determined, by His saying: ﴿until a specified term﴾ [Az-Zumar 42].

* Among its benefits: no one can remain forever in this world. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿until a specified term﴾, a determined term, not an endless one.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that what results from the two deaths contains signs that indicate the perfection of Allah: the perfection of His oneness, the perfection of His sovereignty, the perfection of His management; by His saying: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾ [Az-Zumar 42].

* Among its benefits: the encouragement to reflect, and that it is the key to knowledge; by His saying: ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾ for whom? ﴿for a people who reflect﴾. Reflection is only on the signs of Allah and the meanings of His names and attributes. As for the reality of the attributes or the reality of the Essence, you should not reflect on them. For this reason it is narrated: «Reflect upon the blessings (ala') of Allah», i.e., His favors, «and do not reflect upon His Essence»[[Recorded by al-Tabarani in al-Awsat (6319) from the hadith of Ibn Umar.]]. This is because reflecting on the Essence of Allah leads to abysses of darkness, sometimes leads to doubt, and sometimes leads to ta'til (denial of the attributes). This is what harmed the people of ta'til: reflecting on the Essence. The Essence cannot be encompassed, and what cannot be encompassed, reflecting on it is a waste of time, and in the matter of lordship it is dangerous to a person's creed. You reflect on the signs of Allah, on His names and His attributes in terms of their meanings. But you cannot reflect on the exalted Essence itself. What would you imagine? For this reason, it is obligatory to turn away from this matter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verses 43–44 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Or have they taken intercessors besides Allah?﴾ [az-Zumar 43]. Here "am" (أم) is *munqati'a* (disjunctive, lit. "cut off"). For this reason it is to be interpreted as "bal" (بل, "rather") together with the interrogative hamza (الهمزة), meaning that it carries the sense of "bal" and the hamza. Our saying "munqati'a" implies that there is a counterpart to this meaning, and that is the case. The counterpart is *muttasila* (connective), and at this point we need to distinguish between the disjunctive and the connective. The distinction between them is in two respects. In the Arabic language, "bal" comes in two types, connective and disjunctive. The difference between them is that disjunctive "am" has no *mu'adil* (correspondent), meaning that no correspondent is mentioned with it, unlike connective "am", which requires a correspondent. So the words of the Exalted: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [al-Baqarah 6]. What is this? It is connective. Why? Because the correspondent is mentioned: ﴿whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾. Good. And like His words: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Rather, they do not believe﴾ [at-Tur 33]. This is disjunctive, because it means "bal" (rather): "Rather, do they say he invented it?" Since no correspondent is mentioned in it, it is disjunctive.

The second difference between them is that connective "am" means "aw" (أو, "or"), while disjunctive "am" means "bal" together with the hamza. In ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [al-Baqarah 6], if "aw" were placed after it, that would be the meaning: "whether you warn them or do not warn them". Disjunctive "am" means "bal" with the hamza, not "aw". Let us apply this difference to what we have here: ﴿Or have they taken intercessors besides Allah?﴾ [az-Zumar 43]. What is it then? It is disjunctive. Firstly, because no correspondent is mentioned. Secondly, because it is to be interpreted as "bal" with the hamza.

﴿Besides Allah﴾ means "other than Him". "Dun" (دون) here means "siwa" (سوى, "other than"), not "dun" in the sense of rank; rather, "dun" means "siwa". ﴿Besides Allah﴾ means "other than Allah". The verb "ittakhadha" (اتخذ, "to take") here takes two objects. The first is "shufa'a" (intercessors), and the second is "min dunillah" (besides Allah). That is, they have taken, besides Allah, [things as] intercessors. It is also permissible to say that the first object is omitted, its implied form being "ālihah" (gods), and the second is "shufa'a" (intercessors). That is, they have taken objects of worship which they worship, claiming that they are intercessors for them with Allah. Allah the Exalted said about them: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to Allah in position﴾ [az-Zumar 3]. So they openly declared that they worship these deities, but they want them to bring them closer to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Glory be to Allah! How can one take as a means to draw near to Allah those whom one disobeys Allah about? This is from their foolishness.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: (﴿intercessors﴾ with Allah, according to their claim). The plural "shufa'a" is of "shafi'" (intercessor). The *shafi'* is one who mediates on behalf of another to bring about a benefit or to repel a harm. Intercession for the people of the Gathering (on the Day of Judgment), when distress and grief befall them, is that Allah judges between them, which is repelling a harm. Intercession for the people of Paradise is that they enter it, which is bringing about a benefit. This is intercession. Intercession means that you mediate for someone else, for what? For bringing about a benefit or repelling a harm. Intercession is, without doubt, good: ﴿Whoever intercedes with a good intercession will have a share of it﴾ [an-Nisa' 85], except in some circumstances, such as intercession concerning a *hadd* (prescribed punishment) once it has reached the ruler. Whoever intercedes to prevent one of the prescribed punishments of Allah has indeed opposed Allah in His command, and when the *hudud* (prescribed punishments) reach the ruler, then Allah curses both the intercessor and the one for whom intercession is made. So these people who worship idols claim that they are intercessors. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: "Even though they possess nothing and do not understand?"﴾ [az-Zumar 43]. That is: do you take them as intercessors while they possess nothing, neither intercession nor anything other than intercession? Here He said: ﴿they possess nothing﴾, and "shay'an" (شيئًا, "anything") is indefinite in a negative context, so it is general. The context would have required that He say: "even though they do not possess intercession", but He used the general form to show that these idols bring no benefit at all: they do not intercede, nor do they repel. Intercession has been denied to them because they are included in the generality; that is, they possess neither intercession nor anything else. Yes. ﴿Even though they possess nothing and do not understand?﴾ [az-Zumar 43]. Here "awalaw" (أولو) contains a conjunction after the hamza, and we have mentioned many times what the grammarians say about this construction. Who will recall what we have said? When a conjunction comes after the interrogative hamza, what do the grammarians say in its *i'rab* (grammatical analysis)? We have gone over this many times.

*Student:* We said that the waw is a conjunction joining it to the preceding clause.

*Shaykh:* That the conjunction is joining to what precedes it.

*Student:* And the implied form is: "wa-alaw" (and "alaw").

*Shaykh:* "Wa-alaw"? Or "aw".

*Student:* (...).

*Shaykh:* This is what he said.

*Student:* (...) with an implied verb.

*Shaykh:* Or the hamza stays in its place, and the conjunction joins something implied that suits the context. We have mentioned that the second view is that of the Basrans and the first is that of the Kufans, and we have mentioned that the view that the conjunction joins to what precedes it is preferable, because it spares you the need for an implied element, and because sometimes a person cannot work out the appropriate thing to supply. If he says: the hamza is interrogative and the waw is a conjunction, and what follows it is joined to what precedes, he is relieved. Here He said: ﴿Even though they possess nothing﴾ [az-Zumar 43]. According to the view that the conjunction joins to an implied element, one says: "Do they take them as intercessors, even though they possess nothing?"

According to the second view, one says: the waw is a conjunction, and what it joins is what precedes in the sentence.

﴿Even though they possess nothing and do not understand﴾ [az-Zumar 43]. What do they not understand? That is, they do not understand that you worship them. Idols are stones that know nothing. Nor do they understand anything of intercession by which they could benefit. So they are ignorant of their own situation and ignorant of what they deserve.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: "To Allah belongs all intercession."﴾ [az-Zumar 44]. Who is addressed by "say"? The Messenger of Allah ﷺ, or anyone who is capable of being addressed and whose address is valid. The latter is more general than the former, because it includes the Prophet ﷺ and others.

Well then, He says: ﴿Say﴾, O addressee who is fit to be addressed, ﴿To Allah belongs all intercession﴾. "To Allah belongs intercession" is a declarative sentence that conveys restriction (*hasr*). What is its method? Brother?

*Student:* The operator has been placed first.

*Shaykh:* No, there is no operator.

*Student:* (...) a prepositional phrase. That the predicate has been placed first...

*Shaykh:* That the predicate has been placed first, while its proper place is later. Every fronting of what should be delayed conveys restriction. Well then, "to Allah belongs intercession", not to anyone else. He is the One who possesses it. The "li-" (لِ, "to") in His words ﴿li-llah﴾ denotes ownership. That is, He is the One who possesses intercession, meaning He possesses the authority to permit it. Allah, glory be to Him, has explained that intercession has three conditions:

The first condition: His permission, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah 255].

The second condition: His pleasure with the intercessor, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿On the Day when the Spirit and the angels will stand in rows, they will not speak except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted and who speaks what is correct﴾ [an-Naba' 38].

The third: His pleasure with the one for whom intercession is made, as in His words: ﴿And how many an angel there is in the heavens whose intercession will not avail at all except after Allah gives permission to whom He wills and approves﴾ [an-Najm 26]. This also serves as evidence that Allah's pleasure with the intercessor is a condition. And He said: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya' 28]. So the conditions for Allah's acceptance of intercession are three. Count them for us, brother.

*Student:* Permission for the intercessor, pleasure with the one interceded for.

*Shaykh:* Yes.

*Student:* Permission for the one interceded for.

*Shaykh:* No.

*Student:* Permission for the intercession, and pleasure with both of them, the intercessor and the one interceded for...

*Shaykh:* With the intercessor and the one interceded for. These are three. And you know their evidence. ﴿Say: "To Allah belongs all intercession."﴾ [az-Zumar 44]. Now, if I say: "O Messenger of Allah, intercede for me with Allah", is that permissible? It is not permissible, because he does not possess that. He does not intercede for you or for anyone else except by Allah's permission. An example of this is what some of the mujahideen brothers in Afghanistan do: one of them says to another, "Intercede for me with Allah", because the mujahid has intercession if he is killed as a martyr. You find some of his relatives or companions saying, "Intercede for me with Allah." This is not permissible, because he has asked of him what he does not possess. If he says, "Intercede for me", say: "Intercession belongs to whom?" To Allah. Say: "O Allah, grant him intercession for me." There is no harm in that. Ask for intercession from the One who possesses intercession. As for one who does not possess it, do not ask him. That is a question in the wrong place. So intercession belongs to Allah, and if it belongs to Allah, then it is only to be asked of Allah.

And His words: ﴿Say: "To Allah belongs all intercession."﴾ [az-Zumar 44]. "Jami'an" (جميعًا, "all") is a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of "shafa'a" (intercession). What is the meaning of plurality here? Is intercession plural? The answer: yes, intercession is plural. There is intercession in this world and intercession in the Hereafter, intercession for bringing about a benefit and intercession for repelling a harm. So there is no intercession except that which belongs to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. All intercessions belong to Allah. Intercession in this world is, for example, when a person prays for someone. When a person prays for someone, that is intercession. The Prophet ﷺ said: "There is no Muslim man who dies and forty men stand over his funeral prayer, who do not associate anything with Allah, except that Allah accepts their intercession for him"[[Narrated by Muslim (948/59) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas.]]. So a person's supplication for his brother is intercession for him with Allah. This is intercession in this world.

Intercession in the Hereafter is well known. The intercession in the Hereafter, or the Great Intercession (ash-shafa'a al-'uzma), belongs to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and it belongs to no one else. And what is the Great Intercession? It is that the people on that Gathering, as you know from the texts, are barefoot, naked and uncircumcised, their eyes fixed, their hearts like air. The sun draws close to them to the distance of a mile. The sweat bridles some of them. No one turns to anyone else, and no one seeks help from anyone else. ("To whom belongs the dominion today?" "To Allah, the One, the Subduer.") They are afflicted with grief and distress beyond what they can bear. Some of them say to others: "Look for someone who will intercede for us with Allah, so that we may find rest from this station." They go to Adam, then to Noah, then to Abraham, then to Moses, then to Jesus, and they obtain nothing. Then they come to Muhammad ﷺ, and he asks permission. They ask him for intercession, and he does not intercede until he has first asked Allah for permission, because the sovereignty is great and the authority is complete. He asks Allah to grant him permission to intercede, and He grants it. Then he prostrates beneath the Throne, a long prostration, and Allah opens to him praises that he had not known before. Then he intercedes with Allah that He judge among creation and give them rest from this station, and Allah accepts his intercession. This intercession is called the Great Intercession, because of its generality and the intensity of the need for it. It belongs only to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and it falls under His words: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾ [al-Isra' 79], because in this station the first and the last will praise him, both those of his nation and those who are not of his nation.

In it there is also intercession for those who have entered the Fire, that they may be brought out of it, and for those who deserve it, that they may not enter it. This intercession is of two kinds: intercession for those who have entered it, that they be brought out, and intercession for those who deserve it, that they not enter it. This is general, for the Messengers, the truthful ones, the martyrs, the righteous, the angels, and mankind in general.

However, two groups of the misguided sects within this Ummah deny it: who are they? The Mu'tazilites and the Khawarij. Why? Because they say that the perpetrator of a major sin is eternally in the Fire, sentenced to that by decree and destiny, and if that is so, this decree will not be reversed, and they cannot come out of the Fire. Do you understand? Well then. The Great Intercession is for the one who deserves the Fire so that he does not enter it, and for the one who has entered it so that he is brought out.

The fourth intercession: concerning entry into Paradise. When people cross the Sirat (the bridge over Hell) (may Allah make me and you among those who cross it safely), when they cross the Sirat they do not enter Paradise immediately, but are held back at a *qantarah* (bridge-span), which is the end of the bridge that lies over the Fire, or something else; Allah knows best. Then retribution is exacted from some of them against others. This is *qisas al-tanqiya* (retribution for purification), whereas the retribution earlier on the plain of Resurrection is *qisas al-takhliya* (retribution for clearance). That is: today, on the plain of Resurrection, justice is exacted for the wronged from the wrongdoer. But this is retribution for purification. What does purification mean? It means that the rancour and hatred in their hearts are removed. Because the settlement of a person's right does not necessarily remove the enmity and hatred in his heart. Is that right? Does settling a person's right remove the enmity and hatred in his heart? Yes, perhaps and perhaps not. I might say: "He wronged me, and now I have taken my right from him, but the effect of that aggression remains in my heart." Is that not so? This exists, brothers, no one denies it. But the one who is successful strives to remove it. Yet it must remain: the mark of a wound must remain even when it has healed. If a wound heals, does the thing return to how it was? It leaves marks. Aggression must leave its effect, even if a person takes retribution for himself against another person's heart. So when they exact retribution from one another on the plain of Resurrection and cross the Sirat, they need purification: their hearts are cleansed and purified, so that they enter Paradise with no rancour in their hearts, in the most perfect way.

Well then, after retribution has been exacted between them, they also do not enter Paradise immediately. They find the gates of Paradise closed, so they ask for someone to intercede for them, and the Prophet ﷺ intercedes specifically. This is specific to the Messenger, but it is not the Great Intercession, nor is it the greatest, because it is for the people of Paradise specifically. He intercedes that the gates of Paradise be opened, and he is given permission, and the gates of Paradise are opened. The first of creation to enter it is he, peace and blessings be upon him. The first of the nations to enter it is his nation, immediately after the Prophets. The Prophets first, then the nations. The leader of the Prophets is Muhammad ﷺ, and the leader of the nations is this Ummah, because this Ummah, praise be to Allah, comes late in time in this world, but it is foremost in all the stations of the Hereafter. The Prophet ﷺ said: "We are the last, but the foremost on the Day of Resurrection"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (876) and Muslim (855/19) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. So in all the stations, praise be to Allah, we are foremost in crossing the Sirat, in judgment between people, on the plain of Resurrection, in entering Paradise, in everything. We are foremost on the Day of Resurrection in everything. So they enter Paradise.

Reflect on this in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Allah said about the people of the Fire: ﴿until, when they reach it, its gates will be opened﴾ [az-Zumar 71], while they are unwilling to enter it. From the moment they arrive at it, its gates are opened, and they are driven into it with force. As for Paradise, He said: ﴿until, when they reach it and its gates have been opened, and its keepers say to them﴾ [az-Zumar 73]. So His words ﴿and its gates have been opened﴾ indicate that there is something between their arrival and the opening. Those among the scholars who say that the waw here is superfluous, and that the meaning is "until, when they reach it, its gates were opened", are mistaken. I say: glory be to Allah! Do you know the words of Allah better than Allah does? Allah, Mighty and Majestic, distinguishes in the Fire, saying: ﴿when they reach it, it is opened﴾ [az-Zumar 71], and regarding Paradise He says: ﴿until, when they reach it, and its gates have been opened﴾, and you say that this waw is superfluous! This is dangerous. Even more dangerous is the one who said that the waw is the "waw of eight" (waw ath-thamaniya), claiming that there is a waw in the language called the waw of eight. This claim is false. He said: No, I have evidence: ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will substitute for you wives better than you, submissive, faithful, devout, repentant, worshipping, travelling, previously married and virgins﴾ [at-Tahrim 5]. The waw is the waw of eight, because these are eight. We say: who said this? Say instead: "Zayd and Bakr came", the waw is for two? "And Khalid", the waw for three? Keep going. Who told you this? The correct view is that the waw here is conjunctive, and that what it conjoins to is implied. I have explained what it conjoins to, and I explained it from the Sunnah. On this basis, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ has two specific intercessions: the Great Intercession, and the intercession for entry into Paradise.

There is also a special intercession for him that no one else had: his intercession for his uncle Abu Talib. His uncle Abu Talib died upon disbelief and polytheism, may God protect us, and he is in the Fire. But "God permitted His Prophet to intercede for him, so he is in a shallow part of the Fire, and on his feet are two sandals whose heat makes his brain boil."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3885) and Muslim (210 / 360), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]] He has the lightest punishment among the people of the Fire. So, how many kinds of intercession are special to the Messenger ﷺ? Three kinds. God, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Say: To God belongs all intercession﴾ [Az-Zumar 44]. He is the One who grants it to whom He wills and withholds it from whom He wills. And He has explained the conditions. What are they?
* Student: Permission, His approval of the intercessor, and His approval of the one interceded for.
* Shaykh: Permission, His approval of the intercessor, and His approval of the one for whom intercession is made.
* Student: We said, O Shaykh, that applying a name to God, Exalted is He, without a textual basis is not permitted. As for the expression (...).
* Shaykh: It is permitted, except what is not fitting for God.
* Student: But, O Shaykh, applying (...) to God, Exalted is He, is an overstepping against God.
* Shaykh: No. Informing about Him is broader than naming Him. I do not want to describe God with this in an absolute sense.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, not in an absolute sense. Only what God has described Himself with, in an absolute sense.
* Student: So we do not describe Him (...).
* Shaykh: We do not describe Him in an absolute sense, but we report about Him. For example, the word "existent" (mawjud). "Existent" is not in the Qur'an or the Sunnah. Is it correct to say, "God exists"? Yes, without doubt it is correct, even though He is not described except as "Living, Self-Subsisting, All-Hearing, All-Seeing." And strangely, what people most often seek help with, or some people do, is saying, "God exists." If someone wrongs them, they say, "God exists." This is not the correct approach.
* Student: O Protector (ya Satir).
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, and "O Protector." "God exists." Does this help anyone? "God is a just Judge," this is what helps. Otherwise, for example, "The sultan exists," will he help you? He may help you and he may not. So the word "existent" does not mean help. For this reason we say to some people: be careful with this word. Do not say, "God exists." Say, "God is a just Judge, God is not unaware of what you do, God takes vengeance on the wrongdoer," and similar things.
* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan: ﴿And when God alone is mentioned, the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter shrink; but when those besides Him are mentioned, behold, they rejoice. Say: O God, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You will judge between Your servants concerning that over which they used to differ. And if those who did wrong possessed whatever is on earth entirely and the like of it with it, they would surely ransom themselves with it from the evil of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection. And there will appear to them from God that which they had not expected. And there will appear to them the evils of what they earned, and there will envelop them that which they used to ridicule﴾ [Az-Zumar 45–48].
* Shaykh: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan. God, Exalted is He, says: ﴿Or have they taken intercessors besides God? Say: Even though they possess nothing and do not understand?﴾ [Az-Zumar 43]. What is (am) here?
* Student: (am) here is disjunctive (munqati'a), meaning (bal) ("rather").
* Shaykh: Disjunctive, meaning (bal), and the hamza (interrogative) is there. What is the difference between disjunctive (am) and its counterpart?
* Student: Disjunctive (am) is not preceded by a mention of alternatives, and it is used for a statement of fact. Connective (am) is preceded by a mention of alternatives.
* Shaykh: And it is used with the meaning of...
* Student: "Or" (aw).
* Shaykh: It is used with the meaning of (aw), like the disjunctive.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: And other things.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: What comes before it? ﴿Or do you ask them for payment?﴾ [At-Tur 40].
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: This is disjunctive. Now, connective. Give an example of connective.
* Student: The saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [Al-Baqarah 6].
* Shaykh: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [Al-Baqarah 6]. The saying of God, Exalted: ﴿Say: To God belongs all intercession﴾ [Az-Zumar 44]. This sentence contains restriction (hasr). By what means?
* Student: Its means is that God, Glorified and Exalted...
* Shaykh: It is not needed. This is not a sermon. One word.
* Student: Because the predicate...
* Shaykh: Subhan Allah!
* Student: Fronting of the complement (...).
* Shaykh: There is no complement here.
* Student: "To God is the intercession," "to God" is the predicate.
* Shaykh: Yes, fronting of the predicate. Now why was fronting the predicate useful for restriction?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No. You have a rule for this. There is a rule for which this is an example.
* Student: We said: fronting what should be delayed conveys restriction.
* Shaykh: Fronting what should be delayed conveys restriction. Good. His saying: ﴿Say: To God belongs all intercession﴾ [Az-Zumar 44], the word "all" (jami'an) indicates that there are kinds of intercession. Brother?
* Student: There are types of intercession: the Great Intercession...
* Shaykh: What is the intercession special to the Messenger ﷺ?
* Student: It is his intercession for his community to enter Paradise.
* Shaykh: His intercession for the people of Paradise that they enter Paradise. That is one. And the second?
* Student: Intercession for the people of the Standing Place (al-mawqif) to settle matters among them, and this is the Great Intercession.
* Shaykh: Well done. It is the Great Intercession for the people of the Standing Place, that judgment be passed among them.
* Student: The intercession for his uncle Abu Talib.
* Shaykh: The intercession for his uncle Abu Talib. Good. This is special to the Messenger ﷺ. What is our evidence that the intercession for his uncle is special to him?
* Student: Because it is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he interceded for his uncle.
* Shaykh: That is not sufficient.
* Student: The saying of the Messenger ﷺ: "Had it not been for me, he would be in the lowest level of the Fire."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6208) and Muslim (209 / 357), from the hadith of al-Abbas.]]
* Shaykh: Yes, this is evidence that he interceded for him. But what is the evidence that it is special to him?
* Student: The saying of God, Exalted: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 28], and God approved his intercession.
* Shaykh: The saying of God, Exalted: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 28]. God does not approve of intercession for a disbeliever, so this is excepted. And His saying: ﴿So the intercession of intercessors will not benefit them﴾ [Al-Muddaththir 48], and this is excepted. Therefore, it is special to him.
* * *
God, Exalted, says. We are now at the beginning of the new lesson: ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth; then to Him you will be returned﴾ [Az-Zumar 44]. This sentence contains restriction, which is fronting of what should be delayed. Here the predicate is fronted: ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens﴾, meaning, not to anyone else.
His saying: ﴿the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ includes dominion over their essences, meaning dominion over the very existence of the heavens and the earth, and dominion of disposal over them. He disposes of them as He wills. He is the One who brought them into being, and He is the One who holds them lest they cease. He is the One who manages what is in them, and He is the One who will destroy and annihilate them at the establishment of the Hour.
The saying of God, Exalted: ﴿And those who do not intercede except for whom He approves﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 28]: God does not approve of intercession for a disbeliever, so this is excepted. And His saying: ﴿So the intercession of intercessors will not benefit them﴾ [Al-Muddaththir 48], and this is excepted. Therefore it is special to them.
