If we state this benefit, a question arises: does it mean that we should abandon the means? No, rather we take the means to extend provision so that we avoid its restriction. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿It is He who made the earth docile for you, so walk through its regions and eat of His provision﴾ [Al-Mulk 15]. He commanded us to walk through its regions and eat of His provision, because when we walk through the regions and strive in the means of provision, we obtain and eat of His provision.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the completeness of Allah's dominion and authority, from His words: ﴿extends﴾ and ﴿restricts﴾. This indicates perfection of sovereignty and authority, and that He, the Exalted, has no opponent.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: faith is a means to guidance and to recognizing the signs, from His words: ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe﴾ [Az-Zumar 52]. When this ruling is tied to this attribute, the principle is that whatever is tied to an attribute grows strong with its strength and weakens with its weakness. This is the principle: every ruling tied to an attribute grows strong with its strength and weakens with its weakness. Thus, whenever faith grows stronger, there appear to a person more of Allah's signs than appear to him when his faith is weak. And whenever faith weakens, a person's recognition and perception of the signs that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sends down through revelation and that He decrees through destiny become weaker.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say, "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah"﴾ [Az-Zumar 53]. ﴿Say﴾ means: convey to My servants this matter, convey to them that I say: "O My servants." It is not correct for us to say: "Say, you, O Muhammad: O My servants," thereby attributing servanthood to yourself. No, the meaning is: convey to My servants that I say: "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves." Why did we adopt this interpretation?

Because if the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the people, "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves," the speech would not be coherent. Rather, the meaning is: say to the people, that is, convey to them that I say: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾. Another reading is: ﴿do not despair﴾ [taqnatu]. His words ﴿O My servants﴾ include servants in the specific sense and servants in the general sense; that is, even the disbelievers may be addressed with this speech.

His words ﴿who have transgressed against themselves﴾ mean: they exceeded the limit in caring for their souls. The duty of a person in caring for his soul is to care for it as it deserves, by doing what improves it and avoiding what corrupts it. If he does not do so, he has transgressed against himself. For example: a man who steals; this theft is transgression against himself, because the duty is to protect oneself from theft. A man who drinks wine; this is transgression against himself. A man who prostrates to an idol; this is transgression against himself, because it is going beyond the limit.

﴿Do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾. Al-qunut and al-yas are close in meaning, but they distinguished between them by saying that al-qunut is a stronger form of despair. As for yas, it is well known that it is the absence of hope and the absence of expectation of obtaining a thing. ﴿Do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾: of Allah's mercy toward you. So, is "mercy" here attributed to the agent or to the object?

* Students: To the agent.

* The Shaykh: To the agent, that is, the mercy of Allah toward you. And how does mercy come about?

Mercy comes about when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, guides a man to repentance and seeking forgiveness and accepts his repentance. So you should not despair of Allah's mercy, neither for yourself nor for others, but take the means. If someone who transgresses against himself says: "I do not despair of Allah's mercy," yet he persists in sin and continues upon it, we say: this is a mistake, because if you persist in sin, you are secure from Allah's plan. Both extremes are blameworthy: neither despair of Allah's mercy nor feeling secure from Allah's plan. Rather, we say: take the means, take the means, and do not despair of Allah's mercy.

(﴿Indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾ for whoever repents from shirk ﴿Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾.) ﴿Indeed, Allah forgives sins﴾: ﴿forgives﴾ means He covers them and overlooks them. That is because forgiveness (maghfirah) is derived from what?

* Students: From ghafr.

* The Shaykh: From ghafr.

* A student: (...) derived.

* The Shaykh: (...) the derivation of maghfirah.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, from maghfar. The maghfar is what is placed on the head during battle in order to protect it from arrows, and it is known that this helmet provides covering and protection. Accordingly, when you say: "My Lord, forgive me," you are not asking Allah only to cover your sins, but asking Allah to cover them and overlook them. So His words ﴿Indeed, Allah forgives sins﴾ mean He covers them and overlooks them. As for His words "the sins" (adh-dhunub), is this form general or specific?

* The student: General.

* The Shaykh: General. "The sins" — and He emphasized this generality with His words ﴿all﴾.

﴿Indeed, Allah forgives sins, all of them﴾. Is this forgiveness which Allah the Exalted affirmed inclusive of every sin? The answer: yes, it includes every sin for the one who repents. Whoever repents, Allah accepts his repentance. Do you not see His words, the Exalted: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, nor commit unlawful sexual intercourse — and whoever does that will meet a penalty. Its punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide therein in humiliation, except for those who repent and believe and do righteous work; for those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good ones﴾ [Al-Furqan 68–70]. These combined shirk with the killing of a soul, which is aggression against lives, and fornication, which is aggression against honor and morals; yet if they repent, Allah accepts their repentance.

Scholars have unanimously agreed that this verse concerns those who repent, because Allah says ﴿Indeed, Allah forgives sins, all of them﴾ without restriction, so it concerns the repentant. As for those who do not repent, Allah the Exalted says concerning them: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [An-Nisa' 48]. So for those who do not repent, we are certain that Allah does not forgive shirk in their case, and what is less than shirk is under His will: if He wills, He punishes, and if He wills, He forgives. Thus a person has two states:

The first state: repentance. What is the ruling on his sin then?

* A student: Forgiveness.

* The Shaykh: Forgiveness, however great the sin. The second state: non-repentance.

* A student: Non-repentance (...) due to the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that﴾ [An-Nisa' 48]. As for the rest of the sins (...).

* The Shaykh: How we have understood so far, the answer is not well arranged.

* The student: The major sins (...), so Allah the Exalted forgives them.

* The Shaykh: Major sins, even below shirk?

* The student: Shirk.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: As for what is below shirk, it is under His will.

* The Shaykh: Under His will, exactly. That is, without repentance we say: shirk is certainly not forgiven, and what is below shirk is under His will. And those who transgress against themselves with sins cite as evidence the verse we mentioned: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾. So when you forbid them from a sin, they say to you: ﴿but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾.

We say to him plainly: Do you assert that you are among those whom Allah wills to forgive? The answer: No. Then you are in danger, and you have now done the cause of punishment, and whether you will be forgiven is a matter that rests with the will of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿Indeed, Allah forgives sins, all of them. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾. First, in this sentence, the phrase ﴿Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾: if this phrase were deleted, the sentence would be coherent without it. What is the word?

* Students: "Huwa" (He).

* The Shaykh: "Huwa." ﴿Indeed, He is the Forgiving﴾: the word "huwa" is called by the grammarians a separating pronoun (damir fasl), and some call it an 'imad (support).

* A student: The pronoun of the matter (damir ash-shan)?

* The Shaykh: No, it is not the pronoun of the matter. So what is the benefit of this pronoun?

They say: this pronoun has three benefits. The first benefit: emphasis. The second benefit: restriction. The third benefit: distinguishing between the predicate and the attribute. An example: if you say, "Zayd huwa al-fadil" (Zayd is the excellent one), the pronoun in "huwa" is a separating pronoun. If you say, "Zayd al-fadil" and delete the pronoun.

* Students: It is coherent.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 39, verses 49–60 (part 2 of 7):**

* The Shaykh: The sentence is complete, but it is possible that (al-fadil, "the virtuous one") is an attribute and the predicate is still awaited. It is also possible that (al-fadil) is the predicate. Isn't that so? If you say: Zayd is the virtuous one (zayd huwa al-fadil), the first possibility is removed, namely that (al-fadil) is an attribute, and the second possibility is fixed, namely that it is a predicate. Is this clear, everyone?
Good. What did we gain from this construction? "Zayd huwa al-fadil." First, we gain the affirmation of virtue in Zayd. Second, we gain the restriction of virtue to him. And third?
* A student: Distinguishing between the attribute and the predicate.
* The Shaykh: Distinguishing between the attribute and the predicate. That is, now we no longer have the possibility that it is an attribute. This is the semantic aspect of the separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl). As for its grammatical status (i'rab), is it a noun or a particle? The correct view is that it is a particle with no grammatical position (maḥall), a particle that has taken the form of a noun and has no grammatical position. The evidence that it has no grammatical position is abundant in the Quran and outside it. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Perhaps we will follow the sorcerers, if they are the victors﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 40]. For if it had a grammatical position, its position would be nominative (raf') and what follows would be the predicate. But it has no grammatical position; rather, it came as a support ('imad) or as a separator (faṣl).
* A student: The earlier words of Allah: ﴿but most of them do not know﴾. The author says in the margin that it indicates that the intended meaning of "man" (al-insan) is the species. How did he derive this?
* The Shaykh: The point is that when He said "most of them do not know," this implies that there are some who know, namely the believers. So "akthharahum" (most of them) indicates that the intended meaning is the species, because all non-believers do not know.
* A student: Is that the preferred view, Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: We have already mentioned that the preferred view is that it refers to the disbeliever. The answer to this is that among the disbelievers there are those who know but are arrogant.
* A student: What is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n)?
* The Shaykh: The pronoun of the matter is the pronoun that indicates a story and is not present. The pronoun of the matter is usually omitted.
* A student: Among the believers there are people who, when a blessing comes to them, say: "I was given it only on knowledge I have." These are believers, but deficient in faith. This does not support that the intended meaning of "man" is the species.
* The Shaykh: Yes?
* The student: The intended meaning of "man" is the species, believer and disbeliever alike. Even the believer says: "I was given it only on knowledge I have," but he would be...
* The Shaykh: Yes, but he is a disbeliever by this statement. He is not a disbeliever in a way that expels him from the religion. We say: by this statement he is a disbeliever, and he may be a disbeliever in a way that expels him from the religion, if he believes that Allah has no causal role in the occurrence of this blessing, and that it came about by him and not that he is a means. Then it is disbelief, because attributing blessings to their causes while turning away from the Causer, who is Allah, and claiming or believing that this blessing has no connection with Allah, this is disbelief in lordship (kufr bil-rububiyya).
* A student: If a person repents from a sin, can he be certain that Allah the Mighty and Majestic has accepted his repentance, so that there are no (...) impediments to repentance?
* The Shaykh: We say: Yes. If you repent with sincere repentance (tawba nasuha), Allah accepts it. But who can say that his repentance is sincere? The problem lies in the action of the servant, not the action of the Lord. When the servant's action is what pleases Him, His promise is fulfilled, because Allah does not break His promise. But what is subject to doubt is the action of the servant: is this repentance sincere according to what the Sharia has laid down? So we are certain of the principle, but there may be some defect in a person's heart. He may have some showing off (riya'), some reminding Allah of his favors (mann 'ala Allah), and other causes, and his repentance is not sincere. For example, a person repents from looking at a non-related woman, but he does not repent from touching a non-related woman. Is the first repentance accepted or not?
* A student: No, it is not accepted.
* The Shaykh: No, it is not accepted, because he did not repent from the sin that is of the same kind as his sin. A person may repent from consuming usury of delay (riba al-nasi'a), but he still practices usury of excess (riba al-fadl). This is not sincere repentance. For this reason we say: whoever repents to Allah with sincere repentance, his repentance is accepted, and whoever lacks sincerity in it, his repentance is not accepted (...)

* * *

Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾ [Az-Zumar 53]. What is meant by "israf" (transgression)? "Who have transgressed against themselves."
* A student: They committed crimes (janaw).
* The Shaykh: What?
* The student: They committed crimes (janaw).
* The Shaykh: They committed crimes.
* A student: They wronged (zalamu).
* The Shaykh: They wronged, yes.
* A student: They exceeded the limit in caring for them.
* The Shaykh: Correct: they exceeded the limit in caring for them, and that is by bringing them into sins or depriving them of acts of obedience.
* The Shaykh: Regarding His words ﴿do not despair﴾, what is its meaning?
* A student: Qunut is the most extreme despair.
* The Shaykh: Qunut is the most extreme despair. Good, so the meaning is: do not despair of the mercy of Allah.
The sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾: where does it stand in relation to what precedes it?
* The student: (...)
* The Shaykh: No. I think we did not mention it? Good. Is this verse about all sinners in general?
* A student: This is about those who repent.
* The Shaykh: About those who repent. The exegetes unanimously agreed that it refers to those who repent. What is the situation of those who do not repent, brother?
* A student: Those who do not repent?
* The Shaykh: Yes, what is their situation?
* The student: It differs.
* The Shaykh: Yes, it differs. How does it differ?
* The student: Their situation is in the verse we mentioned in Surah An-Nisa, His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿for whom He wills﴾. Well done, that is their situation.
His words: ﴿Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾. What is the meaning of "al-Ghafur" (the Forgiving)?
* A student: Al-Ghafur is the One who covers the sin and overlooks it.
* The Shaykh: Well done. Why did you add "and overlooks it"?
* The student: (...)
* The Shaykh: May Allah bless you.
Now we take the new lesson. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy﴾. Last night we raised a difficulty concerning His words ﴿Say: O My servants﴾. Does this mean that Allah commanded the Messenger to say "O My servants"?
* A student: (...)
* The Shaykh: He conveys to them that Allah says: "O My servants who have transgressed."
* A student: (...)
* The Shaykh: Good.
The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah; indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾ [Az-Zumar 53]. The position of this sentence relative to what precedes it is that it gives the reason for the prohibition of despair. That is, "do not despair, for indeed Allah forgives all sins if you seek His forgiveness." ﴿Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾. We have already explained this verse. Now we will take its benefits.
* A student: (...)
* The Shaykh: Good. Let us return to the words of the commentator, may Allah have mercy on him. He said: (﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair﴾, with the letter nun pronounced with a kasra and with a fatha). These are two canonical (sab'iyya) readings. The author's practice, may Allah have mercy on him, is that when he says something like this, meaning "with two vowels," or says "and it is read," the reading is canonical. But when he says "and it was read" (wa-qari'a), the reading is irregular (shadhdh). So there are two canonical readings: with a fatha on the nun and with a kasra on the nun.
﴿do not despair of the mercy of Allah; indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾. Yes?
* A student: And it was read with a damma.
* The Shaykh: And it was read with a damma: (la taqnuṭu), and this reading is irregular, meaning it is not canonical.
The scholars differed about readings other than the canonical ones: is it permissible for a person to recite with them or not? The correct view is that if they are authentically transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ), then recitation with them is permissible, because the whole Quran is true. So if it is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited with this reading, it is valid, whether it came through the seven readers or not.
He said: ﴿do not despair of the mercy of Allah; indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾ (﴿indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾ for those who repent from polytheism). Yes, for those who repent from polytheism. Likewise for those who repent from what is less than it. But the author mentioned polytheism because it is the greatest sin, and because it is not forgiven except through repentance. If a person repents from polytheism but remains upon some sins that he used to commit while in disbelief, are these sins forgiven or must they have repentance?
The correct view is that they require repentance, as in the case of someone who drank wine while a disbeliever, then embraced Islam and continued drinking wine. His acceptance of Islam does not cause the sin of drinking wine to be removed from him, because what? Because he did not repent from it. But if he repents from polytheism and does not persist in the other sins, and they do not occur to his mind, then all his sins are forgiven. So the one who repents from polytheism has, in reality, three situations:
Either he is mindful that he repented from polytheism and from all the sins he used to commit. In this case there is no doubt that his repentance covers every sin. Or he repents from polytheism while persisting in some of the sins he used to commit in the state of polytheism. In this case, these sins he persisted in are not forgiven for him, because he continued in them, such as one who was accustomed to drinking wine in his disbelief, then embraces Islam while still persisting in drinking wine. For him, the sins that preceded are not forgiven: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they cease, what has passed will be forgiven them﴾ [Al-Anfal 38].
The third situation: he repents from polytheism, and the remaining sins do not occur to his mind, but he has not committed them since his acceptance of Islam. In this case, what? He is forgiven. All his sins are forgiven, because the small sins are subsumed under the great ones, so all his sins are forgiven.
﴿Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾: the verse ends. His words ﴿Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ give the reason for His words ﴿Indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾, and ﴿Indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾ gives the reason for His words ﴿do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾. So it is a reason for a reason.
* From the benefits of this noble verse: Allah the Mighty and Majestic's concern for this matter, that is, conveying to His servants that He forgives all sins. Yes.
Allah's concern with this sentence, or this matter, is evident in that He commanded His Prophet with a specific command to convey this matter to people. Pay attention: the whole Quran was commanded by the Prophet (ﷺ) to convey: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 67]. But there are particular matters that Allah specifies for him to convey, and this requires attention to them, such as: ﴿Say to the believing men that they lower their gaze﴾ [An-Nur 30], ﴿And say to the believing women that they lower their gaze﴾ [An-Nur 31], ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾. This is a specific charge that the Messenger (ﷺ) should convey to the Ummah, so this requires attention to it. Pay attention to this point, which perhaps has not passed you in recent times. I say: when Allah issues a ruling with "Say" (qul), it is evidence of what?
* Students: Of attention.
* The Shaykh: Of attention to it, because this is a command to convey it specifically. As for the Quran in general, he was commanded to convey it in a general way: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾.
* From the benefits of the noble verse: all creatures are the servants of Allah, ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed﴾, because "servants" here means general servitude.
* From the benefits of this noble verse: whoever repents to Allah, Allah accepts his repentance from polytheism and what is less than it, and this is an agreed matter.
However, the scholars differed concerning one who intentionally killed a soul: is there repentance for him? It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that there is no repentance for a murderer. Some scholars adopted this view and said: the murderer has no repentance, even if he repents. But this is not correct, because it contradicts the verses and hadiths indicating the acceptance of the repentance of one who repents from polytheism and what is less than it. The invalidity of this view is shown by Allah's words: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right, nor commit unlawful sexual intercourse—and whoever does that will meet a penalty. The punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide therein in humiliation, except one who repents and believes and does righteous work; for those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good, and ever is Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Al-Furqan 68–70]. Here Allah mentioned killing, mentioned polytheism, and mentioned fornication, and informed that whoever repents, believes, and does righteous work, he will be given more than his repentance, namely that Allah will replace his evil deeds with good deeds.
From the Sunnah is what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) related to us about a man who was extravagant against himself, and killed ninety-nine souls. Then he asked a worshipper among the devout: Is there repentance for me, having killed ninety-nine souls? The worshipper considered this sin monstrous and said: You have no repentance. You kill ninety-nine souls and then come and say: "Is there repentance for me?" You have no repentance. So he killed him, completing the hundred with him. Then he was directed to a scholar, and asked him: I have killed a hundred souls, is there repentance for me? He said: Yes, and who can come between you and repentance! This shows you the virtue of knowledge and the ugliness of ignorance. Ignorance wrought harm upon its possessor, it wrought harm upon his own soul, and this other man despaired of the mercy of Allah, so his recompense was that he was killed. The scholar said to him: "Yes, and who can come between you and repentance? But you are in a village whose people are wrongdoers. Go to such-and-such village, for it is a fertile pasture for you." So he went, and in the course of the journey death came to him. Allah sent to him angels of mercy and angels of punishment, and they disputed. The angels of mercy said: "I will take his soul, for this man came repentant and emigrating." The angels of punishment said: "No, I will take his soul, for he is an extravagant man and did not reach the land to which he was emigrating." So Allah sent to them an arbiter who would judge between them, and said: "Measure the distance between the two villages. To whichever of them he is nearer, he belongs to its people." They measured and found he was nearer to the righteous village by a small amount, about a span.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3470) and Muslim (2766/46), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]] It has been said that he was nearer to the other village, but at the moment of death, out of his strong desire for the good land and its people, he drew himself toward it while in the throes of death, so the angels of mercy took his soul. They said: If this happened in previous nations, then this Ummah is more honored by Allah than the previous nations. How could there be no repentance for the murderer?
So the preferred view is that this verse is general, and even the murderer has repentance. Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, interpreted what was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas in a good manner. He said: intentional killing involves three rights: the right of Allah, the right of the dead person, and the right of his heirs.
As for the right of Allah, it is removed by repentance without any difficulty, and this would not be hidden from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him. As for the right of the dead person, it cannot be removed now in this world, because he has passed from this world, and he will be held to account for his right on the Day of Resurrection. As for the right of the heirs of the slain, it is fulfilled by his surrendering himself to them. If he surrenders himself to them, this is evidence of the sincerity of his repentance and that his obligation is discharged. This is the interpretation Ibn al-Qayyim gave to Ibn 'Abbas's statement.
My view is that if he repents, Allah accepts his repentance even regarding the right of the slain person, and Allah the Mighty and Majestic bears the right of the slain on the Day of Resurrection and satisfies him. This is due to the generality of the evidences indicating that whoever repents from a sin, however great, Allah accepts his repentance. So if this man comes repentant and surrenders himself to the heirs of the slain and says: "I am now before you. If you wish, retaliation, or blood money, or pardon," this is the utmost that he can do. Allah said: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [Al-Baqarah 286]. So the correct view in my opinion is that he is pardoned even regarding the right of the slain, by Allah the Exalted bearing it on the Day of Resurrection.
* From the benefits of this noble verse: Allah's mercy precedes His wrath, by His forgiving all sins through repentance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verse 49–60 (part 3 of 7):

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the judgments of Allah Most High follow from His names and attributes. Are these judgments here punitive (jaza'iyyah), or decreed (qadariyyah), or legislated (shar'iyyah)?
* Students: Punitive.
* The Shaykh: Punitive. They follow from His names and attributes: because He is Forgiving and Merciful, He is the One who forgives, so He forgives those who repent.
* Among its benefits: an indication that a person after repentance may be better than he was before it and before committing the sin, based on His saying: ﴿the Most Merciful﴾; for mercy entails a new bestowal. This is what is observed. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned of Adam that when he disobeyed his Lord, went astray, and repented, He said: ﴿Then his Lord chose him, accepted his repentance, and guided him﴾ [Ta-Ha 122]. This distinction of being chosen and guided was not mentioned for him before. A person also senses this in himself: when he turns back in repentance and regret, he feels within himself a return to Allah and a great need for Him, unlike when he is steadfast in obedience to Allah, when he does not feel the return to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and turning to Him. Sometimes he is afflicted with conceit, thinking he has never sinned. For this reason, the authentic hadith related by Muslim says: «Were you not to sin, Allah would take you away and bring a people who sin and seek Allah's forgiveness, and He would forgive them»[[(2749/11) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].
So we say: when a person repents to Allah, he may after repentance be better than he was before it. Yes, and it may be the reverse. But this is a matter that occurred by decree in the case of Adam, and likewise by legislation, as this verse indicates: ﴿Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾.
He said: ﴿And turn in repentance to your Lord and submit to Him﴾. Turn in repentance to your Lord: repentance (inabah) means complete return to Allah. By what do we return to Allah? By giving up disobedience and joining the ranks of the obedient. That is, repentance is not truly attained except by returning to Allah from disobedience to obedience. Turn in repentance to your Lord. In His saying ﴿to your Lord﴾, the lordship here may be general and may be specific; it is, after repentance, of the specific lordship.
﴿And turn in repentance to your Lord and submit to Him﴾: He says, submit to Him, i.e., yield to Him. Repentance is in the heart, returning to Allah; a person turns in repentance, i.e., returns to Allah. Submit to Him, i.e., yield to Him, because islam, istislam, and this whole root indicate submission. His saying ﴿and submit to Him﴾, the "lam" in (lahu) is for exclusivity (ikhtisas), and we will mention that it indicates the obligation of sincerity (ikhlas).
﴿before the punishment comes upon you, and then you will not be helped﴾: submit to Him before the punishment comes to you in this world, before you expect it. Then, if it comes to you, you will not be helped, i.e., you will not be prevented from this punishment, because Allah Most High says: ﴿When Allah intends harm for a people, there is no repelling it, and they have besides Him no protector﴾ [ar-Ra'd 11], i.e., no one who takes charge to help them. ﴿before the punishment comes upon you, and then you will not be helped﴾.
﴿And follow the best of what has been revealed to you from your Lord before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive﴾: follow, i.e., hold fast to in action, or hold fast to the practice of the best of what was revealed to you from your Lord. Action requires inward action, verbal action, and bodily action; that is, follow in belief, speech, and deed.
His saying ﴿the best of what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾: is "the best" here a description of the action a person performs, or a description of what was revealed?
* Students: A description of what was revealed.
* The Shaykh: Apparently it is a description of what was revealed: the best of what was revealed to you. When we reflect, we will not find anything better than the Qur'an, as is evident in His saying: ﴿And We have revealed to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it of the Scripture and as a guardian over it﴾ [al-Ma'idah 48], i.e., as a overseer, possessing authority. On this view, the superlative here refers to the Book that is followed, and then there is no difficulty. If we say: ﴿follow the best of what has been revealed to you﴾, i.e., do the best of what has been legislated for you. A difficulty remains: we are commanded to follow the best of what was legislated for us, so does that mean that if we do the good but not the best, we are negligent?
We say: this is the apparent meaning of the verse if we interpret it as we have mentioned. But the texts indicate that whoever limits himself to the obligatory has fulfilled the obligation, even if he does not bring the most perfect, even if he does not bring the best. Indeed the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said to the Bedouin man to whom the features of Islam were described: «If he is truthful, he will enter Paradise»[[Related by al-Bukhari (1891) from the hadith of Talhah ibn 'Ubaydullah.]]. And in light of this (i.e., this possibility regarding the verse), we say: the texts indicate that following the good discharges the obligation, but the more perfect is following the best.
﴿what has been revealed to you from your Lord before the punishment comes upon you suddenly﴾: i.e., unexpectedly. "Suddenly" here means unexpectedly; it may be a verbal noun specifying the type, i.e., that the punishment comes in a sudden manner, and it may be a verbal noun in the place of a circumstantial state, i.e., surprising, and the meaning is surprise: the punishment comes upon you by surprise. ﴿while you do not perceive﴾: i.e., you do not reckon that the punishment will befall you, because you are heedless and have no awareness. This is like His saying: ﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them by night while they are asleep? Or do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them in the morning while they are playing? Do they feel secure from the plan of Allah? None feels secure from the plan of Allah except the losing people﴾ [al-A'raf 97–99]. Generally, one who is absorbed in sins forgets the Creator and forgets the punishment, so the punishment comes upon him while he is at his most immersed in sins and luxury.
* In this noble verse there are benefits. First: the obligation of turning in repentance to Allah, based on His saying: ﴿And turn in repentance to your Lord﴾.
* Among its benefits: the obligation of sincerity toward Him, based on His saying: ﴿and submit to Him﴾, and likewise ﴿turn in repentance to your Lord﴾.
* Among its benefits: that submission to Allah must be both outward and inward. Whoever submits his heart to Allah must submit his limbs to Allah, based on the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: «Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh: if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (52) and Muslim (1599/107) from the hadith of an-Nu'man ibn Bashir.]]. Whoever submits outwardly but not inwardly, his submission does not benefit him, like the submission of the hypocrites. Submission may be inward and followed by outward submission, or it may be outward without inward. Can it be inward without outward? No. How could it be inward without outward? Because if his heart submits to Allah, his limbs submit: «Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh...». As for the one who is coerced, his act has no ruling, because the obligation has been lifted from him.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: caution against opposition, caution against the descent of punishment upon opposition, based on His saying: ﴿before the punishment comes upon you﴾. And who is safe from the punishment of Allah? No one is safe. So if you do not hasten to repent to Allah, punishment may descend upon you.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that when punishment descends from Allah, no one can prevent it, based on His saying: ﴿and then you will not be helped﴾. Consider His saying ﴿and then you will not be helped﴾: he used "then" (thumma), which indicates a delay. That is, however much you seek a helper and however long your search lasts, you will not find anyone who can help you against the punishment of Allah.
* Among the benefits of the second verse: the obligation of following the Qur'an, based on His saying: ﴿follow the best of what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾.
* Among its benefits: the prohibition of following other than the Qur'an, since if following the Qur'an is obligatory, its opposite is forbidden.
But if someone asks: do you say that the law of those before us is law for us?
The answer: there is a difference among the scholars of usul (legal theory) on this, and the sound view is that it is law for us as long as our law has not indicated otherwise. We follow the law of those before us not because it was their law, but because our law has guided us to act upon it. The evidences for this are known in usul al-fiqh, among them His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am 90].
Among them His saying: ﴿There has certainly been in their stories a lesson for those of understanding﴾ [Yusuf 111].
Among them His saying: ﴿There has already been for you an excellent example in Abraham and those with him﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 4].
The point is that the preponderant view is that the law of those before us is law for us by our law, as long as our law has not indicated otherwise; if our law indicates otherwise, it is set aside.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Qur'an is the best of what was revealed, because Allah commanded us to follow the best of what was revealed, and we all know that we follow the Qur'an.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that whoever opposes this and does not follow the Qur'an, punishment may come upon him suddenly while he is unaware.
Here we ask: is the punishment the sensory punishment that corrupts the lands, or does it include both sensory and inner (ma'nawi) punishment?
It includes both, without doubt. A person may be punished with an inner punishment whereby his affairs are corrupted, both his religious affairs and his worldly affairs. Allah Most High said: ﴿So for their breaking of their covenant, We cursed them and made their hearts hard; they distort words from their places and have forgotten a portion of what they were reminded of﴾ [al-Ma'idah 13]. This is one of the punishments that is worse than the punishments of this world: that a person be barred from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. This is worse than losing one's wealth and children.
Some of the early generation (salaf), when they slept through the night prayer, said: "I have only been deprived of the night prayer because of a sin." They took the failure to stand in the night as a punishment for a sin he had committed. Whenever sins multiply, and we seek refuge in Allah, turning away from the remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, increases. Allah Most High said: ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his desire, and whose affair is ever in neglect﴾ [al-Kahf 28].
I think we should read the author's words. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (﴿And turn in repentance﴾: return ﴿to your Lord and submit﴾: sincerely act ﴿to Him﴾). His interpreting "submit" as "sincerity" is open to question; islam is submission, and it is yielding to Allah Most High outwardly and inwardly.
And His saying: (﴿before the punishment comes upon you, and then you will not be helped﴾: by its being prevented, if you do not repent). "If you do not repent" refers back to His saying ﴿before the punishment comes upon you﴾, because when we repent, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, lifts the punishment from us.
(﴿And follow the best of what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾: which is the Qur'an). He did not mention the possibility we mentioned, but made the meaning of "the best" here: the best of what was revealed, not the best of what was legislated. Yes.
(﴿before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive﴾: before its coming at its time, so hasten before ﴿a soul says﴾) [az-Zumar 56], and so on.
* Student: (...).
* * *
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾ [az-Zumar 53]. ﴿Say﴾: the address is to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, because it is he to whom this Qur'an was revealed. Know that the whole Qur'an has been addressed to the Prophet ﷺ with "say," but some of it explicitly includes "say," and some does not, because His saying ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah 67] encompasses the whole Qur'an, so it is obligatory upon him to tell people the entire Qur'an. But some verses or rulings begin with "say" for emphasis on that ruling. So here Allah says: ﴿Say﴾, i.e., say, O Muhammad, ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾, i.e., say to them, conveying from Allah, that Allah said: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾. "My servants" here means general servanthood, not specific servanthood, because it includes the believer and the disbeliever.
His saying ﴿who have transgressed against themselves﴾: i.e., they exceeded the limit in their deeds, by disbelief and what is below it. The root of israf is exceeding the limit; transgression against oneself means exceeding the limit in what is obligatory upon you toward Allah, Mighty and Majestic, or toward other creatures.
(﴿do not despair﴾ with the nun vowelled with kasra and with fatha, and it was read with damma). There are three readings: two sab'i (canonical seven) readings and one shadhdh (irregular) reading that is not sab'i, because the terminology of the author of al-Jalalayn: when he says "in a reading," it is sab'i; when he says "it was read," it is shadhdh; when he says "with fatha and damma," both are sab'i; when he says "and it was read," it is shadhdh. So now (taqnutu) has three vowelings on the nun: ﴿taqnitu﴾ ﴿taqnatu﴾ and these two?
* Students: Both canonical.
* The Shaykh: Both canonical. ﴿taqnutu﴾ is shadhdh, and a shadhdh reading is not recited in prayer, but it may be used as evidence in rulings if it is authentic. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: rather, if it is authentic, it is recited in prayer, just as it is used as evidence in rulings.
If someone asks: what is the difference between the shadhdh and the sab'i?
We say: the scholars have established the terminology that what comes through the well-known seven readers is sab'i, and what comes through another channel, even if authentic, is shadhdh according to them. So the shadhdh is what falls outside the seven readings, but it is used as evidence in rulings and is not recited in prayer, except according to the opinion of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, who says: whenever a reading is authentically transmitted from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, it is recited in prayer, even if it is not one of the seven readings.
The author, in explaining ﴿taqnutu﴾, said: (you despair). The correct view is that this explanation is approximate, because qunut is the strongest despair, the highest degree of despair. So the meaning of "taqnutu" is: despair reaches its utmost extent in you ﴿from the mercy of Allah﴾, i.e., from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, having mercy on you, because when a person despairs of and gives up on Allah's mercy, he does not place himself in the way of mercy, since he is in despair. This is why it is said: despair is the key to abandonment. Let me give you an example: try to untie a knot in a thread; when it defeats you, what do you do?
* Students: You leave it.
* The Shaykh: You leave it. When you despair of it, you abandon it. But regarding the mercy of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, do not despair. However many sins and transgressions you commit, do not despair.
Yes: from the mercy of Allah, we said, its meaning is: from Allah having mercy on you. Do not despair of Allah having mercy on you; rather, try to place yourself in His mercy. So here is the prohibition and the reason. The prohibition: ﴿do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾. The reason: ﴿Indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾. "Forgives" is derived from forgiveness (maghfirah), which is covering a sin and overlooking it. This is forgiveness: covering the sin and overlooking it, and not merely covering it, because it is derived from maghfar, which is what is placed on the head in battle for protection. So it combines two things: covering and protection. For example, this ghutrah we do not call maghfar; the skullcap does not count either, though it covers but does not protect. But the iron helmet placed on the head in fighting we call maghfar, why? Because it covers and protects. So forgiveness of sins is covering them and overlooking them. When you say "O Allah, forgive me," you ask Allah for two things: that He cover your sins from others, and second, that He overlook them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verse 49–60 (part 4 of 7):

His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾ includes minor and major sins. For this reason the scholars said: this verse refers to those who repent. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [An-Nisa' 48] refers to those other than the repentant. This is correct, because Allah does not forgive shirk except with repentance. So if we take the generality in His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾, then we must say: to whom does this apply? To those who repent. It is not for every person. The polytheist will certainly not be forgiven by Allah, but if he repents, Allah forgives him, however great his shirk.

﴿Indeed, Allah forgives all sins; indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾: ﴿Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ is a clause giving the reason for the ruling that precedes it, which is ﴿Indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾. The clause here is emphasized by two emphasizers: (inna) and (huwa), ﴿indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾. As for (inna) being an emphasizer, this is clear, because (inna) is one of the particles of emphasis. As for (huwa), it too is one of the particles of emphasis, because it is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl). What is meant by "pronoun of separation"? It separates between the subject and the predicate, it conveys emphasis, it also conveys restriction (ḥaṣr), and it conveys distinction (faṣl), which is distinguishing the predicate from the attribute. So it serves three purposes; that is, the pronoun of separation has three benefits:
The first: emphasis. The second: restriction. The third: distinguishing the attribute from the predicate. What are the benefits?
* Student: Emphasis, restriction, and distinguishing the attribute from the predicate.
* The Shaykh: Good. This becomes clear through an example. If you say: Zayd al-fādil (Zayd the virtuous), then it is possible that (al-fādil) is an attribute of (Zayd), and the predicate comes afterward, as one says: Zayd al-fādil is in the mosque. But if you say: Zayd huwa al-fādil (Zayd is the virtuous one), it becomes necessary that it be a predicate. So now you have distinguished the predicate from the attribute by means of (huwa). Likewise, when you say: Zayd huwa al-fādil, by bringing in (huwa) you have added emphasis, and likewise by bringing in (huwa) you have restricted the virtue to him alone, to the exclusion of others. So His saying, exalted is He: ﴿indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ has two benefits:
The first benefit: emphasis. The second benefit: restriction. As for distinguishing the subject from the predicate, there is no need for it here, because the pronoun (innahu) — they say: a pronoun is not described and does not serve as a description. The pronoun is not described and does not serve as a description. Is that clear? Accordingly, the benefit in His saying, ﴿indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾, is restriction and emphasis.

As for His saying, ﴿the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾: the meaning of forgiveness has already been explained as covering over a sin and overlooking it. ﴿The Merciful﴾: that is, the possessor of mercy by which the sought-after thing is attained, and by forgiveness the feared thing is removed. So combining the two noble names conveys what? It conveys complete happiness: deliverance from what is feared, in His saying?
* Student: ﴿The Forgiving﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿The Forgiving﴾, because this is forgiveness of sin, and attainment of what is sought, in His saying: ﴿The Merciful﴾, because by mercy the sought-after thing and goodness and blessings are attained.
So combining the two noble names conveys what? It conveys complete happiness: deliverance from what is feared, in His saying?
* Student: ﴿The Forgiving﴾ [Az-Zumar 53].
* The Shaykh: ﴿The Forgiving﴾; because this is forgiveness of sin, and attainment of what is sought in His saying: ﴿The Merciful﴾; because by mercy the sought-after thing and goodness and blessings are attained. And with the removal of what is feared and the attainment of what is sought, success is complete.
Allah, majestic and exalted, said: ﴿So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted into Paradise has succeeded﴾ [Ali 'Imran 185]. ﴿Drawn away from the Fire﴾: what is in it?
* Students: Deliverance from what is feared.
* The Shaykh: Deliverance from what is feared. ﴿And admitted into Paradise﴾: attainment of what is sought. ﴿Then he has succeeded.﴾

Now let us return to the benefits of the verse:
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of the Messenger ﷺ to convey this statement from Allah. From where is this taken?
* Students: From ﴿Say﴾ [Az-Zumar 53].
* The Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿Say﴾, because the basic principle in a command is obligation, especially since this is conveying the message, and conveying the message is obligatory.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the importance of this conveyance, lest we despair of Allah's mercy, and that we know that He, majestic and exalted, forgives all sins. From where did we derive its importance? From its being introduced with ﴿Say﴾, because this is a command to convey a specific matter.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the sinner is one who has been excessive against himself and wronged himself; this is from His saying: ﴿who have been excessive against themselves﴾ [Az-Zumar 53]. What supports this is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves﴾ [Hud 101].
It is strange that the one who wrongs himself through disobedience, when asked: "Why?", says: "This is destiny and fate; perhaps Allah will guide me." Do you understand? And if someone strikes him and wrongs him by beating, and he says: "Why do you strike me?" the other replies: "By Allah, brother, this is destiny and fate." Would he be content with this argument?
* Student: He would not be content.
* The Shaykh: He would not be content, yet by wronging himself he is content. This is a strange contradiction. That is, if you wrong yourself you allow yourself to argue by destiny, and if another wrongs you, you do not allow him to argue by destiny. This is injustice in judgment and contradiction. It is said: How are you content to wrong yourself, yet not content for another to wrong you and argue by destiny?
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of despairing of Allah's mercy, because of His saying: ﴿Do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾. The point of evidence is that the basic principle in a prohibition is prohibition. The Sunnah has indicated that despair of Allah's mercy is among the major sins, because it is an assumption unbefitting to Allah, majestic and exalted. For what is fitting for Allah, glorified and exalted, is that whoever turns to Him, He is the Most Generous of the generous and does not disappoint him. So if you despair of His mercy, you have shown contempt toward Him, glorified and exalted. For this reason despair of Allah's mercy is among the major sins.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of mercy for Allah, because of His saying: ﴿Do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾.
Mercy is of two kinds: created and uncreated. What is of bestowal and kindness is created, and what is an attribute of the Lord is uncreated. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, said about Paradise: "You are My mercy; I show mercy through you to whom I will"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4850) and Muslim (2846/35), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. "You are My mercy" — even though Paradise is created, it is among the effects of mercy. If a person has a child born to him, or a lost item of his property is returned to him, he says: "By Allah, this is the mercy of Allah." Is this mercy created or uncreated?
* Students: Created.
* The Shaykh: Created, because it is kindness and bestowal. So when mercy is applied to kindness and bestowal, it is created, and when it is applied to an attribute of Allah, it is uncreated.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that however great sins are, Allah forgives them: ﴿Indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾. All sins?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, because Allah mentioned them with the definite article (al-dhunūb, "the sins"), and emphasized this generality by His saying: ﴿all﴾. All sins. But this applies to whom? To those who repent.
* Among its benefits: that its apparent meaning is the forgiveness of sins for the repentant, even if the sin was against a created being. That is, if you wronged a person and then repented to Allah, Allah accepts your repentance, even if the sin was against a created being. Do you understand? But we have stipulated that you must repent, and part of complete repentance is to render to the created being his right if you are able to. If you are not able to, then make it up to him even by means of hidden supplication (bi-ẓahr al-ghayb).
We give one example, or two, or three, as the matter becomes clear: if you take property from a person unjustly, this is a sin. If you then repent to Allah, will Allah forgive you the sin or not? Allah forgives you the sin, without doubt. But part of complete repentance is to deliver the property to its owner. If he has died, then to his heirs. If you deliver it to his heirs, your obligation is discharged. But the wrong you did to the deceased, by preventing him from his property, remains: will you be held accountable for it or not? If you say: You will not be held accountable, someone will say to you: How can a person be freed from wronging the deceased who was prevented from his property? Is this correct or not correct?
* Students: Correct.
* The Shaykh: Correct. His obligation is discharged, because he delivered the property to the one entitled to it after the death of its owner. But the difficulty is that its owner was prevented from it during his lifetime. Had he had it, he would have bought a house, bought a car, married. You prevented him from it. Will his right be dropped from you by your repentance or not?
We say: the apparent meaning of the noble verses is that his right is dropped from you, but Allah, exalted is He, compensates him from His own side. Have you understood or not? Now, why? Because you are now unable to reach this deceased person to give him his right, and what you are able to do is to deliver it to his heirs, and you have done so.
Another example: you took property from a person and then forgot the person, forgot him. Then you repented. What is the way to repentance or to getting out of the man's right? You give it in charity on his behalf. And when you give it in charity on his behalf, when does he benefit from this property? In the Hereafter or in this world?
* Students: In the Hereafter.
* The Shaykh: In the Hereafter. But someone may say: You prevented him from it in this world, and he may have had a purpose for the property in this world. I say: Yes, I prevented him from it in this world, but out of my inability to reach him, and what I was able to do of repentance I have done. And what is that?
* Student: You gave it in charity.
* The Shaykh: Giving it in charity on his behalf. So will he be entirely cleared, such that the owner of the property will not demand it from him in the Hereafter? The answer: the apparent meaning of the texts is yes, he is cleared.

Now, suppose you killed a soul and then repented to Allah, mighty and majestic, from killing the soul. Part of your complete repentance is to surrender yourself to the heirs of the slain, saying: "I am the one who killed your companion, and I am now in your hands." If you surrender yourself to them, your obligation is discharged. But what remains is the right of whom?
* Student: The slain.
* The Shaykh: The right of the slain, whom you prevented from remaining in this world. Is he cleared of it by repentance?
The answer: Yes, he is cleared of it by repentance, on account of the generality of this verse and similar verses. He is cleared of it by repentance. But does the right of the slain get lost or not? It is not lost; Allah, glorified and exalted, bears it on your behalf toward him. This is from the bounty of Allah, glorified and exalted, that He pardons his right and bears for you the rights of others.
If someone says: What is the evidence for what you have said? And how is a human's right dropped? We say: The evidence for this is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity, and do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, and do not commit unlawful sexual intercourse — and whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾ [Al-Furqan 68]. Here there is a right of Allah, a right of a created being by blood, and a right of a created being by honor, if he committed zina under compulsion against the woman violated. And Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And whoever does that will meet a penalty. The punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide therein in humiliation, except one who repents and believes and does righteous work; for those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds﴾ [Al-Furqan 68–70]. Even for the killer, Allah replaces his evil deeds with good deeds.
If it is said: How is the right of the slain lost? What is the answer?
* Student: It is not lost.
* The Shaykh: How?
* Student: Because Allah, glorified and exalted, bears it on his behalf.
* The Shaykh: Yes, well said. We say: it is not lost, because Allah bears it on his behalf, and this is from His bounty, blessed and exalted is He. So we say: ﴿Indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾: the apparent meaning of the verse is the generality, that He forgives all sins, whether they relate to the right of Allah or to the rights of the servants. But as for what relates to the rights of the servants, if it is impossible to deliver it to them in this world, then Allah, exalted is He, does what? He bears it in the Hereafter.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of two great names of Allah that frequently occur together in the Qur'an: al-Ghafur and al-Rahim. The reason for their pairing is that in the first there is the removal of what is disliked, and in the second the attainment of what is sought. From their combination arises an attribute beyond the meaning of each when taken alone, because when each stands alone we derive forgiveness from al-Ghafur alone, or mercy from al-Rahim alone. But when they are combined we derive a new benefit: that the forgiveness of Allah, mighty and majestic, is joined with His mercy, so He combines forgiveness and mercy. Are these two names of the transitive names or of the intransitive names?
* Students: Transitive.
* The Shaykh: Transitive: ﴿Indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾. So they are transitive. Good. And ﴿He punishes whom He wills and has mercy on whom He wills﴾ [Al-Ankabut 21]. So they are transitive.
The scholars said: faith in transitive names is not complete except through three matters: faith in the name, faith in the attribute it includes, and faith in the ruling that follows from that attribute, which some call the effect (athar). Faith in the name here, al-Ghafur: we believe that al-Ghafur is one of Allah's names; we believe that Allah has forgiveness, indicated by the name al-Ghafur. Is that right? Now we also believe in what it includes: it indicates forgiveness, and it indicates knowledge, because He does not forgive what He does not know. Is its indication of knowledge by way of inclusion (tadammun) or by way of necessary implication (iltizam)?
* Students: Necessary implication.
* The Shaykh: Necessary implication, because the root (gh-f-r) does not contain the meaning of knowledge ('-l-m), so this is by way of necessary implication. Now al-Rahim: we said al-Ghafur as a name is forgiveness, as an attribute it is forgiveness, and as a ruling it forgives sins. Al-Rahim likewise: we believe in al-Rahim as a name, in mercy as an attribute, and that He shows mercy as a ruling. May Allah forgive us and you, and show mercy to us and to you.
* Student: If a person steals from a disbeliever and the disbeliever does not know of it, what should he do?
* The Shaykh: Yes, this is an important question. He asks: If a person steals from a disbeliever and the disbeliever left without knowing of it, what should he do? The answer: If the disbeliever is a combatant (ḥarbī), then the property belongs to him. If he has a covenant (ʿahd), then he should hand it over to the treasury (bayt al-māl), because the treasury accepts property whose owner is not known. If there is no treasury, then he should rid himself of it by giving it in charity. But the disbeliever is not rewarded for this charity unless he becomes Muslim.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is said: the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is an opinion he held that contradicts the apparent meaning of the texts, and what counts is the apparent meaning of the texts. With this view we find ease. As for Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, his explanation of what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas is that killing involves three matters: a right of Allah, a right of the heirs of the slain, and a right of the slain. The right of Allah is dropped by repentance: when a person repents, Allah accepts his repentance and erases the sin. The right of the heirs of the slain is fulfilled by his surrendering himself to them. As for the right of the slain, Ibn al-Qayyim says: it must be taken from this killer. But it is said: the correct position is that we should not express it this way; rather we say: it must be rendered to him, and who renders it? Allah, mighty and majestic. This is the correct view.
* Student: May Allah be good to you, O Shaykh (...) completion of repentance or condition of repentance?
* The Shaykh: What is meant by "completion" here is not the completion that is preferable, but the completion that is obligatory, meaning repentance is not complete except with that.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No. Did we not say in the tafsir: "Say, conveying on My behalf: ﴿O My servants﴾"? Yes, so the Messenger would say, for example: "Your Lord says: ﴿O My servants who have been excessive against themselves﴾." This is how this verse is to be conveyed. Do you understand?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, with ability.
* Student: With ability?
* The Shaykh: Yes, with ability. This is correct. However, some of them said: if you backbite a person, you must go to him and seek his pardon absolutely. Others distinguished: if he knew of it, you must seek his pardon, because he has resentment against you in his heart; but if he did not know, then praise him in the places where you used to backbite him, and that is sufficient. This distinction is good, because if you go to him and say: "I backbit you," while he did not know, you would create in his heart a resentment against you that you need not create. But if you ask forgiveness for him and praise him in the place where you backbit him, the purpose is achieved.

**Student:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And turn in repentance to your Lord and submit to Him before the punishment comes upon you, after which you will not be helped. And follow the best of what has been revealed to you from your Lord before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive it. Lest a soul should say, "Oh, my regret over what I neglected in regard to Allah, and indeed I was among the mockers." Or lest it say, "If only Allah had guided me, I would have been among the righteous." Or lest it say when it sees the punishment, "If only I had another chance, I would be among the doers of good." [Yes, but] My verses had already come to you, but you denied them, grew arrogant, and were among the disbelievers.﴾ [Az-Zumar 54–58].

**Shaykh:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. It has already been mentioned that Allah, glorified and exalted, commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to say to the people, on behalf of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.﴾ The discussion of this verse, in terms of tafsir (exegesis) and istinbat (deriving rulings and lessons from the text), has already taken place.

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And turn in repentance to your Lord and submit to Him.﴾ The author, the exegete, said: (﴿And turn in repentance﴾ return) ﴿to your Lord﴾. That is, return to your Lord from His disobedience to obedience, and from distance from Him to nearness to Him. This turning in repentance (inabah) is an act of the heart, the heart's return to Allah, glorified and exalted.

﴿And submit to Him﴾, that is, surrender to Him and submit to His law. This is an act of the outward, an act of the limbs. So turning in repentance is with the heart, and submission is with the limbs.

(﴿And submit to Him﴾: make your deeds sincere.) The author derived sincerity (ikhlas) from His saying ﴿to Him﴾, meaning to Allah, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if they argue with you, say: "I have submitted myself completely to Allah, and so have those who follow me."﴾ [Al 'Imran 20]. So this verse contains a command to turn in repentance, which is in the heart, and a command to submit to Him, which is with the limbs. Sincerity is derived from the lam (the particle "to") mentioned in His saying ﴿to Him﴾.

﴿Before the punishment comes upon you﴾ is connected to both (turn in repentance) and (submit), since the two governing verbs compete for it (tanazu', a grammatical term meaning two governing words competing for the same complement). ﴿Before the punishment comes upon you﴾, meaning from Allah. ﴿After which you will not be helped﴾, meaning you will not be protected from the punishment of Allah.

The author's statement "unless you repent" is not needed, because Allah said: turn in repentance and submit before this matter. Whoever turns in repentance and submits before this matter has indeed repented, and then the punishment will not descend upon him.

﴿And follow the best of what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾: ﴿And follow﴾, that is, be followers of ﴿the best of what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾. (The best) is a superlative (ism tafdil) from goodness (husn), and it includes the best in its essence and the best in action. A person is commanded to follow the best. The best of what was revealed to us is, in its essence, the Qur'an. If you examined the heavenly scriptures that were revealed, you would find that the best of what was revealed is the Qur'an. For this reason the author explained it by saying: (and it is the Qur'an). Likewise, the best of what is revealed to us, when there is an act of worship performed by a person in an incomplete manner and another act of worship performed in a complete manner, the one performed in a complete manner is the best. So when there are deeds that differ in merit, a person is commanded to follow the best of them.

﴿The best of what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾. His saying ﴿from your Lord﴾ contains an indication of the obligation to follow the best, because this best has descended from Allah, the Exalted, from the Lord. The Lord is the One who has authority over His servants in management, legislation and judgment.

﴿Before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive it.﴾ In the first verse it was ﴿before the punishment comes upon you, after which you will not be helped.﴾ Then here it is ﴿before the punishment comes upon you suddenly﴾, that is, unexpectedly, ﴿while you do not perceive﴾ that the punishment is coming upon you. This is like His saying the Exalted: ﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come to them by night while they are sleeping? Or do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come to them in the morning while they are at play?﴾ [Al A'raf 97–98]. The one who is asleep does not perceive the punishment except suddenly, and the one who is playing likewise does not perceive the punishment except suddenly.

He, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿Lest a soul should say﴾. His saying ﴿lest it say﴾: the author, may Allah have mercy on him, the commentator and exegete, said: (﴿And you do not perceive﴾ its time before its arrival), that is, you do not perceive its time before it comes. Rather, you have struck the long hope and the false optimism that is out of place, until the punishment comes to you.

He said: (Hasten before ﴿lest a soul should say﴾.) The author estimated what he mentioned because the context indicates it. What the author, may Allah have mercy on him, did is called by the rhetoricians (balaghiyyun) ijaz al-hadhf (brevity through ellipsis). This is because brevity (ijaz), according to them, has two kinds: ijaz al-qasr (brevity through compression), and ijaz al-hadhf (brevity through omission). Ijaz al-qasr is that a short expression includes many meanings. Ijaz al-hadhf is that the expression is present but something that is understood has been omitted from it. An example is His saying the Exalted: ﴿So he watered their flock for them, then turned back to the shade and said, "My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need." Then there came to him one of the two women walking shyly.﴾ [Al Qasas 24–25]. Much has been omitted from this verse, because its estimated meaning is that the two women went to their father and informed him of the matter, then he sent one of them to Musa, and so one of them came walking shyly. So we have two kinds of brevity: brevity of compression, where the expression is short and includes many meanings, and brevity of omission, where what the context indicates is omitted from the speech. Both are eloquent Arabic.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿And in retribution there is life for you﴾ [Al Baqarah 179] is an example of ijaz al-qasr. And ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ [An-Nisa 123] is an example of ijaz al-qasr, because if you wanted to expand this sentence, mentioning all kinds of evil and all kinds of recompense, the speech would be long. But it is limited to these two words, ﴿whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾, and they encompass every detail that could enter this sentence.

Now, regarding the author's statement: (hasten before ﴿lest it say﴾), we say: this is from the category of ijaz al-hadhf, because something that the context indicates has been omitted from the speech. It is possible to estimate something less than that by saying: (out of fear that a soul should say), meaning: follow what has been revealed to you from your Lord, out of fear that a soul should say: "Oh, my regret over what I neglected in regard to Allah." What we have mentioned is more concise than the author's statement.

﴿Lest a soul should say, "Oh my regret"﴾: (soul) here is an indefinite noun (nakirah) in an affirmative context, and an indefinite noun in an affirmative context does not indicate generality. It indicates generality only if it is in a negative context, a conditional context, a rhetorical interrogative, or what is similar to these, as the scholars have mentioned. However, they said that (soul) here is an indefinite noun intended to express generality, meaning that every soul would say, "Oh my regret."

(Its origin is "Oh my regret" (ya hasrati), that is, my remorse.) So regret (hasrah) is remorse. He said: (Oh my regret, yā ḥasratā). This alif has been converted from a yā. Its origin is the yā of the first person: "yā ḥasratī." But in the Arabic language it is permissible to convert the yā into an alif, so one says "yā ḥasratā" instead of "yā ḥasratī." Among examples of this is His saying the Exalted: ﴿O woe to me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman?﴾ [Hud 72]. The estimate is "yā waylatī."

(﴿Oh my regret﴾, that is, my remorse, ﴿over what I neglected in regard to﴾). Tafrit (neglect) means carelessness and losing. Its opposite is ifrat (excess). Ifrat is going beyond the limit, and tafrit is falling short of a thing. So the one who commits tafrit is one who is negligent and falls short, and the one who commits ifrat is one who oversteps the limit. Both are blameworthy, and the best course is the middle way.

﴿Over what I neglected in regard to Allah﴾. He said: (That is, His obedience.) So he explained (jamb, side or regard) here as obedience. This is because it is not possible to mean by it the "side" of Allah that is His own essence, since a person does not feel that he has neglected the very side that is the essence of Allah. However, some scholars say: (jamb) in its linguistic sense means (janib), side. If it means side linguistically, then there is no need for interpretation, and the meaning becomes: in regard to Allah, that is, in the side of Allah, and the side of Allah means His right and His law. The explanation we have mentioned is what the author, may Allah have mercy on him, indicated when he said: (that is, His obedience). But if we explain (jamb) as obedience, we have departed from the meaning that matches the word. As for when we say that (jamb) linguistically means (janib), we have explained it by what the word indicates linguistically, and it is well known that the side of Allah, mighty and majestic, means His right and His law.

﴿And indeed I was among the mockers﴾: (in is lightened from the heavy, that is, and indeed I). (In) in the Arabic language has several meanings. The first: conditional. The second: negation. The third: emphatic. The fourth: superfluous (zaʾida). Four meanings. (In) comes in Arabic with four meanings. Some have added a fifth, that it means "yes," but this is rare.

(In) as conditional, an example: ﴿O you who believe, if a dissolute person brings you a report, verify it.﴾ [Al Hujurat 6]. This (in) is conditional.

It may be negative, as in the words of the disbelievers: ﴿This is nothing but evident magic.﴾ [Al Ma'idah 110]. The negative (in) is always followed by (illa, except).

And it comes emphatic, and this is the lightened form of the heavy (inna), as here. Its sign is that (inna) can take its place, as in: ﴿And indeed I was among the mockers.﴾ This is lightened from the heavy, and it indicates emphasis, because the heavy (inna) is known to be for emphasis. So when this is its lightened form, it is for emphasis.

The fourth: superfluous. Among examples of this is the words of the poet:

*Banu Ghudana, you are not gold,*
*nor silver, but you are mere potsherds.*

The point of evidence is his saying: (ma in antum dhahab, you are not gold). Because the meaning of the speech is: "you are not gold," so it is superfluous. The gold is well known. The ṣarīf is silver, and it was named ṣarīf because a sound of ṣarīf (clinking) is heard from it when counted or weighed. (But you are potsherds.) What is al-khazaf? It is baked clay. That is, your origin is base. The sign of superfluous (in) is that the sentence remains correct when it is removed. If the sentence is correct with its removal, then it is superfluous. Alright.

﴿And indeed I was among the mockers﴾. The author said: (And indeed I ﴿was among the mockers﴾). So he estimated the subject of (in) as a pronoun consistent with the context, saying: "wa innī kuntu" (and indeed I was). This is what the author adopted, and it is the correct view. However, according to the majority of grammarians, the subject of (in) is an omitted pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), so they estimate: "in kuntu" and "innahu" (indeed it), that is, the matter. But the correct view is that we estimate a pronoun consistent with the context, and there is no harm in saying it is omitted, even if it is not a pronoun of the matter. Accordingly, we say: ﴿And indeed I was among the mockers﴾, the estimate being: "And indeed I was among the mockers." The lam in His saying ﴿among the mockers﴾ is for emphasis, and it is also evidence that (in) is lightened from the heavy.

Alright. Is the lam of emphasis required with the lightened (in)?

The answer: it is not required, except if there is a fear of confusion with the negative (in). If there is a fear of confusion with the negative, then the lam must be mentioned. The summary is that the lam often comes in the predicate of the lightened (in), and it may be omitted, except when confusion is feared, in which case the lam must be mentioned. When confusion is feared with what? When there is fear that it could be confused with the negative (in), then the lam must be brought, because when the lam comes, it becomes determined that (in) is lightened from the heavy. The place for this discussion is in grammar (nahw).

He says: ﴿And indeed I was among the mockers.﴾ The sākhir (mocker) means the one who ridicules. Mockers of whom? Mockers of the one who calls to Allah, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Did we take them in ridicule, or have our eyes turned away from them?﴾ [Sad 63]. Mockers of the religion of Allah, mockers of the books of Allah, mockers of the messengers of Allah: ﴿Say: "Was it Allah and His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?"﴾ [At-Tawbah 65]. For this reason the object was omitted in (the mockers), to indicate generality, meaning the mockers of Allah, His verses, His messengers and His allies. It is general. The rest of the discussion of the verse will come, Allah willing.
