**Student:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And follow the best of what has been revealed to you from your Lord before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive it (55). Lest a soul should say, "Oh, my regret over what I neglected in regard to Allah, and indeed I was among the mockers" (56). Or lest it say, "If only Allah had guided me, I would have been among the righteous" (57). Or lest it say when it sees the punishment, "If only I had another chance, I would be among the doers of good" (58). [Yes, but] My verses had already come to you, but you denied them, grew arrogant, and were among the disbelievers (59).﴾ [Az-Zumar 55–59].

**Shaykh:** I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And follow the best of what has been revealed to you from your Lord before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive it. **Shaykh:** Yes, out of fear that a soul should say. What did the author estimate?

Alright. His saying ﴿lest a soul should say﴾, this is an indefinite noun in what context?

**Student:** An affirmative context.

**Shaykh:** So is it for absoluteness or for generality?

**Student:** (...).

Alright. His saying ﴿Oh my regret over what I neglected in regard to Allah﴾. "Yā ḥasratā," its origin is what?

**Student:** "Yā ḥasratī."

**Shaykh:** So it was converted?

**Student:** The yā was converted into an alif.

**Shaykh:** Into an alif, because it is for the lamentation (nudbah).

Alright. His saying ﴿over what I neglected in regard to Allah﴾, what is meant by "in regard to Allah"?

**Student:** What is meant by "in regard to Allah"?

**Shaykh:** Yes.

**Student:** By the side of Allah.

**Shaykh:** By the side of Allah, is that so?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** And the author explained it?

**Shaykh:** That is, whenever it is possible to carry the word on its linguistic meaning, that is preferable. Alright. Is it not possible that it means "the side of Allah" which is His side?

**Student:** (...).

﴿And indeed I was among the mockers.﴾ What is this (in)?

**Student:** Conditional.

**Shaykh:** (In) is conditional? No.

**Student:** (In) is lightened from the heavy.

**Shaykh:** Lightened from the heavy. What does it require? Emphasis. We mentioned in passing that (in) comes with several meanings.

**Student:** Four, or five. It comes superfluous, it comes emphatic, it comes conditional, it comes negative, it may come with the meaning of "yes."

**Shaykh:** What determines these meanings?

**Student:** The context.

**Shaykh:** The context, alright. The example of the lightened form of the heavy (inna)?

Student: Verses like these: ﴿وَإِنْ كُنْتُ لَمِنَ السَّاخِرِينَ﴾ (And indeed I was among the mockers).

Shaykh: What is the estimated (original) form?

Shaykh: Innī kuntu la-min al-sākhirīn, good. And it comes as a negation particle. Its example?

Shaykh: ﴿إِنْ أَنْتَ إِلَّا نَذِيرٌ﴾ — what is the meaning?

Student: "You are nothing but a warner."

Shaykh: "You are nothing but a warner." And what is the sign of this?

Shaykh: That is, what is its sign?

Shaykh: That (mā) can take its place, and it is usually followed by (illā). Good. And it also comes as? Yes.

Shaykh: Its example?

Student:
Banī Ghudānah mā in antum dhahabun ∗∗∗ wa-lā ṣarīfun ..............

Shaykh:
Banī Ghudānah mā in antum dhahabun ∗∗∗ ......................
Good. What is its sign?

Student: Its sign is (...), the context is correct (...).

Shaykh: Yes, that if it is removed, the context remains correct without it. Brother, what does it come as?

Student: Conditional (sharṭiyyah).

Shaykh: Conditional.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Excellent. Now, the conditional's clear sign is that it requires what?

Shaykh: A response (jawāb).

Let us take the new lesson. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿أَوْ تَقُولَ﴾: (aw) is a conjunction particle, and ﴿تَقُولَ﴾ is conjoined to His saying: ﴿أَنْ تَقُولَ نَفْسٌ﴾.

Student: We did not take it.

Shaykh: What did we not take?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: From which place? ﴿وَأَنِيبُوا إِلَى رَبِّكُمْ وَأَسْلِمُوا لَهُ﴾ — did we take this one?

Students: (...).

Shaykh: Good, and up to where?

Students: (...).

Shaykh: Yes, we took the benefits up to where?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: You are now saying: "We did not take the benefits." So from where is it that we did not take the benefits?

Good. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿وَأَنِيبُوا إِلَى رَبِّكُمْ وَأَسْلِمُوا لَهُ﴾ to the end. In it there are benefits:

* First: the obligation of turning in repentance (inābah) to Allah, because of His saying: ﴿وَأَنِيبُوا إِلَى رَبِّكُمْ﴾, and the default in a command is obligation unless there is evidence otherwise.
* Among its benefits: the obligation of submitting to Him (islām), meaning complete surrender together with sincerity, because of His saying: ﴿وَأَسْلِمُوا لَهُ﴾.
* Among its benefits: a warning against not hastening to turn in repentance and submission, because of His saying: ﴿مِنْ قَبْلِ أَنْ يَأْتِيَكُمُ الْعَذَابُ﴾ (before the punishment comes upon you).
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the punishment of one who does not turn to his Lord and submit to Him, since the punishment is a retribution.
* Among its benefits: that when the punishment of Allah comes, there is no repeller of it, because of His saying: ﴿ثُمَّ لَا تُنْصَرُونَ﴾ (then you will not be helped).
* Among the benefits of the following verse: the obligation to follow the noble Qur'an, because of His saying: ﴿اتَّبِعُوا أَحْسَنَ مَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْكُمْ مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ﴾ (Follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord).
* Among its benefits: the praise of the noble Qur'an as the best of what was sent down to mankind. You know that it is best in its essence, its reports, its rulings and its effects, and no nation has attained the honour and dignity that this nation has attained through what Allah has given it of the Qur'an.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, because of His saying: ﴿مَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْكُمْ مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ﴾.

If someone says: We do not grant you this, because among what Allah has sent down are things that are not His speech, such as His saying: ﴿أَنْزَلَ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ مَاءً﴾ [al-Zumar 21], ﴿وَأَنْزَلَ لَكُمْ مِنَ الْأَنْعَامِ ثَمَانِيَةَ أَزْوَاجٍ﴾ [al-Zumar 6], ﴿وَأَنْزَلْنَا الْحَدِيدَ فِيهِ بَأْسٌ شَدِيدٌ﴾ [al-Ḥadīd 25] and similar. So we do not grant you that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah; rather we say it is like the other created things Allah has sent down, for iron is created, rain is created, and livestock is created.

The answer to this is to say: What Allah has sent down is divided into two kinds. The first: that it be a self-subsisting entity (ʿayn qāʾimah bi-nafsihā); this is created. The second: that it be an attribute that subsists only through something else; this is not created. So let us look at the Qur'an: is it a self-subsisting entity or an attribute that subsists only through another? The second. Therefore it is not created; the speech of Allah is uncreated. Is this clear, brothers? Good.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's highness (uluww), because of His saying: ﴿مَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْكُمْ مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ﴾ [al-Zumar 55]; the reason for this is that descent only comes from above.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the virtue of this nation, in that it is the ultimate goal of the sending down of the Qur'an. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿إِلَيْكُمْ﴾, for the sending down has its goal directed to us; so this is an honour for us that we are the goal of the Qur'an's descent.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's lordship (rubūbiyyah), because of His saying: ﴿مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ﴾.
* Among its benefits, among the benefits of this noble verse: that the sending down of the Qur'an to us is from the perfection of His lordship, in that He attributed its sending down to Himself with the attribute of lordship; so from the perfection of His lordship over His creation and His nurturing of them is that this Qur'an was sent down to them.
* Among its benefits also: the obligation to act upon what is in the Qur'an, because it was sent down from the Lord, and the Lord has complete authority over His creation. Consider: if a king issued a royal decree, would it not follow from his authority that we act upon this decree? Certainly. So the requirement of Allah's lordship over us is that we act upon what has been sent down to us, because this Qur'an is in the position of royal decrees that must be executed, and even more so, as is well known, and there is no difficulty in this.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: caution against the punishment of Allah coming suddenly, because of His saying: ﴿مِنْ قَبْلِ أَنْ يَأْتِيَكُمُ الْعَذَابُ بَغْتَةً﴾ [al-Zumar 55]. A sudden punishment is more severe than a punishment that does not come suddenly, because the punishment that does not come suddenly is one for which the person has prepared; but what comes suddenly comes upon a person who is at the utmost of heedlessness and the utmost of delight, as Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿أَفَأَمِنَ أَهْلُ الْقُرَى أَنْ يَأْتِيَهُمْ بَأْسُنَا بَيَاتًا وَهُمْ نَائِمُونَ (٩٧) أَوَأَمِنَ أَهْلُ الْقُرَى أَنْ يَأْتِيَهُمْ بَأْسُنَا ضُحًى وَهُمْ يَلْعَبُونَ (٩٨)﴾ [al-A'rāf 97, 98]. So consider: heedlessness, calm and reassurance, when the punishment comes at that time it is more severe in its impact, and we seek refuge with Allah, than if it came while the person was prepared.

Let me give you a clear, concrete example. If you were descending stairs and became heedless, then your foot slipped on one of the steps, would it be like if you were descending while seeing every step and placing your foot on it? Answer me. So the sudden one is more severe than what comes upon a person who is prepared for it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the sudden one comes without the servant's awareness, because he is heedless and is not thinking that the punishment may come upon him, because of His saying: ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ لَا تَشْعُرُونَ﴾ (while you do not perceive). The grammarians call this clause a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah), meaning "while the situation is that you do not perceive."

Then Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿أَنْ تَقُولَ نَفْسٌ يَا حَسْرَتَا عَلَى مَا فَرَّطْتُ فِي جَنْبِ اللَّهِ﴾ etc.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the explanation of the outcome of the one who neglects, which is regret (taḥassur), and regret is remorse together with grief; regret and remorse together with grief.
* Among its benefits, among the benefits of the noble verse: that the one who neglects will regret his neglect. From this follows a benefit: that a person should be resolute, active and strong, so that matters do not escape him and then he regrets afterward.
* A third benefit branches from this: that one should seize opportunities; whenever an opportunity presents itself to you, do not waste it.
* From this also follows a fourth: that if two needs are before you, begin with what you want first and hasten to it, and make the second a supererogatory matter. This appears in the Sunnah of the Messenger (ﷺ) in several examples. Among them: when ʿItbān ibn Mālik (may Allah be pleased with him) lost his sight and could no longer reach the mosque of his people, he invited the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) to his house to pray in a place he would take as a prayer place. The Prophet (ﷺ) went out to him with a group of his companions. When he arrived at the house, the man had prepared food for them, but the Messenger (ﷺ) did not wish to begin with the food; rather he began with what had brought him, that is, with the primary purpose, and said to him: "Where do you want me to pray?" He showed him the place and he prayed there.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (424), and Muslim (33 / 263), from the hadith of ʿItbān ibn Mālik.]]

This is an example. Based on this, you, students of knowledge, should, when you want to review the fatwās of Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah (may Allah have mercy on him) on a specific issue, look through the index; then a question passes you that tempts you to review it, so you go and review it and leave aside what you were reviewing it for. Without doubt this harms the student of knowledge: it scatters his thought and scatters his time, because his mind, when he first opened the book, was focused on what? On the issue he was seeking. When this side matter presents itself and he turns to it and busies himself with it, and it was not his intended aim in itself, his mind is scattered; then his time is scattered too. Perhaps his session of review was in the span of a quarter hour, and that quarter hour goes while he has not reviewed the issue he was searching for. We have tested this; it has happened to us. We review one issue, then an intriguing heading passes us and we take it up, and it wastes our time. So a person should be resolute and begin with the more important before the important.

From this, that is, from resolution, the Messenger (peace be upon him) would hasten to remove harmful things and not delay, for delay has harms, indeed many harms. "When a Bedouin urinated in the mosque, he immediately ordered that water be poured over it to purify it,"[[Narrated by al-Bukhārī (220), from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah.]] and "when the child urinated in his lap, he immediately called for water and poured it over him."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (223), and Muslim (287 / 103), from the hadith of Umm Qays bint Miḥṣan.]] It was possible for him to leave the place in the mosque until the time of prayer came and people needed to pray in that spot; but he hastened. Likewise it was possible for him to leave his garment until the time of prayer and then purify it; but he hastened. The point is that such incidents should be taken by a person as training for himself; they should not pass by him as merely a jurisprudential matter he has learned, rather his knowledge must appear in his action.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of direction for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because of His saying: ﴿فِي جَنْبِ اللَّهِ﴾. We have said that janb means jānib (side). But those who do not affirm direction flee from this and interpret it differently, as the author interpreted it with his words "in obedience to Allah." This interpretation may be said to be correct, that the side of Allah, Exalted, is His obedience and His right and similar matters. But we know that many people deny that Allah is in a direction, and they say: it is not permissible to say that Allah is in a direction, neither above nor below. Others took the opposite view and said: Allah is in every direction by His essence. Between these two positions, as between heaven and earth, lies the truth.

Others took a middle course and said: Allah is in every direction, but He is above everything: ﴿وَلِلَّهِ الْمَشْرِقُ وَالْمَغْرِبُ فَأَيْنَمَا تُوَلُّوا فَثَمَّ وَجْهُ اللَّهِ﴾ [al-Baqarah 115]. Whether you turn east or west, north or south, there is the Face of Allah; but Allah Himself is not in those directions, rather He is above, and His being above does not contradict that He is in every direction you face. Is this clear, brothers? Good.

If someone asks: how can it be that He is in the direction of the east, for example, or the west, north or south, while He is above everything?

We say: as for "how," do not apply it to what can be described in form; the attributes of Allah cannot be described in form. You must submit. Then we say: this is possible even for the sun: when it rises or sets and you face it, you are in the direction of east or west, and where is its place? In the sky. This is in the case of a creature, so what of the Creator who encompasses everything?

So the correct position is that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, is in a direction, the direction of height; yet whoever turns to Him in any place, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is before his face in any place: ﴿فَأَيْنَمَا تُوَلُّوا فَثَمَّ وَجْهُ اللَّهِ﴾. As for His Essence, Mighty and Majestic, He is above everything.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the acknowledgement by the deniers against themselves of what they were upon of denial, but at a time when it will not benefit them. From where is this taken? ﴿وَإِنْ كُنْتُ لَمِنَ السَّاخِرِينَ﴾, meaning: "Indeed I was among the mockers." This is an emphasis and affirmation that in the world he was among those who mocked the law of Allah and ridiculed it.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the prohibition of mocking Allah, Mighty and Majestic. From where is this taken? From the fact that this mocker regretted and grieved over it, and had he not been struck by a punishment upon him, he would not have regretted.

If someone asks: What is the ruling on mocking Allah?

We say: its ruling is disbelief (kufr). Whoever mocks Allah, His signs or His Messenger is a disbeliever; everyone who mocks Allah, His signs or His Messenger is a disbeliever.

If someone asks: Do you declare him a disbeliever even if he was joking?

The answer: Yes, we declare him a disbeliever even if he was joking, because of the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿وَلَئِنْ سَأَلْتَهُمْ لَيَقُولُنَّ إِنَّمَا كُنَّا نَخُوضُ وَنَلْعَبُ﴾ (meaning: we did not intend it) ﴿قُلْ أَبِاللَّهِ وَآيَاتِهِ وَرَسُولِهِ كُنْتُمْ تَسْتَهْزِئُونَ (٦٥) لَا تَعْتَذِرُوا قَدْ كَفَرْتُمْ بَعْدَ إِيمَانِكُمْ﴾ [al-Tawbah 65, 66].

If it is said: What is the remedy for one who is afflicted with this, that is, who mocks Allah, His signs or His Messenger? What is the cure?

We say: The remedy in this surah is: ﴿قُلْ يَا عِبَادِيَ الَّذِينَ أَسْرَفُوا عَلَى أَنْفُسِهِمْ لَا تَقْنَطُوا مِنْ رَحْمَةِ اللَّهِ إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَغْفِرُ الذُّنُوبَ جَمِيعًا﴾ [al-Zumar 53]. The remedy is that he repents to Allah. When he repents to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and uproots from his heart this mockery and ridicule, and establishes in its place glorification and love, then the ruling of disbelief is lifted from him.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said, and this is the beginning of today's lesson: ﴿أَوْ تَقُولَ لَوْ أَنَّ اللَّهَ هَدَانِي لَكُنْتُ مِنَ الْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ [al-Zumar 57], meaning: "or [lest] a soul should say: 'Had Allah guided me, I would have been among the righteous'." This is conjoined to His saying: ﴿أَنْ تَقُولَ نَفْسٌ﴾, or: the soul says (﴿لَوْ أَنَّ اللَّهَ هَدَانِي﴾ with obedience, so I would have been guided ﴿لَكُنْتُ مِنَ الْمُتَّقِينَ﴾).

﴿أَوْ تَقُولَ لَوْ أَنَّ اللَّهَ هَدَانِي لَكُنْتُ مِنَ الْمُتَّقِينَ﴾: (law) here is conditional; its protasis (verb of the condition) is omitted, and its apodosis is His saying: ﴿لَكُنْتُ مِنَ الْمُتَّقِينَ﴾. Its estimated form, meaning the estimate of the omitted protasis, is: "Had it been established that Allah guided me, I would have been among the righteous." This is an argument from predestination: that is, had Allah guided me and granted me success so that I were guided, I would have been among the righteous. Thus the soul regrets and argues, combining remorse over the lack of piety and guidance with argument, like the saying of one who says: "If you had given me a wage I would have worked for you; if you had fed me I would have been satiated," meaning: you did not feed me and did not give me a wage. So they say: "If Allah had guided me I would have been guided and been among the righteous." Accordingly, the guidance meant here is the guidance of success (hidāyat al-tawfīq), and this is an argument from the soul, using Allah's decree, for going astray, and we seek refuge with Allah.

He says: ﴿لَكُنْتُ مِنَ الْمُتَّقِينَ﴾. The author, the exegete, said: "[i.e., of] His punishment," and this is the object of "the righteous." But the correct view is that we estimate: "I would have been among the righteous of Allah," because the origin is piety toward Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and piety toward the punishment of Allah is part of piety toward Allah. So it is proper to estimate the origin: "I would have been among those who are righteous toward Allah."

What is piety toward Allah?

We know piety toward Allah by knowing its root. The origin of taqwā is taken from waqāyah (protection), its root being waqwā with a waw, but the waw was changed to a tā' for a morphological reason. If it derives from protection, we explain it as taking that which protects from the punishment of Allah, and nothing protects from the punishment of Allah except doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. Therefore the most comprehensive thing said about taqwā is that it is doing the commands and avoiding the prohibitions.

It has also been said: taqwā is that you act in obedience to Allah, upon a light from Allah, hoping for the reward of Allah, and that you abandon what Allah has forbidden, upon a light from Allah, fearing the punishment of Allah. This meaning is longer than what we have said, but what we have said includes it. It has also been said about taqwā:

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verses 49–60 (part 7 of 7):**

*Leave sins, the small of them and the great; that is piety.*
*Act like one walking over thorny ground, wary of what he sees.*
*Do not belittle any small sin, for mountains are made of pebbles.*

This is also a delightful definition, because it is in verse. "Leave sins, the small of them and the great" (*khalli al-dhunub saghirahā wa kabīrahā*). Sins are either the commission of what is forbidden or the omission of what is obligatory. "That is piety" (*dhāka al-tuqā*), the taqwa (God-consciousness). "Act like one walking over thorny ground, wary of what he sees." Does the one who walks over thorny ground walk quickly or slowly?

* Students: Slowly.
* The Shaykh: Slowly.

"Do not belittle any small sin, for mountains are made of pebbles." The great, massive mountains are pebbles gathered together, whether they are lumps or small or large stones.

﴿Would that I had been among the righteous, or [lest] it say, when it sees the punishment: "If only I had a return [to the world], so that I would be among the good-doers."﴾

"Or lest it say" (*aw taqūla*): what is this conjoined to?

* Students: To "lest a soul say" (*an taqūla nafs*).

* The Shaykh: To "lest a soul say." That is, or lest a soul say when it sees the punishment, seeing the punishment with its own eyes, so that what was promised becomes witnessed; it sees it with the eye. "If only I had a return" (*law anna lī karratan*). Seeing with the eye is called the certainty of sight (*ʿayn al-yaqīn*). The promise of punishment is the certainty of knowledge (*ʿilm al-yaqīn*), and touching the punishment is the certainty of truth (*ḥaqq al-yaqīn*). For this reason they said: certainty is of three kinds: knowledge, sight, and truth. All of them are in the Qur'an: ﴿No! If you knew with certainty of knowledge, you would surely see the Hellfire; then you would surely see it with the certainty of sight﴾ [at-Takāthur 5–7], as witnessing. And the Exalted said at the end of al-Wāqiʿa: ﴿Indeed, this is the certain truth﴾ [al-Wāqiʿa 95]. That which occurs at the time of death is the certainty of truth. Which of them is highest in certainty?

* Students: The certainty of truth.

* The Shaykh: The certainty of truth is highest, because the certainty of sight may witness a thing contrary to what it actually is, as you see, especially if your sight is weak. You see a still thing as moving, or a moving thing as still. Yes indeed. In any case, the certainty of truth is the highest. Here, ﴿or lest it say, when it sees the punishment﴾: what is intended?

* Students: The certainty of sight.

* The Shaykh: The certainty of sight. ﴿If only I had a return, so that I would be among the good-doers.﴾ Here "law" (if only) is not conditional; it is for wishing, meaning "would that I had a return."

Let us digress and say: *law* comes in three senses: conditional, optative (expressing a wish), and verbal-masdar (introducing a clause equivalent to a verbal noun). It is conditional when you say: "If (*law*) you visit me, I would honour you." Its sign is that *in* (if), the conditional particle, can take its place: "If you visit me, I would honour you."

The optative sense, which usually comes after *wadda* (to wish), as in the Exalted's words: ﴿They wish you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ [al-Qalam 9]. Its sign is that *an* (that), the verbal-masdar particle, can take its place. If you replace *law* with *an* in ﴿They wish you would compromise﴾: "They wish that you would compromise." Does the sentence hold or not? Good. Could you substitute *an* in the Qur'an?

* Students: It is not valid.

* The Shaykh: It is not valid. Grammatically it works: ﴿They wish you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾. If you replace *law* with *an*, the sentence is sound, but in the Qur'an it is not permissible to substitute *an*. Now, if you say, "I wished you would visit me" (*wadadtu law zurtanī*), is that correct? Good. But here, if you change it to *an*, you change the verb to the present: "I wished that you would visit me." Good.

The third sense is the optative.

* Students: The verbal-masdar.

* The Shaykh: The verbal-masdar? No. I am saying: the verbal-masdar is the one that comes after *wadda*, and the conditional is the other. What remains is the optative, the one that expresses a wish. The verbal-masdar is the one that most often comes after *wadda*, and its sign is that *an* can take its place. The optative means "I wish" (*atamannā*). Its meaning is determined by the context. Here, in ﴿if only I had a return, so that I would be﴾, put "I wish" in its place: "I wish there were a return for me, so that I would be among the believers." Is that clear? The Exalted's words in Sūrat al-Anʿām confirm this: ﴿Would that we were returned, and did not deny the signs of our Lord﴾ [al-Anʿām 27]. So *law* has three senses: conditional, verbal-masdar, and optative.

"If only I had a return" (*karratan*): the commentator said, "a return to the world, so that I would be among the good-doers." That is, he wishes for a return so that he might be among the good-doers.

His words, ﴿so that I would be among the good-doers﴾, and not "among the righteous"? Because *iḥsān* (excellence) is a degree above taqwa. Every good-doer is righteous, but not every righteous person is a good-doer. Excellence is a high degree. The Prophet ﷺ said about it: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him; and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (50), Muslim (9/5), from Abū Hurayrah].

But is this soul sincere in its wish to be among the good-doers? The Exalted said: ﴿And even if they were returned, they would revert to what they were forbidden, and indeed they are liars﴾ [al-Anʿām 28]. But at the punishment, it has nothing to say except this: ﴿If only I had a return, so that I would be among the good-doers.﴾ Then the Exalted said: ﴿Yes! My signs had come to you, but you denied them and were arrogant, and you were among the disbelievers.﴾

* Student: May Allah reward you well. A man was asked, "What is the last joke you heard?" He said: "Two extremists said to each other: 'Straighten up and be even in the row.' Does this fall under mocking Allah and the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ?"

* The Shaykh: This man asks: "What is the last joke you heard?" Yes, indeed. He says he heard a man say: "Straighten up, be even," like this?

* Student: (...) "Straighten up, be even" (...).

* The Shaykh: But did the imam say that? Did the imam say: "Straighten up, be even"?

No, that is not acceptable.

* Student: (...) The last joke I heard, he says: "Straighten up and be even" (...).

* The Shaykh: No. Is it true what he relates about this imam, that the imam says: "Straighten up and be even"?

* Students: He himself is asking.

* The Shaykh: No. In any case, let us set aside whether he depicted it as a boxing match. But if a person said about an imam who said "Straighten up and be even": "This is a joke," and described him as an extremist, would he be a disbeliever or not?

The truth is that this matter is extremely important. Mocking a person who performs an act of obedience or avoids an act of disobedience may be of two kinds. Sometimes the personal aspect predominates, and this does not amount to disbelief. Sometimes the ruling aspect predominates, meaning that he mocks the ruling from whatever source it comes; this is disbelief. An example clarifies this: some people, if they saw a scholar of recognized standing, beloved to the people and trusted, with his garment above the ankle, would never mock him, and could not mock him. But if they saw a young man, they might mock him. So here, the mockery is directed at what?

* Students: At the person.

* The Shaykh: At the person. The personal aspect predominates. This does not amount to disbelief, because he did not hate the ruling; he hated the one who carried out the ruling.

The second case: that he hates the legislated ruling and mocks the legislated ruling. This is disbelief. For this reason the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Was it Allah and His signs and His Messenger that you were mocking?﴾ He did not say "and the believers." The Messenger is known: anyone who mocks him is a disbeliever, even if the personal aspect predominates, because the Messenger is a lawgiver ﷺ, so everything that proceeds from him is legislation. But what proceeds from someone other than the Messenger: if he is trusted by the people, they treat it as a legal ruling and do not mock it. If he is not trusted, they mock him, with the personal aspect predominating, because they do not fully trust him, or they consider him rigid or excessive, or something similar. A person must understand the difference between these two matters, because these issues are very subtle.

For this reason Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned that Imam Aḥmad declared the Jahmiyya to be disbelievers, but did not declare their individuals to be disbelievers, because there is a difference between takfir with respect to the ruling and takfir with respect to the person.

Therefore we warn the students of knowledge against hastiness in declaring a specific individual a disbeliever, because the matter is not trivial. If you declare a person a disbeliever when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has not judged him to be one, the accusation returns to you, and you become a person to be feared for going astray, even in the future, if you do not repent.

[The author's words have been abridged due to their considerable length.]

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verse 61:

When Allah, glorified and exalted be He, mentioned the punishment of those who lied against Allah, He clarified the reward of those who feared Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is the practice (da'b) of the Noble Qur'an: when it mentions a thing, it mentions its opposite. This is part of the meaning of His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech, a Book consistent within itself, repeating (mathani)﴾ [az-Zumar 23]. The scholars said: "Mathani" means that meanings are repeated (tuthanna) within it. So when the description of the believers comes, the description of the disbelievers comes; when the reward of the believers comes, the reward of the disbelievers comes, and vice versa. This is so that a person does not become absorbed in the aspect of hope when the description and reward of the believers is mentioned, and likewise does not despair when the description and punishment of the disbelievers is mentioned.

Here Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And Allah will save those who feared Him by their place of success﴾ [az-Zumar 61]. He says: ﴿Allah saves those who feared Him﴾ from what? From the punishment of the disbelievers, so their faces will not be blackened and their abode will not be Hellfire. Allah, glorified and exalted be He, has clarified in other verses that on the Day of Resurrection some faces will be whitened and some faces will be blackened: the faces of the disbelievers will be blackened, and the faces of the believers will be whitened. So Allah saves those who feared Him from the punishment of the disbelievers in this respect and in that respect.

The author's statement, "(Allah saves from Hellfire)," is correct, but if he had said "from the punishment of the disbelievers" it would have been more general, so that the salvation would include their being saved from Hellfire, from their faces being blackened, and from other things.

He said: (﴿Those who feared﴾ [i.e., feared] shirk). The correct way to put this is: "feared Allah," because taqwa when used without qualification is intended to mean the taqwa of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It may be mentioned in other than Allah's case, as in: ﴿And fear a Day on which you will be returned to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 281] and ﴿and fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ [Ali 'Imran 131], and similar verses. But when used without qualification, it is intended only as the taqwa of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

(﴿By their place of success﴾ [az-Zumar 61], i.e., by the place of their success in Paradise, by being placed therein.) He said: "by the place of their success in Paradise, by being placed therein." Through this explanation, may Allah have mercy on him, he informed us that the letter "bi" (ba') means "fi" (in); i.e., Allah saves those who feared Him from the punishment in the place of their success, which is Paradise. The letter "ba'" comes in the meaning of "fi" in the Arabic language, and among its examples is the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning, And by the night. Will you not then reason?﴾ [as-Saffat 137–138]. ﴿By the night﴾ means: in the night.

He said: ﴿Evil will not touch them, nor will they grieve﴾ [az-Zumar 61]. This is part of their salvation: evil will not touch them, i.e., nothing that would distress them will touch them, neither punishment, nor reproach, nor anything else. For this reason, when the people of Paradise enter Paradise, it is said: "O people of Paradise, abiding eternally, there is no death" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4730), Muslim (2849/40)], and it is said: "Indeed for you is that you will be blessed, and indeed for you is that you will be healthy, and indeed for you is that you will live" – meaning, you will not die – "and you will not fall ill, and you will not be miserable" [narrated by Ahmad (11905) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri]. They are always in bliss. For this reason He said: ﴿Evil will not touch them, nor will they grieve﴾: i.e., they will not grieve over what has passed, because grief is over the past, while worry is for the future. As for the future, He said: ﴿evil will not touch them﴾, and as for the past, He said: ﴿nor will they grieve﴾, i.e., they will not grieve over what has passed, because they were not negligent in it; rather they recognized the value of time and acted in it so that they were saved by it from the punishment of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

* In this noble verse there are benefits:

* Among them: the grace of Allah, glorified and exalted be He, upon the God-fearing, in that He saves them to the place of success.

* Among them: the excellence of taqwa and its effects and fruits; Allah, glorified and exalted be He, has mentioned in the Noble Qur'an many of its fruits.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that these saved ones will not be touched by any evil in the future, nor will they grieve over anything that has passed, and thereby their bliss is complete, because bliss diminishes when a person is afflicted with worry or distress about the future, and also diminishes when he is afflicted with grief over the past. But when he knows that he has earned the past and that no evil will reach him in the future, his bliss will be complete.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is, over all things, Disposer of affairs.﴾ [Az-Zumar 62]. The sentence ﴿Allah is the Creator of all things﴾ is a nominal sentence (jumlah ismiyyah) that indicates permanence and continuity, and that Allah, Exalted is, always and forever, the Creator.

As for His saying ﴿Creator of all things﴾, its meaning is: the one who brings it into existence in the form that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, willed. Khalq (creation) originally means measuring (taqdir), but it is also applied to bringing into existence that is accompanied by measuring, proportioning, perfecting and ordering. So here, khalq refers to bringing into existence in a complete manner, with His measuring, proportioning and arranging.

As for His saying ﴿all things﴾, some people said: Himself is excepted from this. But this is not correct, because it is known that the agent is not the object acted upon, and therefore no exception is needed. Exception is required in a sentence where the excepted item would have been included in it were it not for the exception. Here, however, it is impossible for Him to be included in it, why? Because the Creator is other than the created, so the Creator is not the created, and it is not possible that a created thing exists and then its creator exists after it, so that we could say the sentence needs an exception.

He said: ﴿and He is, over all things, Disposer of affairs﴾, where "He" refers to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿Over all things Disposer of affairs﴾: he said (one who disposes of it as He wills). Had He said ﴿over all things Disposer of affairs﴾ meaning "Guardian over it, managing it," it would have been more general, because wakil (disposer of affairs/trustee) in the language is one to whom a thing is entrusted for preservation and management, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is Disposer of all things in preservation and management. Here, one does not ask: how was He a wakil, and who appointed Him? We say: if wakil means the preserver and manager, then there is no need for someone to entrust Him with it; rather, He Himself took charge of that.

In this verse there are benefits:

* First: the generality of Allah, Mighty and Majestic's creation of all things, from His saying ﴿Allah is the Creator of all things﴾.

* Among them: a refutation of the Qadariyyah, who said that man creates his own actions. The basis for this is that the actions of the servants are included in the generality, for they are a "thing" among things, and so they are included in the generality.

* Among them: that Allah creates substances and attributes, because substances are called "a thing," and attributes are also called "a thing."

* Among them: that the Qur'an is created, because of His saying ﴿Allah is the Creator of all things﴾, and the Qur'an is a thing.

* Among them: that Allah is created, because He is a "thing," as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?"﴾ [Al-An'am 19].

So what do you say about these two benefits, that the Qur'an is created and that Allah is created?

We say: this is not correct. As for Allah being created, you have already known this a little while ago, and it is a necessity, because the agent is not the object acted upon. This is one point.

As for the Qur'an not being created: the Qur'an is an attribute of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the Lord with His attributes is not created; rather He has always been and always will be with His attributes, so His speech is uncreated, and the Qur'an is part of it. In any case, the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and His attributes are necessarily not included in this generality, because the Creator is other than the created.

As for the saying of those who used this verse as proof that the Qur'an is created, that this is general: we say that a general term may be intended to be specific. This applies if it is correct that the mind moves from this generality to every thing. We say that the phrase ﴿all things﴾ is used without intending generality, like His saying, Exalted: ﴿destroying everything by the command of its Lord﴾ [Al-Ahqaf 25]. It is known that it did not destroy the heavens and the earth, nor even the dwellings of the people, as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿So they became such that nothing could be seen but their dwellings﴾ [Al-Ahqaf 25].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the care of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, for what He created, because when He mentioned that He created all things, He made clear that He is Disposer of all things, and this indicates Allah's care for His creation, blessed and exalted is He.

* Among them: that what befalls people of trials and tribulations is from Allah, and it is part of His being their Disposer, due to the generality of His saying: ﴿and He is, over all things, Disposer of affairs﴾ [Az-Zumar 62]. It is known that when a person believes this belief, everything that is difficult will become easy for him; and if he also believes that through patience and seeking reward these calamities turn into blessings, they will also become light for him. For this reason, we find no one with greater ease than one who believes in qadar, its good and its evil. You will find that a person, even when circumstances change over him, is content and tranquil: if hardship befalls him he is patient, and that is better for him; and if ease befalls him he is grateful, and that is better for him.

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Az-Zumar 63]. That is, the keys to their treasuries of rain, plants, and other things. ﴿To Him belong the keys﴾: *maqalid* is the plural of *miqlad*, which is that by which a thing is hung or bound (*yuqallad*). This is the original meaning. The author (al-Mu'allif, i.e., al-Sa'di) takes *maqalid* here to mean *mafatih* (keys). It would have been better to say: "To Him belongs *maqalid* of the heavens and the earth," meaning the management (*tadbir*) of the heavens and the earth, because the word "keys" may lead someone to think that He owns the keys but not the management. The matter is not so. Rather, the management of the heavens and the earth is in His hand, that is, He directs them as He wills.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah, those are the losers﴾ [Az-Zumar 63]. ﴿Those who disbelieved﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*), and the clause ﴿those are the losers﴾ is its predicate (*khabar*). On this basis, this sentence contains two sentences: a major one (*kubra*), made up of the subject and predicate, and a minor one (*sughra*), which is the one that functions as the predicate. Pay attention: ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ is a subject, and (*ula'*) is another subject, ﴿the losers﴾ is the predicate of the second subject, and the clause consisting of the second subject and its predicate is the predicate of the first subject.

The benefit of this construction is that the second clause is attributed to the first, so that the sentence becomes, in meaning, two sentences.

As for His saying ﴿they are the losers﴾: ﴿they﴾ is a separating pronoun (*damir al-fasl*) that has no place in the grammatical structure (*i'rab*). Its benefits are: first, emphasis (*tawkid*); second, restriction (*hasr*); and third, distinction (*tamyiz*), or, if you wish, you may say: separating whether what follows is a predicate or a description (*wasf*). For when you say, "Zayd is the excellent," the word "excellent" may be either a predicate or a description if you omit (...). If you say, "Zayd the excellent," a person may await another word to complete the sentence and think that "excellent" is a description. But if you say, "He is the excellent," this expectation disappears, and it is known that what follows "he" is the predicate of the subject.

He said: ﴿And those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah﴾ (the Qur'an). There is some deficiency in this, because the signs of Allah are in the Qur'an and outside the Qur'an. Moreover, the signs are both cosmic (*kawniyyah*) and legislative (*shar'iyyah*), and disbelief occurs with both of them: with the cosmic signs and the legislative signs, and with the Qur'an, the Torah, the Gospel, and other books which Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed. So the better course, in terms of generality, is to say: they disbelieved in the signs of Allah, the cosmic and the legislative, the Qur'an and other than the Qur'an.

The root of *kufr* (disbelief) is *juhud* (denial), and from it comes *al-kufrara*, which is the sheath of the date-palm spathe, because it covers the spathe and it is not visible. The disbeliever is one who denies and covers the right of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the blessings of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Their disbelief in the signs of Allah occurs sometimes by denial (*takdhib*) and sometimes by arrogance (*istikbar*). In response to news (*akhbar*), it is by denial, and in response to command and prohibition (*amr wa nahy*), it is by arrogance.

﴿And those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah, those are the losers﴾ [Az-Zumar 63]. ﴿Ula'ika﴾ is a demonstrative noun, as you know. Here, is the referent distant or near? The referent is distant, because the particle *ka* does not come except when the referent is distant. The particle *ka* comes to alert the addressee to the referent because of its distance. As for when the referent is near, the *ka* is not used; rather one says *ula'*, like *ha'ula'*, and one says *hadha*. But when it is distant, the *ka* is used. Why? To alert the addressee to the referent, because there is no doubt that when a person is addressed, this is more effective in alerting him. (*Ula'ika*): when you say the *ka*, he will be alert and look to see who is referred to. If the referent can only be distant, then distance is either elevation or lowness, and either sensory or non-sensory (*ma'nawi*). The categories are therefore four. Which category applies to those who disbelieved here? Distant in lowness. Non-sensory or sensory? Non-sensory. And in the Fire? Sensory. But in this world it is non-sensory, because a person may be a disbeliever while he is on the peak of a mountain.

﴿Those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah﴾. So, as we said, disbelief includes two things: either denial, or arrogance. ﴿Those are the losers﴾ [Az-Zumar 63]: they, and no others, are the losers, who have lost this world and the Hereafter. As for the loss of the Hereafter, it is clear. As for the loss of this world, they were only created to worship Allah. Did they worship Allah? No. So have they lost it or not? They lost the purpose for which they were created. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat 56]. And Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: Indeed, the losers are those who lose themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss﴾ [Az-Zumar 15].

The commentator said: (connected to His saying: ﴿And Allah will save those who feared Him by their achievement﴾, and what is between them is an interjection). "Connected" means in meaning, yes, to His saying: ﴿And Allah will save those who feared Him by their achievement﴾ [Az-Zumar 61]. This is what he (may Allah have mercy on him) held. But this may be disputed. It may be said that His saying ﴿And Allah will save those who feared Him﴾ [Az-Zumar 61] is what is connected to what precedes it. Go back to the Qur'an now: ﴿And Allah will save those who feared Him by their achievement﴾ [Az-Zumar 61]. The correct view is that ﴿will save﴾ is connected to what precedes it. When He mentioned those who lied about Allah, that their faces would be blackened, He said: ﴿And Allah will save those who feared Him﴾ [Az-Zumar 61]. As for this (verse 63), it has no connection to what was mentioned; rather its connection to what precedes it directly is clearer and more evident, because Allah said: ﴿Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is, over all things, Disposer of affairs (*wakil*)﴾ [Az-Zumar 62], ﴿to Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Az-Zumar 62-63]. That is: after this explanation and after the affirmation, the affirmation of the disbelievers that Allah is the Creator of all things, there remains no gain for them if they disbelieve; rather they are the losers. So this verse is connected directly to what precedes it, and not connected to His saying: ﴿And Allah will save those who feared Him by their achievement﴾ [Az-Zumar 61], because ﴿And Allah will save﴾ is connected to what precedes it. This is what the structure of the Qur'anic composition requires. As for scattering the verses and saying that this entire statement, ﴿Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is, over all things, Disposer of affairs. To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Az-Zumar 62-63], is an interjected sentence, or that all of this is an interjection with no place here, there is no doubt that this contradicts what the Qur'anic composition and context require. So the correct view is that this sentence is connected to what precedes it. What is the point of connection? What is the point of connection? The author said that His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah﴾ is connected to His saying: ﴿And Allah will save those who feared Him﴾. We have mentioned that there is an issue with this, and that the correct view is that it is connected to what precedes it, and we have explained the correct view. So what is it?

* A student: (...).

A person cannot pay attention while looking right and left. The heart follows the gaze; the gaze commands, then it looks, and the heart follows the gaze and is not concerned with what is in front of it. Who knows?

* A student: Because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: "In His hand are the keys of the heavens and the earth."

* The Shaykh: And that He is the Creator of all things, and they affirm it.

* The student: So they had no argument, and that resulted in (...).

* The Shaykh: So these people, who affirm that Allah is the Creator of all things and that to Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth, and who disbelieve in Him, will undoubtedly be losers. They are the greatest losers. How do they affirm that Allah is the Creator of all things, and that to Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth, and then disbelieve in His signs? The requirement of this affirmation was that they should believe in the signs of Allah. But they lost, so they disbelieved in the signs of Allah. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah, those are the losers﴾ [Az-Zumar 63].

* In this verse, ﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Az-Zumar 63]: among its benefits is that the one who manages the heavens and the earth is Allah alone. The proof that He is alone is that He placed the predicate first in His saying: ﴿To Him belong the keys﴾, and placing the predicate first conveys restriction.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: drawing a person's attention to not seeking help except from Allah, not asking except of Allah, and not relying except on Allah. What is the basis of this? That He is the One to whom belong the keys of the heavens and the earth. So do not turn to other than Him, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas: "If you ask, ask Allah; and if you seek help, seek help from Allah."[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2516) and Ahmad (2763), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the disbelievers are the losers, even if in this world they seem to have won the round. They are losers in this world and the next; this is due to His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah, those are the losers﴾.

* Among its benefits: the obligation of believing in the signs of Allah. The indication is that if the threat is upon the one who disbelieves in them, this shows that belief is obligatory.

* Also among them: the prohibition of disbelief, since it is a cause of loss.

If someone says: where in the verse is the word "prohibited" (*yuharram*)? We say: prohibition is derived in several ways. Among them is the prohibition, like: ﴿And do not approach fornication﴾ [Al-Isra' 32]. Among them is an explicit statement of prohibition, like: ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion and blood﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 3]. Among them is the negation of permissibility, like His saying: ﴿And it is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs﴾ [Al-Baqarah 228]. Among them is a threat upon a thing. Among them is the statement that good is lost. The ways of conveying prohibition are many, but among them is that the imposition of loss upon an act indicates that it is forbidden.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the gain of those who believe, and that they are the winners. From where is this derived? From the implication (*mafhum*) of the disbelievers' loss, that the gain belongs to the believers. Allah has stated this explicitly in His saying: ﴿By time, indeed mankind is in loss, except those who have believed and done righteous deeds and advised each other to truth and advised each other to patience﴾ [Al-'Asr 1-3].

Ibn 'Uthaymin's commentary (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 39, verse 64:

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Say: "Do you order me to worship other than Allah, you ignorant ones?"﴾ [Az-Zumar 64].

**I'rab (grammatical analysis):** ﴿Afa-ghayra Allahi ta'murunni﴾: the *hamza* is the interrogative particle, and the *fa'* is a conjunctive particle. Here a difficulty arises with this analysis, because it is well known that the interrogative *hamza* must come at the beginning of the sentence. In this verse it comes as ﴿Afa-ghayra Allahi ta'murunni﴾. If it must come first, how can the *fa'*, which indicates that the sentence is coordinated with what precedes it, come after it? The answer is that grammarians have two views on this:

The first view: the *hamza* is interrogative and is placed before a sentence that is coordinated with something preceding it, and this sentence is supplied according to the context. On this view, the implied meaning in this verse is: "Say: Are you ignorant, so that other than Allah you order me to worship, you ignorant ones?" The supplied element is chosen in each place according to what fits.

For example, ﴿Afa-lam yasiroo fil-ard﴾ [Yusuf 109] is understood as: "Have they been heedless, so that they have not traveled in the land?" It has also been said that the *hamza* is interrogative and that the *fa'* has been moved from its original place, so the sense is: "So is it other than Allah...", and the sentence is then coordinated with what precedes it. However, the first meaning is preferable when it is easy and possible to supply something suitable.

The author says in his analysis: (﴿Ghayra﴾ is in the accusative, governed by ﴿a'budu﴾, which is the object of ﴿ta'murunni﴾, with the implied *an*; [the verb is read] with one *nun*, or with two *nuns* assimilated, or with two *nuns* separated.) This is in relation to his statement "ta'murunni." The author says in the analysis that *ghayra* is in the accusative, governed by *a'budu*, and the meaning is: "Shall I worship other than Allah by your command?" This is the meaning of the verse. The phrase ﴿Afa-ghayra Allahi ta'murunni﴾ has several readings:

First, reading it with one *nun*: ﴿ta'murunī﴾. Second, reading it with two *nuns* assimilated (*idgham*, the merging of the two identical letters): ﴿ta'murunnī﴾. Third, reading it with two *nuns* not assimilated: ﴿ta'murunanī﴾.

**Meaning:** ﴿Afa-ghayra Allahi ta'murunni a'budu﴾ means: "Do you order me to worship other than Allah?" ﴿Ayyuha al-jahiloon﴾ means: those who are ignorant of the reality of what is owed to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and of the reality of idol worship. It is also possible that the intended meaning of ﴿al-jahiloon﴾ is "the foolish," because *jahl* (ignorance) is sometimes used to mean foolishness and sometimes to mean lack of knowledge. When it means foolishness, it is called *jahalah*, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Allah accepts repentance only from those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon after﴾ [An-Nisa 17].

His words ﴿Afa-ghayra Allahi ta'murunni﴾ [Az-Zumar 64] include everything other than Allah: the living and the dead, the righteous and the corrupt, the inanimate and the animate.

﴿Ayyuha al-jahiloon﴾: *ayyu* is in the vocative (*munada*, the addressed noun), and *al-jahiloon* is an adjective describing *ayyu*; for this reason it is in the nominative. The interrogative here is for rebuke and denial, as shown by his words "you ignorant ones."

* Several benefits are derived from this verse:

* First: the ignorance of those who order the worship of idols.

* Among them: these ignorant people imagined that the Messenger himself worshiped idols, even though he came only to affirm the Oneness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, alone.

* Third: among the benefits of this verse is that the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, whose worship is knowledge, and whose worship is right guidance; since worshiping other than Him is ignorance, worshiping Him is knowledge and right guidance.

* Among its benefits: if the polytheists tried to make the Prophet (ﷺ) associate partners with Allah, how much more so the followers of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him! They will try to make people associate partners with Allah far more than the polytheists tried to make the Prophet (ﷺ) do so.

* A branch of this benefit is caution against the callers to shirk and disbelief, such as the callers to Christianity today. The Christians, may the curse of Allah be upon them until the Day of Resurrection, try by every means to mislead the Muslims and to make them Christians. If they fail in that, then at the least they try to take them out of their religion, even if they do not enter the religion of Christianity. This is now clear: you find them setting up powerful and evident broadcasting stations to call Muslims to Christianity; you find them writing many writings, letters and books, larger ones, which they spread among the Muslims; and you also find them writing the Gospel exactly like the writing of the Qur'an, detailed, vocalized and fully marked, so that the common person who does not know the Qur'an thinks it is the Qur'an. You also find them going to poor and helpless countries and setting up schools and facilities there, then churches, in order to (...) the people. The point is that the enemies of the Muslims spare no effort in taking the Muslims out of their religion and into their own creed which they were upon. And Allah knows best.

**Student:** ﴿And it has certainly been revealed to you and to those before you: "If you associate partners with Allah, your deeds will surely be lost, and you will surely be among the losers." (65) Rather, worship Allah alone, and be among the thankful. (66) They did not measure Allah with His true measure, while the earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand. Glorified is He and exalted above what they associate with Him. (67) And the Trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will fall unconscious, except whom Allah wills. Then it will be blown again, and behold, they will be standing, looking on.﴾ [Az-Zumar 65–68].

Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And it has already been revealed to you, and to those before you, that if you should associate others with Allah, your deeds would surely be nullified, and you would surely be among the losers.﴾ [az-Zumar 65] We mentioned yesterday that this sentence is emphasized with how many emphasizers?

* Shaykh: What are they?

* Student: The second answer (...) it does not necessarily entail the occurrence of the hypothetical.

* Student: His saying: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾.

* Shaykh: Its parallel is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ [az-Zukhruf 81], and it is known that it is impossible for Allah to take a son.

His saying: ﴿and you would surely be among the losers﴾ [az-Zumar 65] is emphasized with how many emphasizers?

* Student: With the lam and the nun of emphasis.

* Shaykh: Yes.

* Student: And the implied oath.

* Shaykh: And the implied oath, because this lam serves as the answer to the oath.

* We take the benefits of this verse:

* Among its benefits: that shirk nullifies deeds, even if it is committed by the best of creation, by His saying: ﴿your deeds would surely be nullified﴾.

* Among its benefits: that this ruling is established in all the revealed laws, by His saying: ﴿And it has already been revealed to you, and to those before you﴾ [az-Zumar 65].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the great gravity of shirk, and that it is the most corrupting of kinds of sin; for this reason it nullifies all deeds.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of revelation to the Messenger ﷺ and to those messengers before him, upon them be peace.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that shirk is a cause of loss in this world and the Hereafter, by His saying: ﴿and you would surely be among the losers﴾.

* Among its benefits: that the disbelievers, even if they profit in this world, are in reality losers in both this world and the Hereafter, because they did not benefit in this world from that for which they were created; therefore they are losers. Allah the Exalted has said in another verse: ﴿Say: Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss﴾ [az-Zumar 15].

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Rather, worship Allah alone, and be among the grateful.﴾ [Az-Zumar 66].

﴿Bal﴾ (rather): this is for idrab (a turning away from what precedes). Is it idrab of nullification (ibtal) or of transition (intiqal)? It is idrab of nullification, because idrab among them is of two kinds: one kind intended to nullify what came before and establish what follows, and another kind intended as a transition from one thing to another.

An example of the first is this verse. An example of the second is His saying: ﴿Rather, their knowledge of the Hereafter has failed. Rather, they are in doubt about it. Rather, they are blind to it﴾ [An-Naml 66]. Here there are transitions from bad to worse. ﴿Rather, their knowledge has failed﴾ means: it has been exhausted, ﴿of the Hereafter. Rather, they are in doubt about it. Rather, they are blind to it.﴾ Here He says: ﴿Rather, worship Allah﴾ [Az-Zumar 66]. This is idrab of nullification of the shirk that preceded; that is, "Rather, leave off shirk, for it is false, and worship Allah."

As for His saying: ﴿Rather, worship Allah﴾, the author said: (alone). From where did he derive this oneness that conveys restriction (hasr)? He derived it from the fronting of the object (taqdim al-ma'mul), and the rule in rhetoric is that fronting what should be postponed conveys restriction and exclusiveness. Everything that should be postponed, if fronted, the judgment is specific to it. It is known that the direct object should be postponed, so when it is fronted before its governing verb, it conveys exclusiveness and restriction, meaning: rather, Allah alone.

﴿Fa'budh﴾ (so worship): the fa' — they say it is brought in to embellish the wording. If it were removed in other than the Qur'an, the speech would still be sound, but in the Qur'an it cannot be removed, because it was revealed from Allah and cannot be altered. Such a particle is called fa' al-tazyin (the decorative fa'), and it has a parallel, such as their saying: "I have such-and-such, only (faqat)," meaning qatt, and the fa' is extra to embellish the wording.

He said: ﴿Rather, worship Allah﴾. ﴿U'bud﴾ is an imperative verb, meaning: humble yourself before Him, humble yourself to Allah. Know that worship ('ibadah) is used in two senses: the first is ta'abbud (the act of worshipping), and the second is al-muta'abbad bih (that which is worshipped).

As for ta'abbud, its meaning is humbling oneself before Allah the Exalted, out of love and veneration, by carrying out His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. So if we see a person praying, for example, we say: this one is worshipping, that is, humbling himself to Allah the Exalted by performing prayer. It is also used for the object of worship, that is, the act itself. Shaykh al-Islam defined it in this sense by saying: "Worship is a comprehensive term for everything Allah loves and is pleased with, of statements and acts, outward and inward." On this basis, prayer itself we call worship, and charity is worship, fasting is worship, Hajj is worship, kindness to parents is worship, maintaining ties of kinship is worship, and benevolence to the poor is worship, and so on. So His saying ﴿fa'budh﴾ means: humble yourself to Him by performing His worship, by carrying out His commands and avoiding His prohibitions.

(﴿Rather, worship Allah and be among the grateful﴾ for His blessing upon you.) ﴿Wa kun﴾: kun is an imperative verb, and ﴿min al-shakirin﴾ means: among those who thank Allah.

Know that when (al) is attached to a participle (mushtaq), it becomes a general relative pronoun among the relative nouns, so it is equivalent to (man) and to (ma) when attached to a participle, such as al-shakir (the thankful), al-mashkur (the one thanked), al-ahsan (the best), and similar words. On this basis, His saying ﴿min al-shakirin﴾ conveys generality, meaning: among those who engage in thanking Allah.

If it is asked: what is shukr (gratitude)? It is said: gratitude is the act of obeying the Benefactor in belief, speech, and action; this is shukr. For this reason a poet said:

"Three things have been gained by you through my blessings: my hand, my tongue, and the concealed conscience."

He means: by your bestowing favours on me, you have possessed my heart, my tongue, and my limbs.

If someone asks: is shukr the same as hamd (praise) or something else?
We say: there is a general and specific relationship between them. They coincide when they are in response to a blessing, for hamd is shukr, since it is praise of Allah by the tongue. If a person eats or drinks and says "Al-hamdu lillah," he is thereby grateful and praising. Hamd stands alone in describing Allah with perfection apart from response to a blessing; so if you praise Allah as "the Living, the Mighty" and similar, that is hamd and not shukr, since it is not in response to a blessing. However, we may sometimes consider it shukr insofar as it is worship, and obeying the Benefactor is part of shukr.

And if you praise Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, or even if you perform obedience to Allah the Glorified and Exalted in return for His blessing, and it was not in your mind (...) perfection, it becomes shukr to Him. In any case, it may be difficult for one to be separated from the other, because praise itself, even if not in response to a blessing, is considered shukr, since it is the performance of obedience to the Benefactor. ﴿Rather, worship Allah and be among the grateful﴾ [Az-Zumar 66].

Then the Exalted said: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure﴾ [Az-Zumar 67]. ﴿Ma﴾ is negative, and ﴿qadaru﴾ means: they magnified. The word Allah is the object of ﴿qadaru﴾, and ﴿haqqa qadrihi﴾ is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), because it is an idafa to a verbal noun, and what is attached to a verbal noun is called an absolute object because it stands in the place of the verbal noun. On this basis we say: ﴿haqqa qadrihi﴾ means: its true magnification.

The commentator said: (they did not know Him with true knowledge, or they did not magnify Him with true magnificence when they associated others with Him). The correct one is the second: that the meaning is they did not magnify Him with true magnificence when they associated others with Him. The evidence for this is that these people knew Allah: ﴿If you asked them who created them, they would surely say, Allah﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 87], ﴿If you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, Allah﴾ [Az-Zumar 38]. But did they magnify the One they knew with true magnification? No, and this is what (...).

So the correct possibility is the second, that they did not magnify Him with true magnificence, by what? By associating others with Him; for whoever magnifies Allah with true magnification cannot associate anyone with Him.

Then He said: ﴿While the earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection﴾. The waw is for the circumstantial clause (hal), and it may be resumptive (isti'nafiyyah) to explain Allah's greatness.

﴿Wal-ard﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), ﴿jamian﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier (hal), and ﴿qabdatuhu﴾ is the predicate of the subject, meaning: the whole earth, all of the seven earths, will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection.

The commentator said: (﴿wal-ard jamian﴾: hal, that is, the seven). ﴿Jamian﴾ is a hal from what? From the earth. From this we know that a hal may come from the subject before the predicate is mentioned, as you might say: Zayd standing is better than him sitting.

He says: (﴿While the earth entirely is His handful﴾ means: held in His grip, that is, in His dominion and disposal). So the author explained the qabd (grip) as meaning dominion and disposal. This is clearly questionable; rather, it is a distortion, because dominion and disposal extend to everything, the earth and heavens both on the Day of Resurrection and before it. Rather, qabda in the sense of the thing grasped, which the hand encloses, is the handful, as one says: a handful of food. What is a handful of food? It means a person grasps food with his hand like this. So the earth on the Day of Resurrection is the handful of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and this has been explained in the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud concerning the Prophet ﷺ and a rabbi of the Jews: "Allah will place the earth on one finger, the trees on one finger, and the mountains on one finger," etc. [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4811), Muslim (2786/19), from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.] So the correct and definite position is that the qabdah means that it is within His hand, Mighty and Majestic.

If someone says: may we depict this handful, by taking a date or an apple and placing it in our hands, and saying ﴿His handful﴾, and then closing our hand on the apple or date?
The answer: No; for if we did that, it would be a likening of Allah's grip of the earth, and this is impermissible. As for explaining the meaning of qabdah, there is no harm, by saying: qabdah is placing a thing in the hand and then grasping it with it. But to specify how Allah the Mighty and Majestic grips the earth is contrary to the belief of the People of the Sunnah and the Community, as is well known to all.

His saying ﴿Yawm al-qiyamah﴾ is a time adverb for the handful; that is, it will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection. The Day of Resurrection is the day when people are raised from their graves to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and it is named thus for three reasons. Enumerate them for us; we mentioned them shortly before.

* Student: the standing of people before the Lord of the worlds.
* Shaykh: for people's standing from their graves before the Lord of the worlds.
* Student: the establishment of justice on the Day of Resurrection.
* Shaykh: the establishment of justice on the Day of Resurrection.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: What? No.
* Student: the standing of the spirits, the angels.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: the witnesses stand.
* Shaykh: "The day the witnesses stand."

﴿While the earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand﴾. The author said: (folded [mijmu'at] by His power). The heavens are "mutawiyyat" (folded). Folding is known: turning cloth over one part upon another is called tayy, and from it: folding a page when the scribe finishes with it, meaning turning part of it over another. Allah the Mighty and Majestic compared His folding of the heavens to the folding of a scroll for books, saying: ﴿On the day We will roll up the heaven like the rolling of a scroll for writings﴾ [Al-Anbiya 104]. Blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds: this great heaven of vast expanse, whose thickness is reported to be five hundred years, Allah the Mighty and Majestic will fold these heavens as a scroll is folded for books, or as the scroll in which cases are recorded is folded: ﴿On the day We will roll up the heaven like the rolling of a scroll for writings﴾ [Al-Anbiya 104], meaning as the scroll is rolled, which is the judge's scribe's record, or as the scroll in which matters are written is rolled. Folding is known; we said it is turning cloth over one part upon another, or paper, or similar.

He says: ﴿The heavens are folded﴾: the agent is omitted, or the form of the passive participle is used for knowledge of the folder. Who is the folder? Allah, as the other verse explains: ﴿On the day We will roll up the heaven like the rolling of a scroll for writings﴾.

The author said: (folded [mijmu'at]). This is questionable, because we say: it is folded (tayyan) as a collection; if we explain it as gathered, we have not given a precise explanation, since a thing may be gathered without being folded. But if it is folded, this is a meaning beyond mere gathering. The correct statement is: ﴿mutawiyyat﴾ means some of them are wrapped up within others.

﴿Folded in His right hand﴾. He said: (by His power). This is a distortion according to the doctrine of those who do not affirm Allah's informative attributes (sifat khabariyyah). The correct view is that the right hand is meant by the yamin, the right hand; He folds them with His right hand, Mighty and Majestic.

He said: ﴿Folded in His right hand, glorified is He and exalted above what they associate﴾ [Az-Zumar 67]. Subhana (glory be to): an ism al-masdar (verbal noun form), its verb is sabbaha, and the masdar of sabbaha is tasbih; the ism al-masdar is subhan, which is always in the accusative as an absolute object and usually attached to a noun. On this basis one should not err in its parsing: parse it always as an absolute object of an omitted verb, the estimate being: he glorifies with glorification.

﴿Subhanahu wa ta'ala 'amma yushrikun﴾ [Az-Zumar 67]: meaning, tanzihan (declaring Him far above) him. What is the meaning of tasbih? We have now explained the word morphologically, but what is the meaning of tasbih? They said: the meaning of tasbih is tanzih (exalting Allah above imperfection), because it derives from sabbaha, yasbahu, when one moves far away in water. So tanzih is distancing from evil. On this basis the meaning of "Subhan Allah" is: declaring Him far above. From what is Allah declared far above?

He is declared far above two things: from resemblance to creation, and from every deficiency and defect in His attributes. His power, for example, is exalted above incapacity; His knowledge is exalted above ignorance and forgetfulness; His strength is exalted above weakness, and so on. His hand is exalted above resemblance to the hands of creatures, and His face likewise. Thus the tanzih of Allah the Mighty and Majestic returns to two things: first, resemblance to creation; second, defect and deficiency.

His saying ﴿Ta'ala﴾: He is exalted in His greatness above what they associate with Him, or above what they associate with Him alongside Him, and there is no doubt this is the reality.

From the two noble verses we take the following benefits:

* First: the obligation of sincerely devoting worship to Allah, from His saying ﴿Rather, worship Allah alone﴾ [Az-Zumar 66].
It follows from this principle that if a person associates someone with Allah, his deeds are nullified: why? Because if he associates with Allah, he performs an act not commanded by Allah and His Messenger, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever does an action that is not in accordance with our command, it is rejected" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2697), Muslim (1718/17), from Aisha]. This is apart from the preceding verse, ﴿If you were to associate others with Allah, your deeds would surely be nullified﴾ [Az-Zumar 65], which is an explicit text. But if we want to derive it from His saying ﴿Rather, worship Allah﴾ [Az-Zumar 66], we say:
* Among its benefits: whoever associates anyone with Allah, his deed is nullified and rejected. The proof is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever does an action that is not in accordance with our command, it is rejected" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2697), Muslim (1718/17), from Aisha].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the obligation of gratitude upon everyone, from His saying ﴿And be among the grateful﴾ [Az-Zumar 66]; and when gratitude is obligatory, its opposite, disbelief, is forbidden.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that sincerity to Allah the Exalted is part of gratitude to Him, since He followed His saying ﴿Rather, worship Allah﴾ [Az-Zumar 66] with His saying ﴿And be among the grateful﴾ [Az-Zumar 66].

As for the second verse: among its benefits is showing the greatness of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, from His saying ﴿While the earth entirely is His handful﴾ and ﴿the heavens are folded in His right hand﴾ [Az-Zumar 67].
* Among its benefits: that whoever associates with Allah has not magnified Allah with true magnification; rather, the opposite, from His saying ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure﴾ [Az-Zumar 67].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the goodness of describing the Qur'an, for when He negated from them that they measured Allah with His true measure, He explained the reason for it: that He, Mighty and Majestic, is greater than everything, ﴿while the earth entirely is His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens are folded in His right hand﴾ [Az-Zumar 67].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that it is obligatory to magnify Allah with true magnification. But someone may say: this involves great hardship, because Allah the Exalted is greater and more majestic than that the deed of the servant could encompass Him. For this reason, when the verse ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah with the fear due to Him﴾ [Ali 'Imran 102] was revealed, it was difficult for the Companions: who can fear Allah with the fear due to Him? It is said that this noble verse is qualified by His saying ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [At-Taghabun 16]. Otherwise, who can compass magnifying Allah with true magnification in the manner Allah the Mighty and Majestic intended? But we say: magnifying Allah with true magnification is by carrying out His command, and this is attained to the extent of one's capacity, by His saying ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [Al-Baqarah 286], and by His saying ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [At-Taghabun 16].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verse 66–67 (part 2 of 2):

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirming that Allah has a hand, based on His saying: ﴿His grip﴾ [Az-Zumar 67], and His saying: ﴿in His right hand﴾ [Az-Zumar 67].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that on the Day of Resurrection Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will grip the earth in His hand, based on His saying: ﴿And the earth entirely will be His grip on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Az-Zumar 67].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the heavens will be folded up on the Day of Resurrection, based on His saying: ﴿and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand﴾ [Az-Zumar 67].
