* The Shaykh: Conjunctive: the waw is conjunctive, "hatta idha ja'uha wa futihat," so it is for coordination.
And according to the author's opinion?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It is opened before they arrive, because he said: the waw is for the circumstantial clause with the implied "qad" (already): "until, when they reach it and its gates have already been opened."
What is the preferred opinion on this?
* Student: The waw is conjunctive, and the response is implied...
* The Shaykh: Omitted before the conjunction. What is the estimate?
* The student: "Until, when they reach it, and they have been purified and cleansed, and its gates have been opened."
* The Shaykh: Excellent. Is there another opinion or a third opinion regarding the waw, the most correct one?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It is for the circumstantial clause. It was also said that it is extra (za'idah). What is your view of this opinion?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No. Do you find this acceptable or not?
* The student: (...).
* Another student: (...).
* The Shaykh: We say: this is not correct, because its use as an extra particle is not known in the Arabic language.
His saying, exalted is He: "Salamun 'alaykum, tibtum" (Peace be upon you, you are good). Is this a supplication or a statement?
* Student: This is a statement.
* The Shaykh: A statement. And "tibtum"?
* The student: "Tibtum" is a circumstantial clause indicating everything that makes you good.
* The Shaykh: A circumstantial clause of what?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, a circumstantial clause of what? A circumstantial clause requires a governing element and a referent. Is there one or not?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The meaning is general, but a circumstantial clause of what? In terms of grammar?
* Student: From the kaf.
* The Shaykh: From the kaf in His saying "'alaykum." Correct.
His saying: "fadkhulu-ha khalidin" (so enter it, abiding forever). Did the author parse it? What is the grammatical status of "khalidin"?
* Student: A circumstantial clause.
* The Shaykh: Of what?
* The student: Of the waw.
* The Shaykh: Of the waw in His saying "udkhulu-ha." Is this circumstantial clause concurrent or anticipated?
* The student: Anticipated.
* The Shaykh: Anticipated.
His saying, exalted is He: "sadaqana wa'dah" (He has fulfilled His promise to us). What is its meaning?
* Student: "Sadaqana wa'dah" means He fulfilled what He promised.
* The Shaykh: He fulfilled for them what He promised, so His promise was true to us.
"Awrathana al-ardh"?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What is it said to mean?
* The student: It is said that it means: He causes to inherit the earth.
* The Shaykh: Which earth?
* The student: The land of the disbelievers.
* The Shaykh: And the second?
* The student: The second shares with the disbelievers in..
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: First, he said: the land of the Garden.
* The Shaykh: It is said: the intended earth is the land of the Garden? And what is said?
* The student: The second opinion: it is the earth on which we are (...).
* The Shaykh: And how did He make them inherit it?
* Student: This earth? By making it exclusively theirs to the exclusion of the disbelievers (...).
* The Shaykh: By what?
* The student: By their being exalted over them in this world; He made them高 over them in the world (...).
* Another student: We said the inheritance of the earth has two aspects: the first is fighting the disbelievers and dwelling in their lands, and the second is that they inherit it rightfully, unlike the disbelievers, who dwelt in the earth falsely.
* The Shaykh: That becomes the earth of this world. Which of them is preferred?
* Student: The preferred view is that the earth is the earth of this world.
* The Shaykh: By what do you prefer it?
* The student: By two things: first, that when "the earth" is mentioned unqualified, it refers to the earth as opposed to the heavens.
The second matter: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mentioned the Garden after the earth; had the Garden been meant, it would not be correct to mention it.
* The Shaykh: How was it mentioned after it?
* The student: "Wa awrathana al-ardha natabawwa'u min al-jannah" — if the earth were the earth of the Garden, one would not say "the earth of the Garden, we settle..." as if in it...
* Another student: The answer has two aspects: first, that when "the earth" is used unqualified, it is meant as the earth opposite the heavens. Second, if the earth intended here were the earth of the Garden, Allah the Mighty and Majestic would not have said "min al-jannah" (from the Garden).
* The Shaykh: "Natabawwa'u min al-jannah" — he would have said "minha" (from it), "natabawwa'u minha haythu nashaa" (we settle from it wherever we will).
But how does He say: "awrathana al-ardha natabawwa'u min al-jannah"? How can their inheriting the earth be the cause of their settling in the Garden?
* Student: It is said for two reasons: by righteous deeds in this world (...) the Garden; and it is said: their settling in the Garden is tranquillity in the place they desire.
* The Shaykh: That is, they take a place in the Garden by their righteous deeds in this world, or wherever they will within their place in the Garden.
His saying, exalted is He: "fa-ni'ma ajru al-'amilin" (how excellent is the reward of those who work). Is this from the speech of the people of the Garden or from the speech of Allah?
* Student: If it is from Allah, the Exalted, then it would be (...).
* The Shaykh: No, I ask: is it from the speech of Allah, or is it the continuation of the speech of the people of the Garden who said: "All praise is for Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us"?
* The student: It is the continuation of the speech of the people of the Garden.
* The Shaykh: It is the continuation of the speech of the people of the Garden. Is there another opinion?
* The student: If it is from Allah..
* The Shaykh: "If it is" is not the point; I ask you whether there is another opinion or not.
* The student: I do not know.
* Another student: The second opinion: it is a beginning from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so it contains an exhortation to us to work and strive in obedience.
* The Shaykh: As for if it is the speech of the people of the Garden, it is a continuation of their speech, and it is in the category of speaking of Allah's blessings.
Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said, and this is the beginning of today's lesson: "And you will see the angels" [az-Zumar 75]. Have we taken the benefits? From where? Subhan Allah.
Allah the Exalted said: "And those who feared their Lord will be driven to the Garden in groups," and so on to the end [az-Zumar 73].
Student: The second opinion: it is guidance from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so it contains an exhortation to work and striving in obedience.
* The Shaykh: As for if it is the speech of the people of the Garden, it is a continuation of their speech, and it is in the category of speaking of Allah's blessings.

The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿Those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups﴾ [az-Zumar 71]. How are they driven?

* Student: They are pushed, shoved forward.
* The Shaykh: What is your evidence for this?
* Student: His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿On the Day they will be pushed into the Fire of Hell with a violent push﴾ [at-Tur 13].
* The Shaykh: Yes. His saying ﴿in groups﴾, what does it mean?
* Student: Companies.
* The Shaykh: Separate companies. How are these companies arranged? Is it according to the sin and its gravity, or according to nations, meaning each nation on its own?
* Student: (...) They are companies according to nations, and others are according to deeds.
* The Shaykh: So there are two opinions. Which is more likely correct?
* Student: According to deeds.
* The Shaykh: What is the evidence?
* Student: His saying ﷺ: "The first group to enter Paradise will be in the likeness of the moon" (ﷺ) [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3246) and Muslim (2834/14), from Abu Hurayrah].
* The Shaykh: Yes. Likewise the Fire: those who are earliest into the Fire are the most gravely guilty, just as those who are earliest into Paradise are the most excellent in deeds.

His saying: ﴿until, when they reach it, its gates will be opened﴾ [az-Zumar 71]. Who opens them?

* Student: Its guardians.
* The Shaykh: Its guardians.

His saying: ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you﴾ [az-Zumar 71]. What is the interrogative here?

* Student: It is for affirmation and reproach.
* The Shaykh: For affirmation and reproach.

What is the benefit in His saying ﴿from among you﴾?

* Student: The benefit in His saying ﴿from among you﴾ is that it is more eloquent than if He had said "from your own midst," because ﴿from among you﴾ is a refutation to them, that if he were an angel they would not accept him.
* The Shaykh: We said this is more eloquent than His saying "from yourselves." How so?
* Student: Because ﴿from among you﴾ indicates (...)
* The Shaykh: That is, from your tribes that you know. That is why He said: ﴿Allah certainly conferred favour upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger from themselves﴾ [Ali 'Imran 164], meaning of their kind, because the Messenger was not from every tribe of the believers. And regarding the unlettered: ﴿It is He who sent among the unlettered a messenger from among them﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 2], because he was an Arab.

I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿And its guardians will say to them﴾, affirming and reproaching and rebuking, ﴿"Did there not come to you messengers from among you, reciting to you the verses of your Lord"﴾ [az-Zumar 71]. The phrase ﴿reciting to you the verses of your Lord﴾ may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and it may be another descriptive clause (ṣifah), because ﴿from among you﴾ is a descriptive phrase, and when an indefinite noun is described, a circumstantial clause may come from it, and the clause may also be another descriptor, since there is no barrier to multiple descriptors. Moreover, the circumstantial clause in reality is a descriptor, as Ibn Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The ḥāl is a descriptive, subordinate, accusative word, conveying "in a state of," like "alone I go."

He says: ﴿messengers from among you reciting to you the verses of your Lord﴾: that is, they recite to you the verses of your Lord. The intended meaning of "verses" here is the legislative verses, because what is meant is what was revealed of revelation.

The author's statement "(the Qur'an and other than it)" means that it includes all the scriptures that were sent down.

﴿And warning you of the meeting of this your Day﴾ [az-Zumar 71]: they warned you of meeting this Day, since they informed you of it and informed you of its great terrors, so no excuse remained for you. That is why they confessed: ﴿They said, "Yes, but the word of punishment has come into effect against the disbelievers"﴾ [az-Zumar 71]. They said "Yes," meaning: messengers from among us have indeed come to us, reciting to us the verses of our Lord and warning us of the meeting of this our Day, but the word of punishment has come into effect against the disbelievers, and this is what prevented us from obeying the messengers.

﴿Haqqat﴾ means "was due and was established." The phrase ﴿the word of the punishment﴾ refers to the word by which they deserve punishment. What is this word? The author said: it is His saying: ﴿"I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together"﴾ [Hud 119]. This is the word: that Allah, glorified and exalted, bound Himself to fill Hell from the jinn and mankind all together. If He has bound Himself to fill the Fire, then He must create for it peoples who deny the messengers, so that they deserve the Fire of Hell, and we seek refuge in Allah.

It was also said that the word is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has come into effect will not believe, even if every sign came to them﴾ [Yunus 96-97], because when the word of Allah came into effect upon them, their belief was prevented.

But here a person asks: is this from the category of arguing by predestination, or from the category of acknowledging the reality?
The answer: the second, because they cannot argue by predestination in that situation.

﴿But the word of punishment has come into effect against the disbelievers.﴾

﴿It will be said: "Enter the gates of Hell"﴾ [az-Zumar 72]. ﴿Qīla﴾ is a past verb in the passive form, whose agent is not named. So who is the one saying it?

Some scholars said: He left the agent unspecified to indicate that the whole creation says this to them. It is said: that is, from the angels, from the people of Paradise, from everyone who witnesses it.

﴿It will be said: "Enter the gates of Hell, abiding eternally therein"﴾ [az-Zumar 72]. ﴿Udkhulū﴾ ("enter") is an imperative for humiliation, not for honour, because whoever is told "Enter the Fire" is not honoured, we seek refuge in Allah, but is humiliated.

﴿It will be said: "Enter the gates of Hell, abiding eternally therein"﴾. The gates of Hell: it has already been mentioned that by the explicit text of the Qur'an they are seven gates. ﴿Abiding eternally therein﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the waw in His saying ﴿udkhulū﴾, meaning: while you are abiding eternally therein.

﴿Abiding eternally therein﴾ means "destined to abide": that is, the circumstantial clause is anticipated, because abiding comes after entering. They enter first and then they abide forever afterwards. So when the circumstance is not simultaneous, it is an anticipated circumstance (ḥāl muqaddarah).

Khulūd (abiding) originally means a long stay, and it was said: a lasting stay.

According to the first view, mentioning eternity after abiding is an establishing statement (ta'sīs). According to the second view, that abiding is lasting permanence, mentioning eternity after abiding is an emphasis (tawkīd). Whichever it is, Allah, exalted, has stated in three verses of the Qur'an that the abiding of the people of the Fire in it is everlasting.

﴿So wretched is the abode of the arrogant﴾ [az-Zumar 72]. Bi'sa is a past verb that is rigid and does not inflect, and it requires a subject and a specified object (makhsūṣ). What is its subject? Its subject is "abode" (mathwā), and its specified object is omitted, which the commentator estimated by saying: "Hell." Mathwā means dwelling-place. The arrogant (mutakabbir): the one who knows him best, Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained it in his saying: "Pride is rejecting the truth and looking down on people" [Muslim (91/147), from Ibn Mas'ud]. So the arrogant are those who reject the truth and look down upon creation. These are the arrogant.

﴿So wretched is the abode of the arrogant﴾. Then He said: ﴿And those who feared their Lord will be driven to Paradise in groups﴾ [az-Zumar 73].

* From this noble verse we benefit: the demonstration of the humiliation of the disbelievers upon their entry into the Fire, since they are driven violently and pushed.
* Among its benefits: that they enter the Fire in groups. The wisdom behind this Allah pointed out in His saying in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿He will say, "Enter into the Fire among nations of jinn and men who passed on before you." Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister, until, when they have all overtaken one another therein, the last of them will say of the first of them, "Our Lord, these are the ones who misled us, so give them a double punishment of the Fire." He will say, "For each is double, but you do not know"﴾ [al-A'raf 38].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the people of the Fire are surprised by it. From the moment they arrive, it is opened, so that the surprise is more severe and its heat more intense, we seek refuge in Allah, and they cannot be given respite from it for the blink of an eye, even though they wish it would not be opened, but the matter is contrary to what they wish. It is opened immediately.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the Fire has gates, from His saying: ﴿its gates were opened﴾ [az-Zumar 71].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the Fire is dark and its depth is far, as is taken from its name in His saying: ﴿Jahannam﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the perfect organization of creation by Allah, glorified and exalted, in that He made guardians for the Fire and guardians for Paradise. Here He says: ﴿And its guardians will say to them, "Did there not come to you..."﴾ [az-Zumar 71].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that these guardians speak as humans speak, with understandable address.

Can it be inferred from this verse that the language of the people of the Fire is one language? Perhaps it may be said that, and perhaps it may be said that their languages are different, and that the angels, due to their great number, each addresses the people in the language they understand. And Allah knows best.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the combination of spiritual and physical punishment for the people of the Fire. As for the physical, it is obvious. As for the spiritual, it is what they experience of rebuke and reproach in His saying: ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you, reciting to you...﴾ [az-Zumar 71]. You know that some people would prefer to have their skin whipped than to be rebuked with a single word. Rebuke is not a light matter, especially in such a situation, because when they are reminded of this blessing in a state where they cannot make up for what they missed, that is more intense regret, we seek refuge in Allah.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the completion of the proof against the children of Adam by sending messengers from among them, as in His saying: ﴿messengers from among you﴾, because if they were not of the same kind, the proof would not be complete. But when they are of the same kind, indeed of the same tribe, the proof is complete.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the messengers, may blessings and peace be upon them, had conveyed the clear message, as in His saying: ﴿reciting to you the verses of your Lord﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that what the messengers brought of revelation is a binding proof, because Allah called it "verses," and a verse is a specific sign indicating what it points to, so it is a binding proof for everyone who hears it.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that there is no messenger except that he brought a scripture, as in His saying: ﴿messengers from among you reciting to you the verses of your Lord﴾ [az-Zumar 71]. This is confirmed by His saying, exalted: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear evidences and sent down with them the Scripture and the balance﴾ [al-Hadid 25], and His saying, exalted: ﴿Mankind was one community; then Allah sent the prophets as bringers of good news and warners, and sent down with them the Scripture in truth to judge between the people concerning that over which they differed﴾ [al-Baqarah 213].

But do we know every scripture that a messenger was given? No. What do we know? The Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, the scrolls of Ibrahim, and the Qur'an. It is no wonder that we know only these five, just as we know only twenty-five of the messengers, and the rest we do not know, because of His saying: ﴿And We have certainly sent messengers before you; among them are those We have related to you, and among them are those We have not related to you﴾ [Ghafir 78]. That is, not all the messengers were related to us.

Some scholars said: Only those who were in the Arabian Peninsula or around it were related to us. That is, the messengers who were in America or the far end of Asia or the like were not related to us; rather, those who were around us were related to us, because those are the ones from whom we can take lessons more than others.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the demonstration of what the lordship of Allah requires, that His lordship is founded on mercy, in His saying: ﴿reciting to you the verses of your Lord﴾. And consider: if Allah had left us aimless, would His lordship be complete? No. But Allah, glorified and exalted, did not leave us aimless; rather, He sent messengers to us, and thereby the lordship whose requirement is guiding creation was completed.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the messengers' concern with the Last Day, in that they warn people of it. The reasoning: if there were no day when people return to Allah and every soul is paid in full for what it did, people would not act nor care about deeds. If the situation were that people live in this world as long as Allah wills and then die and do not return, could anyone then remain upright?

The answer: No, except by what his conscience dictates to him. But to remain upright in what he was commanded is very far-fetched, because a person says, "I will live and then die, and there is nothing." But when he knows and is certain that there will be a day on which he will be resurrected and recompensed for his knowledge, then he must strive to prepare for that day. That is why He said: ﴿And warning you of the meeting of this your Day﴾ [az-Zumar 71].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the full admission of the deniers on that Day through their saying: ﴿Yes﴾ [az-Zumar 71]. Is this "yes" (balā) a response affirming a preceding negation, or affirming a negation introduced by an interrogative?

For example, if you say, "Is Zayd not standing?" and it is answered "Yes (balā)", that means: he is standing. But if you say "na'am (yes)", the meaning would be: he was not standing. That is why it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that regarding His saying: ﴿Am I not your Lord? They said, "Yes (balā)"﴾ [al-A'raf 172], if they had said "na'am", they would have disbelieved, because if they had said "na'am", the meaning would be: You are not our Lord, and that is disbelief. So a negation preceded by an interrogative is answered affirmatively with "balā", and negatively with "na'am." Nevertheless, "na'am" may occur in the place of "balā", but this is rare in the Arabic language. They said: among it is the saying of the poet:

Is not the night gathering Umm 'Amr
and us, so that is nearness for us? Yes (na'am),
and you see the crescent as I see it,
and the day rises over her as it rises over me.

These two verses are well known. This man affirms that he is close to his beloved, because the night gathers them; so as long as the night gathers her, it is as if the bed gathers them.

"Is not the night gathering Umm 'Amr / and us, so that is nearness for us?"
This is evidence of the closeness between us, that the night gathers them together.

The second proof: "and you see the crescent as I see it." And as long as our seeing agrees in sighting the crescent, this is a unity.

The third proof:
.......................... and the day rises over her as it rises over me.
As long as the day rises over her as it rises over me, our day is one, our night is one, our crescent is one. This is one who holds that the sighting of the crescent agrees, so we are... what? Near to one another.

.......................... ... "that is nearness for us"
And this poor man, if he is content with this nearness, then he is very content.

The evidence in the two verses is his saying "na'am" (yes), meaning: yes, the night gathers Umm 'Amr, and this "na'am" is in the place of "balā."

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that whoever the word of punishment has come into effect upon has deserved it, because of their saying: ﴿But the word of punishment has come into effect against the disbelievers﴾ [az-Zumar 71].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the deniers of the messengers will see on that Day with severe sight and know the truth with certain knowledge, because of their saying: ﴿Yes, but the word of punishment has come into effect against the disbelievers﴾. If this confession had been in this world, they would have been saved from punishment. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿You were certainly in heedlessness of this, so We removed from you your covering, and your sight today is sharp﴾ [Qaf 22], meaning on the Day of Resurrection. As for in this world, your sight is dim; but in the Hereafter the sight is sharp and very strong, it sees much more than it sees in this world, many times over.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the word comes into effect only upon the disbelievers, because of His saying: ﴿against the disbelievers﴾.
* A consequence of this benefit: that the word came into effect upon them only because of their disbelief, as in His saying: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [as-Saff 5]. Based on this, the problem is resolved; it is said: how did Allah's word come into effect upon these people and not upon others?

The answer to this is that Allah knew of these people that they were not deserving of guidance. ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [As-Saff 5]. May Allah protect us and you from the deviation of the hearts. This is one aspect.

The second aspect is to ask: did Allah wrong these people by withholding His bounty from them? No. ﴿That is the bounty of Allah, which He gives to whom He wills﴾. We have already passed, shortly before, the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari: "The example of us and of those before us is like a man who hired workers until midday, then until 'Asr, then until sunset. He gave the first group a qirat each, and the second group a qirat each. The first group protested, so he said: 'Have I wronged you in anything?' They said: 'No.' He said: 'That is My bounty, which I give to whom I will.'"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2269) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.]]

Then Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, said: ﴿It will be said: Enter the gates of Hell﴾ to the end of the verse [Az-Zumar 72].

* In this verse there are benefits: when these deniers reach Hell, they hesitate or pause, as it were, and so it is said to them in humiliation: ﴿Enter the gates of Hell﴾. In this there is humiliation of these disbelievers as they enter Hell, since it is said to them: ﴿Enter the gates of Hell﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of eternity, meaning the eternal abiding of the people of the Fire in it, due to His saying: ﴿abiding therein﴾ [Az-Zumar 72].

Is this eternity everlasting or for a limited term? It is everlasting, as indicated by three verses of the Book of Allah: in Surat an-Nisa, in Surat al-Ahzab, and in Surat al-Jinn.

In Surat an-Nisa: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and wrong, Allah will not forgive them, nor guide them to a path, except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [An-Nisa 168-169]. In Surat al-Ahzab: ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blazing Fire, abiding therein forever﴾ [Al-Ahzab 64-65]. In Surat al-Jinn: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, then indeed for him is the Fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [Al-Jinn 23].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the denouncing of the dwelling place of the Fire and the vileness of its residents, due to His saying: ﴿So wretched is the abode of the arrogant﴾ [Az-Zumar 72].
* Among its benefits: the Fire is the abode of the people of arrogance, whereas the people of humility have the Garden as their refuge. Those who are humble before the truth and toward creation are in the Garden, and those who are arrogant toward the truth and over creation, their abode is the Fire.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the warning against arrogance, so that a person does not become one of the companions of the Fire.
* Among its benefits: arrogance may lead its possessor to the deeds of the people of the Fire, even if it appears small in his heart. That is, if you see in yourself arrogance toward anyone, then treat this disease, treat this illness before it spreads, because this disease of the heart is like cancer to the body. If you do not hasten to treat it, it will destroy you. Do not be negligent about arrogance. Arrogance is a vile and blameworthy trait. Try it: when you are humble, you find ease and tranquility. You will find that you will not regret it. But if you were arrogant toward someone and then returned to your senses, you would regret it and seek forgiveness. As for when you are humble, you find ease and tranquility, and love and affection are granted to you in the hearts of the servants. So beware of pride, and adopt humility and gentleness of manner. If you add to that the intention of attaining the honor of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and submission to Allah, you will increase in reward and elevation.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever humbles himself for Allah, Allah will raise him."[[Narrated by Ibn Majah (4176), and Ahmad in his Musnad (11724), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]] The phrase "humbles himself for Allah" has two meanings:

The first meaning: he humbles himself before people for the sake of Allah. A person may humble himself before people not for Allah, but out of greed, humbling himself and submitting to them in order to obtain a morsel of livelihood from them. But if he humbles himself to Allah, complying with His command, that is what becomes the cause of elevation.

The second meaning: one who humbles himself to Allah is one who humbles himself to His religion, in such a way that a person accepts it while feeling that he is in need of it and dependent upon it, and that the station of the religion is higher than himself.

* A student: The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And its keepers will say to them: Peace be upon you﴾ [Az-Zumar 73].
* The Shaykh: (...).
* A student: ﴿You are pure﴾. What is meant by (you are pure) here? The goodness of the station in the Garden?
* The Shaykh: We have not reached it. We have read it, and we have not explained it (...).
* A student: He means by adherence to the religion and prayer. He says: "The Fire, firewood will be sent to it."
* The Shaykh: What?
* The student: He says, "This Fire, firewood will be sent to it." That is, the meaning is he thinks he is going to the Fire. What is the ruling on saying this?
* The Shaykh: He says: when some people are advised, they say: "The Fire has firewood," meaning that he himself is among the firewood of Hell. This is close to being as he said. Like the old man whom the Prophet (ﷺ) visited when he was ill, and he said to him: "No harm, it is a purification, if Allah wills." The man said: "A purification? Rather, a fever that boils, upon an old man whom graves will visit!" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "So let it be that." And the man did not wake up except dead.[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (3616) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] That is, he was treated according to what he wished for himself. Had he accepted the hope from the Messenger (ﷺ), he would likely have been healed. So this man, may Allah protect us, who says that Hell has firewood, is close to being of its firewood, because this indicates one of two things: either mockery or indifference, and both are disbelief. He must repent to Allah and return to Islam after having left it.
* The student: Do you mean he is judged to be a disbeliever, Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* A student: Perhaps this man intended (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes. ﴿As for the deviators, they will be firewood for Hell﴾ [Al-Jinn 15].
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: He means he is of its firewood. When he was advised about sins, he said: "Hell has firewood," meaning that he is of the firewood of Hell. Would a serious person say this, or a believer in the Fire? Never.
* A student: (...) entry without eternity (...)?
* The Shaykh: This is not correct, this is not correct, and this is not the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah (the people of the Sunnah and the community), except regarding the people of major sins. For the people of major sins, entry without eternity is correct. But as for the people of the Fire who are the people of the Fire, their entry is with eternity.

Now we have established for you, we said: some scholars say: eternity is lasting dwelling, and some say: it is dwelling that is not lasting. But according to this view, this eternity is restricted by the other verses that indicate permanence.

* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No. Allah did not say: "abiding therein forever, except what your Lord wills." This is from your own pocket. It was not attached to the exception of will. Bring me a verse from the Book of Allah: "abiding therein forever, except what your Lord wills." Bring it: "abiding therein, except what your Lord wills." O people, I am speaking to one person. Bring it. Give him the Mushaf. What page? Two hundred and thirty-three.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Why did you drop ﴿as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾ [Hud 107]? You say: "abiding therein, except what your Lord wills," and the verse is: ﴿as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾, and there is a difference between them. Because ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ refers to the endurance of the heavens and the earth. That is: except what your Lord wills, beyond that, because the endurance of the heavens and the earth is limited. But the punishment of these people is not limited. ﴿As long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills beyond that﴾, to an endless extent. Do you understand?
﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾. That is, its meaning: abiding therein for the duration of the endurance of the heavens and the earth, or not? Is the meaning clear? The duration of the endurance of the heavens and the earth.
﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, meaning except that which exceeds the duration of the endurance of the heavens and the earth, which is what Allah wills. Do you understand? This is if we make the exception connected. But if we make it disconnected, so that the meaning is: abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, but what Allah wills, then there is no limit to it. Its meaning is also clear. You dropped: ﴿as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾, and so you recited the verse in two ways. The first way: "abiding therein forever, except what Allah wills." When you realized this was not possible, you dropped "forever" and said: "abiding therein, except what Allah wills." But as for ﴿as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾, it is not in your mind.

So what do we say? It is necessary to recite the verse as it is: ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills. Indeed your Lord is the Doer of what He intends﴾ [Hud 107]. Every person forgets, but there is no harm. I did not say it this way except to give him a respite of playful teasing; otherwise everyone forgets (...).

* * *

* A student: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. ﴿It will be said: Enter the gates of Hell, abiding therein. So wretched is the abode of the arrogant (72). And those who feared their Lord will be led to the Garden in groups, until, when they reach it and its gates are opened, and its keepers say to them: Peace be upon you, you are good, so enter it, abiding eternally (73). And they will say: Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us and made us inherit the land, to dwell in the Garden wherever we will. How excellent is the reward of the workers﴾ [Az-Zumar 72-74].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. To what place have we been taken, and have we taken the benefits?

Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And those who feared their Lord will be led to the Garden in groups﴾ [Az-Zumar 73]. Regarding (sīqa), we say what we said before: it is a past-tense verb in the passive voice, or the verb whose subject is not named. It came in the past form although it refers to the future, to affirm its occurrence, as in His saying: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [An-Nahl 1]. The past tense sometimes comes in the form of the present to narrate the situation, and the future comes in the form of the past to affirm its occurrence, as if it were something that has happened and is being spoken of.

His saying: ﴿those who feared their Lord﴾. Taqwa (God-consciousness, piety) is for a person to take a shield against the punishment of Allah, by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. Because if you asked what protects from the punishment of Allah, you would be told: obedience to Him, by complying with His command and avoiding His prohibition.

It has been said about taqwa: that you act in obedience to Allah with a light from Allah, hoping for the reward of Allah, and that you abandon what Allah has forbidden with a light from Allah, fearing the punishment of Allah.

It has also been said about taqwa:
Leave off sins, small and great. That is taqwa.
Walk as one who treads on thorny ground, wary of what he sees.
Do not belittle any small sin, for mountains are made of pebbles.

But what we mentioned first is the comprehensive and exclusive definition: that a person takes a shield against the punishment of Allah by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. If he opposes and abandons some of the commands or does some of the prohibited things, he diminishes his taqwa by the measure of what he neglected. Then taqwa and disobedience may be gathered in a person. This is the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah: that a person may have both qualities of faith and disbelief, qualities of piety and wickedness, and there is no problem, but each has its ruling.

His saying: ﴿those who feared their Lord﴾ attributes lordship to them, because the lordship of Allah toward the pious is a special lordship, not like the general lordship over all creatures. Rather, it is a special lordship: He nurtured them until they feared their Lord.

The author's phrase "(with gentleness)" is the counterpart of his saying about the people of the Fire "(with force)", because Allah explicitly stated that the people of the Fire are pushed forcefully into the Hellfire, whereas the believers are driven in a manner of honor, as if the angels surround them in honor and exalting them.

His saying: ﴿to the Garden﴾. The Garden (al-Jannah) in the language means a garden with many trees, and it was named so because it covers whoever is in it, that is, it conceals him. The root is jim and nun, originally from concealment. For this reason the heart is called janan, because it is hidden. The jinn were called jinn because they are hidden. The Garden was called Jannah because it covers those in it with its abundant trees. This is its original meaning.

As for its meaning in the Sharia, the Garden is the abode that Allah, may He be exalted, prepared for His friends, in which there is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived.

He said: ﴿in groups﴾ [Az-Zumar 73], plural of zumrah. What was said before about the meaning of ﴿zumaran﴾ is that they are separated groups, and these groups are according to their deeds. It has come from the Prophet (peace be upon him): "The first group to enter the Garden will have faces like the moon on the night of the full moon. Then people will follow in succession according to their deeds."[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (3246), and Muslim (2834/14), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]

﴿until, when they reach it and its gates are opened﴾ [Az-Zumar 73]. "Until" (hatta) indicates a limit. "When they reach it": that is, they reach the Garden. ﴿and its gates are opened, and its keepers say to them: Peace be upon you, you are good, so enter it, abiding eternally﴾ [Az-Zumar 73]. If you read the verse like this, your heart will remain suspended, and you will say: where is the answer to "when"? ﴿until, when they reach it, and its gates are opened, and its keepers say to them: Peace be upon you, you are good, so enter it, abiding eternally﴾. All these are conjoined sentences, so where is the answer to (idha, when)?

The grammarians (al-mu'rabun, those who analyse the grammar, i'rab) differed on this. Some said: the answer to (idha) is "were opened," and the waw is extra. But this is a weak view, because an extra waw is not known in the Arabic language.

Others said: the waw is for circumstance, with an implied "qad" (indeed), meaning: until, when they reach it and its gates have been opened. According to this view, the answer is omitted. This is what the author and commentator adopted.

It was also said: the waw is a conjunction, and the answer is omitted and implied before it. The implied meaning is: until, when they reach it, they are purified and cleansed, and its gates are opened. This view is the most correct of the views: that the waw is for conjunction and not for circumstance, and that the answer is omitted and implied before the waw. The implied meaning: until, when they reach it, they are purified and cleansed, and its gates are opened. This view is the preponderant one, because it is indicated by the hadiths. It has been reported in authentic hadiths: "When they cross the bridge, the path extended over Hell, they stop on a bridge between the Garden and the Fire. Then retribution is taken for some of them from others. When they have been purified and cleansed, they are given permission to enter the Garden."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2240) and (6235) from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The believers will be saved from the Fire and held back on a bridge between the Garden and the Fire, where the wrongs they committed against one another in the world will be settled. When they are purified and cleansed, they will be given permission to enter the Garden."]] Furthermore, "when they reach the Garden, they do not find its gates open, but rather find them closed, until the Prophet (peace be upon him) intercedes and Allah opens its gates."[[Narrated by Muslim (197/333) from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I will come to the gate of the Garden on the Day of Resurrection and ask for it to be opened. The keeper will say: Who are you? I will say: Muhammad. He will say: I was commanded regarding you: I will not open it for anyone before you."]] This view is the preponderant and definite one, because the Sunnah indicates it.

His saying: ﴿its gates﴾. It is known that its gates are eight, due to the Prophet's (peace be upon him) saying concerning ablution: "The eight gates of the Garden are opened for him, and he enters through whichever he wishes."[[Narrated by Muslim (234/17) from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir.]]

The wonder is that some grammarians said: the "wāw" here is wāw al-thamāniyah (the "wāw of eight"), thereby giving the wāw a new meaning, and they cited for their claim a strange matter. They said: God said in the Qur'an: ﴿And they will say, "[They were] seven, and their eighth was their dog."﴾ [al-Kahf 22], so the wāw is for eight. It is said: Glory be to God, from where did you get this?

The benefit in His saying ﴿seven, and their eighth was their dog﴾ is the confirmation of what was mentioned, because God said: ﴿They will say, "[They were] three, the fourth of them was their dog," and they will say, "[They were] five, the sixth of them was their dog"﴾ ﴿And they will say, "[They were] seven, and their eighth was their dog"﴾ [al-Kahf 22].

The scholars said: He said "and their eighth was their dog" as an affirmation of this statement; for this reason He said, regarding what preceded it, ﴿guessing about the unseen﴾ [al-Kahf 22], and for this He did not say "guessing about the unseen" [here], because the wāw is a conjunctive wāw indicating that what precedes it is established and settled.

﴿And its keepers will say to them, "Peace be upon you; you have done well, so enter it, abiding forever."﴾ Its keepers are those appointed over it, and they are angels, who say to the people of Paradise: ﴿"Peace be upon you; you have done well"﴾. (Peace be upon you) is an informative statement, and not a supplication, as is apparent; for if it were a supplication, the ones arriving would be the ones offering greetings, whereas here the angels are the ones saying ﴿"Peace be upon you"﴾, as if they are informing them that peace has descended upon them, because Paradise is the abode of peace.

﴿"Peace be upon you; you have done well"﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). ﴿"So enter it, abiding forever"﴾, meaning: peace be upon you while you are good; so the sentence is therefore a circumstantial clause from the kāf in His saying ﴿"Peace be upon you"﴾.

﴿"You have done well"﴾: from what, or in what? You have done well in everything: in bodies, minds, conduct, and everything. They are good; they have alighted in a good place; they have become pure from rancor and envy: ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts, [as] brothers on couches facing one another﴾ [al-Ḥijr 47]. They became pure from every illness; no sickness can afflict them. They became pure from every obscene speech: ﴿They will not hear therein any ill speech or sin, except the saying "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Wāqi'ah 25–26]. So the goodness here is estimated as being in everything.

﴿"You have done well, so enter it, abiding forever"﴾: (enter) is an imperative verb intended as honour, not a real command intended to obligate the addressee; it is an imperative of honour, just as you say to someone who asks permission to enter your house: "Enter."

He said: ﴿"abiding forever"﴾ (khālidīn) is a circumstantial clause from the wāw in (enter it), meaning: while you are abiding forever. Is the circumstance here anticipated or simultaneous? Anticipated; because abiding follows entering.

He said: (anticipating abiding therein; and the answer of "when" is implied, meaning: their entry; and their driving and the opening of the gates before their arrival is an honour for them, while the driving of the disbelievers and the opening of the gates of Hell at their arrival is so that its heat remains upon them, as a humiliation for them).

﴿And they will say﴾ [az-Zumar 74] is conjoined to the implied (they entered it).

("And the answer of 'when' is implied" after the statement "and the answer of 'when' is implied" in the first place (i.e., their entering it), or: (i.e., they entered it)? No: "i.e., their entering it" is an error; "i.e., they entered it" is the correct reading; I have it as "i.e., they entered it".

The wāw, according to the author's view, is for the circumstance: "until, when they come to it and its gates have been opened, and its keepers say to them, 'Peace be upon you; you have done well, so enter it, abiding forever,' and they entered it." You will find that the sentence in this manner is awkward. ﴿Until when they come to it and its gates are opened﴾, meaning: and its gates having been opened ﴿and its keepers say to them, "Peace be upon you; you have done well, so enter it, abiding forever"﴾, i.e., they entered it, does not hold together. But what we mentioned as the preponderant view is wholly consistent with what the Sunnah has conveyed, and the Sunnah explains the Qur'an.

As for the author's statement: ("and the driving of them and the opening of the gates before their arrival is an honour for them"): their driving is derived from His saying ﴿And those who feared their Lord will be driven﴾.

("and the opening of the gates before their arrival") because he says the wāw is for the circumstance, and "its gates having been opened" is an honour for them.

But it may be said: the claim that its gates were opened before their arrival is a claim that the evidence does not support; rather, the evidence is against it, because when they come to it they do not find it open, but find it closed; then the Prophet ﷺ intercedes that the gates be opened for its people (...). In reality this is a doctrinal matter, for we believe and affirm that the Prophet ﷺ has a special intercession, which is the intercession for the people of Paradise that they enter Paradise; but according to the author's statement there is no intercession, because they find the gates open.

Then he said: ("and the driving of the disbelievers and the opening of the gates of Hell at their arrival, so that its heat remains upon them, as a humiliation for them"). The phrasing is open to scrutiny ("so that its heat remains upon them"). Is there not a different version? I say: are all your copies in agreement?

In any case, according to the author's statement, they are opened at their arrival so that its heat touches them directly without delay.

﴿And they will say﴾ (conjoined to the implied "they entered it").

So according to the author's statement: ﴿And they will say﴾ — the wāw is a conjunction, and the verb (they will say) is conjoined to (they entered it): ﴿And they will say, "Praise be to God"﴾ [az-Zumar 74].

The correct view: the wāw is for resumption (isti'nāf), and that after they had entered and settled, they said these words.

﴿"Praise be to God, who has fulfilled His promise to us"﴾ [az-Zumar 74] (regarding Paradise). They praised God, exalted is He, here for His bounty and for His perfection, because God's truthfulness to them in His promise of Paradise includes two things:

The first: describing God as truthful, and this is praise of Him for the perfection of His attribute.

The second: the realisation of that for them, meaning that it is a right owed to them, so it is praise for gratitude. So their praise of God now is for two matters: for perfection and for bounty, or for perfection and for generosity. Where is the perfection?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: What is the attribute here?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Truthfulness: ﴿who has fulfilled His promise to us﴾, and there is no doubt that truthfulness is a perfection.

The second: generosity, in that He caused them to dwell in Paradise, so the praise here comprises both matters, because God is praised for His attributes of perfection and for the completeness of His generosity.

﴿"Praise be to God, who has fulfilled His promise to us"﴾: ṣadaqa (without shadda) is not ṣaddaqa (with shadda); because ṣadaqa means: he informed of the truth; and ṣaddaqa means: he counted as truthful the one who informed of the truth. It is said: "He told me, and he was truthful to me," meaning: he informed me of the truth; and it is said: "I told him, and he counted me truthful," meaning: he said, "I am truthful."

God the Exalted said: ﴿And the one who brought the truth and affirmed it [as true]﴾ [az-Zumar 33]. So the one who brought the truth is the one who ṣadaqa (spoke truly), and ṣaddaqa is the one who affirmed the truth.

(﴿And they will say, "Praise be to God, who has fulfilled His promise to us"﴾: Paradise ﴿and has given us the land﴾, meaning: the land of Paradise ﴿to inherit [it]; we settle in Paradise wherever we will﴾ [az-Zumar 74], because all of it is such that no place is preferred over another.)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and has given us the land﴾, meaning: has made us its heirs. The "land" here, as you know, has the definite article (al-); so is the intended meaning the known land, or the land of Paradise? The commentator holds that the intended meaning is the land of Paradise, and this interpretation is open to two objections:

The first: when "the land" is used absolutely, it means that which is opposite the heaven, namely our land here.

Second: He said ﴿we settle in Paradise﴾, and the context would require, if the land were Paradise, that it be said: "and has given us the land, we settle in it wherever we will"; so the apparent sense would be meaningless in this instance.

What does the author mean by "the land"? The land of Paradise. We said: on this reading two things are objected to:

The first: when "the land" is used absolutely it means that which is opposite the heaven, which is the land we inhabit.

Second: he said "we settle in Paradise"; if the intended land were the land of Paradise he would have said "we settle in it wherever we will." So the correct view is that the intended land here is the land opposite the heaven, and the definite article (al-) is then for previous mention (al-'ahd). Previous mention of which? —

* Student: The remembered one.
* Shaykh: The remembered one; what has been mentioned? Then it is the mental (dhihnī) reference, neither the present (ḥuḍūrī) nor the previously mentioned (dhikrī).

"We settle" — from it, that is, from Paradise. If someone asks: how did He make them heirs of the land? We say: God the Exalted said in His Book: ﴿And We have already written in the Psalms, after the Reminder, that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiyā' 105]. So God's bequeathing of the earth to the believers in this world means that they fight the disbelievers and take possession of their lands; this is one answer.

Second: their presence on the earth, their dwelling in it and their building upon it, is like an inheritance in relation to the disbelievers; because the disbelievers do not enjoy any blessing in this world except that it becomes a punishment upon them. When a disbeliever raises a morsel to his mouth, is he punished for it? He is punished for it, yes; because God the Exalted said: ﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten﴾ [al-Mā'idah 93]; its implication is that whoever is not so, there is blame upon him for what he has eaten. And regarding clothing the Almighty says: ﴿Say, "Who has forbidden the adornment of God which He has produced for His servants, and the good things of provision?" Say, "They are for those who believed in the life of this world, purely [for them] on the Day of Resurrection"﴾ [al-A'rāf 32]. The disbelievers have no share of it in this world, nor is it purely theirs on the Day of Resurrection; they clothe themselves without right, because they enjoy God's blessing while disbelieving in God.

In any case, we say: the inheritance of the earth in this world is what the Muslims take possession of from the lands of the disbelievers; and another inheritance is that their presence on the earth is by right, while the presence of the disbelievers is without right; but God has left them in place for a wisdom.

He said: ﴿and has given us the land, we settle in Paradise wherever we will﴾. His saying ﴿we settle in Paradise wherever we will﴾ means: we dwell wherever we will. Is this on its outward sense, meaning that a person in the lowest rank of Paradise can ascend to the highest thing? He cannot do this. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed the people of Paradise will see the chambers" — meaning those above them — "as they see the bright star that is far away on the horizon" — meaning: distant and shining. These are the people of the chambers they see; and God the Exalted said: ﴿For them are chambers, above them are built chambers﴾ [az-Zumar 20].

But it may be said, in explaining this noble verse, ﴿wherever we will﴾: either the meaning is: we settle in Paradise wherever we will in this world; that is, we do in this world the deeds we will, deeds that secure for us lodgings which are the reward of our deeds.

In this world a person may be with the righteous and the good, and he may be with the moderate, and he may be among those who wrong themselves: ﴿Then We gave the Book to those We chose of Our servants; so among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ [Fāṭir 32]. So a person in this world may settle in Paradise wherever he wills by his various righteous deeds — one who wrongs himself, a moderate one, a foremost one in good deeds. This is one.

The second aspect: we say "wherever we will" means that each of the people of Paradise wills nothing but the place he is in; that is, it does not occur to his heart to wish that he were above; rather he is entirely content in the place where he is, by the saying of God the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds — for them are the gardens of Paradise as a lodging, abiding therein forever, they do not desire to be removed from it﴾ [al-Kahf 107–108]; that is, they do not seek a change; each one of them is content with what he is in, and does not see that anyone is more blessed than he. Even if he sees him with his senses, he does not see him in his heart; for if he saw that someone among people was above him, there would be in his heart some regret and anguish, and this is absent in Paradise.

Thus His saying ﴿wherever we will﴾ may be understood in two ways. The first aspect?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Has the answer become clear, or is it a lame answer? Lame: a broken-winged man. Pay attention: either the meaning of ﴿wherever we will﴾ is in this world, meaning that a person in this world may do the deed that qualifies him for the highest ranks, or the deed that places him in the middle, or the deed that places him at the lowest, is that not so?

The second: ﴿wherever we will﴾ is in Paradise; that is, we in Paradise do not will anything but what we are in, meaning that each of us is content with the place he dwells and does not want another; the proof of this is His saying: ﴿they do not desire to be removed from it﴾ [al-Kahf 108].

Listen to the commentator's statement: ("because all of it is such that no place is preferred over another"). To which of the two possibilities did the author incline? To the second: that each person in his place does not choose a place other than it.

He says: ("﴿So excellent is the reward of the workers﴾, meaning Paradise"). Did they move Paradise? ﴿So excellent is the reward of the workers﴾ [az-Zumar 74]: is "Paradise" vocalised with ḍamma, kasra, or fatḥa?

* Student: With ḍamma.
* Shaykh: With ḍamma; as what?
* Student: As a subject.
* Shaykh: No, it is not a subject; it is as the predicate-specifier (al-mukhaṣṣaṣ). The subject is "reward" (ajr); and "ni‛ma ajr" and "bi'sa" — as we explained to you — require two things: a subject (fā'il) and a specified object (mukhaṣṣaṣ). The subject is clear, and the specified object is generally omitted.

﴿So excellent is the reward of the workers﴾: ni‛ma is an invariable verb used for expressing praise; and "ajr" here means reward (thawāb). God the Exalted called it "ajr" as a favour and a gift from Him, as if we had merited it by obligation, just as the worker merits his wage as an obligation.

If someone asks: is it obligatory upon God to reward us?

The answer: it is obligatory by His promise, for He promised to reward us, and what He promises He cannot break.

So the obligation here is not a favour upon God; rather God has bestowed a favour upon Himself: ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy: that whoever of you does evil in ignorance and then repents after it and makes amends — indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-An'ām 54]. So calling the reward "ajr" is by way of God's bounty, the Mighty and Majestic, that He has made this reward incumbent upon Himself like a wage for the worker — a fixed, binding wage; likewise the reward of the one who does good is a fixed right owed by God through His own obligating it upon Himself, exalted is He, as a bounty and kindness from Him.

On this matter Ibn al-Qayyim, may God have mercy on him, says:

"There is for the servants upon Him no right that is obligatory — He Himself obligated the great, mighty reward;
If they are punished, it is by His justice; if they are granted bliss, it is by His bounty, and bounty belongs to the Bestower."

So He, exalted is He, is the one who has truly bestowed favour upon us twice: the first, by granting us success in acting; the second, by recompensing this good deed tenfold; and consider also the bounty — the third favour: is the recompense for good anything but good? It is as if we were the ones who did good, and He did good to us in return, though the human being belongs to God first and last. So all praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds.

He said: ("﴿So excellent is the reward of the workers﴾, meaning Paradise").

As for His saying ﴿So excellent is the reward of the workers﴾: is it a fresh statement from God, or is it the continuation of the speech of the people of Paradise when they said: ﴿Praise be to God, who has fulfilled His promise to us, and has given us the land to settle in Paradise wherever we will; so excellent is the reward of the workers﴾? If it is from the people of Paradise, it is an additional praise of God, exalted is He; and if it is from God at the outset, it is an exhortation to us that we do this deed whose reward is this.

Has the time ended?

* Shaykh: Yes. This is a good objection: He says ﴿and has given us the land﴾ and ﴿we settle in Paradise wherever we will﴾. He asks: why did He not say "and we settle," so that the conjunction would require difference?

It is said: the clause "natabawwa'" (we settle) is a circumstantial clause (hal) in "wa awrathana al-ardha natabawwa'u" (And He has caused us to inherit the earth, that we may settle [in the Garden] wherever we will), meaning: while we are settling. So we say: the circumstance here is correct, in that we are not settling in the Garden during this very worldly life, but it is an anticipated circumstance, and the anticipated circumstance is that the circumstance occurs after its governing verb.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verses 73–74:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And those who feared their Lord will be driven to Paradise in groups﴾ [az-Zumar 73], to the end of the verse.

* One of the benefits of this verse: the righteous are driven to Paradise just as the people of the Fire are driven to the Fire, but the manner differs.

What is the evidence that the manner differs?

The evidence is His saying concerning the people of the Fire: ﴿On the Day they are pushed toward the Fire of Hell with a violent pushing﴾ [at-Tur 13], and His saying here concerning the people of Paradise: ﴿Peace be upon you; you have been good, so enter it, abiding eternally﴾ [az-Zumar 73]. This indicates that they are driven with a driving of honor.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: piety (taqwa) is a cause for entering Paradise, from His saying: ﴿those who feared their Lord﴾. The reasoning is that when a ruling is attached to a description, this indicates that the description is the cause (ʿillah) of the ruling. So the driving to Paradise here is caused by taqwa. Therefore the verse indicates that taqwa is a cause for entering Paradise, and His saying the Exalted supports this: ﴿It has been prepared for the righteous (133) who spend in ease and in hardship﴾ [Al 'Imran 133–134], to the end of the verse.

* Another benefit of this verse: the people of Paradise enter it in separate groups, from His saying: ﴿in groups﴾ (zumaran). The precedence of these groups is arranged according to their righteous deeds.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: when the people of Paradise arrive at it, they do not find its gates open, from His saying: ﴿until, when they reach it and its gates are opened﴾ [az-Zumar 73]. Rather, they find it closed until the Prophet (ﷺ) intercedes for the opening of the gates of Paradise for its inhabitants.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: Paradise has gates, and it has been established in the authentic collection[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (3257) from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi.]] that "its gates are eight."

From this benefit follows what is established: that the mercy of Allah the Exalted precedes His wrath, and that His giving is greater and more magnificent than His withholding, because the gates of Hell are seven and the gates of Paradise are eight.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the affirmation that Paradise has guardians, from His saying: ﴿and its guardians will say to them﴾.

* Following from this benefit: the perfection of Allah the Exalted's decree over things, and that all things are ordered, preserved and arranged.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the affirmation that the angels speak and talk, from His saying: ﴿and its guardians will say to them﴾.

* Another of its benefits: that Paradise is the abode of peace, peace from every calamity, from the saying of the guardians: ﴿Peace be upon you﴾.

* Another of its benefits: that Allah combined for them, i.e., for the people of Paradise, safety from afflictions and goodness of conditions and times, from His saying: ﴿Peace be upon you; you have been good﴾ [az-Zumar 73]. Thus there is combined for them the negation of afflictions and the goodness of conditions and times.

* Another of its benefits (i.e., benefits of the noble verse): the permission given to them, in a manner of honor, to enter Paradise, from His saying: ﴿so enter it, abiding eternally﴾ [az-Zumar 73].

* Another of its benefits: the complete distinction and great contrast between how the people of Paradise are received and how the people of the Fire are received. The people of the Fire are met with reproach: ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you reciting to you the verses of your Lord?﴾ [az-Zumar 71], to the end of the verse. The people of Paradise are met with honor, care and glad tidings: ﴿Peace be upon you; you have been good, so enter it, abiding eternally﴾ [az-Zumar 73].

* Another benefit of the noble verse: stirring souls and urging them to act as the people of Paradise act, because when a person clearly sees the great difference and the vast contrast between the people of the Fire and the people of Paradise, there must be in him that which urges him, indeed impels him strongly, to act as the people of Paradise act.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the eternal abiding of the people of Paradise in it, from His saying: ﴿so enter it, abiding eternally﴾. This abiding is an everlasting abiding, whether we say that abiding (khulud) is a lasting stay or that it is a stay for a long time, because the mention of perpetuity (ta'bid) for the people of Paradise has been repeated in several verses.

﴿And they will say: "Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us and given us the land to inherit, to settle in Paradise wherever we will. How excellent is the reward of the workers"﴾ [az-Zumar 74].

* One of the benefits of this noble verse: praise of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for His perfection and bounty, from His saying: ﴿who has fulfilled His promise to us﴾. Truthfulness in promise is a perfection, and His giving them Paradise as an inheritance is a bounty.

Thus in this praise they combined praise for perfection and praise for bounty, because Allah the Exalted is praised for both: for His perfection and for His bounty. So this praise combines praising and thanking.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the truthfulness of Allah's promise, from His saying: ﴿who has fulfilled His promise to us﴾. Allah the Exalted has informed in several verses that He does not break the appointed promise, and that is because of His perfect truthfulness and perfect power, for failing to keep a promise is either due to the promiser's lying or due to the promiser's inability, and both are things from which Allah is exempt. So in it is perfect truthfulness and perfect power.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the gratitude of the people of Paradise for their inheriting the land, and for their victory and triumph over the disbelievers, from His saying: ﴿and given us the land to inherit﴾.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: that a person settles in Paradise by himself wherever he wills, and that is by his deeds, from His saying: ﴿to settle in Paradise wherever we will﴾.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: a refutation of the Jabriyyah, who say that a person is compelled in his actions and has no choice in them, from His saying: ﴿we settle﴾, as the verb here is attributed to them, so it occurs by their choice.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the people of Paradise, in their dwellings, do not desire anything other than them, from His saying: ﴿wherever we will﴾. This is part of the completeness of bliss, because if a person looked at the dwellings of others, he would see that his bliss is not complete; he would say, for example, "So-and-so's palace is better than mine, so-and-so has more wealth than me," and his bliss would be spoiled. But when he sees that he is in the place he wills and does not wish to move from it, this is part of the perfection of bliss. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They will not desire any change from it﴾ [al-Kahf 108].

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the affirmation of will for the servant. Thus there is in it a refutation of whom? Of the Jabriyyah.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: praise of this reward that the people of Paradise received, in His saying: ﴿How excellent is the reward of the workers﴾ [az-Zumar 74].

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the explanation of Allah the Exalted's favor in recompense, in that He made it a reward, as though it were an obligation placed upon Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

If someone says: "How do you make something obligatory upon Allah the Exalted?" We say: We did not make it so; rather He is the One who made it obligatory upon Himself.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: encouragement to act, but what kind of action? The righteous action that inherits Paradise, and that a person should not be lazy or slack in righteous deeds.
