Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 39, verse 75 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne﴾ [az-Zumar 75].

﴿You will see the angels﴾ — ﴿you will see﴾, O addressee. It is possible that what is meant is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but the first view is preferable, because the first view includes the second and not vice versa. For when you say, "And you will see, O Muhammad," you restrict this address to him alone, excluding the rest of the Ummah. But when you say, "And you will see, O addressee," it becomes general, encompassing the Prophet ﷺ and others among the Ummah. The principle is that when a word stands between a general meaning and a specific meaning, it is taken to mean the general one, because if you take it as the general meaning, the specific is included in it, and not the reverse.

And His saying: ﴿the angels﴾ is the plural of (malak). The malak, originally, is the messenger. Allah, may He be exalted, made the angels messengers, and they are an unseen world who are charged with the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created from light. For this reason there is no disobedience in them, because they were created from light, whereas the jinn were created from fire. For this reason the original state of the jinn is that there is obedience in them, rather, their father or leader [Iblis] was arrogant toward the command of Allah, which He addressed to him directly.

﴿the angels surrounding﴾ — the author says: (a circumstantial clause, ḥāl). He made it a ḥāl because the seeing here is visual (baṣariyyah), and visual seeing takes only one object, so what comes after it in the accusative is an accusative of circumstance (ḥāl). This is unlike cognitive seeing (ʿilmiyyah), which takes how many? It takes two objects. So the seeing here is visual; for this reason the author parsed His saying ﴿surrounding, from around the Throne﴾ as a ḥāl.

And His saying: ﴿surrounding, from﴾ means encircling it. And ﴿the Throne﴾ is the Throne of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, upon which He rose, and it is the greatest, highest and most extensive of created things. The Kursi encompassed the heavens and the earth, meaning it surrounded and comprised them, and the Throne is greater than the Kursi. It has come in a hadith: "The seven heavens and the seven earths, in relation to the Kursi, are like a ring cast into a desert of the earth"[[Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat (861) from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]]. A ring like the ring of a helmet, a small ring cast into a desert of the earth. "And the excellence of the Throne over the Kursi is like the excellence of the desert over this ring." Thus this Throne is great, whose magnitude none can measure except Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

(﴿surrounding, from around the Throne﴾ — from every side.) The reason for this interpretation is that He stated ﴿around the Throne﴾ without restriction, and in that case this encircling must be from every side, because if they encircled it from only one side, they would not be around the Throne from the side that is empty. So if they are encircling it, they must surround all its sides; for this reason he said: (from every side).

﴿They glorify with the praise of their Lord﴾ [az-Zumar 75]. He said: (﴿They glorify﴾, a ḥāl). That is, this sentence is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿surrounding﴾, meaning "surrounding" is an active participle, and the active participle bears a pronoun just as the verb does.

(﴿surrounding from around the Throne﴾ is a ḥāl from the pronoun in ﴿surrounding﴾; ﴿they glorify with the praise of their Lord﴾ — accompanied by praise.) That is, he took the bāʾ in His saying ﴿with the praise of their Lord﴾ to denote accompaniment (mulābasah), and if you wish, say it denotes concomitance (muṣāḥabah): that is, they glorify with a glorification accompanied by praise. (That is, they say: Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him.) The combination of glorification (tasbīḥ) and praise (ḥamd) is the perfection of the one glorified and praised, because by tasbīḥ the deficiencies and defects are removed, and by ḥamd perfection is affirmed. So combining tasbīḥ and ḥamd conveys a meaning more than if tasbīḥ stood alone, or ḥamd stood alone.

(﴿They glorify with the praise of their Lord, and it is judged between them﴾ — among all creation — ﴿with truth﴾, that is, justice.) ﴿Was judged﴾ — that is, was decided; judgment (qaḍāʾ) means ruling.

And his saying: (﴿between them﴾, that is, among all creation; ﴿with truth﴾, that is, with justice, so the believers enter Paradise and the disbelievers enter the Fire.)

﴿And it will be said: All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [az-Zumar 75]. It is said: the agent is left unspecified in order to be more general; that is, Allah, may He be exalted, in that state is praised by everyone, from every side and every direction. The praise here is joined with (al-), which denotes totality (istighrāq), and the lām in His saying ﴿for Allah﴾ denotes exclusivity and entitlement. If we make ḥamd total, it encompasses all kinds of praise, whether for the perfection of His attributes or for His bounty, benevolence and favors. If we say the lām in ﴿for Allah﴾ denotes entitlement and exclusivity, it becomes clear that absolute praise is deserved by Allah alone, and is only for Allah, exclusively, and none is praised with it in entitlement except Allah.

The difference between ḥamd and madḥ (praise), although they share the same letters, is that madḥ is description with perfection but does not necessarily imply love, so Allah is praised and eulogized, but ḥamd is more specific than madḥ, because madḥ is praise in general, whereas ḥamd is praise joined with love and veneration.

And His saying: ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ means the Creator of the worlds, their Owner, and their Manager. And the ʿālam is everything other than Allah.

(He concluded the settlement of the two groups with praise from the angels.) This requires consideration, and it is not only from the angels, but from the angels and others; for this reason the agent was left unspecified, saying: ﴿And it will be said: All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾.

* In this noble verse there are several benefits:
* First: the affirmation of the angels, based on His saying: ﴿And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne﴾ [az-Zumar 75].
* Among its benefits: the manifestation of Allah's greatness on that day, in that His hosts surround His Throne, and this is among the signs of greatness and perfection of sovereignty, that the soldiers be seen surrounding their Owner, Creator and Master, glorified and exalted is He.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of the Throne, based on His saying: ﴿around the Throne﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: praise of the angels, by their good arrangement in encircling the Throne, which is a good in action, and by their glorifying Allah with His praise, which is a good in speech; so they combine the exaltation of Allah in deed and in word.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the choice of combining tasbīḥ and ḥamd, based on His saying: ﴿They glorify with the praise of their Lord﴾, because tasbīḥ removes deficiency and defect, and ḥamd affirms perfection.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that Allah, may He be exalted, is the Lord of these angels despite their greatness, based on His saying: ﴿They glorify with the praise of their Lord﴾, and that His lordship over the angels is a special lordship, as indicated by the idāfah (annexation).
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that Allah, may He be exalted, after all this, judges among creation with justice, based on His saying: ﴿and it is judged between them with truth﴾, that is, a ruling is made among them.

The divine decree (qaḍāʾ) of Allah is of two kinds: kawnī (cosmic/universal) and sharʿī (legislative). The sharʿī is like His saying: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 23], meaning He enjoined that we worship none but Allah. The kawnī is like His saying: ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book that you will cause corruption in the land twice﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 4]; this cannot be a sharʿī decree, because Allah does not decree corruption, rather it is a kawnī decree.

By this we know the difference between the kawnī and sharʿī decree: the kawnī applies to what He loves and what He does not love, while the sharʿī applies to what He loves. The second difference is that the kawnī necessarily comes to pass, whereas the sharʿī does not necessarily imply that the decreed thing occurs, since it may occur or may not occur.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the judgment on that day is judgment with justice, with no injustice in any way, based on His saying: ﴿with truth﴾.
* Among its benefits: the praise of Allah, may He be exalted, on that day when the matter is completed: ﴿And it will be said: All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. If you compare this with His saying: ﴿All praise is for Allah who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'ām 1], it becomes clear to you that Allah is praised at the beginning and the end of the matter: at the beginning in His saying ﴿All praise is for Allah who created the heavens and the earth﴾, and at the end, after judgment has been passed among creation with truth: ﴿All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the demonstration that Allah, may He be exalted, deserves all praise, based on His saying: ﴿All praise is for Allah﴾. We have mentioned that (al-) denotes totality, and the lām denotes exclusivity and entitlement.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the universality of lordship, based on His saying: ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾. The ʿālamūn (worlds) are everything other than Allah. Some scholars said: they were named thus because they are a sign (ʿalam) pointing to their Creator.

In everything there is a sign for Him
indicating that He is one.

* The student: May Allah be good to you. He said: (...) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They glorify with the praise of their Lord﴾. Verily the tasbīḥ here is for enjoyment, not for worship, because there is no obligation on that day. What is your view?

* The Shaykh: Our view is that this is a false statement; rather it is for worship too, but they take pleasure in worship; that is, they feel that they are humbled and submissive to Allah. As for his saying (there is no obligation on that day), this is also false; on that day there is obligation. Does not Allah say: ﴿On the day when the shin will be uncovered and they will be called to prostration, but they will not be able﴾ [al-Qalam 42]? So there is obligation in it, and whoever denies obligation on that day has erred and neglected the texts indicating that there is obligation in it.

* A student: It is related from some of the early generation that the Kursi is the place of the feet of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, such as Imam Ahmad and others?

* The Shaykh: Yes, and it is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Kursi is the place of the two feet. Some scholars said that in relation to the Throne it is like a step.

* A student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you, the cosmic decree (al-qadar al-kawnī) and the cosmic and legislative judgment (al-ḥukm al-kawnī and al-sharʿī) come up often here. Are the differences between them not really differences?

* The Shaykh: Yes, correct.

* The student: Then what is this?

* The Shaykh: This is it, yes, this is it: the qaḍāʾ, the ḥukm, and the irādah.

* The student: Are they all one?

* The Shaykh: No. The meaning of irādah is not the same as ḥukm. Ḥukm may mean qaḍāʾ, but irādah is other than it. They are divided into this division, as is clear, there is no difficulty.

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Every (...) body; we say: he spoke truly. What is the evidence? Is not its width the heavens and the earth? And Allah places His foot upon the Fire until part of it draws in upon part? Does not a person look upon his kingdom in Paradise at a distance of two thousand years, seeing its farthest end as he sees its nearest? If it is not a body, what are we to make of it? Of air?

* The student: It is a body.

* The Shaykh: By Allah, I do not know; I have not heard it except from you just now.

* The student: Is it said of the angels that they are under obligation?

* The Shaykh: Yes, because they comply with Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿They do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded﴾ [at-Tahrīm 6]. The negation of disobedience from them indicates that they are charged with things, and that disobedience from them is possible rationally, but they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them.

* Student: You mentioned, may Allah pardon you, that the people of Paradise are in complete bliss in Paradise, and that they are content with their place in Paradise. What is your explanation of Ibn al-Qayyim's statement that the remembrance of Allah is a protection from regret on the Day of Resurrection, and he cited the hadith: "The people of Paradise will not feel regret except for an hour that passed in the world in which they did not remember Allah"[[Narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (182) and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab (509), (510), from the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal.]]. Does this regret conflict with our saying that they are in bliss?

* The Shaykh: No.

* The student: They mention this regret because they look at what preceded them, and at one who is higher than them?

* The Shaykh: No, this is not regret; this is wishing (tamannī). That is, they wish that they had done that. Wishing for a thing does not indicate regret, and there cannot be regret in Paradise in the sense of remorse or distress, for example, because that would contradict the completeness of bliss.

* Student: Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne﴾. Does this not indicate that the Throne has sides and corners?

* The Shaykh: Yes, it is so. And the hadith established in the two Sahihs[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2412) and Muslim (2374/162), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]] also: "That Musa will be holding on to the legs of the Throne."

* * *

* The student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful: ﴿Ha, Mim. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the All-Knowing. Forgiver of sin and Acceptor of repentance, Severe in punishment, Owner of bounty. There is no deity except Him; to Him is the destination. None argues concerning the verses of Allah except those who disbelieve, so let not their movement throughout the land deceive you﴾ [Ghafir 1–4].

* The Shaykh: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah send blessings and peace upon our Prophet Muhammad, and upon his family and companions, and those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment.

Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.﴾ The basmalah is an independent verse of the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, not part of the surah before it, nor of the surah after it, but it is recited at the beginning of surahs, except one surah, which is Surat Bara'ah (at-Tawbah), for it has not been reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he placed a basmalah in it; for this reason the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, left it without a basmalah, since this was not established from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

As for what is said, that it was left without basmalah because it was revealed with the sword, this is a false statement; that is not the reason, and the sword against the disbelievers, when it is a mercy, is spoils of war; and it is well known that the sword against the disbelievers is a mercy whose purpose is to elevate the word of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Then the basmalah, as you see, is a sentence with no verb and no active participle; rather it is a prepositional phrase (jār and majrūr), and a annexed construction (muḍāf and muḍāf ilayhi), and an adjective and modified noun. The jār is the bāʾ, the majrūr is a noun, the muḍāf is a noun, the muḍāf ilayhi is the divine name, and the modified is Allah, and the adjective is al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm. So where is the complement (mutaʿallaq)? For every jār and majrūr or ẓarf must have a complement, as the author of the poem of the Jumal (Naẓim al-Jumal) said, let us recite:

* The student:
There must be for the jār a connection (taʿalluq)
to a verb or to its meaning, like "murtaqī."
And exclude every extra particle that has an effect,
like (bā, min, and kāf), also (laʿalla).

* The Shaykh:
There must be for the jār a connection
to a verb or to its meaning, like "murtaqī."
And exclude every extra particle that has an effect,
like (bā, min, and kāf), also (laʿalla).

So where is its complement? Where is the complement of the basmalah, ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾? The best that is said is that its complement is a delayed verb suited to what the basmalah was begun for. So now, when we want to recite, we say: the complement is estimated as "In the name of Allah I recite." When we want to perform ablution, we say: the estimate is "In the name of Allah I perform ablution." When we want to slaughter, we say: the estimate is "In the name of Allah I slaughter." We estimated it as a verb, not an active participle, because the original in action is the verb; and we estimated it as delayed for two reasons:

The first reason: to seek blessing by beginning with the name of Allah.

The second: indicating restriction (hasr). When you delay the governing element (al-'amil) and place the governed element (al-ma'mul) first, this is evidence of restriction, since the well-known rule in rhetoric (balagha) is that placing first what should come later conveys restriction. We estimated the verb to be one that fits what the recitation begins with, because it indicates the intended meaning more clearly. For example, if you say: "The estimate is: 'In the name of Allah I begin,'" that is valid, but begin with what? When we estimate it as a specific verb that fits what one begins with, that becomes a clearer indication of the intended meaning, and it is well known that what more clearly indicates the intended meaning is more explicit in its purpose. This is the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of this basmala.

As for its meaning: (ism, "name") is a singular noun in construct (mufrad mudaf), and every singular noun in construct is general in meaning. Consider the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾ [An-Nahl 18]. Here ﴿ni'mata (favor)﴾ is a singular noun in construct, yet it is not a single favor, because a single favor could be counted; rather, it refers to many favors, encompassing everything Allah has bestowed upon the servant. If a singular noun in construct conveys generality, what then is the meaning of our saying: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful"? Its meaning is: "With every one of Allah's names I do such-and-such," with every name. Thus, you are now seeking help through every one of Allah's names for this action for which you have said the basmala.

As for (ism), it has been said that it is derived from (sumuww), meaning elevation, because the name raises the named and makes it known. It has also been said that it is derived from (simah), meaning mark or sign. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Their mark is on their faces﴾ [Al-Fath 29], meaning their sign is on their faces. Whichever is correct, the name identifies its named and distinguishes it from others.

The names of Allah the Exalted, as we have already learned in the discussion of Tawhid, are not limited to a fixed number, as in the authentic hadith: "I ask You by every name that is Yours, which You have named Yourself with, or revealed in Your Book, or taught to any of Your creation, or kept to Yourself in the knowledge of the unseen with You"[[Narrated by Ahmad (3712), Ibn Hibban (972), and al-Hakim (1898) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud.]].

As for ﴿Allah﴾, it is a proper name (alam) for the sacred, exalted Essence, namely Allah the Exalted. The grammarians said: it is the most definite of the definite nouns (a'raf al-ma'arif). This proper name is the most definite of them, since it does not admit sharing in its reference, whereas other definite nouns may be shared. As you know, they ranked the definite nouns: the most definite is the pronoun, then proper names; yet this proper name is the most definite of them, because it does not allow shared reference, while other definite nouns can.

As for His saying ﴿Ar-Rahman (the Most Merciful)﴾, it is one of Allah's names indicating vast mercy, and ﴿Ar-Rahim (the Especially Merciful)﴾ is one of Allah's names indicating mercy that actually takes effect. So ﴿Ar-Rahman﴾ denotes an attribute and ﴿Ar-Rahim﴾ denotes an action; that is, He is Merciful and He shows mercy. This explains the benefit of combining them: the combination indicates that Allah's mercy is vast. This is in His saying ﴿Ar-Rahman﴾, because the pattern (fa'lan) denotes fullness and abundance, as you say "shab'an (full) and rayyan (sated)" and similar words. As for ﴿Ar-Rahim﴾, it is considered with respect to action, meaning the conveying of mercy to whom Allah has decreed to show mercy.

The basmala has rulings, among them: sometimes it is a condition for permissibility (hill), as mentioning the name over the slaughtered animal is a condition for its permissibility, such that if one omits the mention, even forgetfully, the animal is not lawful. Sometimes it is obligatory but not a condition, as in wudu according to some scholars: mentioning the name in wudu is obligatory but not a condition for validity, since if one omits it forgetfully, the wudu is still valid. Sometimes it is recommended in every matter of importance, as in the hadith: "Every important matter that does not begin with the name of Allah is cut off (abtar)." Or: "Every matter of significance (dhi bal)"[[Narrated by Ahmad (8712) and Ibn Majah (1894) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. That is, an important matter in which one does not begin with the name of Allah is "abtar," meaning deprived of blessing. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) would begin with it in letters to kings and others, and likewise the prophets before him, as Allah says in the Qur'an: ﴿Indeed, it is from Solomon, and indeed it says: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Do not be haughty toward me, but come to me in submission﴾ [An-Naml 30-31].

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿Ha Mim﴾ [Ghafir 1]. This is a word made of two disjoined letters of the alphabet (the ha' and the mim). For this reason we pronounce them by their names, not by their sounds: we do not say "Ha-Mim" but say "ha' mim" by their names. These are therefore two disjoined alphabetic letters, from which human speech is composed.

Does this pair of letters have a meaning? The author says: "Allah knows best what He intends by it," meaning we do not know what He intended.

Did He intend to establish a meaning, or not? Did He intend a specific meaning or something else? The point is that we entrust its knowledge to Allah, and our position on this is like that regarding the other alphabetic letters with which some surahs begin.

However, the requirement that the Qur'an is in the Arabic tongue is that we say these are two disjoined alphabetic letters with no meaning; that is, we affirm that they have no meaning, because the Qur'an was revealed in the Arabic language, and the Arabic language does not give alphabetic letters a meaning. This is related from Mujahid, the imam of the exegetes in the era of the Successors, and it is the truth, because Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down upon your heart, that you may be among the warners, in clear Arabic language﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 193-195].

If someone says: "Against this view it is objected that the Qur'an contains things that have no meaning and no benefit, being merely disjoined letters with no use"?

We reply: The answer to this objection is that Allah the Exalted spoke with this for a purpose, not for a meaning; that is, for a profound wisdom, which is that this Qur'an, which has defeated you, O eloquent Arabs, did not come with any new letters, but with the very letters from which you compose your speech, and yet it defeated you. You were unable to arrange letters to produce something like the Qur'an. If you were unable to do that, your inability to grasp the meaning of these words is all the more so. This is what al-Zamakhshari mentioned in his exegesis, and Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, approved it, and it was also mentioned by others, either originally or by imitation. The point is that this is the correct view according to the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun), namely that Allah the Exalted revealed them for the completion of...
